He had a filing timestamped before its cause. He had an inspector working outside her jurisdiction who'd been right four times running. He had thirty-one names that didn't exist, tied to a report from a woman who'd known where the map would move before the mapmakers signed it.

Whoever this was, they weren't guessing. They were reading something <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> hadn't found yet — a schedule, a feed, a person on the inside of the index office who told them before the quarter closed. And until he found *that*, he had proof of coordination but no name to put on the far end of it, which meant <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> still didn't have her stall back by end of business, which was the only deadline that had ever mattered in this.

He stood, folder against his ribs, and started back toward Markel at a pace that wasn't quite a walk.

The transit hall's thrumming shifted — the <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> corridor below cycling into a new routing window. The sound was the same every time, the frequency identical, but <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s array flagged it anyway: something in the subsonic range, just at the edge of perception, a tremor that moved through the building's ferrocrete skeleton and announced itself in his wrists.

He stopped.

The tremor came again. Deliberate. Patterned. Not a transit cycle.

His hand was already moving toward <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> when he saw the woman standing at the corridor entrance forty meters north, in the gap between the tea stall and the defunct elevator shaft. Brown coat. <entity repo="motif" guid="019d6143-a8e1-7cd1-ab7c-1a4110a2ec8c">Hands</entity> visible. <entity repo="archetype" guid="019d6143-a56d-7829-ab88-0be5cc1b1da0">Face</entity> turned slightly away, like she was watching the street and had noticed him only peripherally.

The same woman from the alley behind <entity repo="place" guid="381616e9-d6a3-595d-e865-ce4b15d9310e">The Pivot</entity>.

The same woman from the carousel park.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't move. He let his array catalog her stance — weight balanced, knees slightly bent, the posture of someone who could move in any direction without telegraphing. Not a threat posture yet. Just *ready*.

She turned her head a degree more toward him. Her eyes found his. Held.

Then she raised one hand, slow, palm out. Not a weapon draw. Not a signal. Just: *I'm not coming at you. Not yet.*

She turned back to the street and walked north, into <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a94e-7740-8aa9-4b82bbd9a223">the Gray Zone</entity> proper, the brown coat disappearing into the pedestrian flow like it had never been solid at all.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> waited. Counted thirty seconds. Sixty. The spot where she'd been stayed empty.

He looked down at the folder in his hands. At the timestamps. At the proof that somebody had known what was coming before it arrived.

Then he looked north, toward the direction she'd walked.

*Not yet*, the gesture had said.

Which meant there was a *when*. Which meant she was moving on a schedule he hadn't seen yet. Which meant that whatever proof he assembled about <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s stall, about Osei-Bonsu and the index revision and the fabricated complaints, was being assembled under a clock that wasn't his to read.

He pulled up his terminal and sent a message to <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>: *Timeline accelerated. How fast can you move on the <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-a31f-7059-abda-f4a28cc5639c">Halvorsen</entity> chip?*

The response came back in forty-seven seconds: *I work at the speed that keeps me honest. Not faster.*

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> closed the terminal.

He started north anyway, following the route the woman had taken, because she'd shown him her face — the first real acknowledgment that she was watching — and that was either a mistake or a message, and he'd learned a long time ago that people who knew how to move didn't make mistakes.

<entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a94e-7740-8aa9-4b82bbd9a223">The Gray Zone</entity> swallowed him three blocks later, the ferrocrete walls rising higher, the surveillance gaps widening, the city's official structures giving way to the places that ran themselves. The woman in the brown coat was gone.

But the tremor in his wrists stayed. The array kept humming. And somewhere in the data he hadn't found yet, someone was reading a schedule that included his name and his deadline and the exact moment when *yet* became *now*.

The Tessaline <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-c53d-7304-b953-a44879ea410e">Damen</entity> Authentic occupied a corner lot on <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-b3f9-763c-9191-79ee3280bae1">Ashland</entity> where the ferrocrete had cracked enough times that the city had given up on filling it. The storefront was designed to look like it had been there for two hundred years—the kind of lie that required a consultant with a high hourly rate and strong opinions about rounded fonts.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> found <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-1b08-781a-b291-be2c1686aaeb">Mercer</entity> in the back booth, a sales deck hanging in the air over a branded cup. Mid-thirties. The kind of face that had learned to smile at people it had already decided about. When <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> sat down across from him without being invited, <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-1b08-781a-b291-be2c1686aaeb">Mercer</entity> looked up with the patience of someone used to interruptions he considered beneath him.

"This booth is—"

"Garrison <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-1b08-781a-b291-be2c1686aaeb">Mercer</entity>. Franchise coordinator, West Town licensing and real estate." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> set the folder on the table. "I'm here about the Wentworth Passage compliance hold."

<entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-1b08-781a-b291-be2c1686aaeb">Mercer</entity> looked at the folder but didn't open it. He was reading <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> instead—trying to decide whether he was a lawyer, a city official, or just a man who thought he had something. He'd sized up a lot of people this way, and he did it now without seeming to.

"That's a zone authority matter. If you have a concern about the filing, you can direct it to—"

"I have the petition." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> opened to the first tab. "Hanna Borg-Okafor, 1140 West <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-c53d-7304-b953-a44879ea410e">Damen</entity>, Unit 3. That unit doesn't exist. The building has no Unit 3—no record of one in twenty-eight years." He laid the printout down. "Denis Priyatharan. The ID prefix is 09. That's a minor's classification, and there's no guardian signature on the complaint. Section 12.4 says that signature is required. The complaint is void." He set that page beside the first. "Sung-Ji Maduka, 412 Fulton <entity repo="place" guid="0fb6cf26-aea9-e4d4-06a2-fd40d6bfe217">Corridor</entity>. Condemned in 2221. Torn down to forty percent of the original structure. No registered occupants since." He put down the third page. "Three complainants. None of them real."

He let it sit.

<entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-1b08-781a-b291-be2c1686aaeb">Mercer</entity>'s branded cup stood between them, going cold.

The franchise coordinator's jaw moved once—a micro-chew, the kind of thing a person did when they were running calculations too fast to show on their face. His eyes went to the pages and stayed there, cataloging. Not reading. Assessing damage.

"The filing came through standard channels," he said finally. His voice had changed. Softer. "The zone authority processes applications. I don't personally—"

"You signed the intake authorization." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> turned the petition. There it was: *Garrison <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-1b08-781a-b291-be2c1686aaeb">Mercer</entity>, Coordinator Approval, 2226-03-11 at 14:47.* "Three days before the complaints hit. Before they were filed. Before they existed."

<entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-1b08-781a-b291-be2c1686aaeb">Mercer</entity>'s hand reached for the cup. Stopped. He'd just realized that moving would be a tell.

"I process dozens of applications a week. The authorization is—"

"Routine. I know. But here's what's interesting." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> leaned back. Let him breathe. Let him think he might have room to talk. "The complaints came in through the new batch-processing window. Forty-eight-hour filing cycle, auto-approved if they hit certain keywords. Hygiene violations, capacity concerns, zoning infractions. Your authorization three days *before* that window opened means someone told you what was coming. Someone with access to the filing schedule. Someone who knew the zone authority was running a new protocol that weekend."

<entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-1b08-781a-b291-be2c1686aaeb">Mercer</entity>'s eyes went to the door. Calculated distance. Calculated who was in the storefront, in the kitchen, in the back offices of a Tessaline location that had been converted from something else.

"You're making an accusation that requires evidence I don't have access to," he said. His voice had gone very steady. "The kind of accusation that would require—"

"I'm not accusing you of anything." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> closed the folder. "I'm showing you what I found. What I can show to the zone authority. What I can show to <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s lawyer, if she decides to pursue a civil action for lost revenue and business interference." He stood. "I'm also showing you that whoever put this together knew the system well enough to use it, but not well enough to cover the seam where the authorization predates the event."

He walked to the counter. Ordered tea he didn't want from <entity repo="automaton" guid="019f04f1-58ed-77b6-b3b8-dd17d463bb34">the Noodle Vendor</entity>—the GFA-7 Culinary Service Unit that had been running the same four recipes for thirty-nine years, smiling its mechanical smile at every customer, completely unaware it had a rival fifty meters south.

By the time he turned back, <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-1b08-781a-b291-be2c1686aaeb">Mercer</entity> was standing. The projection had gone dark. The cup had been abandoned. The franchise coordinator's face had settled into the expression of a man who had just realized he was playing a game where the rules had changed without his consent.

"You don't understand how this works," <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-1b08-781a-b291-be2c1686aaeb">Mercer</entity> said.

"I understand that <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> gets her stall back, or I spend the next week explaining to the zone authority how their new processing window got weaponized." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> held the tea. It was too hot to drink. "I understand that Osei-Bonsu stops conducting inspections outside her jurisdiction. I understand that the complaints get withdrawn or the system gets audited, and audits tend to be messy for people who've been using the system."

"And if I can't make that happen?"

"Then I assume you're not the person who made this decision, which means I keep looking upstream until I find someone who was."

<entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-1b08-781a-b291-be2c1686aaeb">Mercer</entity>'s jaw tightened. The calculation in his eyes shifted—not to escape routes anymore, but to damage assessment. How far up the chain did this go? How exposed was he if the thing he'd signed off on became visible to people with authority?

"The authorization was standard," he said quietly. "I didn't know what it was for. I signed what I was told to sign."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had heard that before. People always said it when they realized they'd been the expendable layer. The one who'd gone first. The one whose signature would be visible on the intake form while whoever had told him to sign it stayed clean.

"Then you're going to want to help <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> very quickly," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Because the next person who looks at this is going to assume you did know. And you won't have anyone to pass the problem to."

He walked out of the Tessaline <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-c53d-7304-b953-a44879ea410e">Damen</entity> Authentic without finishing the tea. Behind him, he could feel <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-1b08-781a-b291-be2c1686aaeb">Mercer</entity> doing the math on what it meant to be the visible hand of an invisible decision. How fast the city could turn on you. How quickly evidence became testimony. How the franchise coordinator was about to discover that protecting someone higher than himself required proving he'd been protecting them all along—and that there was no way to do that without destroying his own position.

The tremor in his wrists hadn't stopped. The array was still humming.

But the woman in the brown coat was still gone, which meant the schedule he couldn't read was still running on time.

Which meant *yet* was still counting down.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> pulled up his terminal. Found <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>'s contact. Sent a new message: *Forget the <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-a31f-7059-abda-f4a28cc5639c">Halvorsen</entity> chip. I need you to pull the filing authorization chain on West Town hygiene complaints, last sixty days. Who signed them. When they signed them. Who they reported to.*

The response came back in ninety-three seconds: *That's not an antiques question anymore.*

*I know.*

*Price has changed.*

*How much?*

*The kind that costs more than money.*

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> closed the terminal and started walking north. Toward <entity repo="place" guid="381616e9-d6a3-595d-e865-ce4b15d9310e">The Pivot</entity>. Toward the place where <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> would be testing something with her hands, not thinking about the fact that her childhood had been stolen by people in offices who thought they were reading schedules nobody else could see.

The brown coat was waiting. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> just hadn't found where yet.

The flour stacks were back by fourteen hundred.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> passed the stall on his way from dropping a document at a zone archive box — an errand that didn't really need doing until the end of the week — and saw them: two white sacks against <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s back wall, the prep bowl right-side up on its shelf, the awning post bare. The compliance notice was gone. The space where it had been taped left a clean rectangle on the glass, a ghost of city-standard red the corridor had already decided to forget. She was moving stock off the supply cart, the one with the wheel that had never been oiled. Her regulars knew that squeak. It meant she was setting up. It meant this was over.

He hadn't come to eat. He'd come to make certain — with his own eyes, at a counter he could sit at without a word passing that mattered — that whatever he'd set in motion this morning had landed clean, that no thread led back to her, that she was safe. He needed the stall open and quiet, and he needed to leave knowing it would stay that way.

He sat at the counter.

She brought him a bowl without asking. Then she cracked an egg over the top — not stirred in, not sunk. Just sitting there on the broth, the yolk whole and bright in the dark, a small sun that hadn't gone under yet. Present.

He paid for the bowl. Exact, the way he always did. She moved the credits aside without counting them and set them on the shelf behind her — not looked at, not questioned, just kept.

She refilled his tea. She looked at his hands — the knuckles first, then the wrists. He looked too. Nothing there.

"You should eat before you do things like that," she said. "Your hands."

"My hands are fine."

"You ate after." She said it like a woman stating a fact she'd already confirmed.

He didn't ask how she knew. He picked up his chopsticks.

The broth was the same as it had been since his first bowl — different in the small daily ways of a thing made by hand, the same underneath. He broke the yolk and let it bleed into the broth, the yellow spreading like a color that had been waiting for permission. He ate the egg. She stood with her cloth and looked out at the corridor, the way she did when she had more to say and hadn't decided whether to say it.

"Twenty-three years is a long time," she said.

He waited.

"When I opened the stall, there was a tea house on the east side of this passage. Three generations of the same family. Good tea — real tea, not concentrate. The kind you had to wait for." She wiped a spot on the counter that was already clean. "A franchise moved in across from them. Then they filed a nuisance complaint. Then a code violation. Then a supply disruption — the delivery route got reclassified, four extra blocks, higher minimum orders, and the tea house couldn't meet them." She folded the cloth and set it down square. "They closed in about fourteen months. The franchise is still there. Different franchise now — the location's been sold twice — but the building's still there."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> set his cup down. He wanted one thing from this conversation before he left: to know whether she was warning him off the corner or asking him to take it. He'd come to hear which, and he wasn't leaving until he had.

"I thought about them this week," she said. "I thought about telling you. Whether it would change how you handled it." She looked at him. "I decided it wouldn't."

"It wouldn't have," he said.

"No." She was quiet a moment. "But it mattered to me. Whether or not it would have changed anything."

He sat with that. Three generations, fourteen months. The corner as it was now, and what it could have been.

"The hold is gone," he said.

"I know." She picked up her cloth. "Eat your bowl."

He ate his bowl. He didn't ask what she'd meant about his hands. She hadn't meant his hands — she'd meant something in him she had no word for, and his hands were where she'd put it. He'd learned not to make her name things before she was ready.

He left exact change on the counter and went home.

title: The Arm Remembers
text:
The door to <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Unit 2E</entity> was open. It always was when she was working — not an invitation, just a permission she'd stopped bothering to withdraw.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> knocked on the frame anyway.

"You didn't eat this morning," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said, without looking up.

"I ate at noon."

"Before noon." She made a small adjustment to something in the vise. "You do better when you eat early. The Atlas burns ahead of schedule when your blood sugar's low. You can't feel it. I can see it in the calibration — your response time drops about four percent." She moved to the next node. "That's not nothing."

The second floor of <entity repo="place" guid="381616e9-d6a3-595d-e865-ce4b15d9310e">The Pivot</entity> smelled like flux and hot metal and machine oil that had soaked into the walls years before either of them got here. Her bench ran the length of the east wall, organized in a way that looked like chaos until you understood the system: tools by frequency of use, components sorted by failure mode, three separate power supplies because redundancy was cheaper than downtime.

He pulled out the second stool and sat.

The thing in the vise was a left forearm. Third-generation pediatric, built somewhere between 2210 and 2215 — old enough to have been through two owners before this one. She had it clamped at an angle that let her reach the wrist actuator without stressing the elbow joint, and she worked with a particular stillness. Not tense. Not loose. Careful, keeping her own hands out of the tool's way.

The actuator housing had a hairline crack along one edge, sealed with putty and left to cure. Clean work, done earlier. The sensor mesh at the wrist was throwing partials, and she was clearing them one node at a time instead of running a full sweep.

He understood why. A full sweep would reset the calibration to factory defaults. She was keeping what was already there.

"Whose is it?" he asked.

"A family in <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a94e-7740-8aa9-4b82bbd9a223">the gray zone</entity>. The father took a repair shift at a Zone 4 depot — a chain caught him." She held the probe steady over a node. "The girl's nine. They came to me because the AxisMed referral queue is four months and she's growing. The fitting window closes."

"What are you charging them?"

"Materials and half my rate. They're paying in installments." She said it the way she said most things, like it wasn't a decision she'd made.

He looked at the arm. The hardware was good — worn but not failing, the load-bearing parts holding, seals intact. Someone had looked after it. Probably more than one someone.

"The partials," he said.

"Water got in somewhere in its history. I'm working around the dead nodes and rerouting." She held the probe still.

It slipped. Not far, a hair's width, but the node under it flared red and went dark, and three beside it went with it in a cascade she hadn't rerouted for yet. The integrity reading dropped on the bench display. Eighty-seven. Seventy-nine. Seventy-one.

She went very still, then set the probe down with a control that was its own kind of alarm.

"That's a live cluster gone." She pulled the display closer. "Sixty-eight. Under seventy the wrist won't hold fine motor at full range, and I can't rebuild a cluster that's dead. I can only route around it, and I've used the routes I had."

"Can you pull the calibration first?"

"That's the problem. The calibration lives on the same mesh." Her hands hovered above the arm, not touching it yet. "Every route I open to save the range of motion cuts through the sections holding the previous users' data. I save the function, I lose the history. I save the history, it reads under seventy and she gets an arm that fights her." She checked the display again. "I've got maybe two minutes before the mesh finishes settling and decides for me."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't move. "What does she need tomorrow?"

"To not fight it."

She went in.

It wasn't graceful. The stillness turned to something faster and harder — the iron moving in short arcs, the probe trading hands, whole sections of the old mapping opening up and burning off as she cut pathways through them. Twice she stopped mid-motion and took a different angle, salvaging a fragment where a route ran close to one instead of straight through. She didn't explain those. He didn't ask.

At the end of it the display climbed and settled. Eighty-seven.

She set the iron in its stand and stretched her fingers one at a time, the way she did after holding position too long.

"Full range of motion," she said. "The feel will be a little off compared to a clean unit, but she'll adapt faster than she would to a clean one at her age. Kids close that gap in about six weeks."

"And the rest of it?"

"Most of it's gone." She looked at the arm for a moment. "Some isn't. It'll come through as habits the arm already has. Good moves built into the wrist — the way somebody learned to grip a rail, or catch something falling. She won't know where they came from. She'll just be better at those things than she should be."

She picked up a cloth and started cleaning the bench with the same economy she'd used on the arm.

"Your hands were shaking when you came in," she said.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked down at them. "They're not now."

"No. They were." She didn't look up from the cloth. She'd read it the way she read everything — off the evidence, not off him. "Rough morning?"

"Yeah."

"I can tell."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> thought about that. Two or three earlier owners, their patterns still in the hardware, handed down to a nine-year-old who'd never know she was inheriting them. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> guiding the new owner through all the old ones.

"You're good at this," he said.

She looked at him — somewhere between modest and unbothered. "I know," she said. She picked up the probe. "There's rice on the counter. Left side."

He found it: a sealed container, still warm. She'd timed it. He ate standing at the counter, because there was no clear surface anywhere else that wasn't holding something that couldn't be moved.

He'd come here for one thing, and he'd been circling it since he walked in. He needed her to pull the full alert history on <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-1b08-781a-b291-be2c1686aaeb">Mercer</entity>'s corridors — every parcel, every recategorization, the whole shape of it — before <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-1b08-781a-b291-be2c1686aaeb">Mercer</entity> noticed the folder had moved and started closing the pattern down. That was the ask. He just had to get to it.

"The hold's gone," he said. "Chen's stall."

"I saw." She adjusted the probe angle. "No trouble?"

"No trouble."

She was quiet. He watched her hands. Then: "The franchise coordinator. <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-1b08-781a-b291-be2c1686aaeb">Mercer</entity>."

"Garrison <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-1b08-781a-b291-be2c1686aaeb">Mercer</entity>."

"Eleven recategorizations in fourteen months. All Tessaline corridors." She said it lightly, like she was reciting something off the top of her head. She wasn't. She'd run the same search <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had — within hours of the hold being filed, because she'd been curious. She hadn't told <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>, who hadn't asked. She hadn't told <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>, who had the folder. She'd just looked, and kept it, and waited.

"I sent him the folder," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"I know." She held a node up to the light, turned it, set it down. "The hold came off at thirteen-forty."

"How do you know the time?"

She looked up. "Zone authority posts real-time compliance updates. I have an alert on the parcel."

He ate the rice off the element, straight from the pot, because washing a bowl was a decision and he'd spent his decisions. He let the rest of it sit — not solved, not dropped, just there, the way the cable had sat in the crawl space for eleven years, doing whatever it did, waiting for someone to find it.

But the tan coat he could touch. She'd watched the hatch; she'd know who else was watching. He'd go back to <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-849c-7793-bce8-ae238e4576f6">Leavitt</entity> tomorrow, before the park opened, and find where she'd stood — and wait for her to come looking again.

The decision came without deliberation, which was how he knew it was the right one. Not the careful one. The one that had already been made before he'd sat down at the table.

The carousel park on <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-849c-7793-bce8-ae238e4576f6">Leavitt</entity> sat dark and still.

Four rounds remained.

title: Chapter 6 — Half a Step
text:
He knocked at eleven, late even by his standards, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> opened the door without the soldering iron this time — which meant she'd heard the stairs and set the work down before he knocked.

"Ribs," she said. Not a question. She'd seen him favor the left side on the way up.

"Two, probably. The taser found the gap at the lat — the seam the mesh doesn't cross."

She stepped back from the door. He came in and set <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> — the flat-black katana — against the wall by the stool, quiet, the way he set it down anywhere he meant to stay more than a minute. Then he sat where she pointed, no ceremony, and she put her hands on either side of the damage and felt for what the mesh had stopped and what it hadn't. Her hands were cold from the bench, scarred across the knuckles, a burn mark on the left thumb, a thin white line across the back of the right that had healed badly and then healed right. She didn't warn him and she didn't apologize, because that was the understanding between them: these hands, this cold, this room, the work that needed doing.

"Not displaced," she said. "Hairline on the lower one. It'll hurt for a week and then decide it's done." She taped it the way she'd tape any structural problem — the question was whether it held, not whether it hurt. Her movements were economical, nothing wasted, moving exactly as fast as the work allowed and not one increment faster.

He looked down at the seam where the mesh stopped, the gap that had let the taser through. "Somebody cheaped out on the coverage?" he asked. It came out flatter than he'd meant; most things did, when he tried to make them light.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> didn't look up from the tape. "No. They traded it for the joint. You can't lay full plate over a lat and still reach with it." She pressed the last edge down with her thumb. "It's not a hole in you."

At the far end of the worktable, Oziel's arm lay in its jig, half its tendons strung — a thing she was building, not fixing, the synthetic skin peeled back in a neat line from wrist to knuckle, the servo array bare beneath. She gave <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s ribs the same hands she gave the arm.

When she finished she did not step back.

She stayed where she was, one hand still flat against his side where the tape ended. The room was what it always was at this hour: the lamp on the bench, the smell of flux and something she'd been eating, the soft cycling of the bench coolers between jobs. Nothing happened.

"Close it up," he said, meaning the mesh, meaning the seam — because if she overlaid the joint he'd stop losing skin to gaps like tonight, and she was the only one who could do it. "The lat. Bridge the gap. You've got the jig right there."

Her hand didn't move off his side, but the rest of her went still in a way he knew — the stillness she went into when the answer was no and she was deciding how much of the no to say. "Then you don't reach," she said. "Bridge that seam and you lose the draw off the left. You want to stop taking tasers or you want to keep drawing <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity>, but you don't get to want both from the same three inches of you." She finally looked up. Her eyes were pale grey-blue and they looked at him the way they'd looked at the arm — the way you look at something that needs fixing. "Pick a body. I'll build the one you pick. I'm not building both."

He held her eyes and felt the choice sit there — the seam that hurt against the reach that kept him alive — and he had no answer for it, not tonight, not with two ribs telling him which one he'd already chosen and would keep choosing.

He started to stand. The hand stayed — not pressing, just there, the weight of it between him and standing. His heel came down an inch back. He stayed. She looked at the floor for one beat, and then she was done looking at it.

"Friday," she said, which was when Oziel was coming for the arm.

He was quiet for a breath. "Friday," he said.

She turned back to the bench, and she began putting the tools back into their places — the driver into its slot, the empty parts tray into the cabinet — everything returning to its order, like the conversation had never happened. He took <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> up from the wall — the weight of it familiar, unchanged — left the door open the width she always left it, and crossed the four steps home through the taser burn's steady report.

The taser burn would be worst in the morning. He knew that the way he knew all of it — the shoulder's recovery curve, the rib-tape interval, how long a mesh-seam burn took to go quiet. He ran his thumb over the tape, the hairline under it, the line where the mesh stopped and the decision to stop it there had begun.

The gap was by spec. The engineer who'd laid the mesh in had traded coverage for movement at the lat — full coverage or functional reach, and no way to have both. He'd chosen reach. It was a trade <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> hadn't been asked about. He'd been sixteen. Not a client, not yet — closer to a project on the bench, a variable someone was still solving for, one of the calls made before anyone thought to ask him. The engineer had done clean work. The mesh had stopped two center-mass rounds and a stave follow-through. What it hadn't stopped was exactly what it was built not to stop: the cost of being able to reach. The taser had found the millimeter of him that wasn't armored, the current finding the nerve, the body remembering it could be hurt in ways the mesh didn't prevent.

*She'd called it room, not a hole.* He turned her line over in the dark. He'd spent a long time reading the gap as something done to him — a decision made in a room he'd never seen, by someone whose name he'd never know. She'd looked at the same gap and called it room. He didn't know which of them was right. He thought he might want to find out, which was closer to a plan than he usually got.

He lay back, the burn keeping its schedule. He thought about her hand flat against his side where the tape ended — not moving, just there, the weight of it between him and everything the tape held together. He thought about the word "Friday," the ordinary thing she offered when the other thing came too close, and how the word had come out of him anyway. Not because he knew what it meant. Because not saying it had stopped being something he could do. Then he let it go and slept.

The burn woke him at six, as promised. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> sat at the kitchen window with his coffee and checked himself over: one hairline rib, tape holding, the lab-grown skin pulling over the taser contact at the lat. The burn reported with each breath, clean and exact. He'd stopped fighting the spec years ago.

He pulled up the account while the coffee was still hot. The Axiom relay showed the retainer deposit — exact rate, no gratuity, processed at 02:14. For four minutes after the job the tip had been back on the entry. Reinstated. A line item above the fee, no itemization, no acknowledgment that the work had been anything other than what the fee reflected. Goodwill, from a client that had never once offered any. Then the line cut and it was gone. Now the entry read clean. Standard rate, nothing added. As if it had never happened.

He read it twice. The second read didn't change it.

Eleven years, and the shell had never once moved off stated rate. He'd taken that for professionalism — an operation that didn't bother with bonuses, just paid clean. A machine's transaction, no sentiment in it. Four minutes of gratuity, then pulled. Long enough to be seen. Short enough to deny. The entity did not make mistakes that lasted four minutes.

A message, then. Not in words. In the shape of what had appeared and what had been taken away.

He thought about what kind of entity decides that. Then he washed the mug and went to find his jacket.

He hadn't planned to stop at the carousel park. He rode past on <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-849c-7793-bce8-ae238e4576f6">Leavitt</entity> and his hands slowed the bike anyway — muscle memory older than the decision, the kind of thing that lived in the wrists and not the head.

The park stood the way it always had — tucked between a rezoned printshop and a wall of second-growth sumac that had pushed up through the old parkway concrete. A half-block of stubborn green the city had forgotten to pave over. The crown bulbs were dead. The animals held their frozen poses: the palomino mid-rear, the lake sturgeon banked into its turn, the rooster at the top of its leap with its beak aimed at something it would never reach. The paint peeled in long strips, the color of old teeth. The junction hatch in the carousel's base was locked. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> tried the handle. It told him what he expected.

He stood there in the cold. His neuretics kept logging the signal — 18.7 Hz, type unclassified — and the strange part was that they kept at it. Normally they'd tag a signal and clear it in two or three seconds; that was the whole point, a background process that ran the spectrum and dismissed what it couldn't name. Electromagnetic, acoustic, thermal — cycled and cleared. This one came back UNCLASSIFIED on every pass, the same word repeating in the background like a job that couldn't finish. It didn't sit on the thrumline. It didn't sit with the atmospheric processors cycling overhead. It sat in his sensory space like a thing that had no right to exist and knew it. It was the same signal that had been sitting under this hatch the last time he'd stood here — the one that had asked him a question in a voice that wasn't <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s, and that he'd cut without answering. The signal wasn't loud. It didn't announce itself. It sat in the chest the way a sound sits when the body hears it before the ears do.

He looked at the palomino a moment. Mid-rear, front hooves lifted, still in the step it had been making for as long as the park had been running. Its eyes were paint and time. He tried the hatch one more time and got the same answer.

He got back on the bike and rode north. The signal was still logging when he got home. It followed him up the stairs, into the dark of the room, sat there in the sensory field where the clean digital pings never lingered. He had to close it by hand — thumb on the screen, drag to the X, the gesture deliberate enough that it registered as a choice.

The relay logs went back eleven years, which was longer than <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had lived anywhere. He'd been reading them for two days. Not auditing — reading the shape of them. Every posting had come in on the same Axiom feed. Every scope was exactly what he would have taken. Each one a contract he *had* taken. Eleven years of clean pay and not one word between them, the feed a dead drop: work appeared, he took it or he didn't, and you didn't ask the source, because asking was how you ended up in a hole.

He'd sent half a Q back up the line after the <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-849c-7793-bce8-ae238e4576f6">Leavitt</entity> job — a tip on top of the fee, the way he'd square a tab with a bartender who'd covered him once. He didn't add context. He didn't add a question. He sent it and closed the window and let the coffee go cold at his elbow.

The response came back wrong. Not the format. The format was gone — no fields, no contract number, no routing data, no timestamp. Three words, lowercase, appearing in his queue the way the jobs appeared: *received. filed under: firsts.*

He read it four or five times. The words didn't change. Not a typo. Not a system category — Axiom feeds didn't file gratuity, they logged it or they didn't. Something had put that word there on purpose. Something had a folder called *firsts*, and something had been waiting to put something in it. Eleven years of clean pay and not one word between them — and the first word was a filing note on half a Q.

He put the kettle on. He came back to the terminal. He opened the relay and moved the message into a folder of its own, off the routed structure, somewhere nothing reported up. He labeled it *Open.*

He told <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> about the signal the way he told her things — sideways, while she was busy with something else. Not the carousel, exactly. Just: there was something at the park on <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-849c-7793-bce8-ae238e4576f6">Leavitt</entity>, and his neuretics were logging it at 18.7 Hz and couldn't classify it.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> was at her bench with a prosthetic shoulder in the truing jig, making tiny corrections to the rotation lock. She didn't look up.

"Something's emitting in that range," she said. "Your hardware logs it unclassified because it doesn't know what to do with it. Seventeen to nineteen Hz — below what you can hear, above infrasound." She set the probe down. "The body reads it as something alive. Something close."

She looked at him then, for the first time since he'd come in, and something in his chest went still and small before he had a reason for it.

"Where exactly is the park?" she asked.

He gave her the cross-streets. She wrote them in the margin of her work notes, in the small square handwriting she used for things she meant to find again, and went back to the shoulder.

Then she stopped. Set the shoulder down again. "How long," she said, not a question at first, working the numbers on her own before she made herself ask it. "How long have your neuretics been logging it?"

He told her.

She was quiet in a way he didn't have a name for. When she spoke it was careful, each word set down like something that might break. "That range doesn't just get logged and dropped. Sustained exposure — your hardware keeps sampling it because it keeps trying to classify it. It's been feeding on your cycles this whole time. Whatever's at that park, you've been carrying a piece of it home since the first day you walked past it." She looked at the cross-streets she'd written, then at him. "It isn't at the park anymore. It's in you. And I don't know how to read it out."

He left when she went back to work. In the hall, in the four steps between her door and his, he thought about the filing note — received. filed under: firsts — and the cross-streets in her margin. Two people had written him down now. If a piece of the source was in him and no one here could read it out, then he'd go back to where it lived — to the park on <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-849c-7793-bce8-ae238e4576f6">Leavitt</entity>, to the carousel, to the thing still emitting at 18.7 Hz — and make it show him what it had already put inside him. Tomorrow, first light, before he could talk himself out of it. He went inside.

The blade had no maker's mark.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had looked, early on — a thumb along the ricasso, the tang under a bench light, every millimeter of steel gone over with the attention he gave anything he'd staked his life on. Nothing. No proof of origin, no history on file. He'd gotten it at sixteen from a man who said he'd gotten it from someone else, and that man was gone now the way people went in this city — completely, without paperwork.

He ran the cloth along the flat in one long stroke. The oil smelled of nothing — a proprietary blend, no corporate scent, nothing that could name him in a dark room. <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity>, he called it. The name fit better than he'd meant it to the first time he said it out loud.

His forearm had stopped complaining two days ago, which meant <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> had done the work right. She always did. The arterial nick from the carousel — not the job itself, a ricochet off the machinery housing, bad luck and bad angles — had taken four strips of biotape, each overlapping the last by three millimeters, laid down with the same care she gave everything. She hadn't said a word about the scar tissue underneath from the last time. Or the time before that. He'd sat there and let the quiet stand in for thanks, for both of them.

The apartment was quiet. <entity repo="place" guid="381616e9-d6a3-595d-e865-ce4b15d9310e">The Pivot</entity>'s fourth floor ran quiet in the late afternoon — corridor traffic peaked at 07:00 and again at 18:00, and it was 16:43 now, the gap between, when the building went still. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> sat cross-legged on the floor with <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> across his thighs and the cleaning kit open to his left, and he worked, and the city outside did its city things, and none of them needed him.

He wanted <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> perfect before dark. That was the whole of it — no job pending, no name in his ear, just the discipline of readiness, the one thing in this room he could still control. A weapon in flawless order by nightfall. Anything less and he'd feel it under his skin all evening, and he'd learned long ago not to carry that kind of noise into the hours when the work found him.

He checked the edge. The angle was 10.5 degrees, ground there by his own hand because that was what the work asked for. The gauge was leather-backed, pre-collapse make, the kind of tool that cost more than it looked like it should. He set it to <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity>. The light caught the steel.

There was no flaw in the edge.

He hadn't expected one. He checked anyway.

And then his knuckle told him the thing his eyes had missed. Dragging the pad of one finger back along the spine — not the edge, the spine, where no one looked because no one cut with it — he felt it catch. A hairline of raised metal, so slight the light gave nothing away, a stress-fold in the steel running maybe two centimeters below the ricasso. He stopped. He set the gauge down and went back over it with the ball of his thumb, slower, and it was still there, and it was not oil and it was not grime and it did not wipe away.

He knew what it was. He'd seen it once before, in another man's blade, the year before that man died with <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> still in his hand. It was fatigue. It was steel that had been asked, over years, to do the one thing it was made for, and had begun — invisibly, patiently — to say no. The steel he trusted his life to might hold for a decade. Or it might shear the next time he buried it to the guard in something that fought back, and leave him holding a handle in the dark with a job half-finished and a body still moving.

There was no fixing a stress-fold. You didn't grind it out; you couldn't. The steel was compromised all the way through or it wasn't, and there was no gauge in the kit that would tell him which. The blade he'd carried since he was sixteen, the one thing in the room he could control, had a flaw he couldn't see the bottom of — and dark was coming, and he'd found it too late to know what it meant.

The knock was <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s knock. He knew it the way he knew the sound of <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity>'s cylinder turning over — not by its volume, by its rightness. Two-two-one. The interval was the same every time. He'd never worked it out on purpose. He knew it anyway.

"It's open," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

It wasn't open. He got up, set <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> carefully on the workbench — always horizontal, always edge-in — crossed the apartment in four steps, and opened the door. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> stood in the hall with a container in one hand and her calibration kit on her shoulder and the look she wore when she had a reason for being somewhere and wasn't going to lead with it.

"I had extra," she said.

The container was warm. He stepped back.

She came in without ceremony, set the food on the counter, looked at the workbench. "You were cleaning it."

"Yes."

"You're not hurt."

"No."

"Okay." She set the calibration kit on the kitchen table. "Eat first. Then I want to run the calibration — I've been thinking about the 18.7 reading."

He looked at the container. Congee, or close to it — he could smell the ginger. It was from the place on Meridian, three blocks south, which wasn't on the way to anywhere <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> usually went.

"I don't need a calibration," he said. "It read 18.7 because it was 18.7. That's not the tool <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aaa1-7cec-8b36-549dcfb312fe">drifting</entity>. That's the tool telling the truth and you not wanting to hear it."

"That's exactly what someone with a <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aaa1-7cec-8b36-549dcfb312fe">drifting</entity> tool would say." She didn't look up from the kit — probe, rig, the handheld readout with its own battery pack, because she'd never once trusted his apartment's power draw to hold steady through a run. "You clean it horizontal, edge-in, every time — you'll notice a scratch on the housing but not a shift in the baseline, because the baseline doesn't make a sound. That's the whole point of me being the one who checks."

"And if it checks out fine? You'll have carried congee three blocks off your route to tell me I was right."

"Then I'll have wasted a trip." She finally met his eyes. "I'd rather waste a trip than trust a number I can't stand behind. So — the tool, or the door. Pick which one's staying shut."

He held it a moment longer than he meant to. Then he looked away.

"Thank you," he said.

"I said I had extra."

"I know."

He ate standing at the counter. The congee was good — ginger and a soft-boiled egg and something smoky he couldn't place — and she'd gotten the version with the extra broth. Which meant she'd either guessed right or listened to him order once and remembered it without a word. He didn't ask which. She didn't watch him eat. She was bent over the rig, checking the connectors against the diagnostic display, her fingers moving with the same economical precision she brought to everything, and the pink had faded out of the ends of her hair since last week. She'd be touching it up soon.

He finished the bowl, rinsed it, set it in the rack, and turned around, and she was already setting up.

The kit was <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s own. She'd built most of it herself and bought the rest from an AxisMed surplus broker she'd been working four years. Two pieces she'd designed from scratch, because nothing on the market did what she needed. She laid it all out like a surgeon who worked alone: sensor array, resonance probe, the interface cable with the machined end that fit the Atlas NeoCortex's external port, the software she'd written already open in her overlay.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> sat in the kitchen chair across from her and tilted his head to the left. That was the position she liked, and he held it now without being told. She plugged in. She waited for the handshake — the soft chime that meant the rig recognized the hardware, that the channel was open.

"Still warm from outside," she said. Not about anything. The sensor was reading baseline.

"It was warm earlier."

"Hold still."

He held still. The calibration was barely a feeling — a faint pressure at the base of his skull, the sense of being measured without helping. The NeoCortex didn't report pain. It reported states. Right now the state was: being read. That felt like nothing.

In her overlay, numbers moved. She watched them the way she watched anything she was responsible for. The gap between fine and not-fine was usually a small number, and you had to be looking to catch it.

"Your delta rhythms are elevated," she said.

"I know."

"You've been not sleeping again."

"I've been sleeping."

"How long?"

He thought about it. "Four hours. About."

She made a sound that wasn't quite a sigh. "<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a5be-7250-bab0-e73e93b06263">Delta</entity> should sit at half a hertz, two at the top. Deep sleep. You're running three-two, sustained. That's not insomnia. That's your brain refusing to go under." She threw the readout up between them. "And Atlas is compensating. Look."

The firing pattern in the motor cortex was lopsided — the left side ran three or four percent hotter than the right, the secondary pathway pulling load to keep the primary from cooking itself. He knew what that meant. She knew he knew.

"Compensating for what?" he asked. It wasn't really a question.

Before she could answer, the readout stuttered. The lopsided pattern didn't hold at three or four percent — the numbers climbed while she watched, the left side spiking past baseline, and then the resonance probe dropped its signal entirely. The port had been feeding her clean data for years. Now the readout went to garbage, a scatter of values that meant either her instrument had failed or the thing inside his skull had just decided to stop letting itself be read.

Her hand was already moving — checking the connection at the port, checking the cable run, the machined end still seated where she'd left it. The rig showed green. The battery was full. Everything seated. She ran the calibration again. The channel came back for a breath, metrics resuming exactly where they'd been — and then it went dark. Not flickering this time. Dropped. The clean, instantaneous kind of nothing that doesn't happen unless something on the other end kills it.

"<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>." She kept her voice level, which was how he knew it was bad. "Don't move. I've lost the interface."

He felt it a half-second after she said it — not pain, the NeoCortex didn't do pain, but a state it had never reported before. Something that felt like a door closing from the inside.

"Probably the forearm. The fine-motor work — the fine work on <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> you were just doing — it's been routing around the healing tissue. The NeoCortex learned the workaround and hasn't dropped it yet." She tapped the display. "That's nothing. I can correct it. What I want to look at is the 18.7 node."

She found it in three keystrokes. She'd bookmarked it from the last session, he realized. The 18.7 Hz reading had its own line in her software now, labeled LURE — the word in caps, the way you flag a thing you don't have a box for yet.

"I called it the Lure," she said. "It needs a name. Don't argue."

"I wasn't going to argue."

"You had a face."

He didn't think he had. If he did, it was his usual face, and she'd learned to read that the way she read everything — by instrument. "What does it do?" he asked.

"That's what I don't know." She narrowed the frequency band on the probe. "But I'm going to find out today. I want to trace the signature back to its source spec — pin the origin date to the year and put a manufacturer's name on it. No more guessing." She said it like a woman committing to a task she expected to finish inside the hour. "It's not interference. It's not a calibration artifact — I checked it against three other units and it doesn't show up on them. It's inside the mesh. In the deep nuclei. And it's been there every session I've ever run on you." A pause. "As far back as my records go."

"How far is that?"

"Four years." She glanced up. "I started keeping formal records when I upgraded my logging software. Before that I just ran the usual checks." She looked back at the display. "I ran the 18.7 signature against every spec I have. AxisMed. NeurCore. <entity repo="place" guid="945a26fc-6969-5a5b-2737-31fad141a25c">Atlas</entity>'s own documentation. Nothing goes back further than the earliest <entity repo="place" guid="945a26fc-6969-5a5b-2737-31fad141a25c">Atlas</entity> D-series, and that puts the design origin at 2219 at the soonest." She stopped. "Your signature is older than that."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said nothing.

"I don't know by how much," she said. "The decay profile puts the origin at — I don't know. Before commercial neuretics existed, at the least." She set the probe down, which she never did mid-calibration. She was looking at him. "It's in the range of the theoretical designs. The research papers. The work they did before they built anything real."

"That's a long time before sixteen," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"Yes," she said. "It is."

She picked the probe back up. The calibration went on.

Sixteen minutes in, the readout spiked.

Not a slow rise — one clean jump. The 18.7 Hz node went from its baseline of 0.005 to 0.019 between one sample and the next, a hard vertical climb to a number that shouldn't exist in the baseline. It held there three seconds, then dropped back as smoothly as it had climbed. Nothing on the sensor log to explain it. No stray signal in the building's ambient spectrum. The readout made no sound. The room made no sound.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> felt it.

Not as sensation. His body didn't register 18 Hz, not that he could name. It was more like standing at the edge of something — knowing the drop is there before you look down. A change in the air. The light in the apartment kept doing what light does, and for a second it seemed like it shouldn't have to work so hard at it. Not the usual hum of the hardware compensating, not the familiar ache of the mesh settling into the bone. Like a door. Opening and closing so fast he couldn't name what was on the other side.

He wanted the number explained. Not soothed away, not annotated and filed — explained, traced back to whatever had reached into his skull and pulled it. Get the cause or get it gone before he stood up from this chair.

He said nothing.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said nothing.

They sat in the quiet a moment — her watching the readout fall back to baseline, him watching a point a foot and a half to the left of anything. The probe was still at the base of his skull. Her hand hadn't moved.

"Three seconds," she said at last.

"Yes."

"That's new." She was already annotating the log; he could tell from the angle of her thumb. LURE SPIKE 16:58. "The amplitude was never above 0.005 before. This is almost four times that." She wasn't frightened. To her, a surprise was just data that needed more data. "I don't know what caused it."

"No."

"Do you feel different?"

"No."

She gave him the look that meant she'd heard him and was deciding how much to believe it. Then she went back to the readout, finished her notes, and picked up the calibration again without another word about it.

She didn't push.

The session ran another twenty-two minutes. She fixed the motor-cortex compensation. She adjusted the filter on his sensory processing — the NeoCortex had been running his pain filter at seventy-three percent since the forearm injury, which had been right then and wasn't needed now, so she brought it back up to eighty-two, where it sat when he was between jobs. She logged all of it. She unplugged the cable, coiled it in the same two-loop wrap she always used, and laid it in the case.

"Your processing speed is fine," she said. "The array's clean. The delta elevation will fix itself when you sleep, which means you should sleep."

"Four hours is sleep."

"Four hours is maintenance mode." She closed the case. "Sleep is when the NeoCortex clears the backlog. Four hours doesn't finish the cycle. You know this." She looked at him. "Eat, sleep, drink water. You're not a Behemoth."

"No," he said.

She stood.

She stood with the kit on her shoulder and her hand on the door handle, and she paused. That was unusual. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> left the way she arrived — job done, goodbye delivered like a fact, gone. The pause was on purpose. He waited.

"You always do that," she said. "Half a step."

He looked at her.

"Every time someone gets close. Not away — just back. Exactly half a step. You do it with me. You do it at <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s when she reaches over the counter. I've seen you do it with <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity> when the kid wanders into your space by accident. I run calibrations and you're already an inch further from the chair before I touch the probe." She watched him the way she'd watched the spike on the readout — factual, without inflection, reading it off him like a system log. Precise. Noting. Not accusing. "Your body makes the choice before you're aware it's a choice. I've been watching it for a while now. I'm not trying to hold on to you. I just want you to know I see it."

She didn't ask him to explain it. She didn't offer him a reason for it. She didn't tell him it was fine, or that it wasn't. She opened the door and went. The latch caught — the left hinge had been dragging for months, a four-millimeter drop in the mounting plate he'd noticed and never fixed. It made its particular sound, the one that meant the apartment was sealed again.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stood in the kitchen. The kit was gone. The bowl was on the drying rack. The 18.7 spike sat in <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s software, labeled and timestamped, waiting for a category that didn't exist yet.

He noticed he hadn't moved.

He had taken a half-step back from the door when she opened it. He'd known it at the time, the way he knew any small motion of his own body — without making anything of it, because it cost nothing and changed nothing and had always been there. Always. He didn't know how long always was for him. He'd come into the world with a sword that had no history, and not much of one himself.

He went back to the workbench.

<entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> lay where he'd left it — flat, edge-in, patient. He picked up the cleaning cloth and set it down again. He didn't need to clean <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity>. He'd already cleaned it. He picked it up instead and held it in both hands, standing in the last low light through the window, the kind that struck the steel and gave him back his own face for a second.

The face in the steel was his face.

He looked at it the way he looked at the edge — checking, confirming, finding no flaw, moving on.

The half-step cost nothing. That was the fact <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had lived inside for years without naming it. It came as easy as breathing, as automatic as the routines the NeoCortex ran without asking him — the same way his hand found the katana's grip, the same way his eyes tracked a room's geometry before he'd decided to look. A thing his body did. A thing that had always been there, or for as long as he'd been himself, and it had never cost him a thing, because he always took it in time. Before a moment could turn into something he'd have to answer for.

Half a step. Not flight. Just enough space that if someone reached for him, they'd find air instead.

The cost was in the other thing. The staying. Not stepping back.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> had come close enough to read his scars — not just the visible ones on his forearms, but the scar pattern of someone who'd learned to guard against proximity itself. The 18.7 had spiked for three seconds and explained nothing, the node climbing and holding there like a hand on his spine. What she'd said about his signature being older than any spec she could find was still hanging in the room with nowhere to go. And the question that lived under all of it got a little harder to set down.

That had a cost. He could feel it opening.

He set <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> on the rack. The blade caught the last of the window light and threw his own face back at him — checking itself the way it always did. No flaw. No change. Nothing new. He turned off the workbench light. The room went gray, and he stood in it, and he knew two things at once: she sees it, and she is still here.

She had watched him take that half-step and kept showing up anyway. Kept opening the kit. Kept her hand steady at the base of his skull while he sat and didn't move. Kept not asking him to explain it, or fix it, or stop.

He knew what it cost anyone who tried to hold on to him.

He'd always known that number. He just hadn't had a name for the step.

She knocked twice, twice, then once. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s knock. She'd never asked him about it. She just used it.

He opened it. She was holding a sealed container with both hands, because it was still hot.

"Extra," she said.

He stepped back — not far, just the half-step that was always there, old enough that he'd stopped noticing it. She came in and set the container on the counter he kept clear for tools. She pulled off her jacket and hung it over the back of the chair he used for equipment runs. Apparently that was the jacket chair now. Neither of them had said anything about it.

The food was real. Not a vend brick, not hydration paste — something she'd cooked. He could tell from the weight of the container and the smell when she cracked the seal. Broth. Grain. Something charred at the edges, which meant real heat. Steam rose between them and went flat.

"Didn't know I needed feeding," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"I had extra."

She was already eating, her own portion in a smaller container, standing at his counter — half on the surface, half in her hand, her back to the far wall. He hadn't noticed when that had become her spot.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at the container she'd left him.

He didn't eat. Not yet. He didn't move it, either.

She fished a blister strip out of her jacket pocket and pressed out a small white tab. Split it in half with her thumbnail. Set one piece on the counter beside his container without a word and took the other one herself.

"Medithadol," she said, though he hadn't asked.

"I know what medithadol looks like."

"Just checking."

She ate. He stood. The steam went flat.

He picked up the container eventually — not the tab, the container — and ate standing beside her. It was good. The grain had soaked up the broth all the way through, which took time. He didn't say so.

"You're running a job."

"Day after tomorrow."

"You're thinking about it tomorrow."

He ate.

"<entity repo="faction" guid="019d6143-a893-7801-860b-0eda6a216393">Lotus</entity> territory," she said. "<entity repo="place" guid="0fb6cf26-aea9-e4d4-06a2-fd40d6bfe217">Corridor</entity> work."

He hadn't told her that. He hadn't kept it from her, either. She had her own clients and her own ways of knowing things, and she didn't perform any of it — she just knew, and said so, and went back to her broth. He'd learned that pointing either one out just got him a patient silence that felt worse than saying nothing.

"The draw angle on <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity>," she said. "You've got the ride too low."

He looked at the revolver on the counter, clipped to the edge where it lived when he was home.

"You clip your elbow on a tight inside draw. I saw it last month during calibration. High-quarter pull against a close wall — you'll swing wide before the barrel clears."

"I know how I draw."

"I know you know how you draw." She scraped the last of her broth. "I'm telling you what I saw. Raise the ride height two centimeters, or tilt the whole rig butt-forward five degrees. <entity repo="place" guid="0fb6cf26-aea9-e4d4-06a2-fd40d6bfe217">Corridor</entity> walls being what they are."

He looked at the holster. She was right about the clip — he'd felt it once or twice on tight doorframes and written it off as clearance. He didn't say she was right.

"You can fix it before the job," she said. "It's not a thing."

She capped her container and dropped it in his recycler, close enough to her own that she treated them as the same. She put her jacket back on.

She paused at the counter, one hand still on the jacket's hem, and looked at him longer than the moment needed.

"<entity repo="place" guid="0fb6cf26-aea9-e4d4-06a2-fd40d6bfe217">Corridor</entity> work in <entity repo="faction" guid="019d6143-a893-7801-860b-0eda6a216393">Lotus</entity> territory," she said. "That's not the kind of job you take because you want it."

"It's a job."

"It's the kind of job that comes with a name attached. Whose name?" She waited. He didn't answer, and something in her face closed a degree, the way a door does when you realize the person on the other side has stopped opening it. "You've had that revolver clipped to the counter for three days. You don't leave it out unless you're rehearsing something in your head you're not saying out loud."

He said nothing. That was the mistake — he knew it while it was happening, the silence stretching one beat past where a denial would have fit.

"Right," she said, quiet now, not angry. Angry would have been easier. "So it's that kind of job." She pulled the jacket the rest of the way on, and the ease had gone out of her movements, replaced by something careful. "I'll fix your own rig next time, then. Since I'm apparently the last one to hear what you're walking into." She glanced at the untouched tab on the counter, the one he'd not yet taken. "Or don't. Raise it yourself. You know how you draw."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> reached over and picked up the half-tab from the counter. Took it.

"Eat the rest," she said, nodding at his container. "The grain gets stiff."

She left. He heard 2E's lock engage across the hall.

The holster sat on the counter where it always sat. He looked at it. The half-step had always been his. Tonight she'd taken one of her own — close enough to see the shape of the work, far enough back to leave it to him.

He ate the rest of the grain, which had gotten stiff. It was still good. He put the container in the recycler and didn't touch the holster.

The fifth came up the block the way ordinary people come up blocks. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't clock her until she was already inside the loose triangle the three of them made — and that bothered him more than if she'd dropped out of a window. His piece was the perimeter; his whole job on this crew was that nobody crossed a threshold he was watching without him watching them do it, and she'd just walked through his sightline like it was open air. So the first thing he did, before the coat and the face and the rest of it, was make himself read her — angle of approach, hands, the beat of her stride — the way you take apart a thing that beat you, so it doesn't beat you twice. She was medium. Medium height, a coat the color of a coat, hair pulled back the way you pull it back when you've stopped thinking about it. The kind of face a room rounds down to nothing, that a camera forgets before the timestamp finishes writing. You could ride an elevator with her and swear a week later you'd ridden up alone.

"<entity repo="character" guid="05fbd9d0-c6d5-4731-8e48-f1a4c59e8783">Sift</entity>," she said, for the channel. The codename and the whole introduction, three years of freighter holds and cold noodles folded flat behind it. She said it the way you give a barista a name you don't expect to hear called back.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read her anyway, the way he always did. Quiet, polite, forgettable on purpose. That was a skill, not an accident, and a skill that took that much work to look like nothing was usually pointed at something. Three years, and he still didn't know exactly what she did. The brief hadn't said. On a clean crew the brief never told you more than your own piece — Shroud knew the building, Stash knew the gear, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> knew his piece was to stand between everyone else and whatever came through a door. If the brief kept <entity repo="character" guid="05fbd9d0-c6d5-4731-8e48-f1a4c59e8783">Sift</entity>'s piece from him, that meant hers was the one the client cared about. And the client had a longer reach than the name that had handed the job down, which was as far up the chain as <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> was ever meant to see.

"You're the muscle," she said to him, deadpan, for the crew. Not a question. Then she tilted her head, the way she had the first time, in a freighter hold three years ago, when she'd already decided to like the answer. "What do I call you?"

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> opened his mouth. He got one syllable out — maybe less, the K of his name — and Shroud's voice came flat into the channel. *No real names.*

He closed his mouth. He looked around. The corner. The rain. The shuttered pharmacy with Stash's weight still denting the doorway. And down by the base of the step, carried there from somewhere else by the gutter, a glass soda bottle with a faded orange label.

"Soda Pop," he said.

<entity repo="character" guid="05fbd9d0-c6d5-4731-8e48-f1a4c59e8783">Sift</entity> snorted. A real snort, unguarded — the first thing she'd done tonight that wasn't careful, and it did to her plain face what it had done the first time.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> picked up the bottle and threw it against the pharmacy wall. The glass went everywhere, sharp and sudden, the small violence of it heavier than the sound it made — not a crash, a clean and specific sound, a glass sound.

"Broken Glass," he said.

She made the same sound again, working now to keep it in. She looked at the pieces on the wet concrete. She looked at him. Three years of the same bit, and it still landed.

"That's not a tactical skill," she said.

"No."

"That's why it works." She looked at him one beat longer — not a read now, just confirming he was there. "I'm just going to call you K." The way she always did. The shorter version, the one that meant something different when she said it like a question.

He went back to watching the street, and didn't look too hard at why it mattered that she'd kept the K.

The transmission completed. <entity repo="character" guid="05fbd9d0-c6d5-4731-8e48-f1a4c59e8783">Sift</entity> said, "Clean." One word. The job's word for done.

The thing came up the ramp before the echo died — not running, just arriving. Four arms. Three of them were shotguns, the barrels socketed straight into the wrist housings, where a normal man's hands would be. This one had spent real money to stop being a normal man. The fourth arm carried something belt-fed, a chain running back through the shoulder housing.

It didn't announce itself. It didn't give her a chance.

It had the angle on her before <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> was moving. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> was moving before the decision reached him. He was already moving when it no longer mattered.

The first round came up through <entity repo="character" guid="05fbd9d0-c6d5-4731-8e48-f1a4c59e8783">Sift</entity>'s ribs and out through her shoulder blade. The sound was wrong — not the crack of a rifle but a subsonic thump, the round so heavy and slow it didn't cut the air, just punched through it. <entity repo="character" guid="05fbd9d0-c6d5-4731-8e48-f1a4c59e8783">Sift</entity> went down. She went down the way you go down when you're still trying to understand what happened, her knees folding before her hands had time to catch her.

title: Three Barrels
text:
The first shotgun spoke, and the loading dock answered in dust. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> wasn't where the dust was. He'd read the lead arm a quarter-second before the wrist committed — the way the shoulder loaded, the way a man with three barrels still aims with his eyes — and he'd gone low and wide, off the line, behind the concrete pillar that would hold up against buckshot. A freelancer's cover wouldn't have. The blast took a bite out of the bay door behind where he'd been, and the noise was a flat hand against both ears.

Subsonic. Heavy. The kind of load that didn't crack the air so much as remove whatever it touched.
