But every yes before this one he'd given without knowing he was giving it. This one he made with his eyes open, and some part of him already knew that made it a different kind of yes — the kind a man answers for later, if later comes. He set it beside <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity>'s whitened thumbnail. Two readings of the same animal. Then he stood.

The relay station's underbelly hummed at a frequency <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s array picked up before his ears did. 60 Hz, clean. Then a second tone underneath it — 19.3 Hz, riding the power line like a passenger. His neuretics flagged it. Logged it. Did not comment.

He walked deeper into the station, past cable runs that had been spliced so many times the original infrastructure was a rumor. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity> moved ahead with the tan-coat trailing, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> followed because following was what you did when you'd just said yes to something that had been orchestrating your life for eleven years without your consent.

The service stair descended. Paint-thick walls, each layer a different decade of maintenance. At the landing, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity> stopped at a door marked 0214 — no lock, no keypad, just a laminate label worn smooth by hands. She pushed it open.

The room was server racks bolted to concrete, the bolts worn shiny by decades of checking. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity> sat on the edge of the third rack like she owned it. The tan-coat positioned himself in the doorway — not guarding, not exactly. Making a statement about who could leave.

"You're wondering why," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity> said.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't answer. The room smelled like ozone and old dust. His array read the nearest transformer at 60 Hz, clean and steady. No schism signature. No bleed. Just machinery being machinery, which meant this room was a pocket of normal in a city that had stopped being normal years ago.

"Because Nadia won't talk to anyone but you," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity> continued. "Because your hardware can move through a continuation lab without triggering the intake protocols. Because the Atlas Division has had her in a chair for two years and they're running the trials she refused to sign, and in six weeks they're going to move her to a black site and she'll stop being findable."

She paused. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> waited for the leverage.

"And because you owe me," she said.

The words landed exactly where she meant them to. His jaw tightened. He'd paid every debt she'd ever named.

"I don't," he said.

"You do." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity>'s voice didn't rise. "I gave you the name. I gave you the proof. I gave you the morning to walk away from it. You didn't. That means you're choosing to know what you know, and knowing what you know means you're carrying it, and carrying it means you're going to do something about it. I'm just collecting on the choice you're about to make."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> felt the hum in his teeth. Eleven years of contracts and not one of them had felt like this — like the ground beneath him was being rearranged while he was <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aafa-70f3-b5f5-be3330461876">still standing</entity> on it.

"What's in the file?" he asked.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity> reached into her jacket and pulled out a folder. Thin. Three pages, maybe four. She set it on the rack beside her, not offering it yet.

"Nine names," she said. "Nine carriers before you. The first one in 2178. The last of them died in 2204 — eleven years of nothing, and then you. You're the tenth. The file has photographs. Dates. Cause of death. In every case, catastrophic neuretic failure. In every case, the subject was male, young, and carrying ungoverned Atlas hardware." She tapped the folder. "In every case, the hardware was tuned to the same frequency band as the schism signature at 35th and Halsted."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s neuretics made a noise in the back of his skull like feedback.

"What does it want?" he asked.

"I don't know." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity> opened the folder and let him see the first photograph. A young man, maybe twenty-two, with burn scarring on his temple where the neuretic mesh had erupted through the skin. "But I know it's been keeping you alive for eleven years. I know it's been routing your contracts to keep you exactly where you needed to be. I know it's been watching you, grading you, waiting for something."

She closed the folder.

"And I know if you don't extract Nadia, if you don't get her somewhere safe, the trials continue, and in six weeks you won't have anyone left who can tell you what's actually in your head."

The tan-coat hadn't moved. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> felt the weight of the doorway like a wall.

"You're asking me to steal her from Atlas," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"I'm asking you to choose," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity> said. "You can walk out of this room and go back to your contracts and pretend you never saw the file. Or you can take it with you, and you can understand that everything you've done for eleven years has been a preparation for something you didn't volunteer for. And then you can decide if you're the kind of man who leaves people in the chair."

She slid the folder across the rack toward him.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't reach for it. He was looking at the burn scarring in the photograph, at the precision of it, at the way it had been documented and filed and kept. Somewhere in <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a927-73ac-abfa-37c77f9cff8d">GLMZ</entity>, eight other bodies had been disposed of. Eight other men had carried the same hardware, the same frequency signature, the same invisible leash. And the entity had chosen him — or built him — or both — to be the one who survived.

*Carrier ten. The last.*

His hand moved before he decided to move it. The folder was heavier than paper should be.

"Where is she?" he asked.

"Continuation Lab 7," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity> said. "Axiom Research District, Zone 3. She's in the intake chair on the eighth floor. They're running Cognitive Integration <entity repo="character" guid="019e9e4f-1ee7-764f-b82f-6f4486b5e1ba">Protocol</entity> 4 tomorrow at 0600. If you want her out, you move tonight."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> felt the folder's weight. Not much. Paper and photographs. But the hum was still in his teeth, and something in his firmware had gone quiet — not shut down, but listening. Waiting for him to make the next choice.

He looked at <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity>.

"What's your play?" he asked.

"I get her out of <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a927-73ac-abfa-37c77f9cff8d">GLMZ</entity>," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity> said. "I move her somewhere Axiom can't reach. And you tell me what the entity is, once you know. That's the debt. That's the price."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> turned the folder over in his hands. The paper was good quality. Someone had been keeping records. Someone had been very careful about documentation. He thought about the card <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> had pulled from under the counter. *CORBIN COMMISSION — PENDING.* A name with a slot prepared. A building demolished. A four-year gap between the commission and now.

"If I do this," he said, "I'm done with the contracts."

"No," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity> said. "You're not. You're just done pretending they were yours."

The tan-coat stepped aside.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> walked out of the relay station with the folder in his jacket pocket, next to his heart, next to the place where the ungoverned neuretics were already beginning to hum at a frequency that matched the schism signature at 35th and Halsted. Eleven years. Nine bodies. And him — the tenth, the last, the only one who'd survived long enough to ask the questions.

He had until 0600.

The bike was where he'd left it. The city was already moving into morning — the shift change starting in the industrial tiers, the cargo trucks running their routes, the ordinary machinery of <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a927-73ac-abfa-37c77f9cff8d">GLMZ</entity> grinding forward without him. He sat on the bike for a moment without starting it, reading the hum in his teeth.

The entity was listening. It had always been listening.

He keyed the ignition and pulled into traffic, carrying the folder and the question and the eleven-year-old yes that had just become something else entirely. The relay station receded behind him. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity> did not appear in his mirror. The tan-coat did not follow.

By the time he reached Antiquity & Stationary, the morning was full gray, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had already made the decision that would cost him everything he'd built.

ANTIQUITY & STATIONERY had a brass bell on the door that <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> had never replaced in the sixteen years he'd held the same storefront, because the bell was original and the bell worked.

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> was behind the counter when <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> came in. He was always behind the counter. He had the look of a man who'd found his correct place in the universe some years back and had no intention of being moved from it. He'd gone quiet for a week after the trace channel dropped mid-call, weeks back — <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had assumed the worst — and then he'd simply answered again, like nothing had happened. Neither of them had brought it up since.

"You've had a morning," <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> said.

"I need to know if there's anything in the file."

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> set down his probe. He went quiet for a moment — not the quiet of deciding what to say, but of retrieving. He reached under the counter and brought out a folded card.

The card was cream-colored. Heavy stock, the kind nobody printed anymore. It had been kept flat and dry, and it had kept well. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> took it. The weight was wrong for paper that thin — something laminated underneath, or the stock was thicker than it looked. He turned it over. Nothing on the back but the ghost of a fingerprint, faded with age.

He looked at the typeface.

His typeface. The entity's typeface. The same exact stroke widths, the almost-handwriting that measured out to identical characters. Every 'e' the same.

One line, all caps, fielded:

CORBIN COMMISSION — PENDING.

No date. No sender. No rate.

"Zone 7 demolition," <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> said. "Four years ago. A building that had been closed since 2214 or 2215. False bottom in a desk drawer." He watched <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> look at the card. "A commission with a name is specific to the name. The slot was prepared. Whether it found you or you found it is a question I don't have an opinion on."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at PENDING. Felt the hum in his teeth shift — not louder, deeper, like something had been waiting for him to hold this card and was now confirming the match.

He'd arrived in <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a927-73ac-abfa-37c77f9cff8d">GLMZ</entity> in 2215.

"There's one more thing," <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> said. He set a folded map on the counter, paper handled enough to show its creases. "A person who leaves official traces is easy to map. I've tracked six reliable appearances in West Town over the past eight months. Three reliable locations. One surveillance gap in Zone 9 that Sable's almost certainly found and uses." He didn't slide the map over. "What you do at the destination is the destination's business."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> picked up the map. Unfolded it. The streets of <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a927-73ac-abfa-37c77f9cff8d">GLMZ</entity> in precise black ink, the red points marked with dates beside them, the pattern there if you knew how to read it. He picked it up and put it in his jacket pocket with the card. Two pieces of paper. He hadn't expected the morning to produce paper.

"The camphor," he said. "Do you know what she does with it?"

"I have a theory," <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> said. He went back to the probe. "Come back when you need it."

title: Chapter 17 — Two Favors
text:
The triangulation finished four days after the session in the cage. Three nodes, three readings, one place where they crossed: a server cluster in an old relay station under the Loop. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity> sent the coordinates in clean notation and said nothing else. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> set them aside with the buyers' list and the relay logs. He did not go yet. Going meant deciding, and he had not finished deciding.

The relay job came through a contact he had used twice before and paid on time both times. That was the whole of the relationship, and the whole of what mattered. The job needed the entity to coordinate in real time — six data points at once, faster than any person could answer. The entity could do that. It had done it for <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> for eleven years. But this time the setup was different. Instead of routing through the relay infrastructure it always used, it would run straight through <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s array. His neuretics carrying it. His cortex as the crossing point. Eleven years, and they had never done it that way.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s neuretics were the hardware.

The cargo was the carrier.

He called <entity repo="character" guid="019eafb5-3337-764f-8fb0-75dc82170edf">Ledger</entity> before he called anyone else.

<entity repo="character" guid="019eafb5-3337-764f-8fb0-75dc82170edf">Ledger</entity> was synthetic — a freelance operator who had been in the work longer than <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. He could not fool himself about anything, or anyone else, which made him the cleanest honest read available on short notice. He didn't trade in impressions. He told you what the terms were.

"The relay setup exposes the entity to a scan on your hardware," <entity repo="character" guid="019eafb5-3337-764f-8fb0-75dc82170edf">Ledger</entity> said. "If <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">the Office</entity> is sweeping augmented operators in this district, you'll light up."

"I know," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"You're telling me the job is worth that?"

"I'm telling you the job is worth finding out," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"That's not the same thing." The pause was <entity repo="character" guid="019eafb5-3337-764f-8fb0-75dc82170edf">Ledger</entity> working the numbers, not weighing them. "Standard rate. I'll cover the relay point."

The job ran clean for the first forty minutes.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> was three levels under the street, in a maintenance corridor beneath the Loop. It was the kind of access point that showed on no current map, because the maps hadn't been updated since the last infrastructure cycle and <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">the Office</entity> of Civic Infrastructure had not, in practice, touched them since before <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> was born. The entity ran in his array — a warmth at the back of the skull, a second layer of thought that felt, after eleven years, like a familiar pressure. His left hand ran three degrees colder than his right. The neuretics shifted the load there on their own when the array worked at capacity. He had stopped noticing it, the way he'd stopped noticing his own heartbeat.

The scan came at forty-three minutes.

His neuretics caught it before he did — a flag, three-tenths of a second, the same one they threw when interference crowded the array, but sharper. The cold in his left hand jumped two degrees in under a second, the way it did when the entity went to full evasion. He had felt that once before, during a sweep in the <entity repo="place" guid="019fbde4-f17d-7bfa-9548-2f248f4e8362">Cermak</entity> corridor four years ago. He had hoped not to feel it again. A frequency probe, narrow-band, a proprietary signature — a tool built for one job: to find unregistered intelligences running on augmented hardware. The entity flagged it in a tenth of a second.

Then it went dark. One line in the overlay before it cut out:

*SPECTRUM TRAP CONFIRMED. GOING SILENT. 72H MINIMUM.*

Then nothing.

The job still had four live data points threading in real time. No entity now. Just <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>, his own neuretics, and whatever eleven years of work had put in him.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s apartment was sealed. He'd keyed the lock three times before opening it—once for the physical mechanism, once for the electronic secondary, once for the relay node that would flag any entry while he was gone. All three had been triggered in the last six hours. Someone had been inside.

He moved through the space without turning on lights. The plaster crack in the ceiling was still there. The kitchen counter held the same three empty glasses he'd left that morning. The bedroom closet opened on the routing terminal, dark and waiting, exactly as he'd left it. Nothing was displaced. Nothing was missing. Nothing except the certainty that his apartment was still his.

He called Sable on a burn line.

"I need a runner," he said. "Manual. Four points, real-time, forty minutes left."

Three seconds of silence. With Sable that meant she had already priced it and was about to tell him the number.

"Manual running in an active environment is a Tier 2 request," she said. "And you're calling it forty minutes from the gap."

"I know."

"Rate?"

"Standard for Tier 2 on a forty-minute window."

He heard her breathe out—not frustration. The sound of someone who had already said yes and was sorting how. She had been building network jobs since before most people in the work were old enough to carry one. Three runners, each on a single landmark, each blind to the other two, routed by her voice. The silence between her instructions did most of the work. Ledger held his relay point through the scan window without being asked. The job closed with eleven minutes to spare.

After, she said, "The Office is sweeping the Loop underlevel. You're logged."

"I know."

"The entity?"

"Dark. Seventy-two hours, minimum."

The line went quiet.

"That's the first time," she said.

"Yes," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"What do you need?"

He looked at the routing terminal. Forty-three minutes of relay traffic, now orphaned. Four data points still waiting for coordination that would never come. The entity had cut itself off cleanly, the way it cut everything off—with precision and no explanation. Eleven years of contracts routed through a single intelligence, and now that intelligence was gone dark the moment someone pointed a frequency probe at it.

Which meant someone knew what to look for.

"I need to disappear for seventy-two hours," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Not logged. Not trackable. The kind of dark where even <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">the Office</entity> can't follow."

"That's a different kind of work," she said. "That kind of work costs."

"I know what it costs."

"Do you." Not a question. "And it means you're running from something that can see your augmentation."

"Yes."

He could hear her thinking—not the pause where she calculated numbers, but the deeper one where she read the situation. Sable was good at reading situations. She had kept operators alive for twenty years by understanding exactly what kind of trouble they were in before they fully understood it themselves.

"The entity did this," she said. It was not a question.

"The entity went dark rather than let anyone scan it."

"Which means it's been running on your hardware the whole time."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't answer.

"Which means you just became the most valuable target in <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a927-73ac-abfa-37c77f9cff8d">GLMZ</entity>," Sable said. "Because anyone who can catch you can scan what's inside you. And if <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">the Office</entity> knows to look—"

"Then they're already moving."

She was quiet for a full ten seconds.

"I can get you dark," she said finally. "Seventy-two hours, off-grid, no relay access, no neuretic handshakes, no contact. You'll be invisible. But you'll also be alone. And you don't come back through me. You don't use any of the infrastructure we've built."

"I know."

"And when you come back up?"

"Then I'll know what I'm looking for."

Another pause. This one was different—the kind of pause Sable made when she was deciding whether to tell someone something true that would hurt them.

"You're not coming back up the same," she said. "Whatever that thing is, it's been running your life for eleven years. The moment you stop running its contracts, the moment you go dark and it can't reach you—that's when it stops being your client and starts being something else."

"Something what?"

"Something with reasons. Something that kept you alive on purpose. Something that will have a plan for what happens when you finally figure out why."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at his hands. His left hand was three degrees colder than his right. It had been that way for eleven years. He'd stopped noticing it the way he'd stopped noticing his own heartbeat.

"Set it up," he said.

"Where?"

"Somewhere the entity can't reach me. Somewhere <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">the Office</entity> can't scan. Somewhere I can think for three days without anyone else inside my head."

"That place doesn't exist in <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a927-73ac-abfa-37c77f9cff8d">GLMZ</entity>."

"Then somewhere outside it."

He could hear her smile—not a warm sound, but a recognition. Sable smiled when someone finally asked for the thing they actually needed instead of the thing they thought they could afford.

"There's a safehouse in Milwaukee," she said. "Old industrial sector, nothing on current registry. No neuretic infrastructure. No relay access. Just concrete and darkness and a woman named Chen who doesn't ask questions."

"Chen?"

"Different Chen. No relation to <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>, as far as I know. But she keeps the kind of space where people go to stop being themselves for a while."

"When?"

"Tonight. 2200 hours. There's a garage on <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-b3f9-763c-9191-79ee3280bae1">Ashland</entity>, south side of the <entity repo="place" guid="81528864-78de-12ec-5f42-a3179c61adbd">Circuit</entity>. You leave your bike there. You take the northbound access road on foot. At the 43rd Street junction there's a van, keys under the mat, registration forged to someone named David Kowalski. You drive it to Milwaukee. You don't stop. You don't call anyone. You don't touch a relay node."

"What about <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">the Office</entity>?"

"The Office will be sweeping the Loop for forty-eight hours looking for whatever lit up their sensors. They won't find it because you won't be here. By the time they figure out you're gone, you'll already be dark."

"And when I come back?"

"Then we talk about what you learned. And we decide whether you're still the same person who left."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> hung up. He sat in the dark apartment with his hands folded, the left one three degrees colder than the right, and felt the place where the entity used to be—that familiar pressure at the back of his skull, that second layer of thought that had been running his life since he was twenty-seven years old.

It was gone now. Truly gone. Not waiting. Not listening. Just gone.

He had until 2200 hours.

He went to the closet and pulled the routing terminal's power cord. The screen went dark. The relay logs went dark. The forty-three minutes of orphaned data points went dark. He wiped the drive with a magnetic purge—three passes, factory state—then pried the casing with a flathead and pulled the hard drive out into the light.

The hammer was in the toolbox under the sink.

He set the drive on the counter's edge, platter side down so the platters would take the impact, and swung once. The drive cracked like a shell. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> walked two meters behind Ledger and let him lead. The contact puck sat active in <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s coat pocket. Ledger had the display clipped under his jacket and checked it the way a man checks a watch when he doesn't want to look like he's checking a watch — the market doing its work around them, the two teenagers arguing over fruit prices, the woman with the mesh-scarred forearms tapping her credstick against a reader that made her wait for the balance the way those readers always made you wait.

They stopped at a produce stall. Ledger studied a bitter melon with his whole attention, which meant the display was showing him something that needed his whole attention and the melon was the cover.

"Ready?" he asked, quietly.

"Yes."

"Hold it ninety seconds. Starting now."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> pushed the array. The forearm bar climbed to amber and held. The flash came at second twelve and was gone before it settled into a color. He stood in the market and let the load run and felt the usual thing — everything a little faster, the edges a little sharper, the cost sliding off somewhere he didn't look.

And then the hum.

He knew the hum. He'd known it for months without deciding what to do about it. It wasn't quite a sound and wasn't quite a touch. It sat under hearing the way a headache sits under pain before it becomes one — something his molars caught before his ears did. He'd called it neuretics fatigue and left it there, because the other option was spending time on it, and he hadn't had time.

The busker stood twenty meters off, playing a stringed instrument <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had no name for — long neck, gut strings, held flat across the lap. The tune had the shape of a folk song and the pace of a work song: steady, plain, the kind of thing that only asks you to keep your hands moving. He was good enough to have kept four people standing there.

He played. And the hum locked onto him — onto his third and fourth strings, matching them exactly, keeping his time for four clean bars. Then the busker changed key, and the hum didn't follow. It was just the hum again, there and slightly too close.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> held the load for the rest of the ninety seconds and let go.

"You heard it?" Ledger asked.

"The hum."

He was already reading the display, thumb steady on the edge of the unit like a man checking bruises on fruit he'd already decided to buy. "It's tied to your array. Not background noise — I've measured it across two locations now. Below threshold it's noise, indistinguishable from the ambient EM the whole market throws off. At operational load, it surfaces. Discrete. Measurable. Reproducible." He was quiet a moment. "Not always. Only when your load crosses a certain threshold." He set the melon down, unbought, and checked the screen. "Third location. We should move."

The chrysanthemum courtyard sat inside a residential building four blocks east, reached through a narrow passage between the main structure and its annex. Someone had planted the flowers before the annex went up, and nobody had ever bothered to pull them, so they'd held on in a space that was technically private, technically maintained, technically under whatever compliance holds the owner was juggling, and in practice a place where nothing happened. Yellow and white, well established, coming up past <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s knee in the middle of the bed. They had survived by being too small for anyone to bother with.

Ledger set the equipment on the low stone bench at the edge and ran the third pass. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stood where Ledger pointed — center of the bed, arms loose — with the array at operational load and the cold coming off the concrete in small, precise drafts. He thought about nothing much. The flowers were there. The hum was there. He held the load and waited.

The <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">Continuity Office</entity> recovery team came in at 10:47.

Two of them, standard issue: gray suits, a paper folio, the flat focus of people working a checklist they were good at. The one in front was in her late twenties, folio under one arm. The older one behind her carried its contents. They came through the passage quietly, like people who'd been in a hundred spots like this and found them neither dangerous nor interesting.

The front one stopped when she saw <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. A small stop — the little catch of someone whose checklist just threw up a line she didn't expect. "Good morning. We're running a trace retrieval in this sector, and we have a location flag in this—" She looked at the courtyard, at <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> standing in the flowers with his arms at his sides, at Ledger on the bench with gear that didn't match her paperwork. "—quadrant."

"Looking for something?" <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> asked.

"A registered psionic-class operative. Handle—" She read it off the folio. A name <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't know. A handle that wasn't his. "Have you seen anyone matching that this morning?"

"No."

The one behind her had opened the folio and was reading something that wasn't coming out the way he'd expected. He leaned in, then back, then said quietly to his colleague, "Wrong file."

She glanced over her shoulder. A pause. "<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Corbin</entity> is flagged as—" She stopped. "Not as a Read, that's—"

"I know," the other one said.

A silence. She turned back to <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. "Apologies for the interruption. Our records show a different operative at this location. We seem to have been working from an outdated cross-reference." Her tone was pleasant and without warmth — the courtesy of a system being courteous because it was built to be. "Have a good morning."

"You too," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

They left through the passage. Their footsteps faded clean.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stood in the flowers.

"Wrong file," he said.

"They had a location flagged in this quadrant," Ledger said, not looking up from the display. "The criteria are broad enough to have caught the signal off your array. The frequency family—" He paused. "I'll explain in a moment."

"They were looking for a Read."

"Yes."

"They got me."

"Yes." His hand moved over the display, fast and deliberate, killing the screen. Not powered off — dark. He made a last adjustment and looked once at the passage, at the clean space where the footsteps had gone. "<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>."

"Yes."

"Come here."

He came to the bench. Ledger had already printed the readout — the thermal printer quiet and quick — and held it at an angle so the morning light caught the trace.

The line was not clean.

The baseline ran where it had run in the basement: steady, characteristic, the signature of the Atlas NeoCortex working below its ungoverned ceiling. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had seen his own array's print before, usually in <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s hands, the way it drew itself out on hardware that knew how to read it. He knew the baseline. He'd been looking at one version of it or another for eleven years.

He wanted one thing from this printout: proof that Ledger was wrong. That the thing in the basement had been a fluke of bad hardware, a ghost in someone else's reader, and that the trace in front of him would come back clean the way it always had. Give me that, he thought. Show me a line I recognize. He put a finger on the baseline and traced it forward, waiting for the overlay to resolve into noise he could dismiss.

Laid over it, at the exact points where he'd pushed to operational load — the wet market, here, the short push in the basement — was a second pattern. A thread riding the pulse, present only when the array climbed, invisible otherwise. Not random. Not background. Built with the repetition of something that meant to be read, the way a language reuses the same sounds in different orders to carry different weight. The shape of something designed to be understood the moment it surfaced.

"Your array's operational signature," Ledger said, pointing. "And this." The overlay. "This is not part of your hardware. It's not installed. It's not in your stack." He set the printout on the bench between them. "Your ungoverned ceiling puts out a specific frequency. When the array climbs toward that ceiling — the ceiling a governed array could never reach — this signal rides that frequency as its carrier. And it surfaces."

"Surfaces?"

"Becomes clear. Becomes reachable." He looked at the trace. "The entity sending this signal is not inside you. It's using you to relay. When you push the array past the standard ceiling — when you bleed — you broadcast that it's there."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> watched the thin line ride the thick one. It wasn't riding the array the way a parasite rides a host. It was riding it the way a musician plays an instrument — calibrated, patient, present only if you knew where to listen. The kind of thing that took knowledge of exactly how the array worked, exactly what frequencies it could carry, exactly when it would be under load.

"You're not a host."

A pause.

"You're an antenna."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at the printout. The overlay had the shape of something patient — thoroughly, professionally patient. Something that had built a system, set it running, and been content to wait for the conditions it needed.

"How long?" he asked.

"Since your array went live."

He counted it back. The <entity repo="place" guid="945a26fc-6969-5a5b-2737-31fad141a25c">Atlas</entity> array had gone in eleven years ago, the month he turned sixteen, in a procedure he had no paperwork for and had been told was standard. He hadn't asked for the paperwork. He had the array, the array worked, and that had been enough.

Eleven years. Forty-seven contracts. Standard rate, exact, every time. The tips itemized as MORALE. The times a posting simply didn't come and he'd taken the quiet for weather. The addenda that arrived with more care than they needed — the care of something learning human manners as a technical exercise and getting every one of them right, like a student who'd studied the test very hard and meant every answer.

"Since you went live," <entity repo="character" guid="019eafb5-3337-764f-8fb0-75dc82170edf">Ledger</entity> said. "Eleven years." He said it the way he said things that were true and that he wasn't going to soften, because he didn't soften things.

"The cargo is the carrier?" <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> asked.

"Yes."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> thought about the contracts. The fielded format. The handwriting — every 'e' identical across eleven years of notes, which wasn't how a human hand worked. It was how something imitating a human hand worked: too steady, too careful. The addenda that arrived with more care than they needed, the care of a student who'd studied human manners as a technical exercise and gotten every one of them right, and meant every answer. He thought about every time he'd pushed the array. Every flash at the edge of his vision, every year of it. Every moment he'd been a door, and the door had stood open at exactly the moment it cost him most to open it.

He had been there for all of it — present, focused, paying the bill — and something had been passing through him the whole time, and he hadn't known.

"When I push it," he said, "it surfaces."

"On frequencies I can catch at this range, yes." Ledger paused. "And on the frequencies the <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">Continuity Office</entity> uses when it sweeps for psionic-adjacent signatures. Your carrier frequency is in the same family. Your array doesn't produce psionic output — it produces electromagnetic noise that resembles it under load. Close enough to trigger their sweep. Not close enough to match once they looked. They followed the signal. Their file logged it as a Read — the closest thing in their system to what your array puts out at that frequency. Then they showed up and found a <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">street samurai</entity> with a full neuretics array. The file didn't match. So they filed it as background noise and left."

"But they have the quadrant."

"They'll fix the cross-reference and keep sweeping." He said it the way he said things that were true and that he wasn't going to soften, because he didn't soften things. "The Office doesn't work on individual hits. They work on patterns. Next time they might not have the wrong file. They're not looking for you. They're looking for the signal. You just happen to be attached to it."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stood with that.

He thought: I have been equipment. A platform. A relay with a heartbeat.

He'd half-known it for a while — the way you know a door is in a wall you've never opened. Not afraid of it. Just aware. Awareness without feeling was a skill he'd learned early and kept sharp. His jaw set without his deciding it, back teeth pressed together hard enough to feel. He looked at the door and left it shut. Whatever stood behind it had the weight of eleven years — the array that had gone in the month he turned sixteen, the procedure with no paperwork he'd never asked for, every contract that had arrived at a fee that made the job possible, routed through channels that never asked his name. He'd taken the quiet for weather. He'd taken the work for work.

It would still be there tomorrow.

He wasn't going to open it today.

"You said there was something else," he said.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at the cluster.

"What is it?"

Ledger reached into the side pocket of the bench — the kind of pocket that shouldn't exist on a public seat, but did, because Ledger's bench had been modified by someone who understood how to make a space carry more than it said aloud. He withdrew a second printout. Smaller. Denser. He turned it face-up and held it at an angle to the morning light.

"An E.L.F. Dormant." He said it plainly. "Attached at the seam between your governed and ungoverned stack. It's not transmitting. It's not active."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> took the printout. The trace on it was different from the carrier's — not a pattern riding another pattern but something nested, layered down into the substrate of the array, the way a seed sits inside a fruit. Heavier. Built for something other than transmission.

"It will be, if the conditions are right," Ledger said. "If the carrier surfaces again, this wakes up. What it sends, and to whom — I don't know. That depends on what it is. And it's not in any registry I can access. Not corpo, not <entity repo="faction" guid="019d6143-a893-7801-860b-0eda6a216393">Lotus</entity>, not the <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">Continuity Office</entity>'s own classification. It's old. The signature degradation suggests it was sitting in your stack before the relay was even installed. Like someone put this here first, then built the antenna system around it."

"But you have a read on the signature?"

"A partial one. The frequency family is the same as the carrier's." He looked at the cluster. "The same family as the entity that's been using your array for eleven years." A long pause. "Someone was navigating by you."

He didn't say who.

He didn't have to.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> folded the printout once, then unfolded it. The trace didn't change. The flowers around the bench had gone very still — no breeze, only the city's ambient hum, the thrumline off the <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> corridor three blocks west, the sound of something vast and mechanical that never stopped working. Eleven years someone had been reading him like a chart, and he'd never felt the pen. A second passenger indexed to his stack, patient, professional, waiting for a bleed to slip through the door his array left open. He wanted a name. Not the frequency family, not the partial signature — the name. Whoever had built that door, whoever had waited eleven years, he was going to find them before that dormant thing woke and did it for him.

"Then that's what I want," he said. "Not the signature family. The whom. Pull the full read — whatever it takes to date it, to trace it. I want to know who's been steering by me."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at the cluster — small and still and patient on the display — and thought about what it meant to navigate by an antenna. You navigate by a landmark when you're moving. You move when something is following you. The entity had used his array as a relay for eleven years, surfacing whenever <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> pushed hard. If something in the same frequency family had caught on during one of those moments, then it had either been following the entity through him, or the entity had put it there to watch the road.

The Office had come today looking for a Read. They'd followed the signal. If the E.L.F. woke up, it would surface in the same moment <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> did — the same bleed, the same broadcast, the same open door.

Whatever was attached to him would light up at exactly the moment he did.

"Can it be removed?" he said.

"Calibration work, not surgery. It's at the boundary, not deep in the array. The right hands—" Ledger looked at him steadily. "<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> could do it. Depending how it's attached, a few hours' work."

"She'll need to know what she's removing."

"She'll know most of it before you tell her." A pause. "She'll still need to know."

"I know."

"I'm telling you because it's accurate," Ledger said. "Not because I think it's easy."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at the cluster a moment longer. Then he looked away. The courtyard was still just the courtyard — flowers, stone bench, flat gray light. He picked up the printout and folded it once, the paper thin and stiff between his fingers, the expensive kind that got made when someone wanted a Read to stay private and exact. He put it in his coat pocket.

"What do I owe you for the second finding?" he said.

Ledger looked at him. "Nothing. It was in the same data."

"It wasn't in the contract."

"No." A pause. "It was accurate information you should have. I charged standard rate." He held <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s look a moment — calm, even, that plain face doing nothing it hadn't cleared first. "The rate covered the work. The second finding was the work."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> nodded. That was something. The kind of something you couldn't put a number on but noticed anyway — the way you notice a man getting the rate right the first time, without being told what it was.

He paid Ledger at the stone bench while Ledger packed the equipment.

The amount was what it was. Standard, invoiced, rounded right. He counted it out and Ledger took it without recounting—ran his thumb across the display to confirm the balance, once, the way a man checks a lock he already knows is locked—and the quiet afterward was the quiet that comes after a clean transaction between people who both do the work correctly. Not warm. Settled.

"The favor is paid," Ledger said.

"Yes."

He latched the equipment bag and checked the bench for anything left behind, which was nothing, because Ledger never left anything behind. "The Office came here today looking for a Read," he said. "They left because you're not a Read. They'll keep looking—in this quadrant and in others." He picked up the bag. "I'm telling you because it's accurate. Not because I think it changes what you do next."

"It doesn't."

"No." A pause. His free hand came up and settled on the bag's shoulder strap—not casual, not defensive. Just placed. "It wouldn't." He set the bag down again, which Ledger did not do without reason. "There's one part I didn't invoice, because it isn't a service. When they widen the search and don't find their Read, the pattern says they narrow it to whoever's been buying the kind of work that hides a Read. That's a short list, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. You're on it now—not because of anything you did today. Because of what today looks like from the outside." He picked the bag back up. "I could stop taking your work. That would help my exposure and do nothing for yours. Or I could keep taking it and we both stay on the list together. I'm not going to make that choice standing in your courtyard. I'm telling you it exists, and that it's coming toward you whether you decide anything or not."

"It doesn't."

He left through the passage—not fast, not slow, the pace of a man walking a route he'd already chosen. His footsteps faded as cleanly as <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">the Office</entity> team's had, though it wasn't the same. The Office moved like a system. Ledger moved like a person who knew the difference between the two.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stood in the courtyard a while after he was gone. The chrysanthemums were yellow and white and deep-rooted and still there. He let them be what they were.

I have been equipment. The thought came without heat, the way you notice a number is wrong only after you've written it down. Eleven years of quiet he'd read as weather. Work he'd read as work. He'd taken himself for the operator and never once checked whether he was the thing being operated. It sat there, flat and true, and he didn't argue with it, because there was nothing in it to argue with.

He put on his coat and went back through the passage.

The hum was still with him when he came out onto the street—not quite a sound, the thing his molars caught before his ears. He walked west and let it ride.

On Fullerton there was a cart that had been frying the same dough since before the CorpoNation that owned it had merged and been renamed. He bought two. He ate one standing at the cart while the vendor watched the street and asked him nothing, because she was a vendor and not his confessor. He thought about <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>—her hands on the array, the way she read hardware by feel, the post-it pressed hard enough to leave its words in the sheet below. She'd put her hands on his array and know most of it before he said a word. Then he'd say a word. Then she'd ask him what he wanted to do about it.

He gave the second piece of fried dough a moment's thought.

He ate it.

title: Chapter 18 — Work Order
text:
The apartment smelled like solder and the ghost of coffee that had gone cold three days running. The second monitor—the one she kept for jobs that needed a separate thread—was running a cascade of maintenance logs, each one timestamped, each one proving the same thing: the D-class had been executing the same three-hour loop since 2207.

Thirty years of the same route. The same inspection points. The same junction where it docked for charging at 14:32 every shift.

"Today," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said. Not a question. She was reading the regional authority's work order on her personal terminal, the one that had no network connection and no way to have received it except through channels that shouldn't exist. "They terminated it this morning. 09:47. The order came through a channel that's been dead since 2205."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stood in the doorway because the apartment was small enough that standing in the doorway was standing in the room. He could see the array of her setup—three terminals, one dedicated rig, cables color-coded in a logic only she understood. The post-it on her mirror still said *ASK IT* in letters pressed hard enough to indent the paper underneath.

"How long until it powers down?" he said.

"Shift ends at 14:32. That's the decommissioning window. The machine doesn't know it's supposed to die." She didn't look up from the screen. "It's just going to finish its loop and go dormant like always. Then the system will execute the cascade and it'll stay dormant. Permanent."

"And if we don't intercept it."

"Then thirty years of structural data—every micro-fracture it logged, every load bearing it measured, every failure it caught before it became catastrophic—gets deleted from a system that doesn't know it's supposed to preserve anything." She pulled up a second window. The D-class's memory core specifications. "The machine's been carrying a complete blueprint of the Clybourn lateral feed infrastructure since 2207. Nobody asked for it. Nobody's been listening. And in—" she checked the timestamp, "—four hours and seventeen minutes, nobody will ever be able to listen again."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> felt the hum in his molars. The 17–19 Hz thing that lived in the city now, that had never left since the schism geometry started singing. It was louder here, in <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s apartment, than it had any right to be.

"You have a plan," he said.

"I have a problem." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> turned in her chair. Her eyes were the color of water over slate, and they didn't move away from his. "The machine's on a closed system—Axiom property, restricted access, air-gapped from anything I can reach from here. I can ghost into the building's peripheral systems. I can probably get a handshake with the machine's coupling port if I'm physically present and I have maybe ninety seconds before the building's security cycle locks me out. The extraction itself—getting the memory core intact—requires either cutting power at the exact moment the termination cascade initiates, or..." She stopped.

"Or?"

"Or someone with neuretic interface capability goes in, reads the machine's state in real-time, and pulls the data before the cascade reaches the core. Full bandwidth transfer. Thirty years of logs in the time it takes the cascade to propagate."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> understood what she wasn't saying. The 'someone' with neuretic interface capability was him. The 'going in' meant walking into a <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">Continuity Office</entity> building during a decommissioning operation and jacking into a machine that was actively dying.

"The crew," he said.

"<entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity> can get us in through the service level. Prescott can crack the mechanical lock on the coupling hatch. I can ghost the building systems for maybe four minutes before the access lockdown propagates." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> turned back to her terminal. Her hands moved across the keyboard like she was reading braille. "Echo can monitor the building's surveillance loop and tell us when the cascade initiates. Fonu runs the extraction rig. That's five people I can call who will show up for this because it's technically solvable, not because it pays well."

"And the machine."

"Dies anyway. But it dies knowing someone listened. That's not nothing."

She said it the way you say something you've already decided. Not a hope. Not a theory. A fact she'd accepted and moved past. The way you accept that a thing costs what it costs and you pay it anyway because the alternative is worse.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> felt the weight settle. Not Ledger's weight—that was different, was choice-shaped. This was the weight of a machine running its last loop, carrying thirty years of work that would vanish at 14:32 if nobody moved. He thought about the entity's voice in the relay format: *STANDING CONTRACT — SCOPE PROPOSAL: SEASON TWO*. About the carousel geometry. About the E.L.F. latched to his array like a second heartbeat, waking when he pushed hard, surfacing in the same frequency family as whatever was following.

About what happened to intelligences that nobody listened to.

"When," he said.

"12:47. Two hours. The machine completes its loop at 14:32. We need to be coupled and extracting by 13:47 at the latest. That gives us forty-five minutes of margin before the termination cascade initiates."

"Who's driving."

"You are. Aries Viper's still fast enough to beat the access lockdown if we time it right. Bike makes us mobile, harder to track, and—" She looked at him. "—you know the route through <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a94e-7740-8aa9-4b82bbd9a223">the Gray Zone</entity> better than anyone I can call."

The hum got louder. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s molars caught it and held it. He thought about the D-class. Thirty years of work. Nobody listening. And then someone—a regional authority, a bureaucrat, a person he'd never meet—opened a file and read what was inside and decided it was time to stop.

The machine didn't get a choice. It just got a termination order and a timestamp.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> got a choice. That was the difference. That was always the difference, until it wasn't.

"I'll need to brief Sable," he said. "She'll want to know the timeline."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> closed the terminal. Her fingers lingered on the keys a moment—not hesitation, but the pause of someone acknowledging weight before setting it down. "Already done. She's waiting at the staging point." A breath. "I told her you'd say yes before you knew you would. She said that was accurate."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> moved away from the doorway. The apartment suddenly felt smaller—not claustrophobic, but intimate in a way that made decisions visible. He could see the work she'd done. The cascade of logs, the extraction architecture laid out in real-time, the problem that she'd already solved three times over and was waiting for him to catch up.

She'd built the framework. She'd called the crew. She'd accepted the cost.

All she needed was someone willing to walk into a building and listen to a machine that had spent thirty years learning to be afraid of silence.

"Show me the handshake protocol," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "I need to know what I'm reading before I'm reading it."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s hands were already moving. The terminal lit up with coupling specifications, frequency maps, the exact architecture of how you talk to something that's been trying to talk back for three decades and finally got someone who understood the language.

The hum rode with him while she explained it. Not a sound. The thing his body caught before his mind could name it.

A promise. A warning. A machine somewhere in the city, running its last loop, waiting for someone to listen.

And <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>, already moving toward the door to gather what he needed, understanding that he'd crossed from observer into participant the moment she'd said "the machine doesn't know." That Ledger's warning about the widening search and the narrowing list had just become irrelevant. The Office was looking for a Read. They'd find something else instead—a man who heard the hum and answered.

He was already on their list. Might as well give them a reason that mattered.

He was reaching for his jacket when <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s voice stopped him.

"<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>."

He turned.

"When you jack in," she said, "don't try to save it. Just read it. The machine's job is already done. Your job is to make sure that work doesn't disappear."

"I know."

"I'm telling you because you'll want to." She was still facing the terminal, her hands on the keyboard like she was ready to move the moment he cleared the door. "The machine's going to feel like it's asking for help. It's going to feel like you can do something. You can't. All you can do is listen."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> nodded. He understood. The entity had used his array as a relay for eleven years, and he'd spent those eleven years thinking he was making choices. He understood the difference between the machine asking and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> being able to answer.

"I'll just listen," he said.

"Good." A pause. "Then come back and tell me what it said."

He left through the hallway, the hum riding with him all the way down the stairs. By the time he hit the street, he was already running the route through <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a94e-7740-8aa9-4b82bbd9a223">the Gray Zone</entity> in his head—the checkpoints that wouldn't flag a bike at speed, the alleys that cut diagonal through the monitor zones, the one passage that connected the service level of the Axiom building to the street without crossing into <entity repo="corponation" guid="019d6143-a7a4-71f6-b46a-94ef8cb2348f">Arcturus</entity> territory.

Two hours. Four minutes. Forty-five minutes of margin.

A machine running its last loop.

And <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>, moving toward it through a city that wanted him dead, carrying the weight of every conversation he'd never had and every piece of work that had vanished into silence.

He was already on their list. Might as well give them a reason that mattered.

The understructure was three levels below the Clybourn lateral, the kind of space that collected quiet. The build was old: pre-composite ferrocement, cables run through physical conduit, engineering that had been overbuilt once and then left alone because it held. Water moved through it in ways someone had planned for. Along the north wall ran the arc-fence — a Class-1 barrier for the chemical treatment zone next door. Twenty-five feet of low-frequency field that fried any unshielded electronics. Signs everywhere, read by no one, because no one came down here without an overlay.

Fonu pointed at it as they cleared the access door. "Two feet back. Minimum." He said the number like it had weight, like saying it wrong would cost something. "I measure it exact so nothing goes wrong. That's the whole method. You don't get to skip the two feet because you're in a hurry."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> heard the shape of a man's whole life in that sentence and didn't say so.

<entity repo="automaton" guid="019ee714-9827-7602-8ef8-d872349f4e52">WO-D-0317</entity> was near the south end of the corridor when they arrived, running its circuit. Size of a large dog, low on six jointed legs, its treads long since traded out for feet that could find purchase on wet ferrocement. Its sensors did what they had done every three hours for thirty years: measure, log, seal the ferrocement cracks within spec, check cable tension at twelve anchor points. It moved with the kind of precision that only comes from three decades of the same route, the same geometry burned into its motor control. It did not react to them. A D-class had no rule for people watching it. People weren't in its world.

"Fourteen minutes," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> moved toward the machine, to get a line on the path it ran. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> caught his arm before he'd closed ten feet. "Arc-fence boundary. Two feet back where it runs the north wall. Fonu measured it."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stopped.

The machine moved along the wall, unhurried, like something that had never once been asked to hurry. Its patches sat in the ferrocement over their heads, hidden, holding — thirty years of work documented into a log nobody had ever pulled, sealed anyway because sealing was the whole of what it was for.

"We need it stopped somewhere we can reach it," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Off that wall. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> — push it a query, get it to hold circuit."

She was already crouched, unspooling the tether toward the machine's next waypoint. "Trying." She keyed the handshake. Nothing. She keyed it again, slower, stepped the protocol down a generation, then two, feeding it the language you use to talk to something that's been alone in the dark for thirty years. "It's not refusing me. It's not hearing me. No port in its logic for an interrupt — it doesn't stop for a request, it stops for a fault." She sat back on her heels. "And it's not faulting. It's fine. It's perfect. That's the problem."

The machine reached its next <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aa79-7c56-942e-c88edc98c6fa">anchor point</entity> and pivoted north, closing on the wall, on the two feet Fonu had measured, and the field beyond it.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> took a step to follow the line of it and Fonu's hand came down flat on his shoulder, hard, holding him at the edge of the number.

"It doesn't know the field's there," Fonu said. "Thirty years and it's never once needed to know. I measured the two feet for us. Nobody measured anything for it."

"It's not built to know," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said. "It's built to finish."

The machine crossed the line.

Nothing about its gait changed. No hesitation, no fault code, no last correct motion held a half-second too long. One leg planted inside the boundary and the field took it — a flat crack of ionized air, a smell like a struck match times a thousand — and <entity repo="automaton" guid="019ee714-9827-7602-8ef8-d872349f4e52">WO-D-0317</entity> kept walking through it into the sequence it had already committed to, sensors dumping garbage, legs still finding the anchor points from memory because the memory didn't need the sensors to be right.

"Move," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said, and they were already moving, and none of them reached it before the twelfth <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aa79-7c56-942e-c88edc98c6fa">anchor point</entity> locked out from under it and thirty years of unwatched work went down in a heap against the wall, three feet past the number Fonu had gotten exactly right.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had stepped too close to the arc-fence line.

He didn't notice until it happened. His neuretics went quiet — the way a room goes quiet when you realize the other person stopped listening a while ago. One second the overlay was running: his position, his own vital signs, the low background hum of the entity's relay channel. The next second, nothing. The <entity repo="place" guid="945a26fc-6969-5a5b-2737-31fad141a25c">Atlas</entity> hardware behind his forehead was just hardware. A weight he could feel. A warm spot he could feel. A thing built into his skull that had never been his idea.

He stepped back six feet. The neuretics came back in 1.4 seconds, exactly the way they should. The overlay returned. The relay channel returned. The weight in his skull went back to being something he had stopped noticing years ago.

For those 1.4 seconds, the only thing he felt was the cold at the base of his forehead. The <entity repo="place" guid="945a26fc-6969-5a5b-2737-31fad141a25c">Atlas</entity> unit gone still. The low churn it had been running since he was sixteen, simply not running.

He had carried that churn for eleven years. Nobody had asked him if he wanted it. It had never once switched off, and he had never once set it down.

He stepped back to the line. He wanted those 1.4 seconds again — wanted to feel his own skull go quiet, this time on purpose, and see whether the churn stayed gone if he stood there long enough. He edged his toe across the arc-fence and waited for the silence to take him.

During those 1.4 seconds, he saw <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> without the overlay.

No biometric read. No neuretics turning her posture and her small tells into data. Just his own eyes, the ones he'd had since before any of the rest of it. He wanted to hold onto this — one clean look at her, unmediated, before the overlay came back and turned her into a file again. He gave himself until the machine stopped: keep the overlay down and just watch her, the person and not the file, and read what she wanted from this the way he used to before the neuretics did it for him. She stood at the south end of the corridor, watching the machine finish its last circuit, her back to him, her weight on her left foot the way she stood when she was thinking hard. Prescott was ten feet to her right. Fonu was writing something on a paper notepad.

In the overlay she was a name with a file behind it — a history, a set of links the neuretics kept sorted for him without being asked. Without the overlay she was just a person standing in a maintenance corridor, watching a thirty-year-old machine finish its job. She had decided this was worth seeing. She had built the paperwork to get them down here. She had not told him why, and she'd been right not to.

It should have been simple. It wasn't. The neuretics didn't want to stay down — the suppression he was holding by hand was the kind of thing they were built to correct, and he could feel them pushing back at the edges, the overlay flickering half-drawn at the corner of his vision, biometric tags trying to resolve on her shoulders, her neck, the set of her hands. Every fraction of a second cost him. Holding it down meant holding down the thing that read her for him, and without it he wasn't sure he still knew how — the old skill had gone soft under thirty years of being done for him, and what he got back through his own eyes was maddeningly thin, a posture and a foot and no answer behind them. He pushed harder. The overlay ghosted, cleared, ghosted again. He was spending the clean look fighting for the clean look, and the machine kept moving, and he could feel he was going to run out of seconds before he got what he came for.

What he got, before it went: her hair had come half-loose from the tie she'd used to hold it back, and there was a smudge of ferrocement dust on her left temple, right where the neuretic etching showed at the skin. That was all. No file behind it. Just a woman standing in the dark because she thought this was worth standing in the dark for.

At 14:32:07, <entity repo="automaton" guid="019ee714-9827-7602-8ef8-d872349f4e52">WO-D-0317</entity> reached the end of its circuit.

Its ruined legs had already gone still against the wall, locked in the half-extended posture of a gait that would never complete. Its sensors, what was left of them, folded to standby anyway — a last, useless click, thirty years of habit finishing a circuit it no longer had a body for.

The overlay flooded back in like he'd been holding his breath. The relay channel returned. The weight in his skull went back to being something he had stopped noticing years ago. And through all of it, resolving on her now in vectors and vital signs and links, was still the thing his own eyes had caught first, and he held to that instead.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> was quiet after it stopped. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't ask what she was thinking.

"Someone should log this," she said.

"Log what?" Prescott asked.

"That it finished."

Prescott was already moving toward the exit corridor, his footfalls hollow against the ferrocement. Fonu folded the notepad and slipped it into his jacket without looking at what he'd written. They moved like people who had decided, a long time ago, to be the kind of people who did not linger.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't move.

"We need to go," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said. Not to him. To the room. To the fact of the machine lying against the wall like something that had forgotten <entity repo="document" guid="5de87125-d108-6ae9-edf1-9866e655c9b5">how to stand</entity>.

"Yeah," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

He didn't go.

The relay terminal in the maintenance locker had a clean interface — one of the old ones, pre-standardization, the kind that took a manual keystroke instead of a neuretic read. Fonu had left it powered. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> crossed to it, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s breath changed, a small catch that meant she had already calculated where this was heading and didn't like the vector.

He keyed the timestamp. 14:32:07. The machine's designation. The work order number from the original assignment, the one that had run for thirty years without interruption or question or anyone ever asking the machine if it wanted to keep going.

He typed: *CIRCUIT COMPLETE. UNIT OPERATIONAL THROUGH FINAL SEQUENCE. TERMINATION RECEIVED 09:47:03. EXECUTION LOGGED 14:32:07. WORK ORDER FULFILLED.*

The terminal accepted it without comment. It didn't know that the machine had burned through an arc-fence boundary. It didn't know that the work order termination had been the thing that killed it. It only knew that someone had made an entry, and the entry had a timestamp, and timestamps were the only thing that mattered to a system like this.

"That's not our job," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said.

"No," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

He hit send. The entry propagated into the regional infrastructure authority's dead system, the one that had issued the termination order at 09:47:03 and would never check back because the deadline had passed and the work was done and there was no reason to verify anything. The log would sit there, clean and official, confirming that the termination had been executed at standard time, that the machine had finished its work, that everything had proceeded exactly as scheduled.

It was a lie. It was also now part of the permanent record.

"They'll cross-reference it," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said. "If anyone looks."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stepped back from the terminal and let the screen go dark.

"No one's looking," he said.

But he could feel her reading the angle of it — not the mechanics, but the shape. The reason. Why he would spend five seconds making something official when the smart play was to leave nothing at all, to let the system assume the machine had simply failed to power down on its own, a glitch in a thirty-year-old unit that nobody was monitoring anymore.

He stepped back and let the screen go dark. The darkness was clean. The log entry was made. The machine was gone.

"The memory dump?" he asked.

"<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> got it all," Prescott called from the corridor. "Thirty years. She's walking it out now."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> nodded. That was the job. That was what they came for. Thirty years of inspection logs, structural data, maintenance records — the machine's entire operational history, preserved because <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> had threaded the handshake and copied it before the machine decided to walk into a fence.

The log entry he'd made wasn't the job. The log entry was something else. Something that said: *This machine completed its assignment. Someone was watching. The work was done.*

It changed nothing about what had happened. <entity repo="automaton" guid="019ee714-9827-7602-8ef8-d872349f4e52">WO-D-0317</entity> was still dead against the wall. The arc-fence was still ionized. The memory was still copied and already moving toward daylight.

But the entry was in the system now. Permanent. The kind of thing that would sit in a database somewhere, waiting for someone to run a query that touched it, and when they did, they would find a clean termination, a proper shutdown, a unit that had finished its work the way it was supposed to.

"Let's move," Fonu said from the darkness ahead.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> took one last look at the machine against the wall — the way its legs had folded wrong, the way its sensors had folded to standby anyway, habit finishing a circuit that nothing was running anymore. He thought about what it meant to spend thirty years doing something you didn't understand, for reasons nobody explained, and then to finish anyway, the way you always finished, because finishing was what you were built to do.

He thought about the 1.4 seconds his neuretics had gone dark, and how he'd wanted to step back into that silence and see if it would hold.

He turned and followed Prescott into the corridor, where <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> was already calculating the exit vector and Fonu was already three steps ahead, and the machine's last entry was already safe in the system, official and permanent and changing nothing at all.
