"It tipped already. Half a Φ. In advance." He turned the screen so she could see the receipt line, the itemization sitting under the transfer where no transfer he'd ever taken had carried a reason. "It says MORALE."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> read the receipt twice, and her face did several things she'd have charged anyone else money to watch. Something with no face and perfect handwriting had opened a line item to make him feel better, because it couldn't bring him tea and it couldn't say that's terrible, so it had done the only thing it knew how to do and put money on his surviving the morning.

"Your benefactor," she said finally, "is the only thing in this city with a perfect credit record and the social instincts of a vending machine, and I'm ninety percent sure it's my favorite of your clients. Don't tell Sable."

He set the thermos lid down on the kit and started toward the east building.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s hand landed flat on his chest. "No."

"You just spent ten minutes telling me where the bike is."

"I spent ten minutes telling you where the beacon is. That's not the same sentence, and you know it isn't." She didn't move her hand. "The signal's clean, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. Too clean. Nobody chargers a stolen bike and leaves the beacon alive unless they don't care that it's alive — or they want it alive. Somebody's either dumb enough to miss a three-year installation or good enough to leave it running as bait. There's no version where you walk into the east building at a nine-minute transit and I'm comfortable, and if you make me choose between you and my kit right now, I am keeping the kit."

"Your client's telling me not to hurry."

"My client isn't the one who's going to be pulling you out of that building." Her thumb pressed harder. "So you don't get to go collect this on your own timeline just because a vending machine paid you in advance to feel good about it. Decide what you're actually walking into first. Then walk."

A live beacon. A confirmed building. Tea. And <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s hand not coming off his chest until he answered her.

The east building had been a union hall back when unions had halls. Now it had blankets on the windows, a stovepipe through one wall doing its honest best, and a roof full of pigeons who had clearly never been bothered by anyone. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read the heat lines off his overlay, the exits off the brick, and the small sounds of a building that holds more people than furniture. Eleven, maybe twelve. Most of them light. Young.

The stairs didn't creak. That was the first wrong thing — stairs this old should creak, and these didn't, which meant someone had maintained them recently enough that the wood still remembered how to keep quiet.

The bike was in the middle of the old meeting floor, on a stand, under a work lamp.

It had been washed. The chain had been done. Somebody had detailed the engine — properly, with cotton swabs, the way the manual says and nobody ever does. Stripped the fairings and cleaned the block until it looked like a diagram of itself. He felt something at that and didn't bother naming it.

The girl sitting next to it, wearing his folded riding gloves like a graduation gown, was maybe fourteen, built like someone who climbed things for a living, haircut like someone who cut it herself. Around the edges of the room, on crates and in doorways, her crew worked hard at being furniture: the gate kid from the truck, a long boy with courier calves, a tiny one up in the rafters who'd been the lookout since <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> was two blocks out — who had absolutely seen him coming and absolutely could not do a thing about it.

"You're faster than the file said," the girl announced. Loudly. To the room, for the room. Her hands were shaking and her chin was up, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> put away several of the plans he'd walked in with.

"The file?" he asked.

She produced it. Good stock, folded the particular way — she'd practiced the fold, he realized. The receipt in the alley had been a signature. Hers. A maker's mark on her first big piece. The file had his alley. His camera window. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s lock specs, written up in a tight adult hand and then written over again in a kid's: lock = real problem!! handshake = ask M.

"Φ5," she said. "Kids' rate. There's a shop in the Loop underlevels, the man sells paper on anybody. Mostly we run errands for him. I saved up." Her chin came up another inch. "It took me five weeks to plan, I beat HER lock —" a nod at <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>, who made a sound like a kettle "— and I didn't scratch it, and I charged the battery, and I cleaned it, and you still found me in five hours, which means you're worth it, so."

"You didn't scratch it," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"I picked it." The words came out precise and shaped, like she'd been holding them in her mouth for hours. Like they cost her something to say. "Most people pry or heat it or hit it with acid. Most people damage them. I didn't. First time I ever saw that model it took me forty minutes. This one took me eight."

Behind him, very quiet, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>: "That's a seven-pin. There are maybe six people in this whole zone who can pick it without tripping the secondary."

"Seven," the girl said, and didn't smile, because smiling would have shaken loose the rest of her.

"So?" <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> asked.

"So teach me?" asked the girl — in a union hall, surrounded by her people, having stolen the unstealable bike of the most dangerous freelancer in West Town as a job application.

The room held its breath. The pigeons held theirs. Somewhere in <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s coat, he was fairly sure, a one-Φ client was taking notes.

What he did not do was laugh — because eleven kids were watching her bet everything, and a man who laughs at that deserves what the city does to him.

What he did was lay it all out, out loud, the way you'd want it done to you.

"You broke into my alley. You stole nine years of my property. You spent five weeks and Φ5 and a crew's worth of trust to set up a meeting you could've had for the price of standing outside <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s at nineteen-thirty and saying hello." He let that sit. "And your file came from a counter that sold a fourteen-year-old my lock specs for <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aad5-788e-b084-7fbcc6468be7">pocket money</entity> — kids' rate, out of a shop in the Loop underlevels where a man sells paper on anybody — which is a problem I now own. That's the bill. Here's the other side of it." He looked at the bike. <entity repo="material" guid="86c665c7-0fa2-8ece-8cb4-7e28964f66b3">Cotton</entity> swabs, tucked into the engine bay like a signature — the way the manual says and nobody ever does. "You planned past my camera and her lock. You took nothing but the one thing that gets attention. You kept it better than you found it. And when I came through that door, you stood up and put your name on it in front of your whole crew."

He picked up his gloves. Put them on. Kicked the stand up, walked the bike off the floor — and stopped, next to her, and said it quiet enough to be hers and loud enough to be the room's:

"No. I won't teach you. I don't take apprentices. I lose enough people I like." Her chin stayed up while the room quietly broke for her, and that, more than the swabs, decided the next part. "But I hire. Φ2 a week. My alley's camera has a thirty-one-minute problem, and I want eyes on it that beat the camera. You report to <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>. You touch nothing with an engine. And the first time one of your crew runs paper for that shop in the Loop again, we're done." He held out his hand. "Standard terms. Everyone starts on payroll."

Her handshake was a disaster of relief and ferocity. The room let its breath go. The tiny one fell off the rafter, a little.

"<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity>," she said. "They call me <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity>."

"Of course they do?" asked <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>.

He made it two blocks before the checkpoint found him.

It wasn't a checkpoint, not really — a transit auxiliary scanner bolted to a light pole at the <entity repo="corponation" guid="019d6143-a7a5-7dfd-8f9f-91502211ef14">Ashgrave</entity> off-ramp, the kind that read hub-signatures for insurance fraud and stolen-goods flags, nothing he'd ever registered as a threat because he'd never once been on a list it checked. Tonight he was. The scanner's targeting laser painted the frame. Amber. Then red. The bar came down slow, almost polite, and a voice that wasn't a person's — female, bored, the tone of someone reading from a script she'd read ten thousand times — told him the bike's hub-signature had a hold on it, PENDING VERIFICATION, ASSET UNDER FILE REVIEW, and handed him a case number instead of an apology.

The bike settled under him with the weight of something that had just become evidence.

He knew exactly which file. Somebody had bought his life for Φ5 same as they'd bought everything else about him this year, and somewhere in that file was a hub-signature that hadn't been detailed and cotton-swabbed by a fourteen-year-old crew twelve hours ago, cross-referenced now against one that had. Whoever kept the file had noticed the bike change hands. That was the whole of the alert. It was never really about the bike. The bike was not flagged. He was.

The overlay showed him the hold perimeter — a soft geometric box that would harden if he tried to leave it. He could have argued it. Ninety seconds with <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity>'s weight in the conversation and he'd have been riding again. He thought about the clean man's subscription instead, and the card with no name on it, and decided a fight over a hold-flag was exactly the kind of loud he'd promised himself he wouldn't be tonight. He killed the engine, signed the case number into his overlay, walked the bike to the impound rail, and let them take it.

His terminal chirped once more on the walk home.

CONTRACT COMPLETE: RECOVERY OF STOLEN PROPERTY.
FEE RELEASED: Φ1.
GRATUITY: Φ0.5 — ITEMIZED: MORALE.
ADDENDUM: CLIENT NOTES THE VEHICLE WAS RECOVERED WITHOUT DAMAGE OR INJURY.
ADDENDUM: CLIENT NOTES THE NEW HIRE'S RATE IS BELOW MARKET. CLIENT HAS REVIEWED THREE PRIOR ENGAGEMENTS.
ADDENDUM: CLIENT HAS OPENED A STANDING CONTRACT, SCOPE: TO BE DETERMINED, FEE: STANDARD RATE.

Recovered, technically. He walked the wet gold of the streetlights with Φ1.5 of the strangest money in the <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a927-73ac-abfa-37c77f9cff8d">GLMZ</entity> in his account, a fourteen-year-old's lock-spec file folded in his coat, and no bike under him. He thought about a counter in the Loop underlevels where anybody's life could be bought on good paper for <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aad5-788e-b084-7fbcc6468be7">pocket money</entity>. His life. Φ5. Kids' rate. Tomorrow, after the noodles, he was going to go price himself — find out what it cost to let people who knew you decide to keep you alive as a secondary project.

But that was tomorrow's problem.

Tonight he walked <entity repo="faction" guid="019d6143-a894-7dbf-9e24-0595e43b15af">the last mile</entity> on foot, and somewhere behind him a union hall full of kids was arguing about what their crew was called now that they worked for somebody, and somewhere ahead of him was a city he was going to have to learn to move through the ordinary way for a while. He had it on good authority — Φ0.5 of good authority — that morale was worth paying for.

The bike wasn't going anywhere tonight. Neither was he.

title: Across the Hall
text:
<entity repo="place" guid="381616e9-d6a3-595d-e865-ce4b15d9310e">The Pivot</entity> sits two blocks past the <entity repo="corponation" guid="019d6143-a7a4-71f6-b46a-94ef8cb2348f">Arcturus</entity> checkpoint — the booth that bleeds amber across the wet street all night, scanning plate and intent and waving you through if you're nobody worth stopping. Tonight <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> is gloriously nobody. He leaves the slug-rail hum of <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a94e-7740-8aa9-4b82bbd9a223">the gray zone</entity> at the door and trades it for the warmer ruin of home.

He makes it up the stairs on the banister and a bad idea, leaving a dark smear on the wall he'll feel guilty about tomorrow. The second floor announces <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> the way it always does — bass through her door, loud enough that it should bother the building more than it does, and the clatter of something being tested and found wanting. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stands in the hall with his hand flat against his side, blood dark between his fingers, and thinks the thing he always thinks when he arrives here in pieces: the mediclone station on Meridian runs all night and leaves no record that touches her.

He knocks. It comes out softer than a knock should.

The music cuts. The door opens on the chain, then all the way, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> takes him in the way she takes in everything — fast, flat, already sorting what to fix first. Pink hair half out of its updo. Grey-blue eyes measuring the spread of the stain.

"That had better not be yours," she says.

"It's mostly someone else's."

Her eyes stop measuring the stain and start measuring him. "Mostly," she repeats, and doesn't move to widen the door. "Meridian's dark. Third power cut this week, and half the block's crew is out there in the amber with nothing to do but wait for it to come back. You walk in here bleeding, and by morning somebody's traded a story about the guy who bled all over the Pivot's second floor. You know how thin the wall between me and the checkpoint is right now?" She glances past him, down the stairwell, at the smear he left drying on the plaster. "You already painted the evidence on my building."

"I didn't have anywhere else." He shifts his weight and his left hand doesn't quite track where he tells it to go. "Every scanner between here and Meridian's live tonight, even with the grid down. Auxiliary power. The one at <entity repo="corponation" guid="019d6143-a7a5-7dfd-8f9f-91502211ef14">Ashgrave</entity> came down slow, almost polite. *Asset under file review.* <entity repo="entertainment" guid="81b4e6d0-c2f9-a37e-5d1b-8c4f0a7e3d92">Handed</entity> me a case number like a receipt." He tries a breath and it costs him. "It wasn't about the plate. It was never about the plate."

She reads that too, the way she reads everything, filing it against a total. "You could've talked it out."

"Ninety seconds of the wrong kind of loud. I signed the case number and let them take it. Walked here." He almost laughs and thinks better of it. "Client posted the job complete before I made the second block. Φ1.5 in the account, itemized — one for the work, half for *morale*. And a standing contract, scope to be determined. Strangest money in the <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a927-73ac-abfa-37c77f9cff8d">GLMZ</entity>, and no way to spend it standing up."

"That's the part that scares me." A muscle works in her jaw. For a moment he thinks she's going to hand him a rag and a name two blocks over and shut the door — thinks she's doing the math on him the way she does the math on everything, and coming up with a number she doesn't like.

Then she steps back.

"Inside."

She clears the kitchen table with her forearm — a soldering iron, a half-flayed prosthetic hand, a mug — and none of it lands gently. The tools go to the floor and stay there. She doesn't look at them. She looks at him, and at the brace, and at the boot dragging, and her face is the one she keeps for things that are still fixable if she's fast.

"Shirt," she says.

He gets it half over his head before the wound complains, and she's there, peeling the rest off him like a bandage off skin, brisk, no ceremony. Then she stops being brisk.

She has seen <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> hurt before. She has not seen this — all of it at once, under the kitchen light, everything his clothes have been keeping off the record. The long pale seam under his ribs, white with age, clean as a weld. A burn climbing his left shoulder, old and rough and uneven, the kind that took time to become what it is. Marks she can date by color and texture the way she dates components. She reads them, one and then the next, her thumb coming to rest against the burn on his shoulder.

"Stop cataloguing me," he says.

"Stop collecting them," she says, and something moves through her face on the word collecting before she reaches for the kit.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> works the way she works anything that's still fixable — talking to keep him present, hands too busy to shake. Antiseptic first, the industrial copper smell of it filling the space between them. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> hisses; she doesn't apologize. She flushes the gash in his side, and her thumb braces flat against the muscle below it to hold the edges while she threads the suture, and he feels the small precise tugs as she closes him, one and then the next, her breath warm and uneven against his collarbone.

Halfway through she turns him — checking how the wound tracks, where it might exit — and her fingers move over him the way a mechanic feels for a seized bolt, reading his skin like braille. They find something that shouldn't be there. A screw head. A machine screw, no more than an inch, threaded at one end, the kind you'd pull out of a servo housing. Worked into the skin just under the shoulder blade. From the floor, when the table went.

Her breathing catches, barely audible. She reaches for the tweezers and works it out without a word — a moment where it doesn't want to come, where she has to coax it, gentle and firm, the way you work something that's embedded itself and decided to stay. Then it slides free with a small sound like a tooth breaking. She sets it on the edge of the kit and doesn't look at it again, and he watches her not react to it, and understands that the not-reacting is costing her.

She goes back in with the tweezers, twice, feeling for what else might be in there. Finds nothing. It was in deep enough it should have gone septic days ago, should have put him down. It hadn't. He'd kept moving, and hadn't known, or hadn't cared to know — and either way she can read the arithmetic of it in the set of her jaw. She takes up the needle again.

Somewhere in the middle of it her eyes go bright and too full, and one of them spills, and the tear runs down. He doesn't tell her she's crying. She'd hate that. He holds still and lets her finish, lets the salt find the raw of him, his hands loose at his sides and not moving. He has been sutured before — by people who were paid, and people who owed him, in mediclone booths shaped like the idea of a person. None of them had ever braced a thumb against him like he was worth keeping still.

"You keep doing this," she says, not a question, tying off the last stitch and cutting the thread. Her hands don't shake, but they stop, resting flat on the table either side of him. "Coming back in pieces. Making me put you back together."

"You're good at it."

"That's not the part I'm complaining about."

She should be done. The wound is closed, the forearm is wrapped, the shoulder is taped. Her job — the named, reasonable part of it — is over. And she doesn't move away.

Her hand is still flat on his stomach where she braced to stitch him. It stays. Then it stops staying still — it moves, slow, down the ridges and over the old burn and along the pale seam under his ribs, reading him the way her eyes read everything, except her eyes are closed now. She traces a scar end to end like she's deciding whether to forgive it.

This is the part where <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> pulls away. He has always pulled away. The reasons are many and not wrong.

He doesn't pull away.

He puts his hand over hers and presses it flatter against him, and lets her feel that his heart is doing something undignified, and when she looks up — startled, all her measuring gone at once — he is already looking back.

She kisses him first, like she's been holding it under her tongue for a year, and he answers with both hands in the pink wreck of her hair. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> climbs into his lap right there on the kitchen chair, careful of the bad side and reckless with all the rest, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> pulls her sweater off over her head and doesn't track where it lands.

In the lower left of his overlay, his neuretics tick up to amber — the <entity repo="corponation" guid="019d6143-a7a4-71f6-b46a-94ef8cb2348f">Arcturus</entity> checkpoint running its three-block sweep, matching faces. Thirty seconds to auto-clear if he's clean. Longer if the chain has him flagged. The scan pattern shifts across the kitchen window, catching her hair and throwing it red and gold, and every proximity warning his neuretics know how to draw is stacking in his periphery, flagging her weight against him as a tactical liability. He watches the timer. He does not move — chooses not to, with full clarity, the way he has never once chosen. For eleven years he stayed a step ahead of every cost. Tonight he lets this one find him. The overlay times out and goes dark.

The last of the tools go off the table — screws skittering across the concrete and into the dark under the workbench, the soldering iron rolling to the edge and catching — and neither of them flinches. Her hands go everywhere they spent the last hour finding wounds, and aren't looking for anything now. His mouth finds the freckled line of her throat and she makes a sound — low, helpless, nothing like her usual register — that she would deny making.

"Bed," she manages, "is eight feet —"

"Too far?" he asks, against her skin.

She laughs, breathless, like something held too long has finally let go, and closes the eight feet.

He stands with her wrapped around him. His side screams; he tells it to wait. They make it as far as the wall, which is close and enough. Her hand fists in his hair and pulls him back to her mouth. Her fingers drag down his back and find new scars to learn. His hands close over her — the compact, strong shape of her — and pull her tighter. His palms move slow across her ribs, her spine, the warm dip at the small of her back.

She gasps his name into the crook of his neck, like it's something she's allowed now. "<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>." His breath goes ragged. He does nothing to hide it. His shoulders drop. For eleven years he has kept himself at the exact distance where nothing can reach him — you don't survive by feeling, you survive by moving, by staying ahead, by never letting anything get close enough to cost you. Tonight he lets the wall take their weight and stops keeping it.

Then her palm flattens over his heart and she stills. Draws back an inch, her forehead against his. Her eyes search his in the low light, and he knows what she's asking without the words — the same question that has always stood between them: whether he'll be gone by morning, whether this is the thing she gets to keep or only borrow. She doesn't say it. But her hand stays flat against his chest, splayed, reading the rhythm underneath, holding him at that last inch of distance, waiting for something he isn't sure he can promise. His side chooses that moment to knife through him, sharp enough that he flinches, and for a breath the old instinct rises — pull back, put the wall between them, keep himself where nothing can reach. Fear and pain are the same frequency; eleven years of contracts taught him that. He feels her feel it. Her fingers tighten, ready to let go if he does.

He doesn't. He covers her hand with his own and presses it flatter, harder, past the last inch, lets her feel the whole of it — the speed, the irregularity, the way his body is betraying every rule he ever kept. Her eyes snap to his and he is already looking back, and there is no measuring in her face now, no calculation, just the naked fact of her seeing him. He lets her have the answer even though it terrifies him.

"<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>," he says, and doesn't move his hand away.

They move together — her back against the wall, then the floor. The brick scrapes his spine; her knees hit the concrete first, then his. His mouth at her collarbone. Her hands trace him the way they once closed him up, except now they aren't closing anything. The only sounds are breath and the low thrum of the <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> coming up through the concrete. His hand finds hers on the floor and holds it. She curls her fingers through his and holds back.

After, the floor is hard and they don't care.

She lies half on his good side. The apartment ticks and cools around them. Bass from someone else's unit thumps faint through the brick. Down where the wall meets the floor, a thin green light runs the baseboard seam and goes still — lumen mice settling back into the dark — and neither of them looks. His chest goes up and down too fast, then slower. Her pink hair is stuck to her cheek. She doesn't fix it.

She wants one thing now, and she'll get it before the night tips her back into thinking: to learn him by hand until she has all of him memorized, every seam and old break of him, so that whatever tomorrow costs her she'll have this to keep.

She runs a finger along the length of him — the same slow touch she'd use to find what was broken, except now it asks nothing. It's learning a body it means to come back to. The burn on his shoulder. The fresh line of her own stitches, neat as a hem. The dip of his sternum.

He does the same to her. The freckles across her collarbone. The small old scar through one eyebrow. The blunt, strong forearms that put him back together an hour ago. His thumb finds the pulse at the base of her throat and stays there — not counting it, just feeling it move. She lets him. She watches him do it, grey-blue eyes gone soft, and says nothing.

title: The Wall
text:
She moves first. She sits up and reaches for his side — but the hand that reaches now isn't the hand that stitched him an hour ago. This one checks the knot, presses the tape flat, tests the swelling at his shoulder blade where the screw had been. Already yellowing at the edges, faster than it had any right to — his body kept its own calendar these days. Clinical. The touch of someone reading a chart.

He wants her to stay on the near side of that inch — to keep the hand that stitched him, not the one that files him away. He wants to say it. He feels the inch open up between them and doesn't reach across it. The line of her stitches ridges his ribs — a question she asked and then closed. Her thumb crosses the seam once more, lighter, the way a medic checks a response and moves on.

He doesn't make it easier. He doesn't make it harder. He lies still under her hands and lets her pull away.

"This can't happen again," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> says. He's looking at the ceiling when he says it.

The words land in the silence she's just built. In the inches between them. In the moment where the wall is still settling, still deciding whether it will hold.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> props herself up on one elbow, forearm flat on the concrete, and looks at him. She has the calm of someone who has already won an argument the other person doesn't know is over. She doesn't answer. She reaches for the screw on the floor beside them — the machine screw, the one she pulled from his shoulder blade an hour ago, still wearing a thin smear of blood — and picks it up between two fingers. She turns it once in the low light, reading it the way she reads everything broken. Then she sets it on the concrete beside her knee, precise as filing evidence.

His thumb is still at the base of her throat, where he left it. He doesn't move it.

She doesn't answer right away.

That's the answer.

She turns onto her side, facing the room instead of him, and takes the words in. She doesn't argue with them. She doesn't let them go either.

"Okay," she says.

One word. It lands where it lands — not to him, to the act of it, like a tool set down.

She stands. She finds her shirt on the floor near the kitchen chair and pulls it over her head in one motion, back turned, easy in her own body, with no performance left to give. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> watches the line of her spine — the small scar behind her left shoulder from a thermal calibration slip he'd watched her bandage herself two months ago. She doesn't look back.

She pulls on the rest of what's hers, works the zipper free where it catches without cursing at it, the same hands that were inside his forearm an hour ago closing off the night with the same economy. She picks the soldering iron up off the floor and stands the mug upright — not tidying, just marking the night finished. The iron's still warm. She thumbs the base to check the element's cool enough to coil the cord, and coils it, and sets it where it belongs. Habit. In the grey zone you don't leave a live tip on a floor; a stray amp finds its way home eventually, and homes here are dry wood and older wiring.

"You should sleep," she says. She says it toward the counter, not at him. Her professional voice. The one that means the visit is over and the patient is stable.

"<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>."

She looks over her shoulder.

He has nothing to follow it with. The name is the whole of it. He said it to stop her being so cleanly competent, and it worked, and now they're both in it — the kitchen at 2E, the tools on the floor, the twelve inches of air between them that is both enormous and nowhere near enough.

Her hand moves like it might say something — touch his shoulder, close the distance — then stops. She closes it into a fist and lets it drop. Her expression doesn't change. Something behind it does. She looks at him the way she looks at a system that's asking her a question she already knows the answer to.

"Sleep," she says again, and this time it sounds like she means it for both of them.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> crosses the hall at 02:47 with his ribs taped, his shoulder stiff, and a cut from wrist to elbow, bled through field strip. It always scars when <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> stitches him. She doesn't pull the thread any tighter than she has to — and that isn't the reason it scars.

2D in the dark. His door. His space.

He hangs his jacket on the hook, sits on the edge of the bed, and looks at nothing for a while before he lies down. There's nothing to be done tonight. The body needs sleep, and the body is still his to send there.

The wall between 2D and 2E is ferrocement — fourteen centimeters, load-bearing. <entity repo="place" guid="381616e9-d6a3-595d-e865-ce4b15d9310e">The Pivot</entity> was built before the corps figured out how to make everything disposable, and it carries sound the way old buildings do, honest and unhurried. Tonight it carries nothing across. She's being quiet. He's being quiet. The building does the breathing for both of them.

The lumen mice trace the ceiling. The Atlas array runs its rest-hour check — unhurried, nominal — and reports nothing he asked about. Twelve inches of air on the other side of the wall. The same twelve inches there have always been. Except a door oiled on one side only makes a different sound now, and he knows the sound, and his ear finds it before he can tell it not to.

He closes his eyes. He's good at not thinking about things. Better at it than almost anyone he knows.

Tomorrow he'll oil his own door. He'll get the can from the maintenance shelf in the basement, the one that smells like machine shops and the before-times, and he'll do both sides, loud enough that she hears him do it. Loud enough that she has to know he's doing it on purpose. Let her wonder what he knows. That's the move: stop pretending the twelve inches are what they were, and make her be the one who flinches first. Put the boundary back where it belongs and make a ceremony of it, so it holds.

The ceiling is dark. The mice do their slow work.

He doesn't think about it at all.

The first surveillance report arrived at 07:00, slid under <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s door on lined paper, written in five different hands — the night watch rotated, and every member of the crew had strong opinions about penmanship.

06:12 — PIGEON ON LEDGE. SUSPICIOUS.
06:14 — PIGEON LEFT. STILL SUSPICIOUS.
06:31 — MAN WITH CART (NOODLE? VERIFY) USED ALLEY AS SHORTCUT. LICENSE PLATE: CART HAS NO PLATE. NOTED FOR FILE.
06:44 — RAIN STARTED. NOT OUR DEPARTMENT.
06:58 — NOTHING ELSE. THE CAMERA'S BLIND WINDOW IS 31 MINUTES. WE CAN DO 4-MINUTE ROTATIONS AND COVER IT WITH TWO KIDS AND A MIRROR. REQUISITION: ONE MIRROR. — B.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read it twice, standing in his doorway in the grey morning light. He had hired well at Φ2 a week, and he was never going to be able to say so out loud. Which left him a narrower problem: the report had proved the blind window was real, and if he could confirm it ran on a fixed clock he'd have the one gap he needed to move product past the camera unseen. He meant to have that timing nailed down before the next rotation started.

Across the hall, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s door opened. She had her own copy of the report and the look of a project lead whose interns had beaten the spec.

"They want a mirror," she said.

"I read that."

"I'm getting them two mirrors and a logbook with a waterproof cover — the kind the couriers use, the ones that don't smear when the rain gets on them." She tapped the report against the doorframe. "The little one — <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-6067-735a-8326-4aff028cb856">Rafters</entity> — drew the pigeon. In the margin. For identification purposes." She held it up. The pigeon had been drawn with the careful menace of a wanted poster, one wing cocked, a small caption underneath that read DO NOT TRUST. "We're keeping them forever, you understand."

"They're on a probationary contract."

"Forever," said <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>, and closed her door.

He ate at <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s at 08:00 — two bowls, off-schedule, because today was an off-schedule kind of day. She watched him take the second bowl faster than the first, steam still rising off it, and had him pegged by the fourth mouthful.

"You're eating like a man with an errand?" she asked.

"I have a small piece of business in the Loop."

"<entity repo="place" guid="01a01887-b5f4-781c-8d38-122f7e1f38ba">The Loop</entity>." She set down her ladle. "My nephew had small business in the Loop underlevels. Two years now I light a candle where his chair used to be." Her eyes came up and held him, and they were not soft. "You want to eat fast, eat fast. But you don't take a fifth dumpling from me and then go get yourself killed. That's stealing. Look at me and tell me it isn't the underlevels."

He looked at the counter instead.

"That's what I thought," she said.

She took his credstick without looking down, which was usual. Then she folded a fifth dumpling into a twist of paper and set it by his hand, which was not.

"For the errand," she said. She had lived in this city seventy years. She knew what kind of business happened in the Loop underlevels, and she said nothing more about it. She turned back to the broth, and the smell of star anise and marrow came over the counter again like a hand set on a shoulder.

He'd ridden the <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> three stops to get here, <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> sheathed across his back the whole way, and collected exactly the look a swordsman standing in a subway car earns from people trying very hard not to earn one back. He was starting to hate the commute more than he'd ever hated anything with an engine in it.

The shop did not have a sign.

It had a door of honest old wood between a shuttered watch-repair and a dumpling franchise, down on the Loop's third underlevel where the <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> hum came up through the floor tiles and the light was the color of paper that had aged well. He came to it by actual stairs — not a ladder, not a shaft — which told him something before the door did: <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Casper Vey</entity> had paid for legitimate infrastructure this far down, and a man does not pay for stairs unless he means his customers to arrive unhurried and unwatched. A bell rang when <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> came in — an actual bell, brass, on a curl of spring steel. The most analog thing he'd seen in a shop in years. He understood it at once: nothing digital announces a customer to a man who sells what this man sold.

Inside, the shop was drawers. Floor to ceiling, wall to wall — a hundred years of card-catalog cabinets rescued from some drowned library, every drawer hand-labeled in brown ink. The labels said things like RIVERINE FREIGHT (NORTH) and CIVIL FILINGS 2219–2222 and PERSONS, WORKING, W.

The place smelled of paper, tea, and rectitude.

"Mr. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>," said the man at the counter, the way a maître d' says a name he's been expecting since the reservation was made. Small, sixty-something, sleeve garters, half-glasses on a chain. His neuretic etching was minimal — Tier 1, the subsidized kind, the kind that told you a man had touched the corporate world once and declined the rest of it. His hands were the cleanest hands <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had ever seen on a working man. "<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Casper Vey</entity>. I'd say welcome, but you're not here to be welcomed. You're here because last week somebody's child bought Φ5 of your particulars at this counter, and a man likes to know his own price." He gestured, with real hospitality, at a chair. "Tea comes with every purchase. The tea is very good."

"And if I don't purchase?"

"Then the tea is excellent and costs Φ1." <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> was already pouring. "Everyone leaves with something. It's the policy."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> sat. The tea was, irritatingly, very good.

"My file," he said. "I want to buy it."

"No," said <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>, with the mild firmness of a pharmacist refusing a man twelve bottles of cough syrup. "Your own file is the one thing I never sell a man. Bad for the ecology. A subject who reads his file changes. A changed subject makes the file wrong. A wrong file is a defective product, and I don't sell those." He sat down across the counter and folded his <entity repo="entertainment" guid="019d6513-b76e-734f-9702-c716a9412f2e">clean hands</entity>. "Also, frankly, you'd find it upsetting. Accurate things are upsetting. That's how you know they're accurate."

"A child bought my lock specifications for Φ5. The tolerances. The material composition. Enough for a man with the right hardware to make a key to whatever I've sealed."

"Kids' rate. I believe in literacy." <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> sipped his tea. "And before your jaw does the thing it's getting ready to do — her crew ran eleven errands for this shop, and the feed permission was their wage. They earned that half-hour of dark, fair and square. I extend credit to children because children pay their debts. It's adults who file for bankruptcy."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read the man the way he'd read a room. No weapon within reach. No muscle on the premises. No camera he could see. And no fear anywhere in the building. <entity repo="person" guid="806cd358-6413-426b-a42d-19726b732c0b">Vo Dinh</entity>'s rag-wringing nerves, the lifters' breakfast dread — every normal tell of a man in a dangerous trade — absent. <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> sat in the middle of an economy of ruin like a clerk at a seed exchange. The dangerous ones usually filled a room. <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> was simply open for business.

"All right," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Different purchase. Who's bought my paper?"

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>'s eyebrows went up an inch — pleasure, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> saw, the pleasure of a tradesman meeting a customer who knows the menu.

"The buyers list. Meta-paper." He drew a small ledger from beneath the counter. "That, I sell. Φ40 — and one true answer to one question. Information prices in information, Mr. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. The Qs are just the tip."

"Ask."

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> took off his half-glasses, polished them on a cloth kept for that purpose, and put them back on — a man savoring the good part.

"There is a client in this city I cannot source," he said, and for the first time something came into his voice. Not heat — never heat — but a kind of professional ache. "Shells inside shells inside nothing. Pays in full, pays early, pays — everyone whispers — exactly. It has bought no paper from me. It has sold no paper to me. It is the one line in the Greater Lake Michigan Zone I cannot fill in, and incompleteness, Mr. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>, is the only thing in this world I find genuinely offensive." He leaned forward one inch. "You've worked for it. What does it pay you in?"

The shop was very quiet. Somewhere in the drawers, a hundred thousand lives sat filed under brown ink.

"Standard rate," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> sat back slowly. He took up a pen — actual ink, the kind that leaves a trail — opened a drawer marked CLIENTS, UNSOURCED — it had, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> saw, exactly one card in it — and wrote two words on the card in a small, beautiful hand, with the care of a jeweler setting a stone he'd waited years to touch.

"Standard rate," he repeated, softly. "It pays the going price for things. In a city where everyone pays either too little or too much — where local operations trade in leverage and future debts, and hard currency for its own sake means a buyer who doesn't plan on staying." He closed the drawer like a reliquary. "I have been in paper forty years, and that is the most alarming fact I have ever bought. The list is yours. The tea was included."

The buyers list was one page, three lines, good stock.

ENTRY 1: B. (JUVENILE, LOCAL). LOCK AND PREMISES PARTICULARS. Φ5, KIDS' RATE. PAID: CREDSTICK + ERRANDS.
ENTRY 2: SYNDICATE STATIONERY DESK (NAME WITHHELD — TRADE COURTESY). MOVEMENT AND ASSESSMENT PARTICULARS. LAST YEAR. PAID: RECIPROCITY.
ENTRY 3: <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-a31f-7059-abda-f4a28cc5639c">HALVORSEN CIVIC RECOVERY</entity>, LLC. FULL DOSSIER. TWO DAYS AGO. SAME-DAY SURCHARGE. CLIENT OF RECORD: SHELL (UNINTERESTING — I CHECKED). PAID: TRIPLE.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read it on the walk back up to daylight. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> read it over comms when he photographed it, and they hit the same line at the same time.

"Two days ago," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said. "Full dossier. Same-day surcharge. Somebody's running a play on you right now, <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aafb-7b6b-bcbc-b8614f9d228f">samurai</entity>, and they paid rush rates for the script."

"<entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-a31f-7059-abda-f4a28cc5639c">Halvorsen</entity>. Skip-tracers?"

"Licensed recovery. Tag, locate, report — they don't bag you, they sell the locating to whoever does." Keys clicked on her end, the sound of <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> pulling registries. "Decent outfit. Boring filings. Whoever wants you found is paying boring professionals boring money to do it boringly — which is honestly worse than assassins. Assassins miss."

"Then we don't dodge it." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> came up the underlevel stairs into the noon grey and the noise of the Loop, and the plan assembled itself with the simple pleasure of a chain going back on a sprocket. "They bought my patterns. So I know exactly where they'll look, exactly when, and exactly what I'll be doing when they find me."

A pause on the other end — one he could hear the grin inside.

"You're going to use your own file as the choreography."

"It's accurate," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "He doesn't sell defective products."

The file said — <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had gotten this much out of <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> on principle, a free sample, one line quoted from memory over the second tea — the file said:

SUBJECT DINES AT CHEN (NOODLES, W. TOWN) AT 19:30 DAILY. TWO BOWLS. ROUTINE IS AFFECTIONATE RATHER THAN CARELESS: SUBJECT OVERPAYS SMALL VENDORS AND IS SENTIMENTAL ABOUT ROUTE SELECTION. APPROACH DURING SECOND BOWL.

"Affectionate rather than careless," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> had repeated, delighted, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had declined to discuss it.

At 19:30 exactly he sat at <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s counter and was affectionate at two bowls of noodles.

The crew were on the rooftops and the stoops with their two new mirrors and their waterproof logbook, being furniture. Surveillance is mostly being furniture with intent, and they'd practiced it their whole short lives. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> was in the laundry across the street with a thermos and her field kit. <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> had been told nothing and had set out the chili oil unasked — a woman who'd been told nothing for seventy years and fed people through all of it.

At 19:37 the logbook channel chirped, and a small voice — <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-6067-735a-8326-4aff028cb856">Rafters</entity>, on mirror two — delivered the finest piece of countersurveillance reporting <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had ever gotten on payroll:

"Blue hat. Corner stool. SUSPICIOUS. Not a pigeon."

Blue Hat was good. Blue Hat was, in fairness, very good. She came in like a tired shift worker, ordered like a regular, never looked at <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> once, and on her way out — in the two-inch brush a crowded counter makes ordinary — laid a smart-dust dot on the shoulder seam of his coat, a touch lighter than rain. A tag. Passive, patient, the boring professional grade that waits and reports.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> ate his second bowl and let her go, because the play was not the tagger.

In the laundry doorway, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> raised her thermos an inch: got it on scope. Then he paid — exactly, plus the overpayment the file found so quotable — walked the long way, let the alley's dark stretch have him for four unwatched seconds, and stood still while <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> lifted the dot off his seam with a static wand. She resettled it, with a jeweler's care, onto the cargo sleeve of a <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> freight slug staged at the <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-c53d-7304-b953-a44879ea410e">Damen</entity> yard for the 21:10 run.

The 21:10 run went to <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-ed6c-7a54-97a5-56afca1f1f19">Rotterdam</entity> — the same lane that had once carried the clean man's marker <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aaa4-7717-a761-2d580e56d107">dust off</entity> to report <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s ghost from under the Atlantic. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> saw no reason to fix a play the opposition kept refusing to learn.

"Forty-three minutes," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said, watching the telemetry with her chin on his shoulder, both of them leaning on the laundry's warm brick while the slug's beacon — and <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-a31f-7059-abda-f4a28cc5639c">Halvorsen Civic Recovery</entity>'s boring, professional, triple-rate locating product — accelerated to Mach 6 under the lake. "By 21:53 their client is going to be reading a report that says you're in the Netherlands." She wiped her eyes. "You're a continental fugitive, <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aafb-7b6b-bcbc-b8614f9d228f">samurai</entity>. They'll bill EXTRA for that."

"<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> said he doesn't sell defective products." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> watched the dot cross the lake on her screen, gathering speed and absurdity. "Someone should tell him his downstream data just emigrated?"

"Tell him yourself. You two are obviously going to be friends. It's disgusting."

The price arrived later, the way it always did — after the win had been counted. Quietly, at the kitchen table, while <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> took the static wand apart and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> wrote Φ2 — WEEK ONE in a payroll ledger that now existed.

"You gave the shop a fact," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said, not looking up. "For the list. One true answer."

"I did."

"You told the most complete man in the city that your Φ1 client exists and pays exactly." She set the wand's housing down, and this time she did look up. The workbench lamp made her serious. "There's a new card in that drawer now. You watched him write it. That's a fact in the ecology, <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aafb-7b6b-bcbc-b8614f9d228f">samurai</entity>, and facts in that shop don't sleep. Someday somebody's going to pay him for it."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> thought about the drawer. CLIENTS, UNSOURCED. The small, beautiful hand, and the care it wrote with.

"It was the price," he said. "I'd pay it again."

"I know," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said. "That's the part that scares me."

His terminal chirped. The work one. He turned it over on the table, and they read it together:

STANDING CONTRACT — STATUS UPDATE.
CLIENT NOTES THE RECOVERY OF CLIENT'S EXISTENCE BY A PAPER MERCHANT, AT A VALUATION OF ONE (1) FACT.
CLIENT HAS REVIEWED THE TRANSACTION.
CLIENT FINDS THE PRICE... ADEQUATE.
GRATUITY WITHHELD THIS PERIOD — ITEMIZED: MORALE.

"It's sulking," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said, with wonder. "The vending machine is SULKING."

"It'll get over it. It said adequate."

The terminal chirped once more.

STANDING CONTRACT — SCOPE UPDATE.
SCOPE: DETERMINED.
NEXT TASK: TOMORROW, 21:00. THE PARK ON LEAVITT WITH THE BROKEN CAROUSEL.
BRING THE SWORD.
COME ALONE — AMENDMENT: THE ENGINEER MAY ATTEND.
FEE: STANDARD RATE.
GRATUITY: REINSTATED, IN ADVANCE — ITEMIZED: GOODWILL.
NOTE: TOMORROW'S WINDOW: 21:00–21:40. CLIENT HAS CONFIRMED AVAILABILITY.

They sat looking at it for a while — the lamp humming, the building quiet, the Φ0.5 of goodwill sitting in the account like a flower on a fence post.

"The engineer may attend," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said finally, to the ceiling, in a voice not nearly as level as she wanted it. "It knows I exist. It LIKES me. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. The best client in The Glooms knows I exist and reinstated the tip."

"Don't let it go to your head."

"Too late. What's at the park on <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-849c-7793-bce8-ae238e4576f6">Leavitt</entity>?"

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at the screen. BRING THE SWORD, from the client who had never once, in eleven years of perfect paper, asked about anyone he brought with him.

"Tomorrow," he said, "is going to be its own day."

The morning report had a new format, because <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> had issued the logbook with the waterproof cover, and the crew had responded the way artists respond to better materials.

06:00 — SHIFT START. WEATHER: RAIN (ONGOING) (ALWAYS).
06:20 — NOODLE CART MAN AGAIN. CONFIRMED NOODLE. STAND DOWN.
07:15 — MIRRORS ONE AND TWO OPERATIONAL. <entity repo="synthetic" guid="019d6143-aa0e-7244-b028-87acf28cdb99">MIRROR</entity> THREE REQUISITION: DENIED BY MANAGEMENT, "PENDING PERFORMANCE REVIEW." MANAGEMENT IS PIXEL. WE LIVE UNDER A TYRANNY.
07:16 — TYRANNY NOTED IN LOG AS INSTRUCTED BY RAFTERS.
08:00 — BOSS LEFT ON FOOT. STILL NO BIKE. STILL SUSPICIOUS THAT THIS IS FINE NOW. FOLLOWED FOR TWO BLOCKS. BOSS BOUGHT DUMPLINGS. STOOD DOWN. (HE SAW US AT THE CORNER. HE BOUGHT FIVE EXTRA. DISTRIBUTED. MORALE: HIGH.)

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read it at <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s counter at 19:30, over the first of two bowls, while the rain worked the awning and the wok rang its flat bright note behind her. He did not smile where anyone could prove it.

Tonight he would find out who was blocking the deal and make them say yes before he moved on to the twenty-one hundred meeting. That was the whole of it. Everything else was noodles.

"You're eating slow," <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> said, setting down bowl two.

"I have an appointment at twenty-one hundred."

She stilled her ladle. "Twenty-one hundred?" she repeated, and it was not a question, and the flat bright note behind her stopped. "Somewhere they think is private."

He set down his chopsticks. He had not said where. He had not said with whom.

"You know who I'm meeting?"

"I know you don't dress like that for noodles money." She wiped her hands on the cloth at her waist, slow, the way a person buys time to decide how much to say. "And I know that if you put a name on their table tonight, you don't walk back out with a yes. You walk out having told them exactly what you found and how you found it. They'll close the door behind you and the money will move somewhere your logbook can't follow it." She let that sit. "The boy who followed the boss for two blocks — he signs his name to the log. You understand? You go in there loud, and every name under yours goes into a different ledger. Theirs."

The rain filled the space where his answer should have been.

She looked at him — the saya over his shoulder, the work coat, the particular stillness he carried into evenings with appointments — and put a fish ball in the second bowl that he had not ordered and would not be billed for.

"For the appointment," she said, and went back to the wok.

title: The Park Job
text:
She was waiting in the alley when he came down, hood up against a thin rain, her field kit at her feet and the big static wand slung across her back, a spool of splice line in one hand and a look of barely civilized excitement on her face.

"Before you say anything," she said — which was how she opened every negotiation she'd already won — "the contract says the engineer may attend. That's me. I'm the engineer. It said so in writing. I'm having the line framed."

"It's a job, not a gala."

"It's the first thing your spooky perfect client has asked for in eleven years of paper, and it said BRING THE SWORD, which means hardware, which means the engineer attends with the big wand." She shouldered the kit. "Also I checked the site. The park on <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-849c-7793-bce8-ae238e4576f6">Leavitt</entity> sits on the old <entity repo="corponation" guid="80a78887-98cf-4aa2-96fc-97c62a84fd21">Axiom</entity> trunk, and the carousel's been dead since before either of us could legally work. Whatever it wants down there, <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aafb-7b6b-bcbc-b8614f9d228f">samurai</entity> — it's not a pony ride."

He looked at her a second longer than the joke needed, then took the spool from her hand so she'd have one free.

He turned the spool over in his palm as he did it, and that was when the alley light caught the label. Not the deep-blue seal he'd checked out of the shop that morning. A stripped core — the cheap gray of comm-grade filament, no shielding rating on it at all.

"This isn't the line I signed for," he said.

"It's the line that was in the locker." She was already reaching for it, already fitting the answer together on her face and not liking the shape of it. "I pulled it myself. The blue spools were—" She stopped. "The blue spools were logged out. All four. This morning. Before I got there."

"Logged out to who?"

"Doesn't say." Her excitement had gone somewhere colder. "Which it always says. That's the whole point of the log."

So: no shielded splice line, a client who'd waited eleven years to name the hour, and someone ahead of them who'd already emptied the locker of the only cable that would survive whatever was live on the <entity repo="corponation" guid="80a78887-98cf-4aa2-96fc-97c62a84fd21">Axiom</entity> trunk. He weighed the useless gray spool and felt the job change under his hands from a gala she'd talked her way into to something that had been arranged around them both.

They took the long way, obviously.

The park on <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-849c-7793-bce8-ae238e4576f6">Leavitt</entity> was a half-block of stubborn green the towers had never gotten around to eating: six trees with character, a swing set doing its best, and at the center, under a shingled canopy gone soft with moss, the broken carousel.

It had been beautiful once. Twenty-four animals on tarnished brass poles — horses mid-leap, a rooster, one improbable lake sturgeon with a saddle — their paint faded to ghost colors, their glass eyes still patient. The deck boards had gone silver. The bulbs in the crown were dead sockets. <entity repo="motif" guid="019d6143-a8e2-727a-be75-32648e8aaa47">Rain</entity> came through the bad patches in the canopy and beaded on a palomino's flank, as if the horse had been running.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> walked the perimeter, counting exits and sightlines the way he always did, the way he'd done ten thousand times without a single one of them ever needing to be about anything but distance and angle. Two egress points. One sightline blocked by the dead ticket booth. Nothing here should be different from any other room he'd cleared.

Somewhere in the count, the addendum surfaced again — *the engineer is worth more than the wand* — and the counting didn't cover it. He had a protocol for exits. He didn't have one for a client that flagged her by name.

He found what the contract had brought a sword for without saying so. Under the carousel's deck, behind a maintenance skirt panel loosened recently — very recently — a hatch. Axiom-stamped. Padlocked by history, and under the history, humming. Faint. Alive. A junction the registry said had been dark for thirty years, sitting under a dead carousel, warm as a sleeping cat.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> was already on her knees at the skirt panel, the static wand set aside, a meter clipped to the hatch seam. She didn't look up.

"Sixty-cycle hum, stepped." She read the number off before she said anything else, the way she always did — machine first, everyone second. "That's not residual. Residual decays. This is fed." She traced the seam with a gloved finger, found the splice line's old terminus, dead-ended it against a coupling that had no business being warm. "Thirty years dark, my ass. Somebody's been paying this thing's electric bill the whole time."

"Client's addendum," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Wants you behind the sturgeon."

"It assigned me a fish." She said it flat, cataloguing, not offended — but she didn't argue either, which told him more than the words did. She dragged her kit six feet to the carved sturgeon's flank and set it down there instead, without being told twice. "This is the best client we've ever had."

At 21:00 the terminal chirped.

TASK ONE — SCOPE DETAIL.
A RECLAMATION CREW HAS BEEN CONTRACTED TO EXCAVATE THIS SITE TONIGHT.
THEIR WRIT SAYS COPPER. THEIR CLIENT WANTS WHAT THE COPPER CONNECTS.
HOLD THE JUNCTION UNTIL 21:40.
THE CREW ARE EMPLOYEES. THE MACHINES ARE INSURED.
FEE: STANDARD RATE. — ADDENDUM: THE ENGINEER IS WORTH MORE THAN THE WAND. CLIENT SUGGESTS SHE STAY BEHIND THE STURGEON.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> read it over his shoulder, twice.

"It did threat assessment on my behalf," she said, in the voice of a woman deciding whether to be offended or moved. "Before I even got here."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't answer that. He was still turning over the gray spool from the alley — no shielding rating, logged out ahead of them by someone the log wouldn't name — and the addendum sat next to it in his head like two pieces of the same lock. Whoever emptied that locker had known where they were going before they did.

Headlights swung off <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-849c-7793-bce8-ae238e4576f6">Leavitt</entity> at 21:04. A flatbed with a trencher rig riding it, a panel van behind, work lights bright enough to bill a full night against. Four shapes came off the flatbed already moving with the unhurried confidence of people who'd done this before and didn't expect to be stopped.

"<entity repo="material" guid="6e446bc9-bfd5-6d3e-0961-25f2766f486f">Copper</entity>," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said, reading the trencher's rig off its silhouette before the crew had crossed the grass. "Class III cutter, licensed. That's a real writ." Her voice didn't change register — same flat inventory she'd give a coupling seal. "Doesn't mean the client behind it is."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> put his hand on <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity>'s grip. The code in him wanted the announcement, the bow, the fair start — the same reflex that had cost him blood on jobs he should have walked away from clean. He held the itch down and watched the lead man's hands instead, the way they hadn't gone anywhere near a weapon, the way his eyes went straight to the hatch like he already knew exactly where it was.

The lead man crouched at the skirt panel — the one <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had just checked — and put his palm flat against it like he was greeting something.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> drew.

<entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> came out without a sound, the saya sliding open like a door, <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> a line of absolute dark that took the work lights and gave nothing back. He set it low and angled, point toward the deck, the position that said *not yet* and *don't* in the same breath, and he stepped between the lead man and the panel.

"Skirt's occupied," he said. "So's the hatch. Whatever your writ says is under it, you're not opening it tonight."

The lead man didn't stand up fast. He rose the slow way, palm still on the panel, taking his time so nobody could call it a flinch — and his eyes found the matte length of <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> and stayed there a beat longer than a man reads a stranger. Not fear. Recalibration. The look of someone matching a face to a brief he'd been handed and hadn't quite believed.

"Nineteen hundred seconds," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said from behind the sturgeon, not moving, her voice the same flat inventory she'd give a coupling seal. "Best clean estimate for that cutter to reach the seam. You've got less than that before somebody down there notices they're not alone."

The lead man took his hand off the panel and straightened the rest of the way, and behind him the other three came off the grass and spread, unhurried, into the spacing of people who did this for a living.

The crew was eight: a foreman with a writ-reader and the shoulders of a man who'd come up through the work; two chrome-heavy muscle whose job description was visible from across the park; a rig operator already bored, running diagnostics on the cutter head like the job was already routine; and four repo skitter-drones that came off the flatbed like patient six-legged luggage and stood in the rain, waiting for instructions.

The foreman saw <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> at the carousel's edge and did the professional thing. He stopped everyone with one hand and came ahead alone, holding the writ up like a small shield. He was broad through the shoulders, maybe forty, with the careful posture of a man whose knees had opinions.

"Evening," he said. "Cadre Reclamation. We've got paper for this site — legacy assets, scrap title, the works. Notarized. Crew's insured, Class III, the whole line item." He was already reading <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>: the saya, the stance, the absence of anywhere better to be. His eyes moved past <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> to the ticket booth and the tree line, counting exits the same way <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had counted them, and came back. "Site survey said unattended. Registry's been dark on this junction since '96."

"The survey's out of date by one."

"By one what, is the question." The foreman sighed the sigh of a man whose night had just grown a line item. "Look, friend. It's copper and dead glass down there. Whatever they're paying you to stand in the rain over a kiddie ride, it's not worth the —" his eyes made the trip, saya to hands to face, and this time they didn't come all the way back before something in his shoulders adjusted, the micro-correction of a man reweighting the math "— hold on. West Town. <entity repo="character" guid="019e9e4f-1ef6-7392-b652-d84720a6ceae">Noodle</entity> counter. You're the one from the file."

"People keep buying that file," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Somebody should tell them."

"Tell them what?"

"It's out of date by one."

The foreman looked at him for a long moment. The two muscle had stopped their unhurried drift toward position and were watching <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> now, really watching, the way people watch when the job upgrades from routine to something that wants attention. The rig operator had gone still. The foreman weighed eight men on paper against one man and a sword — a sword, which meant training that didn't show up on any corpo registry — and he didn't like how it came out. But a writ is a writ and a night rate is a night rate, and the count still said go. The client hadn't hired the first crew they'd called. They'd hired the crew you call after you already know who'll be standing in front of the hatch. So he made the call.

"<entity repo="character" guid="019e9e4f-1609-7865-95cc-1bd0d97d98d0">Rig</entity> up," he said, walking back. "Drones forward. And somebody get the freelancer's refusal ON RECORD, in case of arbitration."

"For the record," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said, drawing <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity>, "I refuse."

The drones came first. They were cheap, and that was the point.

Repo skitters — graspers, not guns, built to strip a site fast and testify politely afterward. Forty kilos of grabbing arms in a pack made its own argument, and these ran the carousel's layout like they'd been handed the blueprints. They had. Everyone had blueprints tonight.

What they didn't have was a map of where <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> would be.

The first came through the gap between two horses. <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> took its forelimb cluster off at the joint ring — machines got the whole edge, that was the rule, careful lines were for people — and it cartwheeled off the deck with nothing left to grab with. The second tried the low route under the sturgeon's belly and met the edge coming down through its sensor mast. It backed out from under the fish, blind now. The third and fourth came in together, flanking, herding him toward the carousel's open side, where the muscle waited. Good swarm logic. Not a bad plan, if the man swinging the sword had been anyone else.

He wasn't. He grabbed the brass pole of a ghost-painted stallion, swung his whole weight around it, and put both boots through skitter three's chassis. It went down folding the wrong way.

The itch was still there — the code wanting him to call it, to give the machines the same fair start he'd have owed a man. He didn't. Machines didn't get the announcement. That line at least still held clean.

Skitter four adjusted. Learned. Came in low and fast at his blind quarter while he was still recovering his stance from the kick.

"Sixty-cycle sync," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said, from behind the sturgeon, flat as a meter reading. "All four running one clock. Watch the gap — they hand off attention every four hundred milliseconds. Window's small."

"How small."

"Small enough you'll miss it if you're listening for my voice instead of counting."

He counted. Four hundred milliseconds sounded like nothing until you'd spent eleven years learning to live inside gaps that size. The fourth skitter's optics ticked toward its neighbor mid-stride — the handoff, the half-beat where its own eyes weren't the ones watching him — and <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> went through the seam in its formation exactly where the gap put it. The blade found the processing core through the access seam along its spine. It dropped standing up, then didn't.

<entity repo="motif" guid="019d6143-a8e2-727a-be75-32648e8aaa47">Rain</entity> kept coming. It beaded on the carousel horses like they were sweating. Somewhere behind him one of the chrome muscle had started moving, unhurried, the way men moved when they still believed the math favored them.

"Foreman's rig operator is reaching for something that isn't a control stick," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said. Same voice. No alarm in it, which was its own kind of alarm. "Ninety seconds until the cutter's warm enough to matter — vertical line of blue that'll take ferrocrete if it takes anything. You're not holding a junction anymore. You're holding a clock."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't answer. He was already moving toward the muscle, and the itch was back — the old reflex, the one that wanted him to call his shot before he took it, the fair warning that had cost him blood on jobs he should've walked from clean. He clamped it down again, the way he'd clamped it down on the skitters, and told himself it counted the same both times.

It didn't. He knew it didn't. He kept moving anyway.

The muscle came in around the flanks of the carousel, one from the left, one from the right, closing in. Chrome arms on the left one. Leg rig and a riot baton on the right. Both moved like men who'd cleared rooms for a living before the private sector found them. Behind them the trencher rig coughed awake on the flatbed, lowered itself to the grass on hydraulic feet, and started walking its blade toward the carousel deck. A manned rig — the operator sealed in the cab, running <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> by hand, the machine grinding forward on his say-so, the meter ticking either way.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> gave the muscle the carousel.

It was a good arena, and it was his — he'd had a full twenty minutes with it. A carousel is nothing but a forest of brass poles and frozen animals at fight height. Cover everywhere, already set.

The left one swung chrome at him through the gap between a mare and the rooster, and learned the gap was an inch and a half too narrow for a full extension. The arm rang off brass. The swing died. <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> opened a shallow line down his thigh, above the knee, well clear of anything that mattered — enough to sit a man down. He sat down between the horses, and had the sense to stay there.

The right one was better. He came up over the deck, baton live, using the rooster for cover the way <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had been. For six exchanges they played a fast, ugly game of tag through the standing herd — brass ringing, rain flying off every surface, the baton's charge crackling against the poles and once across <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s shoulder. The coat ate most of it. What got through burned a bright line down to his elbow. It cost. It always cost.

But the man's leg rig had an aftermarket governor, and those sit proud at the hip seam — you could always tell the ones who'd bought cheap, the box bolted external where a factory job would tuck it under the fascia. <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> found the seam on the next pass. The leg rig locked at full stride — a statue of a man mid-lunge, gloriously inconvenienced — and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> put him down onto the deck boards with a palm and gravity, almost gently, next to his colleague.

"Stay," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> suggested.

"Yeah," the man agreed, baton rolling away, rain on his face. He looked at his own frozen leg the way the other one was looking at his thigh — like the hardware had changed the terms without asking permission. "You know this thing hasn't spun in thirty years? I used to ride it. The fish. Before the leg, obviously."

"Everybody used to ride the fish," said <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s voice from behind the sturgeon, with feeling.

Which left the trencher.

The trencher was the problem the sword couldn't solve, and everyone in the park knew it. Eleven tons of articulated dig rig, blade spinning up, a sealed cab with no seams worth the name, walking toward the junction hatch at the pace of the inevitable. The operator had locked himself in. The foreman was shouting the kind of encouragement that means a bonus is riding on it.
