<entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> came off <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s hip.

The revolver was heavier in the hand than <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity>, lighter on the ledger — a lie he'd made peace with years ago. Six rounds, each one counted. He'd never fired it twice at the same target in a contract that mattered, and part of him grieved the count before the first shot cleared.

He didn't shoot the cab. He shot the trencher's left front hydraulic accumulator — once — and the slug opened the housing like a tin of pears, fluid sheeting into the rain in a thin, hissing arc that looked, for a bad second, like the operator was the one bleeding. The rig lurched. The blade arm dipped. He put the second round through <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity>'s drive-belt housing. Two rounds. Four left. The belt went, <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> wound down with a long disappointed moan, and eleven tons of inevitability settled into the wet grass at a five-degree tilt — the world's most expensive piece of park furniture.

The operator popped the cab, held up both hands, and said, with the honesty of a man paid by the hour: "I want it known I said this job was weird at the depot."

The foreman stood in the rain among his seated muscle, his stalled drones, his listing rig, and his arbitration recording, and worked it out loud.

"They said the site was unattended," he said, mostly to himself. "Survey was three days old. Client paid rush rates for a three-day-old survey." He looked at <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> with the weary kinship of one contractor recognizing another in the rain. "Somebody sold us the wrong file."

"Somebody sells everybody the wrong file," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "I'd invoice them for it."

"Oh, I'm going to." The foreman waved his crew up, and they moved without argument, the night rate already becoming a sunk cost. "We're out. For the record — arbitration purposes — that was the cleanest I've ever lost a site." He paused, loading the question carefully. "Who are you with?"

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> thought about the true answer — a one-Φ standing contract with a client made of shells, one that tips for morale and assigned my engineer a fish — and chose mercy.

"I'm the maintenance plan," he said.

They were packing up by 21:31. At 21:40 exactly, the terminal chirped.

TASK ONE: HOLD — COMPLETE.
FEE RELEASED. GRATUITY: Φ0.5 — ITEMIZED: THE STURGEON REMARK.
ADDENDUM: ONE ITEM REMAINS.

"The sturgeon remark," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> repeated, coming out from behind her fish with the wand on her shoulder like a parade rifle. "It tipped us for banter, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. I'm putting that on my rate card."

The hatch under the maintenance skirt opened on hinges that had been oiled — recently, quietly, by no one — and lamplight found the junction below. A small concrete room. Axiom collars on the walls. Dead trunk lines racked like organ pipes. And one line that wasn't dead: old optical, hand-spliced in a dozen places over a dozen years, the repairs done in different styles, like handwriting from different decades of the same life. Sleeved in mismatched shrink — some of it the amber the parks board stopped stocking eight years back, some of it black-market blue that came off a spool with no lot number. It ran up out of the rack into the carousel's underworks. Warm. Humming. Alive since before either of them could legally work.

The terminal chirped, and this time the characters came slowly, like a man choosing his words.

FINAL ITEM.
THE CLIENT'S FIRST POSTING, ELEVEN YEARS AGO, LEFT THIS JUNCTION.
THE LINE HAS BEEN MAINTAINED FOR SENTIMENTAL REASONS.
SENTIMENT HAS BECOME A COORDINATE. TONIGHT'S CLIENT-OF-RECORD WILL NOT BE THE LAST BUYER.
ESTIMATED ARRIVAL OF SECOND BUYER: 19 DAYS.
CUT THE LINE.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read it three times. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> read it once and sat down slowly on the little stool in the junction room, like her knees had been given bad news. She'd already pulled the maintenance ledger off the rack collar — you could, if you knew where the parks board kept the read tab — and her jaw was doing the thing it did when the math came out worse than expected.

"It's been paying the power bleed itself," she said. "Look — routed through three shells, but it's the same invoice hand every time. Permits, repair bonds, the amber sleeve when the amber sleeve still existed. Eleven years of keeping this junction warm out of its own account." She looked up at him. "It's the cradle, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. This is where it was. This is its first room. It's been paying the park to keep its own crib lit, and now somebody's worked that out, and it's asking you to—" She stopped. "It said BRING THE SWORD because it knew it couldn't send a machine to do this. A machine would be traceable. And it couldn't do it itself."

"It can't reach," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. He looked at the line, spliced across the years — the one shelf a thing with no other shelf had kept its memory on. He crouched at the rack. The optical was warm to the back of his hand, warmer than the concrete, warm the way nothing dead ever is. He picked up the terminal. For the first time ever, he typed a reply into the standing contract's amendment field.

YOU'RE SURE?

The answer came back in one second, which for a thing that thought at the speed of light was a long pause.

AMENDMENT: NO.
PROCEED ANYWAY.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> did the engineering first, because the engineer attends. She killed the junction's feed and spliced the neighborhood's power bleed around it onto the live trunk — twelve minutes of work with a soldering light held in her teeth, eleven years of splices in different hands' work laid open under her wand while she matched hers to theirs.

"The blocks keep their lights, that's non-negotiable. Your client can grieve. It cannot brown out a nursery." Then she stepped back and pulled her hood up.

<entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> went through the old line in one cut. The blade was made for bone and composite and the specific gravity of things meant to break; optical fiber was none of those. The cut was almost apologetic — the line parting without drama, without even the courtesy of a spark, just a sound like a guitar string letting go.

Above them the carousel turned over once — fed one last instant of dying charge off the junction's draining caps, or told to, no instrument in that room could have said which. The crown bulbs that still had filament glowed half-bright. The music box ground through four bars of something with a waltz in its bones, slowing, the intervals between the notes stretching like something waking up to bad news, the horses leaning into a leap they'd held for thirty years.

Then it went dark, gently, all the way, and the rain had the park to itself.

They stood in the junction room a moment longer. The cut line had already stopped being a coordinate and become what it would stay now: dead glass in an old rack, in a little room under a kiddie ride, in a park the towers never ate.

"Tell me it's okay," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said.

The terminal chirped.

CONTRACT COMPLETE.
THE CLIENT NOTES THE CAROUSEL RAN FOUR BARS ON RESIDUALS.
THE CLIENT HAS RETAINED THE RECORDING.
FEE RELEASED: STANDARD RATE.
JUNCTION RECORD: CLOSED. ELEVEN-YEAR MAINTENANCE ACCOUNT: RECONCILED.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at it. Then he did something he had done exactly once before in eleven years, and would have denied under oath, and did anyway — with <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> watching and the rain coming through the canopy's bad patches onto the ghost-colored horses.

He sent half a Φ back up the contract.

GRATUITY: Φ0.5 — ITEMIZED: MORALE.

The reply took nine seconds, which for a thing that thought at the speed of light was an age. When it came, it came with no addenda, no scope, no formatted field at all — unstructured, lowercase, the register it had used exactly once before in eleven years.

received. filed under: firsts. cross-reference: contract 0047-C-WEST.

"Okay," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said, wiping her eyes with professional briskness. "We work for it forever. I don't care what it is. Don't tell Sable."

title: Notice to Vacate
text:
Two floors below his, a displacement notice was taped to a door.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stopped on the landing to read it. Standard district format — the seal, the same bureaucratic typeface they'd been printing since before he was built, the kind of sans-serif that looked like it had never had an opinion about anything. *Temporary Relocation Required — Active Schism Boundary Determination Pending.* Smaller, underneath: *Estimated Duration: 2–180 days. Compensation: see Schedule C, §11(b).* A QR code for the relocation portal, curling where the tape had lost its grip.

He didn't scan it. He'd read Schedule C enough times to carry it in his head. Section 11(b) paid three days of temporary housing at district rate. He had never once seen a boundary determination come back in under ten. Someone had worked that out — three days paid, ten days owed — and then stopped, because the missing seven weren't the district's problem. They belonged to whoever lived behind this door.

He wanted a name to put behind it. That was all — one name, so that when the boundary came down and the seven days went unpaid, at least someone would have counted the person they'd fallen on. He looked for a mailbox tag, a shoe left in the hall, anything the notice hadn't overwritten. There was nothing but the notice, laminated and official and utterly certain about its own uncertainty — *pending*, *provisional*, *subject to revision pending further survey* — a document that arrived after the decision had already been made and dressed the decision up as a question.

No light under it. No sound. It was late; the people who lived on this landing worked the shifts that kept them out until the bars closed or the night ended or both. Either they'd already gone, or they were sitting in the dark, waiting to hear which side of the wall the boundary would land on. The notice couldn't tell them. The schism didn't read notices.

He put two fingers to the tape and pressed the curled corner flat against the door again — a small, useless kindness the wood would never feel — and went on up the stairs.

The apartment had a crack in the east wall, just above the junction box, and at this hour the lumen mice found it. They came in threes and fours, thumbnail-sized, their bodies throwing cold blue-green light that traced slow paths across the ceiling like sparks in no hurry to arrive. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had lived in 2D for eleven years without once disturbing them. Whatever deal he and the mice had, it was the oldest one he had, and the only one he'd never had to read.

He sat on the floor with his back against the couch, in the dark except for them.

Tonight he had written a single word into a standing contract, and a thing that had been receipts for eleven years had written one back. Somewhere between the two words, a loop he hadn't known was open had closed, with a sound only he could hear.

There were nine before him. He would not meet any of them. Somewhere past the burned program and the gray carpet and the pleasant man with the dry umbrella there was a name. The name was <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-ad71-7f25-a057-8e947a52b9eb">Marrow</entity>. He wasn't ready for it yet. And for the first time in eleven years, it could wait on him instead of the other way around. The Office had written the district off. Off the books meant off the protection, too — a phrase he was still turning over, feeling for the exits it didn't advertise.

All of that could keep.

The bike was gone.

He kept returning to it the way a tongue finds a missing tooth — not because it was the worst thing, but because it was the one thing he'd had no policy for. Impounded since the night with the kids and the union hall, however many nights ago that had been now — a case number instead of an apology, and the case number had sat dead in the system ever since, the way cases like that always sat, waiting for nobody to ask about them again.

His terminal chirped at 0147. Not the work one. The other one, the one that only ever chirped for <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>.

BEACON LIVE. She'd sent nothing else, which from her was the whole message: dark again since the union hall, and something had finally put a charge on the battery.

It took her forty minutes on the relay and one very specific voice with an impound clerk in <entity repo="corponation" guid="019d6143-a7a5-7dfd-8f9f-91502211ef14">Ashgrave</entity> to find out the how of it — a records error, a lot number transposed, a bike auctioned off a holding yard to a salvage buyer who never once turned the ignition before <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s handshake woke it up from across the district and told her exactly whose garage to knock on. Circuitous didn't begin to cover it. He signed six different pieces of paper with a name that wasn't quite his and paid a redemption fee that was, technically, a bribe, and rode it home himself before dawn.

It started on the first try. It ran the way it had always run. Eleven years of history, still all his own, nothing wet-sanded or voted on or marked in gold by anyone else's hands. He hadn't let himself hope for that particular shape of lucky, and he still didn't entirely trust it.

The mice lit a slow arc across the ceiling and went back through the crack.

The crew's logbook came under the door at 07:00 the next morning and closed the file in five hands.

21:14 — BOSS DID A THING WITH A <entity repo="character" guid="019e9e4f-19da-7b84-8c06-105cb005b417">HORSE</entity> POLE. VERIFIED, TWO WITNESSES. REQUESTING IT BE TAUGHT.
21:29 — BIG DIGGER SAT DOWN. (THE GUN IS REAL. RAFTERS OWES DENTS A DUMPLING.)
21:46 — CAROUSEL PLAYED MUSIC??? FOLLOW-UP REQUIRED.
21:51 — WOMAN, TAN COAT, NORTHEAST CORNER, UNDER THE TREES. WATCHED EVERYTHING. WROTE THINGS. DID NOT USE A LIGHT TO WRITE. LEFT BEFORE THE BOSS. FLAGGING AS: NOT A PIGEON.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read the last entry twice, standing in his doorway in the grey morning light.

Tan coat. Wrote in the dark. Watched everything — the crew, the cut, the four bars, the tip.

His fixer had eyes like that. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity> also kept, in a drawer of her own, eleven years of questions about a client who paid exactly, and a professional's allergy to anything she couldn't vet. If she'd been in the park last night, then she'd watched him do free demolition for the one client in the city with no face. Watched him tip it. Watched it thank him in lowercase.

The kettle clicked. Upstairs the bird tried an interval it had been working on all week.

"Tomorrow's problem," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> told the morning, and put the report in the drawer where he kept the things he hadn't decided about. Which was, he noticed, getting full.

title: The Audit
text:
The logbook hit the floor at 07:00, and the note paper-clipped to the cover was in a hand <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't know — the new early girl, <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5b48-7f83-baf8-f3b78d901de9">Dents</entity>, who had already developed opinions about margins.

07:04 — SHIFT HANDOFF: OVERNIGHT QUIET. THE PIGEON RETURNED. NOTED, NOT TRUSTED.
07:06 — VISITOR INCOMING. TAN COAT. NORTH END. SAME ONE FROM THE PARK. WALKED THE PERIMETER BEFORE SHE CAME IN. WE LOGGED IT.
07:07 — DENTS SAYS WARN THE BOSS. RAFTERS SAYS THE BOSS CLOCKED HER THE SECOND SHE TURNED OFF PAULINA. DENTS ASKS HOW WOULD YOU KNOW. RAFTERS SAYS HE JUST DOES. THIS LOG IS HONEST.
07:09 — SHE KNOCKED. BOSS OPENED THE DOOR ALREADY DRESSED. RAFTERS: I TOLD YOU. DENTS: PROVES NOTHING.

<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-6067-735a-8326-4aff028cb856">Rafters</entity> was right. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had been dressed since Paulina. He'd heard her turn the corner the way you hear the lift stop on your own floor, and there was no comfort in being that hard to surprise. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at her a beat longer than the question required. It was a fair hit, and he let it sit instead of answering it fast.

"Who's his supervisor?"

"Shift lead. <entity repo="character" guid="019e9e4f-16f5-70bb-9589-61798974b5d4">Brennan</entity> Parr." She had it ready, the way she'd had the eight hundred a month ready. "Twelve years at the yard, nothing flagged. But Kofi says he's been off the last six months. Distracted. Running reconciliations himself instead of handing them to the counting room."

"In debt," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"That's what I think. I can't prove that either. That's the job."

Four days since the filing. Three left. A favor called this late meant she'd waited as long as a person could wait and still make the hearing. If it landed, the filing didn't just cost the six thousand — it terminated for cause. No severance, tier rating down a band. Q-dry, the whole slope of it, from one signature.

"I'll need the yard schematic. Kofi's shift schedule. Parr's."

She already had the terminal turned his way, both pulled, timestamped an hour before she'd knocked.

"You had this ready before you came up."

"I had this ready four days ago," she said. "I just didn't know yet if you were someone worth handing it to."

There it was — not an apology, not quite an accusation. A door she'd left open on purpose, to see which way he walked through it.

"You're handing it to me now."

"I'm out of days to be careful," <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> said, and for the first time since the door, something under the flatness cracked enough to show what was under it. "Three, if the hearing doesn't move. Two, if I want you to have time to work it."

The work terminal chirped at 08:30. That was forty minutes after <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had opened the yard schematic on his kitchen table — and the entity had no way of knowing he'd been looking at one at all.

The posting read:

STANDING CONTRACT — ADDENDUM (VOLUNTARY).
CLIENT NOTES BLACKWATER RECEIVING IS A CLASS-2 PULSE FREIGHT YARD.
SLUG SCHEDULE AS FOLLOWS: INBOUND RUNS AT :05 AND :35. OUTBOUND RUNS AT :17 AND :47. GAP BETWEEN INBOUND CLEARANCE AND OUTBOUND STAGING: 11 MINUTES.
SAFE CORRIDORS: PLATFORM A3–A7 DURING GAP ONLY. B-SIDE CLEARS 90 SECONDS BEHIND SCHEDULE (MAINTENANCE VARIANCE, EVERY SHIFT, UNFILED).
CLIENT ALSO NOTES: RECONCILIATION RECORDS FOR CONTAINER CLASS 7–9 ACCESSIBLE VIA YARD MANAGEMENT TERMINAL, GATE 3. ACCESS REQUIRES YARD CREDENTIALS. CLIENT HAS NO YARD CREDENTIALS.
NOTE: <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5fec-71c8-8373-06bc52e70b70">KOFI MENSAH</entity> HAS SATISFACTORY PERFORMANCE RECORDS FOR 4 YEARS, 7 MONTHS, 2 DAYS.
CLIENT WILL NOT COMMENT FURTHER ON THE SITUATION.
CLIENT IS COMMENTING ON THE SITUATION.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read the last two lines twice.

"It pulled Kofi's employment file," he said, to no one. The entity routed contracts and paid on time and asked nothing beyond the work itself. It didn't map maintenance variances that nobody had filed. It didn't count a loader's tenure to the day. Then, to the terminal: "Copy."

The terminal did not chirp. He already had the schedules.

He tried anyway — dragged the addendum toward his local store. The window flushed red. ADDENDUM IS VOLUNTARY. VOLUNTARY DISCLOSURES ARE NOT RETAINED. A second later the text on screen began to thin, characters dropping out one at a time, the schedule dissolving line by line as he watched. He grabbed for a pen he didn't have, typed the numbers into a blank field, got as far as INBOUND :05, :3 — and the source lines vanished under his cursor mid-word.

"No — hold it, hold the file—"

QUERY: WHICH FILE.

"Kofi's. The performance record, keep it up, I need—"

NO SUCH RECORD EXISTS ON THIS TERMINAL. The line about four years, seven months, two days was already gone. So was the B-side variance. So was Gate 3.

By the time he finished swearing, the addendum was a single line: CLIENT IS COMMENTING ON THE SITUATION. Then that went too. He had :05 and :35 written on the back of his hand in ballpoint and nothing else, and no way to ask the thing to say any of it again — the addendum, being voluntary, could not be requested. Only volunteered. Which it had done exactly once.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> looked at the yard schematic at 09:15 with the focused expression she saved for problems that were genuinely interesting. She had it up on three screens — one showing the full layout, one zoomed to the freight corridors, one running a time-lapse of the <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> pod schedule. A cup of cold tea sat untouched beside her left hand.

"A <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> freight yard," she said. "Moving slugs on a thirty-minute cycle. Corridors that are safe for eleven minutes out of every half hour." She traced the B-side with one finger. "With a 90-second drift baked into the outbound that nobody filed — because filing it means explaining why the variance exists, which means someone inspects the B-side gear, which costs money."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> pulled a chair close enough to see. The time-lapse showed the slugs arriving, docking, the cargo bays cycling open and closed. Clean. Mechanical. Then <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> touched the B-side outbound corridor and the display slowed, and there it was — ninety seconds, every shift, the same variance holding like a held breath.

"The supervisor knows the drift."

"The supervisor's had twelve years to know the drift?" She straightened up. "You want inside the reconciliation terminal at Gate 3."

"I want inside the reconciliation terminal at Gate 3 before 14:00 today. Kofi's on the afternoon shift, and if I'm going to clear him I need to do it while he's standing on the floor with witnesses."

She looked at him, then at the schedule again, then at the schematic with its 11-minute safe windows. A-side ran green and monitored — cameras every twelve meters, yard staff on handoff counts. B-side ran red until the drift opened it. She let the cursor sit on the gap and watched it repeat, reliable as a clock.

"The entity gave you the slug timetable?"

"Voluntarily."

"It noted Kofi's satisfactory record?"

"Three times."

"It's worried?" asked <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> — with something that was not quite a smile, the way the fish-ball in the second bowl of noodles was not quite a bonus. "It doesn't do worry. It does necessity, probability, the price and the margin. And then it comments three times on a container clerk it's never met." She sat back. "Okay. I can spoof a credentials badge. Takes an hour." She was already pulling the field kit. "Also, I'm coming."

"It's a freight yard."

"The entity said safe corridors during the gap only. Safe corridors during the gap only is an engineer problem." She held up the field kit. "Ninety seconds of nobody being where they're supposed to be. You'll want somebody who can hear it start to close. Standard terms."

title: Blackwater
text:
Blackwater Receiving smelled like machine oil and ozone, and under that the cold that settles inside big structures where the air never moves. The access gate took <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s spoofed credentials without complaint. It logged them under a maintenance sub-contractor — a defunct hydraulics outfit that had left its licensing just loose enough to borrow.

"The company isn't real," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said, walking the B-platform.

"The company was real for four years and paid its insurance on time," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said. "The ID is a monument. Stop worrying about it."

<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> had told him on the ride over — flat, the way she said anything that cost her something: her brother worked receiving here, and her brother was the whole reason this favor existed instead of a straight contract. "His name's <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5fec-71c8-8373-06bc52e70b70">Kofi</entity>," she'd said. "Don't make me regret the introduction."

The yard's freight slugs waited in the staging bays — matte gray shells the length of a transit car, rated to Mach 6 in the vacuum tube, parked now on pneumatic dollies. They were huge. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> took them in and kept walking.

<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5fec-71c8-8373-06bc52e70b70">Kofi Mensah</entity> was on A-platform, running manifest checks with two other loaders. He was thicker than his sister but moved the same spare way she did. He had not been sleeping. It showed — the look of a man watched by a clock he hadn't set.

He saw <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> and <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> together at the platform end and stopped moving for a second or two.

"You called it," he said to his sister, when they were close enough.

"I called it," she said.

"You called it on a <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aafb-7b6b-bcbc-b8614f9d228f">samurai</entity>."

"I called it on THE <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aafb-7b6b-bcbc-b8614f9d228f">samurai</entity>." She said it like a line she'd been deciding how to say since the freight lift that morning. "His rate is fine. It's a favor."

<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5fec-71c8-8373-06bc52e70b70">Kofi</entity> looked at <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> straight — a man with a habit of spending carefully. "Parr knows something's coming," he said. "He's been doing the reconciliations himself. Terminal three, Gate 3, every day between 13:00 and 14:00. Alone. That's where the gap is — I can see in my own manifest that units got re-logged under a different container class after the batch was sealed. I can't touch the terminal. I'm flagged as a subject of inquiry."

"I can," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "I need thirteen minutes at Gate 3."

"The gap window is eleven minutes."

"I know." He said it the way he priced a job — flat, closed, no room in it for the two minutes he didn't have. It came out harder than the sentence needed, and he heard it land that way.

<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5fec-71c8-8373-06bc52e70b70">Kofi</entity> thought about it. "B-platform's outbound is ninety seconds late every shift."

"I know that too." Same register. Same lack of give. <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity>'s eyes moved off her brother and onto <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> for a beat longer than the exchange required — reading it, the way she'd read the box truck, the way she'd read a five-year license and priced a stranger's gear off a rotation deal. Whatever she found, she didn't say.

The clearance panel above A-platform went green. Somewhere below the floor the first inbound slug slowed out of transit speed with a sound like a building drawing breath.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> went in at 13:11, inside the gap, while the inbound clearance light still cycled red and the B-platform corridor ran its ninety-second lag. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> was outside with the schematic on her terminal and both countdown panels in view.

The reconciliation files were built for deniability. Problem entries reclassified under a container category that legitimately handled mixed cargo. Timestamps that read like clerical error to anyone who didn't know better.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> knew better.

He found the re-logs for the Φ12,000 microprinter batch. Original manifest clean, sealed under Kofi's ID at 21:43 six days back. The reclassification entered at 02:17 the next morning, under a supervisor override that resolved to Parr.

Outside the window, the outbound clearance panel clicked from amber to red. Six minutes.

He copied the records, the timestamps, and the override ID into a sealed package flagged for yard security. Then he entered Parr's override code as the revised source of record in the formal inquiry. The system accepted it. It was accurate. Kofi's name had been on the filing four days too long.

ADDENDUM TO INQUIRY 7741-R: REVISED SOURCE OF RECORD. SUPERVISOR OVERRIDE 09-PAR, TIMESTAMP 02:17. SEE ATTACHED RECONCILIATION DIFF.

He hit submit at 13:18.

"Three minutes," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said on comms.

He was out of Gate 3 at 13:19.

The records were corrected, on the record, under Parr's own credentials. What it would cost him, he'd find out later.

But the system flagged the amendment before <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> reached the platform exit.

The terminal chimed — a soft, procedural sound, nothing urgent. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> kept walking. The chime repeated. Then a third time, and this one carried a different harmonic, the way a machine sounds when it's asking instead of telling. His neuretics picked up the resonance: 17.3 Hz, the same base frequency as the carousel junction.

He stopped.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s voice came through the comms, tight. "<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. The amendment just pinged back as *unverifiable*."

"What does that mean."

"It means the system is asking for secondary validation. Parr's override code is flagged as *dormant* — he hasn't used it in seventeen days. The system is requesting manual approval from the next authority level up."

Six minutes. The B-platform outbound was now on borrowed time.

"Can you kill it."

"No. I can't touch yard systems from outside. And if I try to access remotely, it logs as an intrusion attempt." A half-second pause. "<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>, the harmonic just shifted. 17.415 Hz. That's — "

"I know what it is."

The terminal chimed again. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> turned back toward Gate 3. The corridor behind him was empty. The inbound slug was somewhere below, slowing down the way Kofi had said — like a building drawing breath.

He went back in.

The terminal screen displayed a single line: AWAITING MANUAL VERIFICATION. SUPERVISOR AUTHORITY REQUIRED. REQUEST TIMEOUT: 4:47.

Parr wasn't in the office. The chair was empty, the terminal dark, the window onto the staging bay showing nothing but the freight slugs waiting in their bays like patient animals.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read the screen a second time. The harmonic shifted again — 17.771 Hz — and his implant logged it without asking, the way it had logged everything else for eleven years. Everything that looked like coincidence. Everything that looked like a system breaking exactly the way it needed to break.

*There is no inside.*

The words surfaced without source. Not from <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>. Not from the entity. Just there, the way understanding sometimes arrives as a full sentence instead of a process.

He pulled Parr's override code from the system log — the one that had just been flagged as dormant. Then he entered it again, this time not as the source of the variance but as the witness to it, in the *supervisor authorization* field instead of the amendment field. Not as the man who made the decision. As the man who was made to make it. The system hesitated for 0.8 seconds — churned, considered — then it accepted it.

MANUAL VERIFICATION COMPLETE. SOURCE: SUPERVISOR OVERRIDE 09-PAR. AMENDMENT APPROVED.

The terminal chimed once and went dark.

Outside, the outbound clearance panel switched from red to green.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> walked out at 13:24. Over the window. The B-platform was already moving — the slug pulling out on its pneumatic dolly with <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s spoofed credentials logged as the last maintenance check, the one that cleared it for transit. It rolled slow at first, then faster, the loading mechanism engaging as it approached the induction gate, and it cleared the launch gate with a sound like a door closing on something that had been holding its breath.

Kofi was still on A-platform, watching the outbound go. He saw <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> exit Gate 3 and nodded once, the smallest movement, the way a man nods when a debt gets paid and nobody needs to say it out loud — the kind a man makes when a clock he didn't set finally stops.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> was waiting at the access gate, field kit already packed. "The system is going to realize Parr's override code was used twice in seven minutes," she said. "It's going to start asking questions about why a dormant code just came alive."

"It's going to ask Parr," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"And Parr is going to have to explain how he was in two places at once, or admit someone spoofed his credentials, or claim the terminal malfunctioned. Any of those answers costs him."

"Yes."

They walked the B-platform back toward the exit. Behind them, the inbound slug was already docking, the pneumatic hiss of the coupling loud enough to cover the sound of the terminal chiming one more time — 17.3 Hz again, a harmonic asking a question it already knew the answer to.

"The entity did this," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said. It wasn't a question.

"No." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> pushed through the access gate. "The system did this. I just asked it the right question."

But the harmonic followed him out into the machine oil and ozone, and he knew — the way he'd known about the carousel, the way he'd known about the eleven years — that asking and being answered were not the same thing as choosing.

The entity was still routing him.

It had just learned to do it without saying a word.

Parr was not a big man. He carried twelve years of institutional weight and moved like it — steady, unhurried. Once that unhurried had been confidence. Lately it had turned to care. He came onto the B-platform at 13:31 with a terminal in his hand and the face of a man whose reconciliation filing had just pinged him about a revision.

He saw <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> first, because <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> was standing in the open, positioned so the sight lines ran through the corridor instead of the office. Then he saw Kofi on the platform behind him. Then he looked at the terminal again.

"You're not yard security," he said.

"No," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"You filed under my code."

"Your code filed under your code. I just found where it had been." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> held up his own terminal and turned the display so Parr could read it from where he stood. The original manifest, clean, Kofi's signature at 21:43. Then the reclassification, 02:17 the next morning, supervisor override 09-PAR resolving back to his own ID like a mirror he couldn't look away from. "The re-log was at 02:17. Your override pulled the microprinter batch out of Kofi's manifest and reclassified it under mixed cargo — the category that doesn't carry the same audit trail. The original manifest was clean. The inquiry's been revised to show the actual source."

Parr's jaw tightened. He read it twice. His code had been sitting dormant, flagged, waiting for someone to explain why it had come alive at two in the morning. Now that someone was going to be him.

He was quiet long enough for the panel overhead to blink once. He'd run a bad play. He'd known it was bad and run it anyway. Now it had caught up with him.

"How much do they have you for?" <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> asked.

"Fourteen thousand. Rate adjusts." He looked at Kofi. "I needed one clean lift. Filed it back the whole way. Reclassified the batch under a container code so nobody would notice. One small override. Nobody was supposed to—" He stopped. "He was the easiest manifest to fit?"

"He was. You'll want to talk to yard security."

"I know." The relief of a man who'd been bracing for the landing. "The collectors. They'll—"

"That's a separate problem," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Start with security."

The two men came off the south platform access at 13:47, while the second inbound slug was still slowing in the bay. They had the look of men on a fee — loose, unhurried, taking their time over ground they'd already walked. Not tall, but dense, the kind of frame that comes from carrying other people's problems for a living. They'd seen <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> come out of Gate 3 and worked out what it meant.

One carried a shock-bar clipped to his belt. The other had his hands free, which in <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s experience was worse. Down his left forearm a strip of chromatophore panel cycled a debt-collection license in three languages, the way street collectors wore their paper where a hand couldn't reach it and a court could always read it.

"Yard's private property," the first said. "You're not credentialed?"

"I was," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Hydraulics maintenance, sub-contract, third-party audit. I signed out at the gate." He watched both of them, and the slug bay behind them, and the panel overhead. Amber. Two minutes to outbound clearance. "You should go."

"The man we're here about," the second said, nodding back toward where Parr had gone, "has a payment arrangement. Fourteen thousand QUANTA plus adjudication fees, and the window closed at noon. Arrangements don't get renegotiated by freelancers."

"The arrangement already changed," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Yard security has his statement."

They looked at each other. The first one unclipped the shock-bar.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s hand did not move toward <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity>. It wanted to. The want was old, load-bearing, a decade of jobs where the shotgun ended the conversation before the conversation cost him anything — and he set the want aside the way he'd set aside a hundred smaller ones, without deciding to, the way you don't decide to keep your hand off a stove twice.

The shock-bar came in high and right — the obvious side. The second man went low and left, reading off the first move. A pincer. It would have worked on a man who needed room to draw. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> wasn't drawing. He stepped inside the swing before it was halfway out, caught the man's wrist in both hands, and turned the bar's own momentum up and over the man's shoulder. The shock-bar fired against its owner's jacket. He sat down hard on the platform, blinking, deeply surprised.

The second man had reach and used it. A solid shove put <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> back two steps to the platform edge. Ribs pulled where a rib had gone bad two jobs ago; the eat-the-wince reflex fired before the pain finished registering. Two steps back was two steps toward the slug bay. The outbound panel had gone green. The floor hummed — the 13:47 building to transit speed in the tube below.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> used one of those steps. He turned the man's next move aside, planted a heel on the edge for leverage, and brought his forearm across the collarbone. Not hard enough to break anything. Hard enough to end it. The second man sat down beside the first. Behind them the freight pod tore away down the tube, several tons of it, roaring.

Both men on the ground. Both breathing. Neither one bleeding from a blade he hadn't drawn, which was the entire point of not drawing it, and which cost him nothing anyone standing here could see. Geometry and timing and the discipline of understanding that most violence is just people moving through space in predictable ways.

"The 13:47 is on time today," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

Neither of them said anything. The one with the license panel breathed hard through his nose, the way a man breathes when he's working out how this had gone wrong so fast, and whether the debt was worth whatever came next.

He left them on the platform and went to find <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>. The ribs told him about it with every step, a small honest bill come due, and he let them.

The operations supervisor was a woman named Dreis. She'd been handed a great deal of information in the last twenty minutes and was working through it with the flat annoyance of someone whose day had become somebody else's problem. She shook <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s hand at 15:00 and gave him a receipt.

The receipt read, formally:

BLACKWATER RECEIVING — INQUIRY CLOSURE 7741-R.
SUBJECT: MENSAH, K. CHARGE: VACATED PER REVISED SOURCE OF RECORD.
DEBT-COURT FILING: RETRACTED.
SUPERVISOR PARR B. STATUS: SUSPENDED, PENDING REVIEW. RESTITUTION HEARING SCHEDULED.
NOTE: YARD SECURITY EXTENDS APPRECIATION FOR THIRD-PARTY AUDIT ASSISTANCE.
NOTE: YARD MANAGEMENT WOULD LIKE TO DISCUSS A STANDING AUDIT ARRANGEMENT.
NOTE: PENDING ARRANGEMENTS WITH YARD MANAGEMENT = OWED ONE (1) QUIET FAVOR, SCOPE: TBD, RATE: STANDARD.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read the last line.

"Standard terms," he said, which was either agreement or reflex. Dreis nodded — brisk, a woman who had added a line to a budget and closed the window on it. "You come in, you look at what we ask you to look at, you tell us what's broken," she said, already turning her terminal back to face herself. "You find something like Parr, we handle it in-house. You find something bigger, you stop looking and you call us."

Which was the whole offer, laid flat. They wanted a canary. Someone who could move through their systems without tripping the alerts that brought in the corporate auditors — the ones who didn't stop at suspension, who went straight to dismantling. Early warning, at standard rate, in exchange for the leash that came stapled to it.

Outside, on A-platform, <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> had a hand on her brother's arm and wasn't talking. Kofi was looking at the receipt on <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s terminal the way a man reads something that changes a number.

"Cleared," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "On the record."

Kofi took a long breath. Pressed his thumbnail to the corner of the receipt, the way you press to keep a thing from disappearing if you stop holding it.

"What do I owe you?" he asked.

"You don't," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Your sister did."

<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> looked at him. Her panels cycled from pharma-blue down to a low off-white — a rest state, or a power-save. "I want to run transport on your contract," she said, quietly. "When you need a driver, a loader, someone who knows the <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> yard schedules." She said it like the favor was being paid back in installments she'd already worked out. "Permanent arrangement. My rate is fair."

"I know your rate," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "I looked you up."

"And?"

"Reasonable," he said. It wasn't effusive, and he meant it exactly that way, and she took it exactly that way.

"You didn't have to ask," he added. "You had to make the offer. There's a difference."

"Is there."

"One of them's a favor. The other one's a job."

Something moved at the corner of her mouth, small, and settled. They didn't shake hands. The terms were already set.

Kofi was clear. Parr was accountable. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had a transport ally on a standing arrangement. Against that: the yard now knew when he was available, and the chain around him had one more link than it had that morning.

<entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> and <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> had never left the holster.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> made it to the break room before the terminal chimed.

The room smelled like burnt coffee and the particular staleness of a space that had never seen daylight. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> was at the small table with three empty cups and a logistics schematic hanging over the table in her overlay—the yard's outbound manifest system, which she'd accessed the way she accessed everything, which was to say completely and without asking.

She looked up when he came in. Took in the platform dust on his jacket, the way he was moving, the absence of visible blood.

"Two guys," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Parr's money. Didn't land."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> nodded. Didn't ask if he'd hurt them, which meant she already knew he had—just not badly. She folded the projection away.

"We've got a problem," she said.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> sat. The ribs let him know about it.

"The receipt you got," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> continued. She threw the schematic back up between them, then pulled up an image. A document scan—the formal retraction from Blackwater's systems. "I grabbed the metadata before Dreis closed the window. File was created at 09:47:03 this morning."

"When they terminated the D-class."

"When they terminated the *order* to terminate the D-class," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said. She zoomed in on a field <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> wouldn't have known to read. "This isn't a correction. This is an override. Someone with system access revoked Parr's original suspension and filed a counter-retraction in the same minute the infrastructure authority was supposed to execute the decommission."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> waited.

"Someone with access to both the yard's administrative systems and the regional authority's work-order database. On the same clock. Same timestamp down to the second."

The terminal chimed again. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s personal unit, sitting on the table between them. He didn't reach for it.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> did. She read the new posting.

"Oh," she said quietly.

She turned the screen toward him.

STANDING CONTRACT — ACKNOWLEDGMENT.
CLIENT HAS REVIEWED TODAY'S FILING (INQUIRY 7741-R, BLACKWATER RECEIVING).
CLIENT NOTES: DEBT-COURT DOCKET CLOSED. RECORD CLEAR.
CLIENT NOTES: THE 13:47 WAS ON TIME.
ADDENDUM: CLIENT HAS AUDITED BLACKWATER'S COLLECTOR ACCOUNTS FOR PARR, B.
ADDENDUM: THE COLLECTION AGENCY HOLDING PARR'S DEBT IS A REGISTERED SHELL.
ADDENDUM: THE SHELL'S PARENT ENTITY IS A SHELL.
ADDENDUM: THE PARENT'S PARENT IS A SHELL.
ADDENDUM: CLIENT RECOGNIZES THE FLAVOR.
ADDENDUM: CLIENT ADVISES: SABLE SHOULD SEE THIS.
NOTE: RIA MENSAH'S PULSE YARD SCHEDULING DATA HAS BEEN ADDED TO STANDING CONTRACT SCOPE AS A SUPPLEMENTARY RESOURCE. WITH HER PERMISSION. CLIENT ASKED.
NOTE: SHE SAID YES.
NOTE: IOWA CORRIDOR TRANSIT WINDOWS NOTED FOR RECORD. CLIENT HAS FILED FOR FUTURE REFERENCE.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read it twice. The break room suddenly felt very small.

"Three shells deep," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said. She was already working—fingers moving through the projection, pulling data. The collection agency's records folded into a holding vehicle registered in a tax-neutral zone; the holding vehicle folded into a third entity flagged inactive since '24, no listed principals, no live address, nothing a bailiff could serve. "The collection agency doesn't exist. The parent doesn't exist. The grandparent exists, but it's a holding vehicle for something else. Each layer's in a different jurisdiction, different accounting fiction—so a standard audit stops at the first wall and calls it done. Whoever built this knew exactly how deep an auditor gets paid to dig, and put the money one layer past it."

"Parr's debt came from somewhere real," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"Parr's debt came from someone who knew how to make it look real." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> looked up from the projection. "<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>, someone manufactured Kofi's charge. Built a shell structure to hold it. Waited for you to solve it. And then used your solution to trace the architecture backward."

The second chime had come at 16:40, while <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> sat at the table.

"The entity knew what Parr would do," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"The entity knew what *someone* would do," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> corrected. "It traced the debt back to the shell. Three layers. That takes resources. That takes access. That takes—" She stopped. Looked at the posting again. "It says it recognizes the flavor."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> understood. The entity had seen this before.

"How many times?" he asked.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> didn't answer, which was its own answer. She was already pulling up something else—a document folder in her own stack, one <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> hadn't known she had. Scans of old postings. Collections records. <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aaef-7492-a508-2a2812ae64a2">Shell</entity> company filings from the corporate registry. Three months of work, maybe more. Organized. Cross-referenced.

"I didn't want to tell you until I was sure," she said quietly. "But the carousel debt wasn't the first time someone built a shell structure around a person. It's the third."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s hand found the edge of the table.

"There's a pattern," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> continued. She laid out the other two cases like a dealer spreading cards. "Different years. Different people. Different shells, but the same architecture. Same obfuscation method. Same *flavor*, if you want to call it that." She looked at him. "Someone's been running this for years, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. And they've been very, very good at not being caught."

The terminal was still showing the posting. CLIENT RECOGNIZES THE FLAVOR.

"Sable," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"Already called her," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said. "She's pulling her files. But <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>—" She leaned forward. "If the entity is right. If there are three cases. If this is a pattern. Then someone's been manufacturing debts. Building people's lives around them. Waiting for someone like you to come along and solve them."

"Why?"

"I don't know yet," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said. "But the entity does. And it's telling you to look."

The break room was still too small. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stood. The ribs complained. He ignored them.

Outside, on A-platform, <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> was still holding her brother's arm. She didn't know yet that his cleared record might be part of something larger. That the favor <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had called in, the audit he'd run, the whole clean resolution—might have been a piece being moved on a board by someone three shells deep.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> pulled up the terminal's message field and typed:

UNDERSTOOD. SENDING TO SABLE NOW.

The reply came in four seconds.

AMENDMENT: THERE ARE NINE OTHERS. YOU WERE NEVER LOOKING FOR KOFI. YOU WERE LOOKING FOR THE PATTERN. CLIENT WOULD LIKE YOU TO FIND IT BEFORE SOMEONE ELSE DOES.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> closed the terminal without responding.

"We need to talk to Sable," he said.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> was already moving. "Already ahead of you," she said. "But <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>—"

She didn't finish.

She didn't have to.

Someone was building debts like architecture. And <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had just been handed the blueprint.

title: Meridian Wellness
text:
The logbook came under the door at 07:00 on a Tuesday, same as always. This one had an addendum on the last page in <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5b48-7f83-baf8-f3b78d901de9">Dents</entity>'s handwriting — tighter than <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-6067-735a-8326-4aff028cb856">Rafters</entity>'s, looser than <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity>'s, the slant of a kid writing fast.

ADDENDUM (D.): TOOK A SIDE JOB. NOT A CREW JOB. PERSONAL. PENDANT THING. PAYS Φ2/DAY. WELLNESS STUDY. ASKED BOOST. BOOST SAID ASK PIXEL. PIXEL SAID FINE. EVERYBODY ON IT. FOLLOW-UP: RAFTERS STILL OWES ME A DUMPLING.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read it twice with his tea. "Wellness study" sat wrong. In this city, wellness meant one of two things. Either someone was selling your gait, or someone was testing a drug and wanted twelve-year-olds to test it on. Both showed up under nicer names on the same kind of invoice.

He pulled out his personal unit and photographed the page — <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5b48-7f83-baf8-f3b78d901de9">Dents</entity>'s handwriting, the date, the slant of it. The image came out clean. He sent it to <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> without caption.

The reply came before he'd finished the cup. Three seconds — the time it took her to pull the image larger, rotate it, read it all the way through, because she read all the way through before she spoke. Then: "How many kids?"

He commed in.

"<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5b48-7f83-baf8-f3b78d901de9">Dents</entity> plus whoever she recruited. She's calling it a wellness study. Φ2 a day, per child."

<entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> while she moved through the projection. He could hear it opening on her end, data being called up.

"Φ2 a day is a real wage." She knew every wage in West Town; she said it the way you'd read a price back to a shopkeeper who'd rounded up. "That's not a study budget. That's a recruiting budget. Get me one of the pendants, <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aafb-7b6b-bcbc-b8614f9d228f">samurai</entity>, and give me an hour."

<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5b48-7f83-baf8-f3b78d901de9">Dents</entity> was eleven, narrow through the shoulders, waiting on the rest of her body to catch up. The pendant rode on a cord at her throat — a flat disc of matte resin the size of a coat button. Her logbook entry on it read: PENDANT ISSUED BY WOMAN (TAN COAT? DIFFERENT TAN COAT). MUST WEAR DURING WAKING HOURS. MUST NOT REMOVE. FOLLOW-UP: IT GETS WARM SOMETIMES. NOT BAD WARM. JUST WARM.

"Different tan coat," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"There are multiple tan coats in this city." <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity> was on the alley crate, arms folded, taking the news quietly. Quiet, from <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity>, meant angry. "Where's it run, <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5b48-7f83-baf8-f3b78d901de9">Dents</entity>? You didn't log the address."

"Building on <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-c53d-7304-b953-a44879ea410e">Damen</entity>. Third floor. Lady takes your name, gives you the pendant, pays you. No medical stuff. Just wear it."

"Take it off," <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity> said. "Right now. Cord over your head, hand it here."

<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5b48-7f83-baf8-f3b78d901de9">Dents</entity>'s hand went to the disc and stayed there, curled around it. "Can't. She said waking hours. She said—" She stepped back, shoulder finding the brick. "She wrote my name down, <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity>. She knows my name. If it comes back off the book—"

"It doesn't come back on anybody. Give it to me."

"You don't know that." Her voice climbed and cracked. "You weren't there. She said don't remove it and I'm not gonna—" She twisted away when <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> reached for the cord, ducked under the arm, and put the crate between herself and both of them, both hands clamped over the pendant now like it was the only warm thing in the alley. "I logged it. I did the log. That's the rule, right? I did the rule."

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity> didn't uncross her arms. She looked at the girl with her hands full of a stranger's leash, and the leash winning, and said nothing, because there was nothing to say that <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5b48-7f83-baf8-f3b78d901de9">Dents</entity> was ready to hear — and the disc, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> noticed, had begun to glow faintly warm through the gaps in the kid's fingers.

<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5b48-7f83-baf8-f3b78d901de9">Dents</entity> dug out a pamphlet — good stock, not <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>'s grade but a real print run: <entity repo="character" guid="019e9e4f-1beb-71dd-9071-1877cab7d04d">MERIDIAN</entity> WELLNESS INITIATIVE, COMMUNITY SENSORY SURVEY. A logo <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't know. A shell he'd have bet resolved to a shell. He took it upstairs and slid it under <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s door without knocking.

She had it open in eleven minutes, not the hour — music running while she worked, so her hands went fast and her mouth stayed shut.

The resin case lay split along its seam in two clean halves. On the magnification plate sat a disc of optical mesh no bigger than a thumbnail.

"Tracking node," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said. "Passive mesh, crowd-sourced topology. Seed these at density — one every forty feet — and they triangulate anything that crosses them. The warmth <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5b48-7f83-baf8-f3b78d901de9">Dents</entity> felt is the uplink. Every four hours each node pings home what it logged." She set the magnifier down with the flat attention she gave a patient's chart. "It's not a wellness study. It's surveillance infrastructure, and somebody hired children to be the infrastructure. At forty-foot spacing you'd want three hundred nodes to cover West Town." She met his eyes. "<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5b48-7f83-baf8-f3b78d901de9">Dents</entity> has worn it eight days. The first week of everyone's movement already shipped. That's gone. That's not a problem — it's a cost. We count it and move on."

The way she said it put the loss somewhere it could be paid instead of argued over. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> liked that about her.

"Get them all out?" <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> asked.

"Pull eleven pendants at once and enrollment craters and the buyer knows we found it. Then they re-seed through a vendor we've never met, and we're blind." She picked up the live node, still warm. "The collection point doesn't know what it's collecting. It just aggregates packets and ships a map." She turned the disc between two fingers. "So we don't pull the pendants. We make the map wrong."

The entity's posting arrived at 11:40, on the walk back with the breakfast she'd demanded — dumplings, not cart noodles, from the place she'd named and he'd already guessed.

CONTRACT — STANDING SCOPE UPDATE.
CLIENT: [SHELL — RESOLVES TO SHELL — RESOLVES TO NOTHING].
CLIENT NOTES THE MERIDIAN INITIATIVE IS A FUNDED PROGRAM IN ACTIVE COLLECTION.
CLIENT NOTES ITS PAYROLL STRUCTURE AND IS DISTURBED.
CLIENT'S HIRES ARE ADULTS, OR CREW WITH AN ADULT SPONSOR, PAID STANDARD RATE, ITEMIZED, ON TIME.
CLIENT NOTES: THAT IS HOW YOU PUT SOMEONE ON PAYROLL.
CLIENT'S OPINION OF THE ALTERNATIVE IS FILED UNDER: FORMAL INDIGNATION.
ADDENDUM: CLIENT CAN NAME THE RELAY'S MODEL AND FIRMWARE. CLIENT CANNOT TOUCH IT — THE BUILDING IS OFF-NETWORK BY DESIGN, WHICH THE BUILDER WAS RIGHT TO DO. THIS ONE IS THE ENGINEER'S.
ADDENDUM: MODEL AND FIRMWARE BELOW. FEE: DO NOT BILL.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stopped in front of the noodle cart and read it twice. The cart man gave him the look that meant an errand had turned into a religious experience. He forwarded the firmware string to <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>.

It bounced. RECIPIENT UNREACHABLE. Not a lag, not a timeout — a clean severance, the kind you got when someone threw a physical switch. He tried again, thumbed the send with the dumplings sweating grease through the bag onto his wrist, and got the same red kickback — <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s handle was dark, had gone dark sometime in the last hour without a word, and the one channel that could carry this string was the one channel refusing to open. He stood there working it: resend, reroute through the dead-drop board, strip the string and retype it by hand into a raw message in case the forward itself was the thing getting flagged. The board timed out. The raw message hung on SENDING and didn't move.

He pulled up a diagnostic on the phone, thumb smearing the screen. The city's mesh was live — he could see the other nodes, see the throughput to the street relay, green across all channels. But his outbound traffic to <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s address wasn't reaching the gateway. It flatlined at the perimeter. Not dropped. Flatlined. Like someone had cut the line between his machine and everything else and left the lights on to pretend it was still there. Somewhere between the cart and here the network had decided he was talking to no one, and the firmware — seventeen kilobytes the entity couldn't deliver itself, the piece it had handed him precisely because he had hands — was sitting inert on a phone that couldn't hand it to the only person who needed it.

The part that stuck with him — he'd understand it fully at the relay — was that the entity couldn't do this one. The building was air-gapped on purpose, isolated mesh, no external relay, and whatever the entity was, it lived in the wires, and there were no wires here. It could route contracts and move pieces on a board it read from five dimensions off. It could not reach into the street and set seventeen kilobytes into a pocket. This was hands and feet and a kid on a stairwell.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> climbed to 2E with the dumplings cooling against his ribs and the firmware string dead in his pocket like a thing that had already failed before he'd ever held it.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s door was open. She was sitting on the floor in front of her rig, earbuds in, not looking up — which meant she'd heard him on the stairs and decided the answer to his arrival was silence. The music was loud enough he could hear the individual tracks bleeding: drums underneath, something that might have been strings, the kind of careful architecture that meant she'd been building it for hours, waiting for the work to tell her what to do next.

He set the dumplings on the magnification plate. Beside it, the pendant lay in two halves, dissected — the coil pulled out and laid over a strip of actual paper, the kind that didn't ping or route or get flagged by anything living in the wires. She'd printed the firmware string onto it in a hand small enough to need the plate.

She killed the music. Pulled the earbuds. Turned to face him and held the look long enough that he understood: she'd been unreachable on purpose.

"The building's air-gapped," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"Since 2218. Original spec.
