He was cataloging something small, the work taking his whole attention the way it always did, his fingers moving with the precision of someone who believed accuracy was a form of prayer.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> waited. The shop smelled like paper and dust and something older — the specific cold of a sealed room where nothing moved without permission.

"The carousel," <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> said finally, still not looking. "You want to know who paid for it."

It wasn't a question. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> moved to the counter anyway, keeping his hands visible. <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> had a Faraday vault behind his left shoulder and a philosophy about information that didn't include apologies.

"The funding chain," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Everything upstream from the salvage writ."

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> closed his ledger with a deliberate motion. The sound it made was final. He turned to face <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>, and there was something in his expression that <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> recognized the way you recognize a door you've already walked through — the look of a man who was about to tell you something he'd been holding too long.

"You know who authorized Meridian Wellness," <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> said. "The pendant distribution. The site selection."

"I know."

"Do you know why?"

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't answer. The silence stretched between them like a thing with weight.

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> moved to the Faraday vault. His hand found the lock without looking — muscle memory built over decades of transactions nobody was supposed to witness. When he came back, he was carrying a file. Not thick. Just thick enough.

He set it on the counter between them.

"The funding traces through four shell companies," <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> said. "All of them registered to a procurement office in the Loop. All of them authorized by one signature." He opened the file. The paper was old — not ancient, but old enough that <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> could see the difference between the printing date and the authorization date, the way you can see the difference between a thing that was planned and a thing that was inevitable. "The authorization happened in 2219. Three months after a woman disappeared from <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a91a-7aeb-870e-990413666429">Geartown</entity>."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s eyes found the signature — careful, precise, the hand of someone who believed in documentation the way other people believed in God.

*<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Casper Vey</entity>*.

The name was already there. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had known it was there before the file opened. The knowing didn't make the seeing any easier.

"After the authorization ended in 2220, the trail went dark," <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> continued. His voice was level. Professional. The voice of a man delivering bad news to someone who'd already guessed it. "But the pendants kept shipping. The program kept running. Someone else picked it up."

"Who?"

"That's where the trail stops being mine." <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> closed the file. "The authorization chain traces through <entity repo="corponation" guid="019ef728-3e8a-7d69-9543-777e7c718174">Tessera Industries</entity>. That's public record — municipal procurement, all documented. But the successor program? The one that kept the children marked after the official study ended?" He tapped the file once. "That's private. That's the kind of infrastructure that doesn't show up in ledgers."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s hand moved to the file. <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> didn't stop him. The pages were warm — still holding the vault's climate control, that careful neutral temperature <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> maintained for documents that couldn't survive normal air.

The carousel park hatch was marked with a red vector. Same vector <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> had drawn. Same geometric center.

But <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> had added something else — a circle, large enough to encompass the entire West Town sector. Inside the circle, concentric rings. Data points. Coordinates.

"Every location marked on that map," <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> said, "is a place you've taken a contract."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s chest went tight. He knew this already — <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> had shown him the relay logs, the way the geometry centered on the carousel. But seeing it mapped this way, his own movements traced as data points, his own route through the city rendered as a lattice that someone had built deliberately around him—

"Forty-three coordinates," <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> said. "Over eleven years. All of them within walking distance of the carousel center. All of them positioned to move you through the geometry in a specific sequence." He let that sit. "You weren't investigating the carousel. You were part of its infrastructure."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at the map. At the concentric rings. At the single point in the center that was marked with a notation in <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>'s careful hand: *FIRST ADDRESS — 2178*.

The same year the entity's contract history began.

"You knew," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. It wasn't a question.

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> didn't answer for a moment. When he did, his voice was quieter. "I knew someone had built something in this neighborhood. Something old enough to have infrastructure predating the current commercial zoning. Something that mattered enough that a woman disappeared trying to document it, and someone spent a funded program and eleven children to mark the location." He met <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s eyes. "I didn't know it was you until <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> brought me the relay logs. Until I saw the geometry and recognized the pattern."

"The pattern?"

"A man being positioned," <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> said. "Deliberately. Over years. Like you were being grown into something specific, and the carousel park was the soil."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s hand closed on the edge of the counter. The file was still open. The map was still there — his life rendered as data points, his choices rendered as coordinates, his entire existence rendered as infrastructure for something else's purpose.

"<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s mother," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "The woman from <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a91a-7aeb-870e-990413666429">Geartown</entity>."

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> nodded. "She was documenting the program. Building her own map. She got far enough to see the geometry before she disappeared." He paused. "I think she found the same thing you found. I think she understood what the carousel meant. And I think someone decided she understood too much."

The shop was very quiet. Outside, muffled through the copper-lined walls, the noodle cart made its endless circuit — thin and wrong, a hum that shouldn't have reached this deep. Inside, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stood holding a map of his own life rendered as someone else's infrastructure, and understood — with the clarity that comes from seeing a door you've already walked through — that he'd been standing in the middle of it the whole time.

"What do you need?" <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> asked.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked up from the map. The question was simple. The answer was not.

If he closed this file and walked out, the carousel stayed dark. The entity stayed hidden. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> never learned what happened to her mother, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> never understood why eleven years of his life had been spent moving through a geometry that wasn't his.

If he didn't close this file — if he asked <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> to trace the successor program, to follow the funding after 2220, to find out who picked it up and why — then he was asking the entity's questions. Then he was becoming visible to something that had kept him invisible for eleven years precisely because invisibility was how it kept him alive.

The distinction was the same one that sat in his chest after the buffer authorization: the difference between a system you trusted and a system someone had arranged to be exactly as trustworthy as it needed to be.

Except now the system had a name. And the name was looking at him from a map drawn by a woman who'd disappeared.

"Everything," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said finally. "Trace it all."

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> didn't argue. He just closed the file and carried it back to the vault.

When he returned, he was carrying something else — a second file, thinner, older, the paper yellowed to the color of old teeth, waiting a long time for someone to open it.

"I've been holding this for six years," <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> said. "Since a woman came in asking about property ownership records for the carousel park. She paid me in cash. She asked me not to sell the information to anyone else. She said if anything happened to her, I should give it to the person who came looking for the geometry."

He set the file on the counter, bound with a string that had been tied so many times it was fraying.

"She said you'd come looking eventually," <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> said. "She said the carousel was your address too."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s hand moved before his mind caught up. The file was warm — not from the vault, from something else. His fingers opened it and found a photograph. A woman. Young. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s face rendered in someone else's bone structure, someone else's eyes.

Beneath the photograph, a name written in the same hand as the carousel map: *Lena Vasquez. Missing, 2219.*

And below that, in different handwriting — <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>'s hand — a single line: *She knew what the carousel meant. She knew what you were.*

The copper mesh held his silence the way it held everything else — completely, without echo. Outside, faint through the grounded walls, <entity repo="automaton" guid="019f04f1-58ed-77b6-b3b8-dd17d463bb34">the noodle vendor</entity> was singing its cheerful loop. The kids were still carrying their pendants. And somewhere in the geometry that <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had walked for eleven years, a woman's disappearance and a carousel hatch and a first address from 2178 were all the same thing — all the same answer to a question <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had been asking without knowing he was asking it.

He was standing in the middle of it.

And now <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> was too.

title: The Taste-Off
text:
<entity repo="place" guid="01a01887-b5f4-781c-8d38-122f7e1f38ba">The Loop</entity>'s third underlevel had its own ecology. A paper shop, a shuttered watch-repair, Vong's Dumpling Franchise #7 on the right under a red awning, and Mei's Dumplings on the left — no franchise, no awning, forty stolen inches of counter she'd annexed off the watch-repair's wall by leaning on it hard for years. The stationer's honest door sat dead center.

The two men stood in the middle with their backs to that door. Backs to <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>, in other words. A careless place to stand.

Vong was a compact sixty-year-old with the posture of a man who'd been taking bad news standing up for decades. The clipboard man wore a gray suit tailored to fit like a threat, and he held out a form the way a doctor holds out a chart. "—monthly insurance assessment. Standard for all food vendors on this underblock. The Tsui Group's protective services, standard rate—"

"Φ35 a week?" <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said from behind them, reading the figure upside-down. "Four hundred percent over the Meridian Merchant index. And your policy number's nine digits. <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a927-73ac-abfa-37c77f9cff8d">GLMZ</entity> policy numbers run eleven. That's somebody's neuretic handle on a form."

The clipboard man turned. He'd been in the work long enough to have stopped enjoying it. His face carried the apparatus of legitimacy — Tsui Group letterhead, a municipal seal, all of it official enough to survive a glance. "Not your stall."

"The coverage you've been operating under lapsed on the fourth," he went on, sliding his attention back to Vong. "Forty-two days ago. The protective license contingent on it is now void."

"Thirty-day grace period," Vong said, level. "Statute reads twenty-eight days left on the clock."

"The grace period applies to active licenses. Yours was lapsed. There's a distinction." He tapped the form without pointing at the number in section three. He didn't have to. Vong could see it from where he stood, and it was a number high enough to close the shop — high enough to make the calculation simple: pay the fraudulent claim, or spend six months in litigation nobody down here could afford.

"Go, Mr. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>," Vong said quietly. "This is mine to carry."

"I eat here," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. That was the whole of his position.

He'd half-expected the paperwork to end it. He pulled up the Tsui Group's public filing anyway — every collection franchise filed public or didn't operate — and it took under three minutes to find the part that mattered. The NeoCortex arranged the fields faster than conscious thought could follow: date, policy number, status.

"Your protective license lapsed," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said, turning the screen. "The fourth. Not expired — lapsed. You've been writing paper on a dead license for eleven days. There's no reinstatement pending; the portal would show it."

The clipboard man looked at the screen for a long moment. He knew the number format. He knew what it meant. Not expired — lapsed — the difference between a renewal you'd missed and a standing you'd let die. Any form filed under it was a fraudulent document. Any Φ35 taken on it was restitution-eligible the second someone objected in the district record.

Then he handed the clipboard to his partner — the big one, the expensive shoes — and rolled his neck.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read it as a man getting ready to leave. He was wrong.

"License is for the ones who pay clean," the clipboard man said. "Vong's not paying clean anymore. So this is the other visit." He looked at his partner. The big one didn't go for <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> — a professional, and professionals understand leverage. He came forward with the intention of making somebody stop being vertical, and he went for Vong's broth pot.

Forty liters of scalding pork-bone stock. A sixty-year-old man standing next to it.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> was moving before the big one's hand finished closing on the rim.

He didn't draw <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity>. A drawn blade in an underlevel full of lunch customers was a conversation he'd have to finish, and this didn't need finishing. It needed interrupting. He crossed the three meters in the time it took the big one's shoulder to commit — the man hadn't lunged at the pot, he'd pivoted into it, shoulder-first, the kind of redirect that would tip forty liters of scalding stock across Vong's counter and Vong's legs in one smooth motion. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> took the wrist off the rim — not a block, a redirect — and steered the shove ninety degrees into the franchise's steel prep counter. The stock rocked on its ring and held. One tongue of it slopped over the lip and hissed across the floor, where Vong had been standing half a second before. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s other hand had already moved him.

The big one came off the counter fast and threw the elbow. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had left him the room to throw it. It caught <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> across the cheekbone — a real hit, a bright white line of pain, a mark by evening — and the cost bought the opening. Weight forward, lead knee proud. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> took the knee from the side with the flat of his boot. Not the joint. He'd walk with a limp for a week and tell the story straight; ruin the knee and he comes back, and he brings people. The big one folded into the spilled stock, swearing, done.

The clipboard man's hand went inside his jacket. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at him.

"<entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> holds six," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. He hadn't drawn it. The sentence drew it. "You came to scald a sixty-year-old over Φ35 a week. Take your partner, take your dead license, and tell Marcus Tsui that Vong's block is documented now — times, faces, the shoes." A beat. "There's a kid on that roof who drew the shoes."

The hand came out empty. They hauled the big one up between them and left, tracking wet bootprints and the smell of spilled stock, and the underlevel breathed out. <entity repo="automaton" guid="019f04f1-58ed-77b6-b3b8-dd17d463bb34">The noodle vendor</entity>'s cheerful loop played on outside, indifferent.

Vong stood by his rescued pot with both hands flat on the counter. Steadying it, or himself.

"The tea stall on sub-two," he said. "Lin's. Forty years. She told them no, same as me. They didn't burn it. They just visited, and visited, and one week the customers decided sub-two wasn't worth the walk, and then Lin decided too. Now it's a jack kiosk and nobody remembers there was tea." His hands weren't quite steady. "That's how it's done now. Not a fire. An erasure. You wait for the block to forget."

"It's documented now," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "The next visit isn't a visit. It's a filing." He looked at the blood on his thumb without surprise. "Lin's mistake was being the only no on her block. You've got a whole block, Vong. Bill me for the dumplings I'm about to eat."

From his doorway, <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> made a small sound that was not a cough.

They came back at 14:00.

No clipboard this time. Three of them — the clipboard man, the big one moving carefully on his bad knee, and a third <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> hadn't seen before. Chrome thumb-rings, the flat affect of a man brought in for one purpose. The underlevel had thinned out after lunch. The third man's eyes went to Vong's counter first, then to the stairwell on the far wall, marking the ways out. That told <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> more than the chrome did.

"Marcus Tsui filed a complaint," the clipboard man said. He was talking to the room, not to any one person. "Assault of a licensed representative. Interference with contracted services. You've got a warrant flag running on your neuretics, <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aafb-7b6b-bcbc-b8614f9d228f">samurai</entity>. Check it if you want. We'll wait."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't check it. A warrant flag cost sixty Φ to file and twenty to pull. It was a stall, not a threat. He also didn't move from where he stood, which was between the third man and Vong's pot.

"The complaint went to a licensing board that hasn't had a quorum since the fourth," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Same day your license lapsed. So the filing is stuck behind the lapse review. It's paperwork with nothing behind it. It dies the moment your reinstatement is denied, and it will be, because I've already sent the eleven-day gap documentation to <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">the Office</entity> of Merchant Protections." He hadn't sent it yet. He was going to, in the next forty minutes, which was close enough. "You want to check THAT warrant, I'll wait."

The third man looked at the clipboard man. The clipboard man looked at his shoes.

The chrome rings were the tell. This one wasn't here for paper. He was here to stand in Vong's stall and let the afternoon customers see what they'd be walking into. He wouldn't touch Vong. He'd just be present, every afternoon, until keeping the franchise cost more than giving it up.

The same erasure Vong had described. Patient, and technically legal.

"Vong," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said, without turning. "Is there a back entrance to this underlevel?"

"Loading dock. Service corridor, behind the watch-repair."

"The watch-repair's shuttered?"

"Three years."

"Whose lease?"

A pause. "Mine. I took it when they left. Cheaper than advertising."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at the third man. "You're standing in an extended franchise footprint. The loading dock, the service corridor, and the six feet of watch-repair wall all come off the same lease. You can stand here, but you're standing in his house. You want to tell Marcus Tsui you held a loitering position inside a vendor's licensed space, in front of witnesses, on the day I filed that lapse paperwork? That's intimidation after filing. Different charge. Higher one. They read it off a different shelf downtown."

The third man had the chrome rings and the flat affect and nothing else. He'd been hired for presence, not decisions. He looked at the clipboard man, who had been wrong about this block twice now.

They left.

Vong sat down on his prep stool and said nothing for a while. From the service corridor below, faint and steady, the <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> ran its hum through the tiles — thirty meters down, Mach 6, the whole moving world.

"Every time I tell them no," Vong said, "I think about Lin."

"You're not Lin," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Lin didn't have the service corridor and a kid on the roof and a <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aafb-7b6b-bcbc-b8614f9d228f">samurai</entity> who eats here on Tuesdays."

He went upstairs and filed the documentation.

The Office of Merchant Protections portal loaded slow, the way it always did, a public docket built to discourage the people it was meant to protect. The form was the same every time: date, location, names if available, what happened, who witnessed it. He typed Vong's block number. Uploaded the screenshot of the dead license — no reinstatement pending, eleven days of nothing where a credential should have been. He filled the witness line: six lunch customers who'd confirm it if asked, and <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-6067-735a-8326-4aff028cb856">Rafters</entity>, who'd drawn the big one's shoes off the rooftop log while <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> was still reading the clipboard. That was the leverage. Not the violence. The paperwork. You broke the paperwork, you broke the system's claim to anything.

The filing cost Φ8.50. He paid it from his personal account and hit submit.

The confirmation code populated — a case number, a line drawn in the underlevel's invisible architecture that said Vong's block was not erasable, not this week, not without leaving a mark someone downtown could read. A small stone set in a current, changing nothing except the angle at which the water fell.

He wrote the number on the back of a receipt — <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>'s paper, because <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>'s paper had weight — and went back down to leave it on Vong's counter.

By 14:00 there was a chalk line on the floor. By 15:30 there were two, with a disputed strip between them and three customers eating in the gap, braced to be told to pick a side.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> was at Mei's — he alternated weeks, had for six years, and both owners knew it — with a cut cheek and a late lunch when <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> came down the stairs. Somebody had sent for her. She came down the way a woman does when she's been handed a job beneath her skill and above her patience, carrying a wooden spoon she hadn't put down before leaving her own counter. She stopped on the neutral chalk and let the quiet do half the work.

"Both of you have sold dumplings down here longer than half these buildings have stood," she said. "You've both overcharged me. I paid, because the food was worth it." She looked at the two lines, then at the three customers wedged in the gap between them. "I'm not an arbitrator. I'm a customer owed better than this."

"You're the only one on this block both stalls will hear," Vong said.

"You started it," Mei said.

"The awning—"

"The broth pot—"

"The awning was over the line by a hand," <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> said, without turning to either of them. "The broth pot's been in that corner since before the strip mattered. I know because I've been paying you both to feed me since the year the water came up to the second level. That's not a claim I made lightly and it's not one you'll argue." She tapped the spoon once against her palm. "A block runs on people who don't ask each other for receipts. You've made everyone down here reach for a wallet twice — once for the food, once to guess whose side of the chalk they're standing on. That's the part I won't pay."

She turned to <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. She didn't ask. She had spent seventy years not asking for things, and the not-asking was the request. He finished his dumpling and stood up. His cheek had stiffened to a dull throb that woke when he chewed. A fair price, for an afternoon that had twice nearly cost Vong his hands.

The taste-off was <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity>'s idea, and the speed with which the logbook made it official suggested it had been everyone's idea at once.

DUMPLING COMMISSION: OFFICIAL RECORD. CHAIR: MR. KYLE (VISIBLE INJURY, SEE 11:40 ENTRY). RECORDER: RAFTERS. PANEL: DENTS, BOOST. OBJECTIVE: BETTER DUMPLING, FOR BLOCK PEACE. NOTE: BOSS GOT HIT TODAY. ONCE. WE LOGGED IT. THIS LOG IS HONEST.

Both stalls cooked. Vong ran his standard pork-and-chive — thicker wrap, machine-even pleating, corners sealed with the precision of someone who'd done it ten thousand times, every inspection star it had ever earned. Mei brought the original: thinner wrap, hand-crimped in a pattern <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-6067-735a-8326-4aff028cb856">Rafters</entity> sketched in the margin for the record, ginger-forward with something older underneath. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> ate four of each. Vong's wrapper held the filling's heat longer; Mei's broth was cleaner, the salt distributed so it didn't land all at once on the tongue. Different choices. Different hands. The cut in his cheek woke at every one of Mei's. He took that as evidence of the ginger and kept it out of the minutes.

The crew filed scorecards, from TWO POINTS AND A STAR up to a drawing of a thumbs-up with a Φ1 price tag. A crowd had gathered — chalk lines and official proceedings will do that, word moving through the underlevel the way it does, *taste-off, somebody's going to lose* — and <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> had migrated from his doorway to the building's first inside window for the better angle.

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity> tallied the cards twice, then a third time, her pencil going slower each pass. When he finally turned the logbook around, the count was a dead tie — and every one of Vong's points, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> saw, was clustered on the crew's own cards. The neutral crowd, the strangers who'd wandered in off the chalk lines, had scored Mei's to a person. Vong saw it the same instant <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> did.

He set down his ladle. Wiped his hands with great deliberation. And said to the whole gathered block that a rigged panel of <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s own people wasn't a taste-off, it was theater — that he'd had to prove he was better, and instead a room of <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s crew had proved they were the same — and he'd take the real verdict, the crowd's, as proof the Commission had picked its winner before the first dumpling hit the water.

"A tie is a loss for me," he said. Flat, the way accusations come out when the accuser already knows the words won't stop. Half the crowd murmured agreement. The line was already re-forming on Mei's side of the chalk, feet voting where scorecards hadn't been trusted to.

<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-6067-735a-8326-4aff028cb856">Rafters</entity>' pen stopped over the honest log with nothing fair left to write, and the block peace the whole thing was supposed to buy was now visibly worse than when they'd started.

"For the record," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said, to the chalk and the crowd and both owners, "Vong's franchise makes a technically excellent dumpling. Consistent. Well-priced. You know exactly what you get, any day of any week." Vong nodded with professional dignity. "Mei's original is better."

Mei made a sound that was not quite a sound. Vong's jaw went through an expression and out the far side.

"By a margin that doesn't justify a chalk line," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> went on, over the crowd's murmur. "Vong, your guarantee covers the gap — inspection rating, delivery network, the app. Mei's got seventeen years of recipe folded by hand. Two stalls, two reasons to buy a dumpling. You're both leaving money on the floor fighting over an inch." He let that sit. Then he said the part that was the actual point. "This afternoon Marcus Tsui sent three men to stand in Vong's stall and wait for the foot traffic to decide it wasn't worth the walk. They left because the paperwork went in and the stall had footage to stand on. That changes nothing about next week, or the week after, or Lin's tea stall on sub-two that's a jack kiosk now and will never be tea again." He looked at both of them. "A block with one stall is a block that can be made to forget it. A block with two stalls arguing about awnings at lunch is a block that's LOUD. People come to it on purpose. You two are each other's insurance, and you've been drawing a chalk line down the middle of it."

He looked at <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-6067-735a-8326-4aff028cb856">Rafters</entity>. "That how the minutes read?"

<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-6067-735a-8326-4aff028cb856">Rafters</entity> consulted the logbook with the gravity of a senior analyst. "Exactly how they read. I can charge for certified copies."

The chalk was gone by 16:30. Vong sent one complimentary order of pork-and-chive to Mei's counter without a word; Mei took it without a word. Closest the underlevel had come to a diplomatic event in twenty years. Vong put the franchise testimonial card in his window — cheap stock, the kind that yellowed in a month, printed on the same run as the inspection rating so the ink matched. Beside it he set a second card, hand-lettered, that hadn't been there this morning, the letters pressed hard enough to leave indents on the back: BEST ORIGINAL ON THE BLOCK — SEE MEI, NEXT COUNTER. He positioned it to catch the afternoon light coming down the stairwell, where the foot traffic from street level would read it before it read anything else. Insurance, posted where the block could read it.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> was leaving at 17:20 when <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> opened his door the particular width of a man who'd been saving something all day.

"Come in. The occasion warrants the good shelf." Inside, the labeled drawers sat in their brown-inked rows, dates running back forty years, indexed by a system nobody but <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> could read. He poured without asking and pushed the cup handle-first. "The Tsui Group isn't my clientele — impersonation filings are public, and I don't sell what I can read for free." He settled onto his stool. "I watched the whole thing. Morning and afternoon. The license. The pot. The chrome thumb-rings." His eyes went, briefly, to <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s cheek. "The interruptions, plural."

"You watched a man go for a sixty-year-old and made tea?"

"I sell maps, Mr. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. I don't walk the territory. A stationer who picks up a weapon is a stationer no one trusts with a secret again." He said it without apology. "But I noticed you didn't draw the sword. A man went for Vong's pot — twice, two different ways — and you put them down with paperwork and a boot and a sentence. The leverage was real. The filing was real. The sub-two corridor was real. Three kinds of paper and one measured piece of violence, in order." He polished his glasses. "The Tsui Group needed a reason to stop. The stalls needed a verdict. Your standing client needed" — the smallest brightness — "a dumpling methodology, apparently."

He turned back to his desk, where three forms sat stamped and dated in that small, precise hand. "There are two kinds of people who last in a place like this. The ones who don't move unless the contract says to move, and the ones who move and then write the paper to cover what they've already done. I'm the first. You're the second. That's why your afternoon holds up and mine only records it." He dipped his pen. "Two stalls arguing is noise, Mr. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. One stall is silence, and silence is what makes a block disappear off the district roll. You kept the noise. That was the work. Don't tell me it was an accident."

"Don't."

He said it about all of it, and <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> — who understood the word the way he understood filings — didn't press.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> drank the tea, which was from the good shelf, and set the cup down square.

The terminal chirped on his way to the stairs.

STANDING CONTRACT — AMENDMENT. CLIENT HAS REVIEWED TODAY. CLIENT NOTES: THE INJURY WAS AVOIDABLE IF THE ENGINEER'S DRONE PROPOSAL (FILED, DECLINED) HAD BEEN ADOPTED.
CLIENT HAS RE-FILED THE PROPOSAL.
GRATUITY: Φ0.5 — ITEMIZED: THE CHEEK. ADDENDUM: CLIENT NOTED THE CHEEK AT 14:40.
CLIENT DISLIKES THE CHEEK.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read it twice on the stairs. The gratuity wasn't payment — Φ0.5 was insulting as payment. It was a record, logged so a street cut became a documented injury that might one day bear on his ability to work. Corpo files didn't care about a man bleeding in a stall. They cared about the same blood once it had a line item.

The cut was stiffening, tight enough now that turning his head pulled at it, and behind him the underlevel settled into its evening — Vong's closing sequence, Mei's last fold, the <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> dragging its Mach-6 tremor through the floor thirty meters down. He decided the client could dislike the cheek all it wanted. A cut cheek was cheap. Vong still had his hands.

title: The Forger's Ledger
text:
The stairwell smelled like machine oil and cold concrete, the recycler drums somewhere below still running their angry twenty-fourth hour. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s terminal chirped again before he reached street level.

Not the client. A relay tag he half-recognized: FERENTI, C. - ARCHIVIST, DETROIT SPUR.

He'd taken the man's forty-one pages three weeks back, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity>-routed, unremarkable - historical utility surveys, a security flat on top of the Read's rate. Paid, filed, done. Except <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5f86-7b4e-ba08-349d6ddac1c7">Ferenti</entity> didn't ping closed contracts. Nobody did.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> opened it standing on the landing, one hand still on the rail.

FERENTI: THE PAGE CLEARED YOUR SCREEN. IT DID NOT CLEAR MINE. I AM ASKING YOU TO LOOK AGAIN BEFORE I FILE IT AS TRUTH.

He read it twice, same as the client's amendment, except this one didn't feel like weather. He thought about <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5f86-7b4e-ba08-349d6ddac1c7">Ferenti</entity>'s tea cup turning its quarter-turn, the room he'd lost to his own archive, the man's voice going flat on *I become the reason the claim is clean.* <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had heard that shape of fear before - not the fear of getting hurt, the fear of being used as the good name on a bad thing. It was Vong's fear, some version of it, standing over a pot with his own franchise stamped on the side. It was, if he let himself sit in it for half a second on a stairwell that smelled like plastomer, his own.

He didn't sit in it. He typed back one line - *sending someone* - and thought about <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-602e-7a47-a1ec-61747fc9d537">Marisol</entity>.

She worked jobs like this cold, no names exchanged that mattered, and she never once needed the client to explain what "wrong" meant before she found it. Everyone <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> knew who'd used her once came back, and nobody had a bad word to say. If forty-one pages had a seam in them, she'd find which one, and she'd tell him after, exactly as promised, the way she told everyone after.

He pinged her handle. No preamble - she didn't like preamble.

KYLE: Archive job. <entity repo="place" guid="03964523-e47c-306f-ce05-cc8b80500139">Detroit</entity> spur. Forty-one pages, paper stock, already cleared once. Someone thinks a lie is sitting in a trusted stack. Need the page that doesn't belong.

The reply came back in under a minute, which for her was fast.

MARISOL: Anyone can take. The trick is putting something back. Send the address. I'll tell you after.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> sent it and kept moving, down through the recycler heat and out into the evening cold, the <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity>'s tremor climbing up through his boots from thirty meters under the street. <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5f86-7b4e-ba08-349d6ddac1c7">Ferenti</entity>'s forty-one pages were three weeks gone and none of his business anymore, except the man had asked him to look again, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had already decided to spend someone else's evening doing exactly that.

Behind him, the terminal chirped once more. He didn't look. Whatever the client wanted next, it could wait for the stairs to end.

She was already in the lobby, finishing a warm bun from the cart two doors down. Mid-forties, warm-faced, field coat the brown of autumn mud. She brushed the crumbs off her lapel and gave him a handshake that lasted the exact professional fraction of a second — the grip of someone who'd sized him up before he crossed the floor. She wasted no gesture. Her hands were steady and unremarkable until you noticed that.

"Marisol."

"<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>."

"I know." No agenda in it. "You held the carousel park last month. The whole block talked about it. The carousel ran music."

"Four bars."

"Four bars," she agreed, and they went upstairs.

He needed her signature on the records-access form before noon — one name in ink, and the sealed inventory would open to him for the rest of the case. That was all. Get the form in front of her, get it signed, get out before the screening flagged anything he'd rather keep unlisted. <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5f86-7b4e-ba08-349d6ddac1c7">Ferenti</entity> had rented this floor eleven years ago and spent every one of them turning it into the kind of place where paper lived longer than people did — sealed windows, the air dry enough to make <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s throat tight, the whole careful architecture of a life spent making sure nothing got lost.

The scanner on the third-floor landing gave its institutional chime — STANDARD SCREENING INITIATED — DOCUMENT INVENTORY — PSYKER ON PREMISES — VISITOR CONFIRM. Marisol confirmed without breaking stride, the way a woman does when she's been thumbing that same word since she was twenty-two. She didn't roll her eyes. Something in the set of her jaw took the word, weighed it, and decided not to spend the afternoon on it.

On the ride over he had thumbed <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> back to six. The trencher had cost him two, and he didn't walk into archives light.

The records room smelled of conservation solvent and old paper, which was better than the two floors below. <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5f86-7b4e-ba08-349d6ddac1c7">Ferenti</entity> ran the intake briskly and left them to it.

Marisol pulled on cotton archival gloves — soft, worn thin from use, worked on one finger at a time — and looked at <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> over the first tray. "The way I work: I go through in order and tell you what I get. An authentic page has a whole person in it — the hands that made it, what they had for breakfast, whether they hated the job. A fake is just a job. Clean in a way nothing real is clean." She turned the first page. "I charge by the touch because it costs me by the touch."

Page one: clean.

Page fourteen: clean.

A knock at twenty-two — <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5f86-7b4e-ba08-349d6ddac1c7">Ferenti</entity>'s runner, twelve or so, sleeve patches from a Spine courier house, the face of a kid who'd been doing piecework since he was ten. He held out more documents. "Broker says these came with the load. The <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="3b153287-1c59-41b7-8773-e63a11aea945">Psyk</entity> verify these too, or just the primaries?"

"Primaries," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said, and tipped him Φ2, above rate.

When the door closed, Marisol said without looking up, "He'll grow out of the word or he won't. Not my afternoon."

Page twenty-three: clean. Eleven more after that. She moved through them methodically, one hand flat on each sheet, no half-second pause, no hitch that would mean the thing was telling her something.

At thirty-eight she stopped.

She held the page by its edges and laid her palm flat, fingers spread, and went still — the stillness of a woman listening to something that made no sound. Her breathing slowed. Her jaw tightened. "This one."

It was a utility survey of the carousel junction on <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-849c-7793-bce8-ae238e4576f6">Leavitt</entity>: the underground chamber, the trunk lines, the sub-floor hatch under the maintenance skirt. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> knew the room. He'd bled there. He knew the width of that hatch and the passage behind it and what the junction smelled like when the line was warm. He knew the half-block of stubborn green above it that had never made economic sense to any of the towers, and four bars of music that had played there before the mechanism wound down.

The survey read: SITE ASSESSED — NO ACTIVE INFRASTRUCTURE — DEAD GLASS — NO RELEVANT ASSETS.

He had stood in that room six weeks ago. The line had been humming.

"It's beautiful work," Marisol said. It was not a compliment. "The fiber, the aging chemistry, the hand — almost right. The paper's old, the ink's old. But the hands that made it didn't care about this survey. They cared about making a survey." She set it down like it was contaminated. "The gesture is wrong. The pressure is wrong. Whoever filled this out never filled out a survey before in their life." She lifted her palm off it. "There's your forgery. One specific lie: there's nothing at this address."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at the date stamp. Three months old. Three months this page had sat in <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5f86-7b4e-ba08-349d6ddac1c7">Ferenti</entity>'s archive, patient and filed, waiting for a demolition order that would find its provenance already clean. Dead glass on the record. Officially gone. No acquisition needed, no permit required — just a site that had never existed to argue with.

He held on to that.

Then the smell came in through the ventilation slit above the third tray: acetone, and something flatter under it — the chemistry of a fire agent primed and waiting.

Four seconds between the smell and the door.

The woman came first — chrome running her whole left arm, shoulder to fingertip, the hardware expensive enough not to show at the joint seams, a multi-tool already open on her palm with the incendiary trigger showing. Three men behind her. All four moved with the rehearsed economy of a team that had learned the room off a floor plan.

They did not say get away from the paper.

She said: "<entity repo="vocabulary" guid="816dbd83-fa5a-4ccb-9b58-b353707146d3">The Read</entity> comes with us. Principal wants her able to talk."

It landed on <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> all at once. The fire wasn't for the forgery. The fire was cover. The principal had decided that a woman who could touch a forged survey and feel the lie in its fiber was worth more than the paper. Paper you could burn. A witness you could carry, and the authentication walked out with the crew. No one else in <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a927-73ac-abfa-37c77f9cff8d">GLMZ</entity> was going to authenticate that forgery by hand.

"Marisol," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "The window."

"I have eight pages and the forgery," she said, already moving, "and I am not leaving the forgery."

The tool discharged. Blue-white in the back corner, the third tray catching. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> put <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity>'s first round through the multi-tool at the wrist joint — the percussion enormous in the narrow room — and the augmentation's servos screamed, a high mechanical shriek under the roar of the fire, and the woman sat down hard around the nerve hit, the tool spinning off into the flames. One spent. Five left. The room was burning now.

Two of the men moved to bracket Marisol, not <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. A mistake. <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> came out and wrote a clean line across the nearer one's wrist flexors — wide of anything that wouldn't grow back — and he found a new priority and took it to the floor. The second got a hand on Marisol's field coat and got <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s elbow across the hinge of his jaw. The cheap fast answer, when the clean one would cost tenths of a second the room didn't have.

The fourth — hired for position, slowest to commit — watched three colleagues turn into problems and put his effort into the door.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> let him go. There was no version of this where chasing him put the fire out.

His left shoulder had taken the woman's elbow on the way down, outside the mesh. It hurt in a clean, specific way: bruised, not broken, still working. He set the pain aside and kept moving.

"Extinguisher," Marisol said. "Beside the door."

She had the forgery and a stack of pages under her arm and was working through the surviving trays with the calm of a woman who charged by the touch — fingertips skating each sheet, reading the weave for heat damage the way she read it for forgery, salvaging by feel what the <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aa93-73ed-b61d-b7955f44a2d8">cold storage</entity> had kept at fifty-two degrees and thirty-five percent for a century because that was the temperature old paper liked to stay honest at.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> found the extinguisher and killed the blaze — blue, then grey, then out.

One round spent. Five left. The shoulder would keep. Third tray gone.

The fourth man had a van, and the van had a frequency <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> could track. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had pulled the plate off the lobby scanner — <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a927-73ac-abfa-37c77f9cff8d">GLMZ</entity> registration, recent, a gray panel job with no markings, the kind of vehicle built to dissolve into traffic because it looked like every other panel-side van in the city. Marisol had the forgery. <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5f86-7b4e-ba08-349d6ddac1c7">Ferenti</entity> had his surviving thirty-eight pages and his grief for the Domazinski surveys, gone to ash in the third tray. Somewhere below them the extruder drums were still running the twenty-third hour without a pause.

He put the page on the desk instead of the drawer and left it there, face up.

He looked at the forgery in the morning light. The handwriting was perfect — engineer-grade, municipal, right in every detail except the one thing the whole page existed to lie about. <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-60c7-75e9-8bc1-df94f90ec0b0">The Glove</entity> had known the hatch dimensions down to zero deviation and still drawn a survey that swore the site was dead glass. <entity repo="archetype" guid="019d6143-a570-7f99-8349-1341d88cbbcb">Forger</entity>'s rates, spent across three months, one filing at a time, feeding that nothing into the registry before the job ever reached <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5f86-7b4e-ba08-349d6ddac1c7">Ferenti</entity>'s archive.

Seven pages of it were already in the record. This was the eighth — the one that had slipped, the one that ended up in the wrong hands.

The shoulder visit had cost twelve Φ. He drew it from the operating account, put on his coat, and went downstairs.

CONTRACT ADDENDUM.
CLIENT NOTES SEVEN REGISTRY FILINGS REMAIN OUTSTANDING.
CLIENT NOTES STANDARD RATE APPLIES.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stood in the stairwell with the terminal in his good hand and read it twice, the way he'd read the logbook twice, looking for the thing he'd walked past the first time.

Standard rate. Not a bonus for the eighth page, not a flag on the woman in the brown coat, not one word about a read who'd been working a crew's blind side for three months and gotten close enough to touch the hatch dimensions without anyone clocking her face. Just the outstanding count, filed the way a client files anything — clean, procedural, no weight on it at all.

Seven filings gone. A woman walking west at odd hours who wasn't going anywhere a courier would go. And somewhere upstream of both of them, an entity that had been asked to stand down on the sighting and had chosen the word *flagging* instead of *closed*.

He put the terminal away and went to find B.

title: Halvorsen & Sons
text:
The appointment was 09:00, on the record.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> walked to <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-95c2-7084-bc60-1d8cb35562ed">Bucktown</entity> and took the stairs at <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-a31f-7059-abda-f4a28cc5639c">Halvorsen Civic Recovery</entity> two at a time. The firm still listed itself in the directory in that careful serif font that said *we have been here longer than you have* — third floor of a corner block, the kind of place where the filing system predated cloud storage and nobody had bothered to argue about it. On the second-floor landing he had the work terminal out before he'd decided to reach for it — habit. The way you check for a pulse on something that might already be dead.

He expected it to have something to say. A meeting at the firm behind the <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-ed6c-7a54-97a5-56afca1f1f19">Rotterdam</entity> job should have pulled a scope update out of the client, or a query, or at least the dry territorial note it had sent the morning he first walked into <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>'s shop. It had opinions about where he took its business.

The screen was blank.

Not locked. Not sleeping. Not stalled, not loading. Blank the way a room is blank after someone has quietly stood up and left it — the kind of blank that meant the device had stopped talking to whatever it had been talking to for eleven years. He held it, waiting for the flicker of a boot sequence, the return of the standing contract, the amendment that had started as logistics and become something else entirely.

Nothing came back.

He read the empty screen twice. 08:58. He put the terminal away and went up.

The office had two desks. Blue Hat — her professional name was apparently beside the point for both of them — sat at the nearer one with all her attention aimed at anything except <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. It was costing her something.

Her boss was a big man going gray at the temples, both hands flat on the desk before <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> sat down. It was the posture of a man holding himself back — not a threat. Something closer to embarrassment doing its best to pass as composure. He had an <entity repo="corponation" guid="019d6143-a7a4-71f6-b46a-94ef8cb2348f">Arcturus</entity> cert on the wall, forty years of work behind the name on the glass, and red at the corners of his eyes. Not today's red. The kind that builds up over years.

"<entity repo="character" guid="019fbde4-d680-7bb7-b9f5-5f28c3b8f705">Breckenridge</entity>," he said. "Walt. Operations foreman." He shook hands without theater. "The <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-ed6c-7a54-97a5-56afca1f1f19">Rotterdam</entity> run."

"Mach six," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"Mach six," <entity repo="character" guid="019fbde4-d680-7bb7-b9f5-5f28c3b8f705">Breckenridge</entity> agreed, with the tiredness of a man who has said those two words in front of lawyers. "My father started this company. Forty-one years ago, him and a partner. Never a finding. Never a suspension. Not one." He pulled a breath that didn't quite settle. "The insurance carrier sent their first letter eight days after <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-ed6c-7a54-97a5-56afca1f1f19">Rotterdam</entity>. Their second ran nine pages. I've been on the line with our council rep three times, explaining why a fish-box truck was hauling <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-a31f-7059-abda-f4a28cc5639c">Halvorsen</entity> work product the night your tag went to the Netherlands." He looked at the desk a long moment. "We were used. Somebody walked a fake job through my intake process, and we didn't catch it, because we were good and trusted and didn't ask the question you always have to ask."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at the cert on the wall instead of at <entity repo="character" guid="019fbde4-d680-7bb7-b9f5-5f28c3b8f705">Breckenridge</entity>'s face. Forty-one years. His own client had opened its screen nine days back and said nothing at all — the first silence in eleven years — and here was a man who'd built something clean for four decades watching it come apart from the inside because somebody needed a name to hide behind. He filed the coincidence and didn't reach for it.

"You're asking it now," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"I'm asking it now." <entity repo="character" guid="019fbde4-d680-7bb7-b9f5-5f28c3b8f705">Breckenridge</entity> lifted a folder. "My intake desk found the sloppiness first. A client-reference header that carried through from their own internal system. An export error — the kind that happens when someone forgets to clean the metadata before sending a file to a firm they mean to use once and throw away." He set the folder down. "Two words on the header line."

He waited.

"<entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">Continuity Office</entity>."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> let the words sit. The building carried someone else's morning up the stairwell, boiler heat and old paper. It was a tidy operation up here — a board of open jobs behind <entity repo="character" guid="019fbde4-d680-7bb7-b9f5-5f28c3b8f705">Breckenridge</entity>, each one numbered instead of named. Forty-one years of not getting sloppy, and then sloppy once, from the outside, in a way that would never show up as theirs on any ledger but the one that mattered to them.

"I'll deal with that separately," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. It came out flatter than he meant it. <entity repo="character" guid="019fbde4-d680-7bb7-b9f5-5f28c3b8f705">Breckenridge</entity> didn't need to know he was already carrying two other threads with the same two words woven through them, or that he had no idea yet how many hands they touched.

"One job. One clean credited recovery, on the public record. Something a court reads and files under routine." <entity repo="character" guid="019fbde4-d680-7bb7-b9f5-5f28c3b8f705">Breckenridge</entity> produced a second folder, thicker, sealed. "A clinic in West Town — <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-849c-7793-bce8-ae238e4576f6">Leavitt</entity> Free Medical. Grant-funded, run on goodwill. Kessler and Sons in the South Loop impounded their med-printer. Kessler works with a distress-paper broker named Arpad Fekete. Fekete scouts clinics behind on their lease maintenance, buys the paper before the grace period closes, and tips Kessler the window."

"The lapse on the clinic."

"Fourteen days. The grace period is ten. The paper sold to Fekete's broker on day nine — inside the window, before it closed." His mouth was flat. "The printer's a Lenz-Haas RP-7. The clinic financed it at Φ640 through the Territory Health Co-Op. Two payments left, and nothing to make them with, because the printer's sitting in bay three of Kessler's yard." He pushed the folder over. "I've had the chain documented for a month. I can't move on it alone. Kessler's yard is family-staffed, and the family has a cousin on the <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-95c2-7084-bc60-1d8cb35562ed">Bucktown</entity> council."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> opened the folder. Financing certificate. Maintenance log. The distress-paper sale, timestamped day nine — a single day inside the window. A photograph of the RP-7 in institutional white, the clinic's intake number taped to the chassis, hand-labeled, the tape cut with scissors instead of torn. The kind of label that comes from a place doing its best. Below it, the Co-Op's own repayment card, the boxes filled in by hand and initialed each month — the sort of clinic that still kept a paper ledger because half its patients didn't carry terminals and the other half didn't trust the ones that did.

He thought of the Glove's survey — engineer-grade, correct in every particular except the one that mattered — and set the thought down before it could turn into a speech. <entity repo="character" guid="019fbde4-d680-7bb7-b9f5-5f28c3b8f705">Breckenridge</entity> didn't need the comparison. He needed the printer back.

"Standard rate," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "And I keep a copy of your engagement file."

<entity repo="character" guid="019fbde4-d680-7bb7-b9f5-5f28c3b8f705">Breckenridge</entity> reached into the same drawer and set a second folder on the desk, already prepared.

"Had two copies made," he said. "Yours is on top."

The logistics took the rest of the morning.

A writ at the <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-95c2-7084-bc60-1d8cb35562ed">Bucktown</entity> filing desk: Φ40, forty minutes, a clerk who triple-dated every document on principle and brought the stamp down like accuracy was a physical discipline. A truck from <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity>'s pool: Φ25, four hours, matched to Kessler's yard specs so nothing would flag at the gate.

He messaged <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity> a time and a place. She was already on the <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-849c-7793-bce8-ae238e4576f6">Leavitt</entity> apron when he arrived at noon, reading the clinic's posted hours like a woman memorizing a load spec.

Six feet of canvas work jacket, pockets reinforced twice over. Her eyes crossed the front of the building and came back to the angle of the apron, already working out how the printer would ride. She spent forty words a day and wouldn't waste one indoors.

"Bay three," she said. Seven down, thirty-three to go.

"Bay three," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> confirmed.

At the clinic door, a nurse in green scrubs was talking a patient down over the threshold. Both of them wore the look of people used to checking the apron for something that should have been there and wasn't.

<entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity> read the sign — NO FEE FOR CARE, hand-painted, black on white, the letters thinning where the brush ran low. She looked at <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>.

"Good printer?" she asked.

"Financed clean. Two payments left."

She nodded once, like that settled something, and went to check the rigging. She coiled the crane cable first, each loop exact, no slack, no kinks — the same care she'd have given a wound.

The truck was where <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had left it. A yard coordinator from the neighboring depot had planted himself behind the rear gate, clipboard out, young, pressed uniform, the kind of posture that came from a training manual instead of years on a dock.

"Who authorized a four-hour hold on a Kessler-spec vehicle without a counter-signature from Kessler's logistics chain?"

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> pulled the writ and held it out flat, letting the man take his time.

The coordinator read it. Read it again. Checked the seal against a reference card from his own pocket. Found nothing actionable and went looking anyway — turned the page over, checked the back for a signature that wasn't required, held it up to the light like the paper itself might confess something the words hadn't.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> watched him do it. Recognized the shape of it: a man who'd been told competence meant never letting a thing through, and had built a whole morning's worth of authority on top of that instruction, and couldn't tell the difference anymore between diligence and stalling. Bay three was thirty minutes out. Every minute this cost was a minute <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> didn't have to spend somewhere else, a minute the clinic's printer sat further behind on its own clock.

He didn't raise his voice. He didn't repeat himself. He stood with the writ still out, arm level, and waited the way he'd waited on a dock ramp for a countdown to hit one second — patient because patience was the only lever that worked, and because the paperwork existed for exactly this, a wall he could put between himself and a fight that wouldn't get the printer to bay three any faster.

The coordinator found a third thing to question — the truck's registration date, two years old, nothing to do with anything — and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> handed him that answer too, and watched him run out of things to ask before he ran out of wanting to ask them. His jaw worked once, then settled.

Forty minutes gone. The gate came down. <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity> was already moving before it finished rising, the rigging in her hands like she'd been holding the shape of it in her head the whole time she stood there reading a sign about free care.

Kessler and Sons took up a quarter-block on the South Loop fringe: cracked concrete apron, chain-link fence rusting at the joints, three cameras someone had aimed at the street instead of the lot — installed for the look of liability coverage, not the fact of it. The gate was the old kind: a clip-framed window, a hand-lettered sign, a yard dog chained behind the shed that had given up barking at strangers and now just watched.

The old man behind the window had the face of someone who'd sat in that chair thirty years and watched better paper than this come through. He read the writ. Read it again. Found the line he wanted: RECOVERY AGENT OF RECORD: <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-a31f-7059-abda-f4a28cc5639c">HALVORSEN CIVIC RECOVERY</entity> LLC, BUCKTOWN.

"Arpad's paper," he said.

"Sold inside the grace window," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Timestamps are on page two. The co-op filing desk is open until seventeen hundred if the yard wants to contest it."

The yard manager turned the writ over. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> kept his eyes moving across the lot. Two cameras with clear sightlines. One blind corner behind the office shed. Three vehicles in pieces with their hoods up. At the back, in the repair corner, a young man in a work shirt had been shuffling parts around an engine block with more energy than the job called for. He'd stopped. He was standing up.

The son. Not small. Not slow. Reading the gate the way a young man reads it when he thinks his odds are better than they are.

"My own son says we should push back on this," the yard manager said. He was still holding the writ. His eyes went to <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s shoulder — the sheathed sword — then to <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s face. "Arpad's been a good customer. Eight years."

"Arpad bought paper that sold inside a grace window," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "That's a problem between Arpad and the co-op. Not the clinic's problem."

The son came around the engine block. He hadn't picked up a tool. Both hands empty and held wrong — too still, too deliberately open — which meant the wrench on the oil drum was the thing he was thinking about.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> moved without announcing it. One step right, so the gate post wasn't behind him anymore. <entity repo="motif" guid="019d6143-a8e1-7cd1-ab7c-1a4110a2ec8c">Hands</entity> open at his sides. Weight balanced. Nothing drawn. He kept his voice flat and easy.

"Your father's going to tell you to sit down. Listen to him the first time."

The yard manager looked at his son. Something passed between them in the silence — a fight they'd had before today, in a kitchen, at the end of a shift, and were having again now in the way they stood next to each other.

"Sit down," the yard manager said.

The son stopped. Two feet of distance, the wrench on the drum, and the anger with nowhere to go. His eyes went to the sword, to <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s hands, to his father's face.

"We should contest it?" the son asked. To his father, not to <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>.

"We're going to let the man take the printer, and we're going to call Arpad and tell him he's got a co-op problem," the yard manager said. "And you're going back to that engine block until I say otherwise." He let go of the writ. "Bay three. My employee will walk you in."

The son set the wrench down on the oil drum with a sound that said everything he wasn't going to say in front of his father, went back to the engine block, and picked up a socket he didn't need.

<entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> stayed on <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s hip. No rounds drawn, none spent. The son's anger was fair, and it had cost nobody anything.

The gate was open.

<entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity> had the RP-7 loaded and strapped in eleven minutes, talking to the printer the whole time in a low, even voice: "easy with the corner — that's the corner, the corner's fine — we're going to set you on a pad, not the bare deck." When the last strap was set she patted the chassis once with a wide hand, the way you'd settle a nervous horse, and climbed up front without ceremony.

The drive back to <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-849c-7793-bce8-ae238e4576f6">Leavitt</entity> Free Medical took twenty-two minutes. <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity> spent most of it explaining the weight-distribution tolerances of the RP-7's chassis to the printer, in the second person, as a professional courtesy.

The intake nurse took delivery on the apron at 15:40. Signed three copies. Stood a moment with her hand flat on the chassis before the bay doors rolled and it went inside.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> sent <entity repo="character" guid="019fbde4-d680-7bb7-b9f5-5f28c3b8f705">Breckenridge</entity> the confirmation at 15:43. Three words came back at 15:44: FILED AND CREDITED.

The crew logbook pinged at 15:51. He hadn't told <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity> about the job.

15:40 — PRINTER RETURNED TO CLINIC. BIG WOMAN TALKED TO IT (PRINTER). PRINTER SEEMED FINE.
15:41 — THE SIGN ON THE CLINIC DOOR SAYS "NO FEE FOR CARE." DENTS ASKS: HOW?
15:44 — DENTS ALSO SAYS RAFTERS IS NOT CRYING. RAFTERS NOTES THIS IS A FACTUAL DISPUTE.
FILING SEPARATELY: BOSS DID NOT USE THE SWORD. REQUESTING EXPLANATION. — B.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> pocketed the terminal and totaled the day on the apron. Writ, Φ40. Truck, Φ25. <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity>'s afternoon, Φ80. That was Φ145 out against <entity repo="character" guid="019fbde4-d680-7bb7-b9f5-5f28c3b8f705">Breckenridge</entity>'s standard-rate fee of Φ400 — a Φ255 margin. No injury. No rounds spent. A clinic with its equipment back before the end of shift.

Then the intake nurse came back out through the bay door, and she wasn't holding a clipboard anymore. She was holding a diagnostic slate, and her face had gone the color of the apron concrete.

"It won't calibrate," she said. "The head's out of true. Whatever moved it, moved it hard." She turned the slate so he could see the fault cascade scrolling red down the screen. The print head had shifted in its carriage — not catastrophically, but enough. A millimeter, maybe. A millimeter was all it took. "We can't print on this. Not until it's re-shimmed, and we don't have the tech, and the nearest one who does is contracted to the people we took it back from." She looked at him the way you look at a man who has just handed you a debt. "It'll still print. Every line offset the same distance. Every document that comes out of this machine reads forged — timestamps, signatures, the chain of custody, all of it staged in the queue and all of it about to come out crooked. You logged it returned. <entity repo="character" guid="019fbde4-d680-7bb7-b9f5-5f28c3b8f705">Breckenridge</entity> logged it credited. As far as the writ's concerned, this job is closed and this printer works. It doesn't work. And now I've got a signed intake saying it does."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at the three copies she'd signed. At the FILED AND CREDITED still glowing in his pocket. At the margin that had, thirty seconds ago, been clean.

The clinic's writ was official because the clinic's writ *was* official — every line true, every stamp earned. That was the whole trick of a place with NO FEE FOR CARE nailed to its door. You couldn't buy trust here, so you documented it, one honest form at a time, on a machine two payments from being owned outright. And now the machine would make every honest form look like a lie.

<entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity> came up beside him, both hands buried in her jacket pockets, and looked at the clinic door.

"Clean," she said. Thirty-two down, eight to go.

"Clean," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> agreed.

He typed back to <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity>: SWORD STAYS SHEATHED WHEN THE JOB DOESN'T NEED IT. THAT'S THE EXPLANATION.

She nodded once and walked toward the <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> station like a woman with three more jobs before dinner who'd already arrived, in her head, at the first.

He read the <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-a31f-7059-abda-f4a28cc5639c">Halvorsen</entity> engagement file on the walk back.

Twelve pages in <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-a31f-7059-abda-f4a28cc5639c">Halvorsen</entity>'s intake format, put together by someone who understood that in the end the paper is the only argument that holds. The first eight pages were operational: scope, authorization, the tracking-dot delivery chain, the <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-ed6c-7a54-97a5-56afca1f1f19">Rotterdam</entity> timestamp.

Page nine was where the sloppiness lived.
