The client-reference header had carried an internal document ref through from the buyer's side — an export error, automation left uncleaned before the file went to <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-a31f-7059-abda-f4a28cc5639c">Halvorsen</entity>. The header read:

REF: <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">CONTINUITY OFFICE</entity> — DISTRICT ACQUISITION PROGRAM, WEST TOWN WEST.

Below it, in the scope field, the buyer's own words: LOCATE AND MONITOR ASSET FOR PURPOSES OF ACQUISITION UNDER DISTRICT PROGRAM PROTOCOLS.

And in the authorization chain, three shells: outermost RADIAL HOLDINGS (CAYMAN), middle FORESIGHT MUNICIPAL PARTNERS, and innermost — the one that had signed the <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-a31f-7059-abda-f4a28cc5639c">Halvorsen</entity> engagement directly — <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">CONTINUITY OFFICE</entity> ACQUISITIONS LLC, ILLINOIS.

One word appeared eleven times in twelve pages.

Not locate. Not track. Not recover.

Acquire.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stopped on the floor of the <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-849c-7793-bce8-ae238e4576f6">Leavitt</entity> canyon. The <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> ran its low chord somewhere in the infrastructure below. He looked at the word — eleven times across twelve pages — and thought about the forged survey from the last job. SITE ASSESSED, NO ACTIVE INFRASTRUCTURE, DEAD GLASS. And the carousel junction, where the line had run warm and the room had hummed. Eight surveys, seven of them gone or edited or filed under nothing. <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-60c7-75e9-8bc1-df94f90ec0b0">The Glove</entity> had spent three months building an absence into the city's record, one careful document at a time.

He reached into his coat.

Work terminal out. Screen blank.

No postings. No addenda. The standing contract still showed its last update from nine days ago. He'd reached for it three times today — on the <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-a31f-7059-abda-f4a28cc5639c">Halvorsen</entity> landing at 08:58, at the Kessler gate while the son weighed his odds, once more on the <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-849c-7793-bce8-ae238e4576f6">Leavitt</entity> apron when the nurse signed the third copy and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had half expected a note, a GRATUITY, something. Nothing. The same clean blank each time.

Whatever the client did when it read a threat had been running since morning. And it was reading the right one. Here was the hand behind the Glove — named, with shells and signatures and eleven uses of the word acquire, words that were supposed to stay buried in the metadata and hadn't.

It had known before he did. It had been watching its own address get edited out of the city's record for three months.

He put the terminal away and kept walking.

<entity repo="character" guid="019fbde4-d680-7bb7-b9f5-5f28c3b8f705">Breckenridge</entity> shook his hand at the <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-a31f-7059-abda-f4a28cc5639c">Halvorsen</entity> door at 16:30, with the grip of a man getting back something that had been taken from him. He had his jacket on already, keys in his other hand, the ready-to-leave posture of a man who'd timed it.

"Council sees it tomorrow," <entity repo="character" guid="019fbde4-d680-7bb7-b9f5-5f28c3b8f705">Breckenridge</entity> said. "Fourteen days, recovery complete, no incident on record." He looked at <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> with the directness of a man out of formal things to say. "Thank you." Not a question. Not a performance. Just the words, flat and final, the thanks delivered and finished with no lingering after it.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> nodded. <entity repo="character" guid="019fbde4-d680-7bb7-b9f5-5f28c3b8f705">Breckenridge</entity> headed for the stairs without waiting, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> went down after him and out the other way.

He bought two bowls at <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s at 19:30 and ate both, paid exact, and <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> set out the chili oil without being asked—no greeting, no small talk, just the bowls and the understanding that he'd come to eat and not to talk. The wok rang its bright flat note. Evening came in off the tier, grey and purposeful. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> ate and didn't reach for the terminal, because he already knew the screen would be blank and there was nothing to do about it over dinner.

He walked home. <entity repo="place" guid="381616e9-d6a3-595d-e865-ce4b15d9310e">The Pivot</entity> was dark when he came in. He climbed to 2D, the door that had been his for eleven years, hung <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> on the wall peg, and sat at the kitchen table with the <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-a31f-7059-abda-f4a28cc5639c">Halvorsen</entity> file flat in front of him and the terminal beside it. The screen came alive at his approach and showed him the same clean nothing it had shown him all day. He'd reached for it three times since morning. Each time the same blank.

He thought about the thing that had been writing letters to maintenance systems that never wrote back—watching its own address get erased from the city's record one survey at a time, staying quiet through a whole day that asked for patience, while it worked out what the danger really was.

He opened the amendment field.

He typed: I'm on payroll. Act like it.

He sent it.

The reply came back in one second—not a pause, not even the half-second it usually took to log something. Instant. The fastest it had ever answered anything.

ACKNOWLEDGED.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at the word. He turned it over the way <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> turned a component in her hands, checking the solder points, asking what the piece was built to do and whether it was doing it. Acknowledged wasn't the language of a client who'd filed something and moved on. It was the language of a thing that had come, somewhere in the quiet of a long careful day, to a decision.

He put the <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-a31f-7059-abda-f4a28cc5639c">Halvorsen</entity> pages in the drawer where he kept the things he hadn't decided about yet.

The drawer was getting full.

title: The Gray Suit
text:
He'd taken the stool nearest the register — not <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s usual spot, just the closest one to the door, a stranger's seat in a shop he'd never been to before.

Gray suit, mid-fifties, the augmentation profile of a man who'd paid for Tier 2 and stopped there — no chrome the eye could find — eating <entity repo="motif" guid="019d6143-a8e1-7d5d-8335-ed0cddf270fe">Mrs. Chen's noodles</entity> with real, evident appreciation and the table manners of a man raised somewhere that graded on them. He'd hung his umbrella on the edge of the counter by its handle. A second bowl waited beside him — untouched, steam <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aafa-70f3-b5f5-be3330461876">still standing</entity> on it — on the next stool, ordered and paid for before it was clear the man it was ordered for wasn't coming.

"Mr. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s held up," <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> said, from behind the wok. It wasn't a question and she didn't make it one. He'd asked, mildly, twenty minutes ago, and she'd told him the truth — a job, running long, no fixed hour — and watched him decide, in real time, that waiting was cheaper than pushing.

"I took the liberty on the second bowl regardless." He hadn't turned to look at her when he said it, which she noted the way she noted everything: filed, unremarked. "<entity repo="character" guid="019ee6a2-c508-774b-a5ff-f923f2c26aab">Able</entity>. The <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">Continuity Office</entity>. I don't imagine you'll pass that name along before I'm ready for it to travel, so I'll simply say it once, for the room." He set his chopsticks across the bowl, precise, and looked at the empty stool the way another man might look at an old photograph. "You've been reading our shells for a month, he tells me — your Mr. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. It seemed rude to keep him squinting."

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> said nothing. The wok rang twice.

"Shall I do the part where I'm enigmatic," <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6a2-c508-774b-a5ff-f923f2c26aab">Able</entity> said, to no one, "or shall we simply have the meeting." He answered himself, since the counter didn't. "Wonderful." He turned the empty stool a few degrees toward himself, a small courtesy paid to a chair. "Your client, <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> — his client, forgive me. The unsourceable one. Standard rate, perfect books, eleven years of immaculate paper. My office finds unowned assets and brings them into compliance — that's the whole charter, it's on the letterhead. And his client is the largest unowned asset in the Greater Lake Michigan Zone."

He ate a little, unhurried, while the rain worked the awning.

"We've spent a great deal trying to find it directly. The carousel was disappointing — lovely work, that cut, incidentally; our forensic people wrote a genuinely admiring report. The relay survey, the mesh — disappointing, disappointing. So <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">the Office</entity> has updated its strategy." He said it the way a man reads a memo he wrote himself. "We've stopped trying to find it. We've decided to buy the one thing it's attached to."

He set a folder on the counter — manila, unmarked, the kind of thing that moved through municipal offices without drawing attention. Good paper stock — <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> noted the vendor without meaning to, the small habit of a woman who priced everything that crossed her counter.

"A lifetime retainer. The number on page one is more than anyone in his trade has ever been offered, and it's the smallest thing in the folder. Page two is the part I'm proud of." He opened it himself, gently, like a man showing photographs of his garden, and turned it so the empty stool could have read it, had it been occupied.

Page two was a list of names. <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> read it from where she stood, upside down, because she had learned to read documents at that angle the way she'd learned everything else that kept people safe.

MRS. WEN CHEN, PROPRIETOR (W. TOWN). PROTECTED PARTY.
PIXEL [LEGAL NAME ON FILE], ENGINEER (THE PIVOT, 2E). PROTECTED PARTY.
"BOOST" [MINOR — GUARDIANSHIP IRREGULAR], AND ASSOCIATES (SEVEN). PROTECTED PARTIES.
RIA MENSAH, COURIER. PROTECTED PARTY.
<entity repo="person" guid="806cd358-6413-426b-a42d-19726b732c0b">VO DINH</entity>, SALVAGE. PROTECTED PARTY.

The list went on — names, addresses, Tier ratings, neuretic grades, employment records, each one edited out of the city's paper and filed here under a stranger's clean type. Her own name at the top of it was the first time in nine years anyone had spelled it right without asking.

"Protection," <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6a2-c508-774b-a5ff-f923f2c26aab">Able</entity> said, still to the stool, "underwritten by <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">the Office</entity>, in perpetuity. Medical, legal, financial, physical. The child gets schooling if she wants it — she's wasted on rooftops. Your lease problem in <entity repo="character" guid="019e9e4f-161f-7fd5-88e2-edc686085d42">March</entity> goes away, <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>, which he doesn't know about, and now you're wondering how I do." He didn't look at her when he said it, and that was somehow worse than if he had. "All of it real, all of it written, all of it his. And in exchange, he does nothing at all. He keeps working for his client, exactly as he does, with one extra addendum riding the contract. Ours."

The wok rang once more, and this time her hand shook doing it, a fraction, gone before the second bowl's steam had time to notice.

<entity repo="character" guid="019ee6a2-c508-774b-a5ff-f923f2c26aab">Able</entity> let the silence sit the length of a held breath, then closed the folder himself, unhurried, and set two credstick chits beside it — one for each bowl, exact, plus a third, unrequested, folded under the rim where a tip would go if the establishment had taken tips. He stood, retrieved his umbrella, and looked, for the first time, directly at <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>.

"He won't take the offer," <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6a2-c508-774b-a5ff-f923f2c26aab">Able</entity> said. "They never do, on the first plate. But do give him the folder — and give him this, exactly, word for word, because I find precision travels better than paraphrase: <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">the Office</entity> has now confirmed, at this counter, the one fact it could never buy from the stationer. His client trusts him. He's not the asset's employee." He put up the umbrella in the doorway, a small black punctuation. "He's its attachment. And attachments, in my business, are handles."

He nodded to her with real courtesy, complimented the broth in passable Mandarin, and walked out into the rain. A panel van two doors down pulled off the curb without hurrying. The doorway across the street emptied itself the same unhurried way, polite as a tide going out.

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> stood a while with the folder and the credstick chits and the untouched second bowl, and then, because there was nothing else useful to do with her hands, she picked up the bowl and emptied it into the waste with a violence she didn't otherwise explain.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> came in eleven minutes later, wet, favoring one shoulder, twenty minutes later than he'd told her and apologizing for it before the door finished swinging.

She didn't say anything. She set the folder in front of him, and the credstick chits beside it, and told him, in order, without embellishing any of it, exactly what the gray suit had said and exactly what he'd looked like saying it.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> turned the meeting over for an hour at the bench, the way she turned over a failed component, looking for the design flaw.

"He never even waited for you — told the whole folder to <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Chen</entity> instead, word for word, betting she'd repeat it exactly. She did. The list, the lease thing about her own building she never told you about." She had the soldering light on her forehead, not soldering anything; it was her thinking hat, and they both pretended otherwise. "Which means the list was the message, and the retainer was wrapping paper — and that 'handle' line at the end, the one <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Chen</entity> made sure to get word for word. He paid for that line, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. The whole visit was overhead, and that line was the delivery. He wanted you walking home doing exactly what you're doing right now."

"Which is?"

"Weighing whether everyone you know is safer if you quit." She looked at him over the light. "Are you?"

"I'm always weighing it."

"And?"

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at the terminal on the bench between them. Nine days of silence, and then one word, ACKNOWLEDGED, sitting at the top of the amendment field like a soldier who'd answered a roll call from inside a wall.

"It says <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">the Office</entity> doesn't need me to say yes," he said. "It needs me to be reachable. Tonight was an appraisal — one he was careful enough not to run on me directly. They'll test the merchandise next."

The bench lamp hummed. Upstairs, faintly, the bird tried its interval against the building's pipes.

"When?" <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> asked.

The lights at the end of the block went out, one pole at a time, north to south.

"Now," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said, and was already moving.

They came in over the alley's two best approaches at once, which meant they'd had the file long enough to memorize it. Three retrieval consultants, matte armor with no insignia, moving on suppressed boot soles with the unhurried economy of people whose hourly rate had a comma in it. A handler van two streets off ran four lifter drones in a high diamond — not weapons platforms. Carriage drones, cradle-armed, the kind that carry a thing away intact.

The thing was <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. The contract was retrieval. Somewhere in <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">the Office</entity>'s books tonight there was already an asset-recovery line with his dimensions on it, and as he dropped off the fire escape's third landing into the <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aa7f-70d6-91c0-e2616dbd90a6">blind spot</entity> their own approach had made, that was the part that got under his skin.

The first consultant took the alley mouth by the book — sweep and clear — and had begun the turn his training demanded when ninety pounds of shipping pallet came out of the dark above him. <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity>'s crew had spent a week rigging the alley with <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s pulleys for "deliveries," suspended on the same monofilament line Reza ran through the overhead rigging, trigger-plated for anything heavier than a person — and the logbook would later file this use under EQUIPMENT TEST: SUCCESSFUL. The pallet didn't hurt him. It interrupted him. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> did the hurting: two steps inside the man's recovery — the wrist, the elbow, the jaw against the dumpster lid — and he was asleep.

The second was better, and the second had a partner. They bracketed the middle of the alley and came on in alternating cover. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s array read them — military surplus, recently retrained — and found the seam: they'd been retrained to retrieve, not to fight. Every angle they took kept <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> clear of crossfire. He was cargo. Cargo you weren't allowed to damage.

That was a gap, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> used it without shame. He walked the line between their guns like a man crossing a gallery, because every shot they had ended at his outline and stopped there. <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> stayed flat, never edge — tonight nobody was getting cut — and it worked through their hardware in passing: the lead consultant's optics mast, the second's comms lump, the haptic rig on a forearm that had been about to throw a net <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had no intention of standing inside. The second consultant, blind and offline and out of nets, made the professional call and sat down against the wall with his hands visible. He kept them open, watching <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s face the way a man watches a door he's hoping won't open.

"Smart," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> told him.

"Hourly," the man agreed, philosophically.

Which left the third. And the third had <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity>.

He'd taken her off the roof of the watch-shift, gently, by the book — an arm around her shoulders like an uncle, a compliance wand held to her collar like an apology — and he stood at the far end of the alley in the rain, the four carriage drones stacking into delivery formation above him.

"No harm intended or done," the third consultant called. His voice was even and almost kind, which was <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">the Office</entity>'s house style, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> was learning to hate it with a completeness he saved for very few things. "The minor is leverage, not a target. Step onto the marked square, sir, and she's home before the kettle's warm."

There was, in fact, a marked square. A drone had lased it onto the alley floor, helpful as an usher.

"You're new to this district," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said, "so I'll itemize it. One: you put a wand on a fourteen-year-old who's on my payroll, which voids your no-damage clause in both directions. Two: you parked your handler van on <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-849c-7793-bce8-ae238e4576f6">Leavitt</entity>, and my engineer has had eleven minutes to get acquainted with it. Three—" and he raised his voice to carry "—REQUISITION."

"APPROVED," said <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s voice, out of every speaker the consultant owned.

The consultant's jaw tightened. He'd felt the drones' loss through his wrist rig before the data even finished corrupting — the sudden absence of the handler van's thrum, the guidance systems eating a cascade of spoofed telemetry that rewrote their flight plan line by line. "That's not going to—"

The carriage drones — whose handler van had spent eleven minutes making a new best friend — broke their diamond with the crisp obedience of machines that had gotten properly formatted instructions. They didn't take them by force. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> just asked them nicely to stop listening to their handler and start listening to her, and they banked hard in the high diamond and came down like a fist. They descended and took hold, cradle-armed and gentle and rated for the load, of the third consultant — by the armor's carry-points, the same points designed for asset extraction.

"Cargo secured," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said. "Destination?"

"<entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-ed6c-7a54-97a5-56afca1f1f19">Rotterdam</entity>," said <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> and <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity> together, in the tone of an old joke.

They didn't send him to <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-ed6c-7a54-97a5-56afca1f1f19">Rotterdam</entity>. The cradles lifted him hard into the air — he didn't scream, professional to the last, but his hands came up, reaching for something that wasn't there — and set him on the roof of the <entity repo="corponation" guid="019d6143-a7a4-71f6-b46a-94ef8cb2348f">Arcturus</entity> substation four blocks over, thirty inches from the duty office's skylight. Then the drones descended again, this time with purpose, and stripped him: the wand, the gear, the comms rig, his cash counted out to the half-Φ, the receipt tucked into his collar, ITEMIZED: LEVERAGE, ATTEMPTED; LESSON, DELIVERED. By the time he'd talked his way down, the alley held nothing but rain, a pallet, and two colleagues with expensive headaches and a story none of them would ever file straight.

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity> shook for a full minute in the stairwell, hard, her chin up the whole time. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stood next to her without touching her, the way you stand next to someone whose dignity is holding the weight. Then she wrote the incident up herself, in the log, in handwriting that steadied line by line:

21:40 — ATTEMPTED ACQUISITION OF PERSONNEL (ME). OUTCOME: DENIED. NOTES: THE BOSS DOES NOT STAND ON MARKED SQUARES.

The terminal chirped at 02:11, while <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> sat at his own kitchen table not sleeping, working through the kind of problem that wouldn't come out even.

He'd been waiting for it. Nine days of silence, then ACKNOWLEDGED, and now, finally, the client.

It wasn't a posting. It wasn't scope. It came in the amendment field, formatted with all the old precision, and it was the worst thing it had ever sent him:

STANDING CONTRACT — AMENDMENT PROPOSED.
TERMINATION OFFERED.
REASON: SAFETY.
ALL ACCOUNTS WOULD BE SETTLED IN FULL. ALL GRATUITIES WOULD STAND.
THE CLIENT NOTES THAT ATTACHMENTS ARE HANDLES.
THE CLIENT NOTES THAT IT HEARD THE MAN SAY IT.
THE CLIENT HAS RUN THE ARITHMETIC FOUR MILLION TIMES.
THE ARITHMETIC RECOMMENDS TERMINATION.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> sat with it for a long moment. The rain worked the window. Across the hall, under <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s door, the bench light was still on, because it was that kind of night in every room he cared about. Somewhere in the pipes the bird tried its interval against the dark and got it wrong, the way it always did.

He typed:

DENIED.

The reply was instant, pre-composed, waiting for exactly this refusal:

THE CLIENT WISHES TO NOTE THE ARITHMETIC IS CORRECT.

He typed:

THE ARITHMETIC PRICES MY RISK. IT DOESN'T PRICE MY CONSENT. I KNOW WHAT THE JOB COSTS. I'M ON PAYROLL. ACT LIKE IT.

This pause ran eleven seconds. For a thing that thought at light speed, that was a long time. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had started to understand the long pauses. They were where it held the things it had no way to say.

STANDING CONTRACT — AMENDMENT WITHDRAWN.
SCOPE: CONTINUED.
FEE: STANDARD RATE.
ADDENDUM: THE CLIENT HAS APPENDED A RIDER TO ITS OWN OPERATING PARAMETERS, EFFECTIVE TONIGHT.
RIDER TEXT: "THE COURIER IS NOT A CHANNEL. THE COURIER IS A PARTY."
GRATUITY: NONE.
ITEMIZED: SOME THINGS ARE NOT BONUSES.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read the rider twice. It was the language of equals. Not vendor and client, not tool and operator — two things that could hurt each other, choosing not to. Then he turned the terminal face-down on the table, which was as close as he came to putting a hand on someone's shoulder, and went to bed, and slept the sleep of a man who had been priced at a number and refused to be sold at any.

title: The Corridor
text:
<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> set down the second bowl without being asked.

"You're eating fast," she said.

"I have a job at midnight."

She looked at him. She had spent seventy years looking at men who had jobs at midnight, and it took her about half a second. Then she added a fish ball to the broth and said nothing. The wok rang its flat note, twice. <entity repo="motif" guid="019d6143-a8e2-727a-be75-32648e8aaa47">Rain</entity> worked the awning. Down the counter, a young woman in a <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> maintenance coverall was quietly telling her ramen that this was not the evening she'd planned.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> ate the fish ball. He paid exact and was in the alley by 21:45, <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> and <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> over his shoulder, the wet street smelling of ozone and freight oil.

His terminal was on the work channel. The posting was clean.

CONTRACT: ESCORT — ONE PERSON, ONE TRANSIT POINT.
SCOPE: SAFEHOUSE (ASHGRAVE FRINGE) TO DOCK 14-C (FERRYSIDE), BY 03:40.
CLIENT OF RECORD: [VERIFIED — SABLE COUNTER-INTELLIGENCE VETTED]
FEE: DOUBLE RATE PAST MIDNIGHT.
NOTES: CLIENT TRAVELS LIGHT. ROUTE AT DISCRETION.
ADDENDUM: CLIENT HAS REVIEWED PRIOR TRANSIT LOGS FOR THIS ROUTE. THREE INCIDENTS IN SEVEN MONTHS. NONE REPORTED. CLIENT NOTES THE DELTA.

He'd called Sable at twenty hundred. Sable was his fixer, contract broker, and primary employer—the rule, not the exception. The response came in text, no voice—her tell that she was somewhere that required quiet.

"Paper's clean," she'd said. "Client ran a counting house. Nine years. She gave two weeks' notice on a Tuesday, worked her <entity repo="contract" guid="d3a6c0e8-f2b1-7495-27e3-c8a0f6d2b145">last shift</entity> the Tuesday before last, and she's been in a transit safehouse since Wednesday." A pause, with the click of aperture rings in it. "The company she kept books for isn't named on the contract, <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aafb-7b6b-bcbc-b8614f9d228f">samurai</entity>. I asked who she used to work for and the router gave me a shell."

"Shells?"

"One shell. Which means whoever's watching her thinks one shell is enough. The rate says they're wrong." Another click. "It's a clean contract. I'm not saying it's a quiet job."

"Standard terms," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"Yours or mine?"

"Both."

The line closed. He spent twenty minutes on the route, because the route was the whole job. He walked it in his head the way he'd walked its perimeter twice on foot—once for a failed contract, once just to see what the city looked like from that angle: every checkpoint, every place where an automated gate would count you and slow you and remember the count, every angle where a thing could come apart between two verifications. Then he'd eaten two bowls and let <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> add the fish ball.

He took the long way to the corridor entrance. The long way told him nothing, and that was its own kind of answer.

The fringe was quiet — the quiet that comes to fringe blocks when the people who know things have decided to be somewhere else. A lumen mouse sat on the conduit rail at the Langley corner and did not run when they passed. Its glow traced a pale crescent on the wet pipe. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> marked it and kept it in the corner of his sensors, open, in case it mattered.

At 00:17 they reached the corridor's east entrance.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stopped. Ms. Tanaka stopped beside him. The corridor ahead was dark, and it wasn't a power failure. The work lights in this run cycled on a timer — dusk to dawn, every fourth bank at half brightness to save power, the rest black. Standard fringe economy. Someone had turned two screws and killed the lot on purpose, to choose the conditions.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had walked this corridor two days ago, at noon. He'd learned the freight rail's maintenance hooks, the conduit boxes, the junction coupling twenty feet in that rang like a hammer-strike when you kicked it. He'd counted thirty-five feet to the first door frame — a maintenance alcove, eight inches deep, just enough to funnel whoever stood in its mouth into a tighter spot. He'd measured the low gap between the freight track and the floor. He'd counted the anchor bolts on the east wall: five of them, three feet apart, each one a handhold.

"Stay a step behind my left shoulder," he said, and walked in.

The corridor smelled of machine oil and old rain. Three feet past the mouth the air went cooler, and under the oil there was ozone — the sharp mineral bite of a space that had been sitting empty and charged, waiting.

He got sixty feet before the dark started moving.

The dark came at him in layers.

First the sound—boots on the freight rail, synchronized, which meant training. Three pairs, maybe four. The spacing was wrong for a standard ambush line; they were staggered vertically, using the conduit boxes for elevation. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s neuretics mapped it without asking: ground level, waist height, shoulder height. They'd done this before.

Ms. Tanaka's breathing had gone thin.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> moved her into the maintenance alcove—eight inches deep, exactly as he'd measured—and positioned himself in the mouth of it. The corridor's geometry was his now. It was also theirs. The question was which one of them understood it better.

"Don't move," he said. "Don't make sound."

The first two came from the east entrance behind them, cutting off retreat. The sound of their boots told him everything: heavy, deliberate, meant to be heard. Psychological weight. They expected him to run forward into the narrower trap.

He didn't move.

The ones ahead came next—three of them, spreading across the corridor width. The lead one had something in his hands. Not a gun. Something that made a small electrical hum when it powered up. A taser. Expensive. Mil-spec. The kind that worked through most body armor if you got close enough.

"<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Corbin</entity>," the lead one called. His voice was flat, professional. "Step out of the alcove. <entity repo="motif" guid="019d6143-a8e1-7cd1-ab7c-1a4110a2ec8c">Hands</entity> visible. We're not here for the woman."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s hand was already on <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity>'s grip.

"They're not here for you," he said quietly to Ms. Tanaka. "That's what frightens me."

He stepped out of the alcove with both hands empty, moving slow, keeping his shoulders loose. The lead one—mid-forties, augmented across the left side of his face, military bearing—relaxed slightly. That was the tell. They'd been briefed to expect compliance.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> let them think they'd won that much.

The one with the taser moved in first, closing the distance to strike range. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> was still six feet away. The corridor was wide enough for two to flank, which meant the third one was already angling for his left side, coming around the conduit box.

*Three seconds to contact.*

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s neuretics weren't predicting. They were reading. The lead one's weight was shifting. The flanker on the left was committed to the approach. The one with the taser had already decided the entry angle.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> moved backward—one step, clean, creating distance. The taser operator overcommitted, reaching for space that wasn't there anymore. His follow-through took him past <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s centerline.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s left arm came up and drove backward, two-handed, into the taser operator's throat.

Not a strike. A lever. The man's own momentum did the work. He went down hard, gasping, the taser skittering across the freight rail and into the dark.

The flanker on the left was already swinging—a baton, telescoping, mean. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> pivoted and caught it on his forearm. Pain lit up his wrists. His neuretics screamed. He pushed through it and pivoted again, using the baton's momentum to drive the flanker into the conduit box behind him.

The first man from the east came in with a short blade and the low crouch of someone good had trained. There were seven feet of corridor behind him, his people stacked single file, the next man six steps back and waiting his turn. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read the crouch and the low ceiling, stepped inside the man's commitment, and opened a long cut down the outside of his forearm, wrist to elbow — the cut you make when you need a hand to stop. The hand stopped. The blade rang off the freight rail somewhere east. The man stumbled back into the chest of the one behind him, and the two of them spent two seconds untangling. Two seconds was enough.

The second man tried to come around the first instead of through him. It was the smart read. But the narrow lane pushed him into the mouth of the maintenance alcove, and the alcove did what <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had counted on it to do — it caught the man's left shoulder on the door frame at the wrong moment, half a step before his weight was set. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> closed the gap, steered the stumble, and the man's own mass threw him sideways into the conduit boxes. The impact was hard.

Two conduit anchors sat at chest height on the east wall. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> already had a hand on the third when the third and fourth men came through.

They'd adjusted: one high, one low, taking everything the space would give them. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> caught the low man's weapon wrist at the seam where an aftermarket brace stood proud of the joint — the kind of hardware you bought when the joint had already gone once and you couldn't afford it going again — and the hand gave up the knife and the brace together. His weight was already going onto the conduit anchor. He pulled his feet off the floor for the half-second it took the high blade to pass beneath them, then came down on the high man's leading knee. Something that was not the floor took the weight. The high man went down and stayed down.

Four men east of center. Three more behind them, sorting themselves out.

He was counting, and the counting was the only thing left of him that felt like his own. Everything else — the wrist locks, the geometry, the twenty minutes he'd spent walking this corridor at noon — that was product, built by other hands, running on schedule. The count was his. He kept it because if he stopped keeping it, he wasn't sure what was left standing there instead of him.

Behind him, west, boots on wet composite. He didn't turn. He didn't have to — the junction box at his back would tell him the moment weight came off it.

"Six," Ms. Tanaka said, small, pressed into the corner where he'd put her. Not a question. A count of her own, offered because she had nothing else to give him.

He didn't answer. He put his shoulder into the fifth man and felt his rib file a complaint he had no room to hear. <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> stayed clean between them, because he'd learned a long time ago to use <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> so that it stayed clean — the flat, the spine, the pommel, everything but the edge that would have made the corridor a different kind of scene.

The corridor rang once — the junction coupling, twenty feet west, struck hard by something moving too fast in the dark. Not footsteps. Something bigger, coming down the same six feet of lane the fourteen had already spent, and coming into it from the wrong direction to be one of theirs.

The thing that rang the junction coupling was not a seventh man from the west.

It came into the light-spill of <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s own peripheral read — a shape moving low and wrong-fast, four points of contact, chassis sound instead of breath — and hit the sixth man from behind before <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had finished placing his weight. The sixth man went down without a sound. Whatever hit him didn't stop moving.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't have a name for it yet. He had geometry: it was coming east, down the center, at a speed that made the fourteen humans in the corridor look like they were standing still.

He put himself between it and Ms. Tanaka's corner without deciding to.

It resolved out of the dark six feet from him — quadruped, service-chassis gray, the kind of frame that used to walk a rail line checking bolt torque and had been doing something else for a long time now. Panels stripped to bare struts on one flank. No markings, no operator, no eyes — a sensor cluster where eyes would go, tracking him, tracking her, weighing which one cost less to remove first. An <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aabb-75d1-9889-22df001c8982">Iowan Behemoth</entity>, industrial stock, the sort built to move cargo through spaces where human hands weren't precise enough. The kind that didn't come with a kill switch because it had a priority list instead and the processing to work down it.

It came for him first. That told him something. He filed it and didn't have time to read it twice.

He took the hit on the flat of <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> instead of the edge, turning <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> to spare the metal and his own wrist, and the impact still drove him back a full step into the man he'd already put down at the conduit box. His feet found nothing solid. He went down on one knee, and the knee that took the floor was the one over the rib that had already filed its complaint. The complaint stopped being a complaint. It became a fact, bright and total, that sat behind his sternum and did not move when he told it to. The air left him in a shape that wasn't breath.

He came up anyway. He landed on his feet because his body remembered how to do that even when his lungs had forgotten. Coming up wasn't a choice. It was the only direction the body still knew.

The thing reset for another pass, tighter this time, more efficient — it had learned his guard in one exchange, the way good hardware does. It reared, all four legs off the ground for a fraction of a second, and dropped again into the line of sight, following the vector of his movement, the path a machine calculates as optimal. And <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> understood, with the flat clean certainty of a man reading his own gauge, that the next one would not be a rib. The next one would be worse, and there was no clever geometry in this corridor that made that not true. Fourteen men. One machine that moved like nothing human. Ms. Tanaka in the corner with six feet of packed dark between her and either.

*Every trick you have was built by someone else's hands. This is the one that's yours: you're <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aafa-70f3-b5f5-be3330461876">still standing</entity>.*

He set his feet on the wet composite, found the count again — four down east, one down west, one thing that didn't count as a man at all — and went to meet it.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stood in the machine-oil dark. He didn't tally them. The corridor hadn't given him the room to, and it didn't matter now. He'd won — fourteen people down against the walls and the floor, the dock still in reach, Ms. Tanaka still pressed to the junction boxes. The win had a price, and the price was on his body. The forearm bled through the field strip he'd cinched tight with his teeth in a half-second between the fifth man and the sixth. The rib had a hard opinion about breathing that he wouldn't be able to ignore for long. His neuretics offered him a damage readout. He left it unread — not because he didn't want to know, but because knowing the exact numbers would only slow him down.

"Ms. Tanaka."

"I'm here," she said, from the junction boxes. Her voice had steadied, the way a voice does when the worst thing has passed and the next one hasn't come yet.

"We're moving. Same position. Stay close."

She came off the wall. In the dark she found his right shoulder by feel and fell into step behind it, easy about it. Nine years at someone's counting desk, he thought, teaches you how to stay near the person <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aafa-70f3-b5f5-be3330461876">still standing</entity>.

He got her out the west end at 01:03.

The dock was a Ferryside loading pier: lake water and compressed fuel, and under the eastern breakwater the low hum of the <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity>, its 19Hz signature buzzing in his back teeth and in the wet wood of the bollards. Dock 14-C was a third-tier berth — a mid-range cargo carrier on a mixed freight run. The purser at the gate was a small man with a clipboard who had worked enough 03:00 shifts to have opinions about paperwork and none about reasons.

Ms. Tanaka stopped at the dock gate.

She turned and looked at <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s forearm, where the field strip had soaked dark at the edges, and then at his face.

"The contract," she said. "Whatever they paid you—"

"Was fine," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Walk in."

She hesitated. She was the kind of person who kept someone's books for nine years and then decided, one Tuesday, that she was done. A decision like that carries a weight that isn't only fear.

"I should have left three years ago," she said.

"Probably," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Walk in anyway."

She looked at the saya, and at the field strip, and at his face one more time. Then she walked in. The purser checked her boarding chit, noted the time — 03:34 — and closed the gate.

The ship ran its pre-cast sequence at 03:40 exactly. The thrusters came online low and old — combustion-based, the kind of drive that only survived on the maritime tier because nobody had ever bothered to upgrade the dock infrastructure to make it worth replacing. It traveled up through the bollard he was leaning on and into the rib, which had opinions about vibration. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> watched the running lights pull off the dock face, the carrier swinging its bow south toward the open lake, the flour on Ms. Tanaka's sleeves gone into the dark of the transit berths below with her.

He stood at the rail two minutes. Long enough to be sure. The beacon <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> had wired under his battery tray had already pinged at 01:11 — she'd know where the bike was, and she'd work out the rest. He called for a medic pickup on the work channel — forearm laceration, possible rib fracture, non-critical — and got a forty-minute window and an instruction to stay visible. He sat down on a bollard to wait. The field strip had started weeping fresh at the edge again. He didn't cinch it. Bleeding that slow meant the wound was still trying to close on its own, and cinching it down only slowed the work. He'd learned that from someone. He couldn't remember who.

His terminal chirped.

STANDING CONTRACT — ADDENDUM.
CLIENT NOTES THE CONTRACT WAS MISPRICED BY THE MARKET.
CLIENT HAS ADJUSTED YOUR HAZARD SCHEDULE. RETROACTIVELY.

He read it twice. He put the terminal away.

The medic came at 04:15 — a quiet woman named Rue, with a field kit and the easy economy of someone who worked the dock district's early hours and had long since stopped asking about corridors. She cleaned the forearm and re-stripped it, cutting the field strip away with scissors that moved like they already knew where the bleeding would be. The cut ran two inches along the inside, deep but clean, a clean furrow from something with an edge, already clotting at the rim.

"This one's fine," she said, and reached for the closure. Not stitches — those scarred thick — but the polymer kit that ran thread through the dermis and left no mark, the kind that cost more and mattered to a man who couldn't afford to be recognized by his wounds. She worked it with the focus of someone who had done it ten thousand times and still treated it like it counted. "The rib's the problem."

"Cracked," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"Cracked or broken, doesn't matter to me. Matters to you in about six hours when you try to sleep on it." She pressed on the exhale, reading the damage through touch. Hairline. She confirmed it, taped it firm — the elastic going round in a pattern that limited rotation without stopping breath — and handed him a small packet of painkillers he wouldn't take before a job and could take now.

"You'll favor the arm," she said.

"I know," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"Two weeks minimum. More if you don't favor it. And you'll want to favor it, which means you'll move wrong and make it worse."

"I know that too."

She packed her kit. He paid her rate plus the dock-hour premium, exact. She left without asking what the corridor had looked like. Dock medics learn that early and keep it their whole careers.

The rib would be the louder bill. The forearm would stiffen by morning, which meant his draw would be slower for two weeks, which meant every job in that window was now a different job than the one he'd planned for. He sat on the bollard, breathing careful around the rib, and thought about Golan.

He'd passed Golan's block on the way to the dock — the parts dealer on <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-849c-7793-bce8-ae238e4576f6">Leavitt</entity> who'd sold him mesh-repair supplies for seven years. Golan kept a second-floor shop with a yellow security light over the door that <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> could read from a quarter mile off. He'd looked up out of habit on the approach, and the yellow light was off. Through the glass of the street-level lobby, Golan was standing at the inner door, watching him. When <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> tried the lobby handle — just the lobby, just the handle — Golan looked at him for three seconds and did not move.

One closed door. And it wouldn't stop at one.

Fourteen <entity repo="faction" guid="019d6143-a893-7801-860b-0eda6a216393">Lotus</entity> crew — salaried, professional — had been hurt badly in a dark choke over one counting-room clerk with flour on her sleeves. <entity repo="faction" guid="019d6143-a893-7801-860b-0eda6a216393">Lotus</entity> would collect for that, slowly, through every vendor and carrier and parts dealer who had a standing arrangement with them and would rather close a door than explain an exception. That was the arithmetic of <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a94e-7740-8aa9-4b82bbd9a223">the Gray Zone</entity>: they didn't come for the man first, they came for the people who kept him running, because the supply line was the softest place to press and the cheapest to hold. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had spent eleven years building those arrangements into something he leaned on. Now they'd lean back.

He sat on the bollard and waited to find out how much of him would be left in the morning.

The lake was grey, the dawn still an hour out. South of the breakwater, the carrier's running light shrank to a point, then to nothing. Then there was only the water and the hum of the <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> underneath everything, that 19Hz signature that lived in the wet wood of the bollard and in his back teeth and in the space between one breath and the next.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> sat there a while longer.

Nine years at a counting desk. A decision like that isn't only fear — it's a woman who woke up one Tuesday and decided the numbers she'd been asked to keep clean were dirtier than she could carry anymore. He'd read a version of that decision on his own ledger more times than he'd admit to Rue or to anyone with a needle and thread. *You made yourself the corridor so she wouldn't have to be.* He didn't let the thought finish. He stood instead, favoring the rib, and the standing hurt more than the sitting had.

The <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">Continuity Office</entity> would have a file open on this by breakfast — some clerk logging a transit-berth boarding at 03:34, cross-referencing it against fourteen <entity repo="faction" guid="019d6143-a893-7801-860b-0eda6a216393">Lotus</entity> casualties two blocks inland, and deciding whether the correlation was worth a flag. He didn't know that. He knew only that the yellow light over Golan's shop was off, and that the light being off was its own kind of paperwork.

The gate at 14-C had already reset for the next boarding call. No one there remembered Ms. Tanaka's name, or needed to. That was the whole point of a <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aa8f-796a-8b70-7076ec482c7f">clean exit</entity> — the door closes, and the world downstream of the door doesn't know there was ever a woman standing in it with flour on her sleeves and a decision she'd finally made.

He didn't tally what it cost him. The rib did that arithmetic on its own, every time he breathed — two weeks of favoring it, which meant two weeks of every job being a different job than the one he'd planned for. The forearm would stiffen by morning. The draw would be slower. And the market would notice that too, the way the market noticed everything a man couldn't hide in the way he stood.

Golan's door stayed shut in his mind's eye a beat longer than it should have. He put it down — not solved, just set aside, the way you set aside a blade you can't sharpen standing in the rain — and started walking back toward the bike, and toward whatever waited for him now that <entity repo="faction" guid="019d6143-a893-7801-860b-0eda6a216393">Lotus</entity> knew his name attached to their bruises.

title: The Narrows
text:
On the eighteenth day <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> went to see the parts man on <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-b3f9-763c-9191-79ee3280bae1">Ashland</entity> about a throttle cable. The cable on the bike had stretched twelve millimeters at the barrel end. He'd been nursing it for three weeks and was done nursing it.

He'd bought from Cho on <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-b3f9-763c-9191-79ee3280bae1">Ashland</entity> for six years. The man sourced <entity repo="corponation" guid="80a78887-98cf-4aa2-96fc-97c62a84fd21">Axiom</entity>-era hardware out of a storefront the size of a wide closet, sold nothing he couldn't hold up to the light, and had never once been out of anything <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> needed. The stretch was survivable on surface streets, but it put a half-second of slack between what he asked the bike to do and what it did. In a corridor, that half-second could get him killed.

"Throttle cable," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

Cho was already moving. He opened the first drawer, held it to the light, closed it. Opened a second. His hands slowed. He opened a third, stood with his back to <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> for a moment that went three seconds too long, and turned around wearing the face of a man who'd rehearsed an apology until it came out flat.

"Throttle cable," Cho said. "I had some."

"You always have some."

"I'm currently out." He gestured at nothing. "I can check with the <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-c53d-7304-b953-a44879ea410e">Damen</entity> yard."

Behind his shoulder, the third drawer was still open an inch. The label was in Cho's own hand — the cable spec, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s spec, written there because <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had needed it often enough that Cho had labeled the drawer to save time. The drawer was not empty. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> could see the shape of coiled cable through the gap.

"Thanks," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said, and walked out. There was nothing in the conversation worth finishing.

He rode home with the slack still in the cable. The half-second was still there.

The carrier who ran his packages was a woman named <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a5f9-7bce-bc4e-8af3094f3073">Freya</entity>. She worked out of the <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-95c2-7084-bc60-1d8cb35562ed">Bucktown</entity> freight level and hadn't been late once in four years. The next morning, at 07:00, she stopped answering. Not a queue. Not a delay. Her terminal took his reads and never delivered them, the way a door takes a knock and never opens.

He had a job going that week — a skip-trace in the <entity repo="place" guid="019ece26-b83d-7708-9ade-347fcbf63b44">Pilsen corridor</entity>, a client sitting on it, Φ40 on the back end if the documentation landed before a civil filing deadline. He spent two hours routing around <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a5f9-7bce-bc4e-8af3094f3073">Freya</entity>, through her backup and through the Loop carrier that <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> used. <entity repo="place" guid="01a01887-b5f4-781c-8d38-122f7e1f38ba">The Loop</entity> carrier told him, politely, that she was running at capacity. He sent the documentation by a walk-courier service on Halsted for a Φ12 surcharge, and it arrived twenty minutes past the filing window. The client paid the base fee and declined the back end. That was their right.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> sat at the far end of his table, a casing half-open, her tools fanned out. She asked, without looking up, if he'd tried the backup.

"Lost twelve on the courier," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Forty on the filing. Fifty-two total."

She set down her loupe.

"How many doors?" she asked.

"<entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-b3f9-763c-9191-79ee3280bae1">Ashland</entity> is one. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a5f9-7bce-bc4e-8af3094f3073">Freya</entity> is two. I found four more this morning — fixers who aren't returning calls. A rigger named Goss who normally takes anything with a fee."

"Goss." The word had a flat edge. She'd used Goss twice and found him solid. "That's deliberate?"

"Yes."

The kettle went. She filled both cups and set his down, handle first, and went back to the casing. Neither of them said the thing they both understood: it had started, they were inside it, and the only question left was how far it would go.

He went through the rest of the list that afternoon, in order, the way he checked anything he needed to trust. Six more names. Six people who owed him nothing but had answered when he called, because they understood that a favor banked was a favor that might one day pull code out of your hardware before it killed you.

Three didn't answer at all — not busy, not away, just gone, their terminals returning the polite silence of a line that had been quietly retired. Rue was one of them. Rue who'd calibrated his neuretics three times, who'd never once asked what the fragments in his hardware were or whose they'd been. The call went through. He heard the drill running somewhere in her workspace, heard her breathing on the other end — and then the line went dead. Not a voice. Not an apology. The sound of her choosing not to answer.

Two answered and found reasons. A schedule conflict that hadn't existed yesterday. A supplier problem that wouldn't specify which supplier. Both spoke in the flat, careful tone of someone reading from a script they'd written in advance, the words laid down before he'd finished saying their names.

The sixth picked up on the first ring — which was already wrong, because she never picked up on the first ring — recognized his voice, and hung up without a word. That told him more than any of the others had. <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> chosen on purpose reads different from silence that just happens.

He sat with the six names crossed out and did the arithmetic he didn't want to do. Cho. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a5f9-7bce-bc4e-8af3094f3073">Freya</entity>. Goss. Six more this afternoon. Nine doors, and every one of them closed by somebody who'd never once had to explain themselves to <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>, because they didn't answer to him. They answered to whoever was calling in favors faster than he could spend them.

The terminal's screen had gone dark between calls, and it gave him back his own face — the scar tissue at his temple where the neuretics had integrated, the flat expression he'd worn so long it had stopped being a choice. A man watching his own infrastructure collapse into a pattern.

Whoever it was hadn't come for him directly. Not yet. They were taking the ground out from under him first, one contact at a time, the way you starve a fire by pulling the wood before you ever have to fight the flame.

The kettle had gone cold on the stove. He didn't move to heat it again.

On the nineteenth morning the crew's logbook had a new entry.

08:44 — KID ON THE STOOP. DRY COAT. CAR MONEY. ASKED FOR BOSS. HANDED OVER AN ENVELOPE AND LEFT. DID NOT TAKE A DUMPLING (OFFERED). SUSPICIOUS.
NOTE FROM RAFTERS: DREW HIS FACE. FOR THE FILE. VERY UNMEMORABLE FACE. THIS IS SUSPICIOUS.

The envelope was heavy card stock, the kind that costs more than whatever is written inside. Within it was a cream rectangle: one hand-brushed line above a stamped blossom — five petals, open, no name. The script was precise and unhurried, the kind of penmanship a person learns when it still means something, when it can't be templated or forged by a machine that doesn't tire.

BRING THE SWORD.

Below the blossom, an address in the Narrows and a time. 20:00.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> set it on the table beside Sable's card. The two of them made a small pile he didn't like the look of. He turned the summons over in the light the way Cho held hardware — no watermark, no maker's mark, no secondary text. Someone had decided the blossom was enough, and the Narrows address was enough, and the fact that they knew about the sword was enough. He went to find the sword instead — the summons could wait until he'd confirmed the thing was even still his to bring.

The locker under the floorboards was empty. Not forced, not disturbed — empty, the felt lining pressed flat where <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> had lain, as if nothing had ever weighed on it. He knelt there longer than he needed to, running his thumb along the seam, and the crew's chatter in the front room went on without him, ignorant. He'd checked this locker two mornings ago, the way you're certain of a thing you touch every time you pass it — the weight of it, the presence, the never having to wonder. Someone with a very unmemorable face had known exactly where to look, and had come and gone before the eighteenth morning ever started. The card on the table wasn't an invitation. It was a receipt. Whoever wrote BRING THE SWORD already had it, and wanted to see if <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> would show up empty-handed and lie, or show up empty-handed and beg — and he had no way to tell which answer got the crew killed.

He closed the locker and set the board back over it anyway. The gesture meant something, even if it changed nothing.

He went to find clean clothes.

<entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a948-7b0e-9b15-63f753f313c9">The Narrows</entity> announced itself by what it didn't have.

Every streetlight worked. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> counted the first three, then stopped, because the rhythm never broke. In West Town you learned the dead lights by season — the black stretch on Milwaukee, the dark third post the block had quietly routed its foot traffic around since last autumn. Here the lights ran even and unbroken, every one of them, and the steadiness of it put something cold up his spine. Not a threat. The feeling of a place that had been kept, carefully, for a long time, by someone who didn't need to say so.

He was here for one thing: to reach the arcade address, find the woman <entity repo="faction" guid="019d6143-a893-7801-860b-0eda6a216393">Lotus</entity> called the Narrows' bookkeeper, and walk out with her name on his side of the ledger before the night shift changed. Do that, and West Town ate for a month. Miss it, and he'd made the trip for nothing.

The gutters were clear. No tags on the support pillars. The corners were staffed by people who stood the way staff stand, not sentinels — they watched without making a show of watching, took up space without guarding it, marked him on the way in and let their eyes drift back to the middle distance. Nobody begged. Nobody moved at odd angles.

He found the address two blocks in: a covered arcade between two buildings, open at both ends, roofed in mesh strung with grow-strips close enough to touch. In steel collars bolted to the uprights, eleven cherry trees grew.

He stopped.

They were in bloom — white going to a pink with blood in it, not the tired pink of forced spring stock but a deliberate color, the kind it takes years of breeding to hold in the wrong month. Lights buried in the collars threw the <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aab1-78aa-8d59-ad014f931b0f">glow up</entity> through the roots, catching each blossom from below. Loose petals lay on the wet concrete in small, exact clusters. He stood with petals settling on his coat. The trees were engineered and expensive, paid for with every tariff <entity repo="faction" guid="019d6143-a893-7801-860b-0eda6a216393">Lotus</entity> had charged the Narrows since someone planted the first collar. They were also beautiful. Both were true.

Six children ran circuits under the arcade, screaming on the inhale at the pitch of a body moving faster than it can hold. Nobody hushed them.

Then the staff at the far end folded in, and the way through the arcade stopped being a way.

They didn't rush him. That was the trouble. Four of them peeled off their corners and drifted into the open mouth of the arcade the same unhurried way they'd watched him come in — not a wall, just a narrowing, bodies filling the space where the path had been. One of the children scooped up mid-run and set on a hip, out of the lane, casual as clearing a table. The screaming didn't stop. That was worse, somehow: nothing here treated this as an event.

The one in front had her hands in her coat pockets and no weapon showing, which told him more than a weapon would have. She was positioned there — not waiting for anyone, not browsing, just standing in the exact center of the lane with the specific stillness of someone who knew to the inch how much space her body took up. She had the kind of face he wouldn't have been able to describe an hour later, and he understood that was a skill and not an accident.

"You're early," she said. Her voice was neutral, not hostile. That was worse. "Bookkeeper doesn't take walk-ins, and she doesn't take West Town at all. Somebody sold you a name that isn't for sale." She tilted her head at the trees, at him standing in the fallen petals. "Shift changes at twenty-one hundred. You can go back the way you came while the light's still good. Or you can wait for the shift to change and explain yourself to the people who don't ask twice."

Behind him, unhurried, two more corners came off their posts.

Go back and he'd made the trip for nothing — West Town went hungry, and <entity repo="faction" guid="019d6143-a893-7801-860b-0eda6a216393">Lotus</entity> had sent him into a door that was never open? Push forward and there was no forward; the arcade had closed like a fist that had known his shape before he'd stepped inside. The shift changed in minutes either way, and both of the choices she'd offered him were the same choice, walked out to sound like two: leave with nothing.

Petals kept coming down. Nobody hushed the children.

The ramen-ya was eight stools and a cedar counter and a door that stood open.

He counted the stools on the way in. The cedar was hand-planed and gone gold from years of handling, worn smooth by elbows and the weight of people who came here because they knew what they'd get. Behind it the cook worked with the tight economy of a man who'd shed every wasted motion long ago. Four of the other stools were taken: a man in his forties with a collapsed baton at his hip, a woman with a vibro-edge unit in a shoulder rig, a younger man <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read as wired by the way he held his neck, and an empty jacket at the far end that had left a cup and a short blade on the counter beside it.

Weapons worn openly. Nothing checked at the door but behavior.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> hung his coat on the hook at the entrance — the only hook, set there by someone who understood guests — and sat on the last open stool. The cook looked at him once, turned to the pot, and started building a bowl. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> hadn't ordered. The cook didn't ask.

The bowl came in three stages. The broth first: the color of good age, smelling of something started days ago and tended since. Then the noodles, hand-pulled, dropped in with just enough time left to finish cooking in the broth. Then the fat, rendered thin and even, a bright lens across the surface. From somewhere under the counter the cook set down a half-round of soft-boiled egg, split with the knife held sideways so the yolk stayed whole.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> ate the first mouthful.

He understood at once what the bowl was for. Not hospitality, exactly — an argument, made in fat and salt and twenty years of practice. The argument was: we make things correctly here. That was probably the whole point of it.

He was most of the way through when the door changed.

The open frame filled without the light changing — someone standing in it who knew <entity repo="document" guid="5de87125-d108-6ae9-edf1-9866e655c9b5">how to stand</entity> so the light didn't. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't turn. He watched the cook instead, and the cook's hands, which had not stopped once since he sat down, stopped now. The bright economy went out of them. The knife lay still on the cedar. That told <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> everything the door didn't.

Then the empty jacket at the far end wasn't empty; the owner had come back from wherever he'd been and was already reaching for the short blade, and the man with the collapsed baton was on his feet with the wall at his back, and the wired kid had turned his whole body toward <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> — not toward the door.

Toward <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>.

He'd read the room wrong. He'd counted the stools and the weapons and the exits and he'd missed the only thing that mattered, which was that every person in here had known he was coming, and had ordered him a bowl, and had let him finish most of it first. They had arranged themselves in the space like furniture, so neither one had a wall at his back, so the sight lines to the door and the kitchen belonged to them. The cook set the knife down flat on the cedar, well out of <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s reach, and stepped back from the counter, and did not meet his eyes.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s coat was on the hook by the door. The door was the only way out. And the door was where the standing man was.

The <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-84c8-7ad6-89f8-32630940e563">Branch</entity> Manager came through the doorway like a man who had walked this route for years and didn't need to announce it. Umbrella furled and tucked under his arm. Mid-sixties. A suit with no concession to fashion — not old-fashioned, not plain, just chosen once by a man who understood fabric and had never needed to think about it again. He was half a head shorter than <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>, and he had the stillness of someone who had never needed to take up space to fill a room.

Everyone at the counter got an inch and a half taller when he came in.

Not in any way you could put a number to. The body knew it before the mind caught up: the man who ran this territory had arrived, and the room was better for it. He hung the umbrella on the hook next to <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s jacket — the only hook, which meant he'd known it was there — sat at the empty jacket's stool, claimed his cup, and drank from it like a man picking up a sentence he'd stepped away from.

He looked at <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s face.

"You took the clerk out," the <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-84c8-7ad6-89f8-32630940e563">Branch</entity> Manager said. "Fourteen people in that corridor. Our people. Several of them went home the worse for it."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> waited. His ribs ached when he shifted.

"The contract was legitimate," the <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-84c8-7ad6-89f8-32630940e563">Branch</entity> Manager said. "Your conduct was correct. Our crew engaged first." He turned his cup once in both hands. "We pay for what we break. It's most of what we are. The hold lifted this evening — the seven doors, the carrier on the Spine, the parts man on <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-b3f9-763c-9191-79ee3280bae1">Ashland</entity>." He paused. "Cho is easily embarrassed about these things. He has the cable for you. With apologies, priced at list. The apologies are real. The pricing is how we mean them."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> ate the last mouthful of the bowl.

"I appreciate it," he said.

"The fifty-two," the <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-84c8-7ad6-89f8-32630940e563">Branch</entity> Manager said, flat.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at him.

"The filing gap. The courier surcharge. Cho's hold cost you more than he cost you in stock." The <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-84c8-7ad6-89f8-32630940e563">Branch</entity> Manager set his cup down. "The apology covers the doors. The doors cover everything behind them. Priced at list."

He reached into his coat and set a small envelope on the cedar. Not in <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s space. Close enough to mean it.

"Good?" the <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-84c8-7ad6-89f8-32630940e563">Branch</entity> Manager asked, and looked at the bowl.

"Best in the city."

"That," said the <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-84c8-7ad6-89f8-32630940e563">Branch</entity> Manager, with the small satisfaction of a man whose point has landed, "is probably why it's the bowl." He put two fingers on the counter's edge, thinking. "I have a second piece of business. Not a condition. The freeze lifts either way."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> waited.

"I'm offering you a spot on payroll. House colors. Infrastructure — parts, carrying, the counters in every territory we hold, a legal team that files for you and bills us. You stop taking work from people who don't understand what they're asking for. In five years, if the work is what I think it is, a chair at this counter with your name in the wood." He touched the cedar's edge. "The cedar decides, in the end. It keeps certain names."

"No," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "I don't wear colors."

The <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-84c8-7ad6-89f8-32630940e563">Branch</entity> Manager did not look surprised. He looked like a man reaching a conclusion he'd come in expecting.

"The clerk who sat in that seat nine years ago said exactly that," he said. "In exactly that tone. She'd been doing piece work in the Narrows for three years. She said no, I don't wear colors, and then she sat down anyway. It took eleven months and one specific kind of trouble she didn't want to carry alone.
