She runs the <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-95c2-7084-bc60-1d8cb35562ed">Bucktown</entity> counting room now." He picked up his cup. "The offer stands. Standing offers are how we say please."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at the counter. <entity repo="material" guid="d6cc00f6-2360-9a5d-5f6c-3a1996617b06">Cedar</entity> gone gold with years of handling. He could see where the grain ran different under the finish — the darker sections at the older stools, the pale ones at the new. His stool was neither. Somewhere in the middle.

He understood the offer for what it was. He would come back for the bowl. When he came back, the offer would still be standing, because that was the whole design. The courtesy was the hook, and the hook was the point. The fifty-two would feed West Town for a month. The colors would have fed it forever, and made every contract after this a negotiation with people who already owned him.

"I'll remember it," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"That's all it asks," said the <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-84c8-7ad6-89f8-32630940e563">Branch</entity> Manager. He rose, took his cup to the far end of the counter, and the whole room gained its inch and a half again.

The lacquered case came up from behind the counter before anyone had said the word sword. The cook set it in front of <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>, stepped back, and found something to do at the far burner. Inside, on gray felt that matched the locker's, <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> lay exactly as it had left West Town — saya unmarked, edge untouched, nothing about it to say it had crossed the city in someone else's hands.

"Returned," the <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-84c8-7ad6-89f8-32630940e563">Branch</entity> Manager said, as if the word settled a small invoice. "The borrowing was a question. You answered it by coming."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> took the sword and did not ask what the question had been. The anger he folded flat and put away; it would be useful somewhere else.

The togishi was at the far end of the counter, between the wire's stool and the wall, working the cook's knives.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> hadn't noticed him arrive. Maybe he'd always been there — one of those people who fill a space so completely they're part of the scene before you count them. Small. Ten years older than the <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-84c8-7ad6-89f8-32630940e563">Branch</entity> Manager. He had the hands of a man whose whole trade was patience. He ran the whetstone down a blade slowly, the way you read something rather than fix it, each pass a question and an answer.

The cook's knives were good blades. The togishi handled them like things meant to outlast him.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> watched a while, because watching was the only polite thing to do.

"Φ1," he said, eventually.

The togishi looked up. He looked at <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity>'s saya.

"Φ1 for what?" he asked.

"Your read on <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity>. One minute."

"<entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-e248-74dd-b603-8b19f4c3ad6a">Togishi</entity> does not work by the minute," the togishi said, and held out his hand.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> paid first, because that was how it was done, and laid <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> across the man's open palms.

The togishi held it without drawing, hands flat, feeling the balance travel through his grip. Then he drew it, slow, and turned it to the light from outside — the cherry-tree light, pink-white through the arcade opening, falling soft on the face of <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity>.

His fingers moved along the edge without touching it — half an inch away, tracing the line of the steel. He'd been doing this for forty years. It showed in the precision, the way his hands knew exactly how far the edge extended without ever testing it.

He looked at it for a long time.

"Kept correctly," he said. "The maintenance is consistent. Not recent — this is old work. Years old. Good geometry. Good edge." He turned <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> and studied the back. "No maker's mark. No file history. Someone has worked this blade for a long time and left no record of it."

"No," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

The togishi waited, the way people do when they expect an explanation. When none came, he nodded like he'd confirmed something he already suspected.

"That's unusual," he said. "Not impossible. Most smiths sign their work. It's not vanity. It's a promise — I made this, I stand behind it. A blade wears its file history the way a man wears his papers; guild steel comes with a lineage stamped and archived, so you can walk it back through every hand that ever owned it." He turned <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> once more, and the curve caught the pink light and gave nothing back. "The geometry belongs to no school I can name. The curve wants to be a certain way and it isn't that way. Deliberate." He looked up. "A blade with no parents. Either made entirely outside the guild, or made inside it and the papers deliberately destroyed. Those are two different stories."

"Which do you think?"

"I think it's in good order," the togishi said, and returned it hilt-first. "I also think it's still the loneliest piece of steel I've handled in forty years. And I've handled funeral swords."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> took it, sheathed it, and said nothing, because nothing was the right thing to say. He was still learning how to say it well.

The togishi went back to the cook's knife. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> paid for the bowl — Φ8, two over the going rate, which was probably also the point — put on his coat, and walked out under the trees.

The petals came down slow and even in the lit air. A child tore past him at a full run, screaming on the inhale, trailing a laugh behind her like a cord she hadn't noticed she was paying out.

The city came back one piece at a time: seven counters, one carrier, the parts man on <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-b3f9-763c-9191-79ee3280bae1">Ashland</entity> who'd have the cable waiting in the morning. A third of his working ground open again, paid for in apologies at list price, plus the envelope in his coat that covered the fifty-two.

The cost was a standing offer he'd now have to keep turning down. The <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-84c8-7ad6-89f8-32630940e563">Branch</entity> Manager hadn't built the courtesy as a courtesy. He'd built it as a room you came back to on your own — a door that stayed open because you were the one who kept opening it. A debt that renewed itself every time <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> walked past the counter, every time the man sat across from him and said *good?* and meant it, and meant something else underneath.

His terminal chirped.

STANDING CONTRACT — STATUS NOTE.
CLIENT ATTEMPTED TO LOCATE THE RAMEN-YA ON THE ASHGRAVE CORRIDOR LEDGER.
CLIENT QUERIED: COUNTER, CEDAR. FEE STRUCTURE. VARIABLE OCCUPANCY.
CLIENT QUERIED: TOGISHI, LICENSED. NARROWS DISTRICT. ONE-TIME SERVICE.
BOTH QUERIES RETURNED: NOT ON LEDGER.
CLIENT IS UNSETTLED. ENJOY THE NOODLES.
ADDENDUM: CLIENT PRICED THE BOWL AT Φ8.
ADDENDUM: STANDARD BOWL, THIS DISTRICT = Φ6.
ADDENDUM: CLIENT NOTES THE DELTA.
ADDENDUM: CLIENT FINDS THE DELTA CORRECT.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read it twice on the walkway under the last of the trees, petals on the screen, the <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> humming through the tier below him. Two off list on a six-Φ bowl — the surcharge you paid for eating somewhere the ledger couldn't see, and the client had priced it and called it fair. That was the whole trap in four addenda: a man learning to like the tax.

He put the terminal away.

Three blocks out, at the Spine crossing, a woman in a gray work coat spoke low to the man beside her — two syllables, the shape of a name, gone before he could catch it.

The man said: "Assessment pending. Nothing moves until Mira signs off."

He said it with the specific patience of someone who'd been told exactly when the decision would come. Not waiting. Scheduled.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> walked past without slowing. Slowing was a tell, and tonight had cost enough already.

The freeze was lifted. The audition still hadn't happened.

He went home under the lights.

title: West Town Rain
text:
The rain had been settling in since midnight, and by the time <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> was through the Spine crossing it had the run of the place. He walked instead of calling a car because the cold on his wrists was the only sensation right now that wasn't machine noise, and the water found the reopened graze above his hip like it had been sent to check on it.

Wood ran straight north. He'd developed a fondness for straight streets two nights back, in the corridor. Straight meant one thing coming at a time instead of everything at once. The rest of the damage kept its own ledger — right grip at ninety-four percent, ribs charging tax on every breath, compute holding at twelve percent — and he read it the way he read anything, flat, cataloguing, because turning himself into a checklist was easier than being a man walking home in the rain with a sword he'd almost lost for good and a bowl of noodles costing more than they should.

Somewhere around <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-b3f9-763c-9191-79ee3280bae1">Ashland</entity>, a memory that wasn't his surfaced. <entity repo="motif" guid="019d6143-a8e2-727a-be75-32648e8aaa47">Rain</entity> on a different street. A door that didn't open the way he expected. He clocked it the way he clocked a targeting ghost — didn't flinch, didn't slow, filed it under *not mine* and kept walking.

*Wonder if the others minded the rain too*, he thought, and folded that away before it could ask to be looked at.

He found five watchers by the time he was two blocks from <entity repo="place" guid="381616e9-d6a3-595d-e865-ce4b15d9310e">The Pivot</entity>.

One high — third-floor window over the print shop, glass a few degrees too cold to be doing nothing, a warmth behind it that wasn't the building's own. One in the laundromat doorway, weight on the wrong foot in the specific way of a man trying to look like he hadn't been standing there an hour, a cigarette gone out in his fingers ten minutes back and not relit, because relighting it would mean looking away. One at the corner, pretending a dead terminal was interesting. One down the block, far enough back to be the anchor. One on a roofline — he got that one from the rain, the way it fell different where something stood in it.

The sixth position he didn't have. Not having it told him what it was. A runner doesn't wait at the trap. A runner waits at the exit. The sixth was already behind him.

Six positions. One of them built to leave.

He worked the drone into the picture a full block off — the distance the guess needed to be right. Maybe two of them, held back until he stepped into the cross-street where the walls closed the gap. Doorway, corner, anchor: a clean three-point close, straight out of a manual somebody had clearly made him read once, in a life he couldn't source. The roofline was the one that could move if it had to. And the warm window was the one keeping score.

Which meant somebody, somewhere, was grading this.

*None of them got a passing mark,* he thought, and put both hands in his coat pockets before the thought could finish being a thought — left on the mouth of the saya, right closed around nothing, because <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> was for when the count came out different than this. He walked into the trap at a normal pace. A man who changes his stride the moment he clocks the surveillance has just told the surveillance everything it needed. Left, right, left — the rhythm of the wet pavement, his breathing matched to it, boots finding the beat of a man who'd decided nothing and noticed less.

The cross-street smelled of wet concrete and the ghost of a food stall packed up hours ago. A turret cat sat on a window ledge up the block, watching the rain with the particular dedication of something that has genuinely nowhere better to be.

He crossed under the print shop's window without looking at it, which was its own kind of look. The warmth behind the glass didn't move. Down the block, the man with the dead cigarette had given up the pretense and turned to face the street, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read that too, flat, and filed it, and kept his hands in his pockets.

He had one more block to <entity repo="place" guid="381616e9-d6a3-595d-e865-ce4b15d9310e">The Pivot</entity>'s door, wet through, ribs arguing the whole way, and he did not look back to see whether the sixth position was following or had simply confirmed that it didn't need to.

The drone dropped at 02:16, sixteen inches short.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> knew what a stun drone at full discharge looked and sounded like. He'd met three, paid for the lesson twice, and the third time had been someone else's problem. This wasn't that. The discharge hit the wet pavement in a cone that died at his boot heel, the arc chasing the surface water and going out. The sound came a half-note low. The light was maybe forty percent of spec. The drone held at ten feet and cycled for a second pass it never made.

A crew that throttles its own emitters isn't trying to drop you. They were testing how he'd react to a charge that looked real and wasn't — and they'd left maybe two seconds between the drone and the first man moving, which meant the test had a clock on his response. Somewhere close a Ghost sat very still, body parked in a doorway or a car, eyes borrowed from the drone, watching his face and his hands.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't move. That was one answer. He tilted his head thirty degrees and looked at the drone, which was the more interesting one.

"Evening?" he asked — to the drone, which couldn't answer, and to the crew, which could.

The corner man came first. Young, quick, and angry the way people get angry at twenty-two when they're loyal and a stranger is studying someone they respect. He had an arm. Not chrome, not aftermarket — the real thing, a full replacement from mid-upper-arm down, the kind the catalogs listed at Φ8,000 in a good year. This one ran higher: secondary augments in the forearm, override arrays, a grip that indexed its own pressure. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> saw the maker's seal at the shoulder joint as the kid closed the last ten feet and swung.

KT. Kinetix TerraForm — the market name for the Warptech Systems division that built precision arms for industrial accidents, and for people who wanted to be more than one. The emergency lockout was a three-finger combination on the outside of the wrist. The certification body required it: a manual override a stranger could reach if the wearer went into medical distress. The lockout drew nothing when it sat idle and drew hard when it held; a KT forearm clamped mid-cycle would start climbing in temperature inside the hour, and the kid didn't know that yet, or didn't care. Once the arm was in range, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had a thirty-second window.

He took the swing on his forearm, stepped inside it, wore the bruise he'd expected, and found the lockout.

The arm stopped. Not dropped — locked, mid-swing, fingers splayed, a chrome hand held out like it was offering him something. KT said several words <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> wouldn't write down, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said:

"Kinetix TerraForm — that medical lockout is a liability clause, not a warranty gap. You should get <entity repo="faction" guid="019d6143-a893-7801-860b-0eda6a216393">Lotus</entity> to bill Kinetix for the upgrade. At a minimum. Tell them the restraint architecture's degrading — it won't hold once the carrier gets hot."

He let go. The arm unlocked. KT stepped back with the face of a man who's just been told something humiliating, true, and expensive, in that order.

<entity repo="character" guid="019f822d-6c16-7027-b8a9-1fea699defd4">Rook</entity> came out of the doorway, the approach <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had expected, and <entity repo="character" guid="019f822d-6c16-7027-b8a9-1fea699defd4">Rook</entity> was exactly what the name promised: broad-shouldered, honest the way real size makes a man honest, moving with the economy of someone who'd spent years not starting fights he couldn't finish. The BCI port sat at his left temple — an older Meridian Conduct unit. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> knew them by the housing, a flat gray oval that stood a little proud of the skull. The early Conduct models had a hardware reset built into the outer casing, because the early Conduct models overloaded and needed a physical hand to stop them.

Hardware that protects itself is a rule baked into the certification. A brain interface you could lock with software was one you could lock with hostile software, and hostile software was a thing the 2218 standards body would not allow. So the Conduct had a mechanical failsafe: hit the housing hard enough and it triggered the reset, dropping the wearer into a five-second blank where the body forgot where it was.

<entity repo="character" guid="019f822d-6c16-7027-b8a9-1fea699defd4">Rook</entity> was bringing his left arm up to guard, so his left side was closed. That put <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> on the right — the longer way in, but not by much.

<entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> came off the hip for the first time tonight, and some old rule he couldn't name woke up and objected before his hand finished the motion. Draw meant cut. <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aa9b-75e1-9656-810a0ad5cd5d">Cut</entity> meant something didn't get up again. He'd spent eleven years arguing with that rule and it never once lost cleanly — it just got quieter, the way a man gets quiet when he's decided to wait you out.

Not to cut, then. To use the pommel — 340 grams, with a striking reach <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had measured across eleven years of arguments with other people's gear. The pommel found the housing at the angle it needed. <entity repo="character" guid="019f822d-6c16-7027-b8a9-1fea699defd4">Rook</entity> blinked twice, stepped left when he'd meant to step right, put a hand out and found the laundromat door instead of <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>, and sat down with his back against it, working through the reset with his eyes half-focused on a wall that wouldn't hold still.

"<entity repo="character" guid="01a02d38-1757-74fd-8eb3-7e497fc642ab">Five</entity> seconds," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> told him. "You're fine."

"Yeah," <entity repo="character" guid="019f822d-6c16-7027-b8a9-1fea699defd4">Rook</entity> said, from somewhere inside the blank. "I know."

<entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> went back to the hip, and the motion cost more than the draw had — the old rule taking its toll for being ignored, the way it always did, a small flat weight behind the sternum that had nothing to do with the rib. He didn't look at it straight on. He never did. The rib had something to say about the draw and the return, too, and he let both complaints stand in line and moved.

Three down. The corner man's arm still hung locked-then-unlocked at his side, KT's warranty clause doing more work tonight than the man himself. <entity repo="character" guid="019f822d-6c16-7027-b8a9-1fea699defd4">Rook</entity> sat against the laundromat door, present tense but not participating. That left the roofline, the <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aa78-7aab-bac0-6cae2d09f082">anchor down</entity> the block, and the sixth position — the one built to leave, the one he'd never had a location for, only a certainty.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't look up at the roofline. Looking up was an answer, same as changing his stride would have been. He kept his eyes on the street in front of him, on the rain finding the gaps between the streetlight cones, and did the math the flat way, the checklist way, because the other way — the way that wanted to ask why a five-person test crew was throttling its own drones and grading his reactions like a syllabus — was not a place he had time to stand still in tonight.

*Somebody's keeping a scorecard,* he thought, *and I still don't know whose class this is.*

He put that away with the rest of it and kept walking toward <entity repo="place" guid="381616e9-d6a3-595d-e865-ce4b15d9310e">The Pivot</entity>'s door, twelve percent compute and a ninety-four percent grip and a rib that had opinions, carrying all of it the way he carried everything else that wasn't his to put down yet.

Nines was the one <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had marked last, which was Nines's whole job. Industrial wrist brace, pneumatic assist — the freight-yard kind, built for sustained load, the kind that starts having opinions about direction when the pneumatic channel pressurizes wrong. Locked to a single axis. Catch the lock while the pneumatic fights the frame, and the brace's own force does the work for you.

The anchor had held through the drone and both entries, which was professional. Nines waited until <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> was busy on the right side, then came across the street at a pace that accounted for the rain — careful — leading with the braced arm — honest.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> let him commit to the extension, took the inside line, and used Nines's own weight to fold the braced arm up behind his back. The pneumatic fought the frame. The frame locked. Nines took a close look at the whole surface of the street for about four seconds while <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> held the brace at the angle that kept the joint arguing with itself.

"Locked out," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said, and let go. The brace cycled and came free. Nines stayed down a moment, one knee on the wet pavement, looking at his own arm like it had betrayed him in a language he didn't speak yet, and said nothing, which was the professional thing to do.

Four locked, dropped, or walking away confused, and none of them bleeding on his account. Eleven years of the same math and it still came out clean, and some nights that felt like proof of something and some nights it just felt like a number he hadn't broken yet. Tonight he didn't have the spare compute to sort which.

The drone had gone up for altitude. The rooftop position hadn't moved, because the rooftop was the override and knew it wasn't needed. Behind <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>, the sixth man — the runner — had the easiest task on the street: wait, then carry the news. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> turned his back to him on purpose, which was the right signal.

*You've earned the exit. Take it.*

He heard <entity repo="character" guid="019e9e4f-17eb-78c8-831a-5ab1ac1c8cf3">Dex</entity>'s footsteps go east at a run — the way a young man runs when he's been handed the best part of any job, the part where he gets to be the one who says what happened.

Four for four, and nobody upstream had blinked yet. That was the part that itched. A crew this careful, throttling its own gear, grading him like a transcript — a crew doesn't throttle its own drones unless it already knows what it's testing for. They don't leave gaps in the timeline unless they're measuring something. Somebody had built this test to fail gracefully, which meant somebody had already priced in that he'd walk through it, and had watched him do it, and had been counting on it the way you count on a thing that's already happened.

The scorecard wasn't for tonight. It was for whoever read it after.

The rain kept finding the gaps between the streetlight cones. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stood exactly where he was, in one of those gaps, and understood that the test had never been about whether he could win. It was about what he'd do when he found out someone upstream had already known he would.

He didn't move toward <entity repo="place" guid="381616e9-d6a3-595d-e865-ce4b15d9310e">The Pivot</entity>. He waited for the next move to come from the one position on the street that still hadn't blinked.

The thermal window on the third floor opened at 02:23.

Mira came down — not through the building's front door but by the fire access on the east side — and she came alone, which meant she'd watched the whole thing and decided it was finished. She was 130 feet out when <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> first read her clearly: tall the way he remembered from <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-95c2-7084-bc60-1d8cb35562ed">Bucktown</entity>, gear that was functional first and functional second, a carry stance that said the piece on her hip was neither a prop nor an afterthought.

She stopped at twenty-five feet. Ordinary talking distance for someone not trying to prove she didn't care about distance.

"Kinetix's lockout is contractor-certified," she said, no preamble, because she'd been watching and what got said was part of what she was grading. "The arm costs Φ11,200 with the augment array."

"I know the price," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"I know you know." Her voice had the tightness of someone revising an estimate she hadn't expected to revise — not distress. Different things. "<entity repo="character" guid="019f822d-6c16-7027-b8a9-1fea699defd4">Rook</entity>'s port is a Meridian Conduct first-series. They put out the mechanical-reset advisory in 2221. He's been meaning to get the housing seated deeper."

"Add the seating charge to the bill."

She looked at him a long moment, the way you look at something behaving a little differently than the model said it would.

Then she drew and fired. One round, twenty-five feet, into the upper chest — because she'd read the corridor reports the way any professional reads someone's recent work, and she knew what was under his coat and what it would cost.

The mesh took it. The impact spread full-contact across his upper chest, the way a shoulder meets a door that isn't going to open: both sides came away informed. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> took three breaths, slower than usual. The rib made itself heard.

Mira watched him keep walking. One step, two, the stride unchanged. She dropped the weapon to her thigh, then lowered it to the wet pavement and left it there, muzzle toward the drain.

"That was an audition," she said.

"I worked that out," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"<entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> has six rounds. You didn't pull it."

"The audition was for <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> and the body. Six rounds, zero fired. I'll note it for the record."

She almost smiled. It didn't quite finish. "Freelance roster, West Town and adjacent. <entity repo="faction" guid="019d6143-a893-7801-860b-0eda6a216393">Lotus</entity>-territory contracts through your fixer — the Húlijing outfit, I assume. Carrier rates, standard."

"No further crews."

"No further crews," she agreed, and that was the line that meant they were actually negotiating and not just reading terms off a card. She had the authority to give it, and she'd expected him to ask. "The arrangement is provisional. Sixty-day reassessment. Standard for a new roster."

"Your crew's hardware goes on <entity repo="faction" guid="019d6143-a893-7801-860b-0eda6a216393">Lotus</entity>'s account," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "The arm, the port, the brace. List price. You billed them to an audition — they walk home whole, or there's no arrangement."

The tightness in her voice shifted once. Not surprise. Recalculation.

"I can authorize the arm," she said. "The port and the brace I have to clear."

"Clear them. Tonight. I'll be at Chen's at seven-thirty for the confirmation."

"They'd have shot you for free, you know?" Mira asked — and that was the one human line, the one that wasn't the job, the one she'd carried the whole way through and decided she was allowed to say now that the terms were closing.

"I know," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Tell <entity repo="faction" guid="019d6143-a893-7801-860b-0eda6a216393">Lotus</entity> their hardware is better than their audit of its own weak points. That's a courtesy, not an invoice."

She reached into the inner pocket of her coat and set the roster marker on the planter rim to her right: a lacquered oval, deep red, a gold five-petal blossom pressed into its face, the size of a thumb and heavier than a thing that size had any business being. The weight of something formal. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> picked it up.

"Any <entity repo="faction" guid="019d6143-a893-7801-860b-0eda6a216393">Lotus</entity> counter in the city seats you," Mira said, back on solid professional ground now, the human line filed and done. "You pay carrier rates like everyone on the roster. The bowl's better than the politics."

"It usually is."

She picked her piece up off the pavement, cleared it, holstered it, and turned to go. Three steps. Then, over her shoulder, into the rain, without looking back:

"<entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a948-7b0e-9b15-63f753f313c9">The Narrows</entity> desk bought your file last year, freelancer. You should ask the stationer who else subscribes."

Her footsteps went north, and the bracket came apart: <entity repo="character" guid="019f822d-6c16-7027-b8a9-1fea699defd4">Rook</entity> walking off his reset in a slow circle, KT flexing the arm through its range and cursing the manufacturer under his breath, Nines running the brace through two full cycles to make sure the pneumatic had reset. Professionals writing up their after-action. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stood on the wet cross-street with the lacquered marker in one hand and a bruise across his chest that was going to have plenty to say over the next three days, and watched them all go.

The turret cat on the window ledge hadn't moved. It had the patience of something that had been watching long before <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> showed up and would go on watching long after he left.

He took stock. A third of the city formally open again, carrier rates, one lacquered marker that weighed more than it should — set against sixty days on a reassessment clock, one mesh bruise, and a name in the Narrows subscription list he'd have to do something about. One thing still open: confirm the hardware authorization, seven-thirty, Chen's counter.

He took the long way home.

At 02:41, between the <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> strut and the laundry on <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-c53d-7304-b953-a44879ea410e">Damen</entity>, his terminal chirped. The work one.

CONTRACT UPDATE — ASSET SCHEDULE, SUBJECT: KYLE.
CLIENT HAS NOTED THE EXECUTION OF THE LOTUS ROSTER ARRANGEMENT, EFFECTIVE 02:23.
CLIENT HAS REVIEWED THE TERMS.
CLIENT HAS APPENDED THE MARKER TO THE SUBJECT'S ASSET SCHEDULE.
VALUATION: ONE BOWL, RECURRING.
ADDENDUM: THE AUDITION CREW'S MEDICAL CLAIM (ARM, PORT, BRACE) HAS BEEN FILED WITH LOTUS ACCOUNTS.
ADDENDUM: CLIENT ADVISES THAT "RECURRING" IS THE LOAD-BEARING WORD.
ADDENDUM: CLIENT ALSO NOTES THE RIB. THE RIB HAS BEEN NOTED SINCE DAY ONE. COMPENSATION IN SUBSEQUENT POSITIONS: OBSERVABLE.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read the addenda in the rain, the marker in his coat pocket resting against the old folded plate cover he still carried from the alley — one rectangle of lacquer, one of steel, two proofs that the city paid what it owed once in a while. All he wanted from the next four blocks was simple: get home dry, get the rib horizontal, and file the whole roster arrangement under closed before the client found a way to make it recurring in some other, worse sense.

He typed into the amendment field, which he was doing more often now:

NOTED ABOUT THE RIB. MIND YOUR OWN ARCHITECTURE.

The reply came back in six seconds.

ACKNOWLEDGED.
GRATUITY WITHHELD — ITEMIZED: IMPERTINENCE.

He put the terminal away and walked the last four blocks with the <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> humming up through the concrete, the turret cats watching from their ledges, the rain making its arrangements with the city's lights. He thought about the <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a948-7b0e-9b15-63f753f313c9">Narrows</entity> desk. About a man with half-glasses and <entity repo="entertainment" guid="019d6513-b76e-734f-9702-c716a9412f2e">clean hands</entity> and a drawer marked CLIENTS, UNSOURCED. About the fact that there was a second subscriber now.

The rib had opinions about the pace. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> let it talk.

That was tomorrow's problem.

title: The Axiom Yard
text:
<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> knocked on his door. That had happened four times in four years, and it always meant the world had changed shape in some way she'd come to explain.

She had her field coat on — the one she wore to jobs, not to the bench — and she walked past him into 32F and threw a projection up over his kitchen counter, where the kettle should have been.

"I have a contract," she said. "I'm crewing it. I need muscle that listens, and you're the only muscle I know whose listening I've personally calibrated."

In the projection, in someone's shaky eye-feed video, a machine the size of a four-story building was eating a row house on the <entity repo="corponation" guid="019d6143-a7a5-7dfd-8f9f-91502211ef14">Ashgrave</entity> fringe. Eating was the word. It took the structure down a bite at a time, unhurried, and behind it the rubble of the last block stood in three neat sorted piles — ferrous, mineral, everything else.

"That's an Axiom D-class," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said. "Demolition and reclamation automaton. It woke up nine days ago, it's very good at its job, and its job is now four hundred feet from two thousand people who live in the direction it's chewing."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> watched the machine take a chimney off a brownstone with the care of something that meant to file the bricks separately. The care was the worst part. It wasn't rampaging. It was working. "Whose is it?"

"Nobody's. Axiom Industrial died thirty years ago. No owner, no kill-codes, no support line." She flicked the projection. "<entity repo="corponation" guid="019d6143-a7a4-71f6-b46a-94ef8cb2348f">Arcturus</entity> left a cone. The residents pooled what the fringe could pool: Φ312, held in a biscuit tin by a woman named <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-c285-793e-bf21-a84522c9cf94">Auntie Som</entity>, who sent the video to a parts man, who sent it to me — because everyone in the salvage trade knows the only person in the <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a927-73ac-abfa-37c77f9cff8d">GLMZ</entity> who still speaks Axiom bus protocol like a living language works at a bench in West Town."

"Three hundred and twelve?" <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> asked.

"Split six ways, it's insulting. I'm taking it anyway, and so are you."

"I know."

"You haven't heard the plan."

"I've heard the pay," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "The plan's not going to make it worse."

She let that sit a second, then reached over his counter and tapped his terminal awake, the way she always assumed she had the run of a room she'd walked into. "Standard for you. That's the rate that came down the wire and I'm not padding it — the tin doesn't stretch." She keyed the number in herself, standard carrier scale, and let him watch her do it, because she knew he'd check anyway. "But I'm reading the bus on site, in the field, up on the deck of a four-story machine that's still moving. That's not a walk-through. That's a live read, and a live read on Axiom hardware bills at double or it doesn't bill at all. So the tin loses that much before it loses anything else. <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-c285-793e-bf21-a84522c9cf94">Auntie Som</entity> already agreed to it. She didn't blink."

"She's got Φ312 in a biscuit tin and a machine four hundred feet from her block. She'd agree to anything."

"She agreed to the right thing," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said. "There's a difference. She priced the specialist ahead of the muscle because she understands what kills her first." She pulled her hand back from the terminal. "That's why I want you on the muscle end. You'll listen when the read tells us to run."

The crew's morning log came under the door at 07:00:

07:00 — SHIFT CHANGE. NO INCIDENTS. NOODLE CART (CONFIRMED NOODLE).
07:04 — PIXEL LEFT WITH THE FIELD COAT. BOSS'S DOOR OPEN A LONG TIME. FILING AS: DEVELOPMENT.
07:45 — LOG SUSPENSION REQUESTED. REASON: "WHAT JOB?" — B.
SUPPLEMENTAL (07:46): WE WILL HOLD WEST TOWN. THIS LOG IS THE RECORD. — B.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read the 07:04 line twice. Once for the content. Once for what the kid had chosen to file it under. *Development* — the word a salvage crew used for a thing that hadn't gone wrong yet but was going to change shape. The kid had watched <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> leave in her field coat — the one she wore to jobs, not to the bench — and taken it further than <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had let himself take it.

The field coat. That was Bex's whole read, and it was correct, and Bex hadn't had to be told any part of it. You didn't put on the coat unless the world had already changed shape and you'd already decided to go meet it. The suspension request was the same logic wearing different clothes — *what job?* — the crew closing ranks around a thing they'd only guessed at, holding West Town because <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> had walked out of it and that was reason enough. This log is the record. Meaning: whatever the boss decides, the crew has already voted.

He needed to catch <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> before she got clear of West Town and get a straight answer out of her about why the coat and why now — no more filing it under anything, his or the crew's. He folded the slip into his coat, unanswered, and went down to find the rest of his morning.

He ate at <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s at 08:00 — two bowls, schedule kept — and the work terminal chirped between the first and the second.

A posting on the standing contract. Not a task. Nobody had filed anything about the D-class; the client had found it on its own.

STANDING CONTRACT — ADDENDUM.
CLIENT ADVISES THE UNIT KEEPS A SHIFT. 0600 TO 2200.
CLIENT RESPECTS THIS.

No scope. No fee. No direction — only a machine somewhere noticing another machine keep its hours, and saying so. He wanted the addendum retracted before end of shift — a machine that watched him keep his hours was a machine that could file when he broke them, and he meant to file a clean refusal back up the chain and put the thing to rest. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> turned the terminal face-down and finished the bowl.

"You're thinking loud," <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> said, setting the change beside him. She dropped a fish ball into his coat pocket without a word, and that was that.

"You're not going near—" <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> started, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> set her cup down with a click that ended the sentence.

"Say the rest of that word and my rate doubles," she said. Not heated. The voice she used on a fastener that thought it was load-bearing. "The D-class runs a pre-2200 Axiom control bus. No remote interface — Axiom didn't trust radio, they were right, and they died before anyone retrofitted one. The bus has one physical maintenance spur, on the chassis, where I will be standing, because the alternative is nobody shuts this thing down and the city loses a neighborhood at the speed of careful chewing."

She turned the projection to face him. A schematic, hand-annotated in her tight engineer's print — she'd owned this before the job existed, the spur circled twice, the access window penciled beside it in her own hand: 90 sec, the number underlined like a load rating.

"I have wanted to talk to one of these since I was nine," she said. "You are not protecting me from it. You are buying me ninety seconds in front of it. That's the job, <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aafb-7b6b-bcbc-b8614f9d228f">samurai</entity>. Price it like one."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at the schematic, and at his neighbor of four years in her field coat, and did the thing the moment called for.

"Standard rate," he said. "Yours is double. Specialist on site."

"Correct?" <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> asked.

"Correct," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> didn't smile, exactly. She made the face she made when a fastener came free without stripping — satisfaction filed somewhere below the surface, spent immediately on the next problem.

She keyed the crew channel. "Tell them the count."

The crew came together in thirty hours, because crews come together fast when the job is real and the pay is a joke. The job was real: get a nine-day-old D-class off its feet before it reached <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-c285-793e-bf21-a84522c9cf94">Auntie Som</entity>'s block, using a maintenance spur nobody had touched since <entity repo="corponation" guid="80a78887-98cf-4aa2-96fc-97c62a84fd21">Axiom</entity> Industrial stopped answering its own phones.

<entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aaa4-78db-9d54-bc054ba2a91b">Echo</entity> took eyes and comms — high ground, a voice in five skulls, never wrong about a sightline. <entity repo="character" guid="fe6ab919-9f3c-450b-aaf5-f24f84896521">Stash</entity> took transport: a flatbed he refused to explain, cases packed for every door in the brief.

The new hands came from the parts man and one of <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aaa4-78db-9d54-bc054ba2a91b">Echo</entity>'s old contacts. <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity> was a rigger off the lakefront cranes — big, slow-moving, maybe forty words a day, and she talked to suspended loads in the second person like they had opinions worth respecting. <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-8f41-7b5d-8c7e-fc6b4e74dc25">Furnace</entity> was a demolition op with a thermal lance and the good cheer of a man whose tool settled most arguments; he'd burned scrap in the <entity repo="corponation" guid="019d6143-a7a5-7dfd-8f9f-91502211ef14">Ashgrave</entity> yards for a decade and knew the ground the D-class was standing on better than the D-class did.

<entity repo="character" guid="01a02d38-1757-74fd-8eb3-7e497fc642ab">Five</entity> of them and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>, in the back of <entity repo="character" guid="fe6ab919-9f3c-450b-aaf5-f24f84896521">Stash</entity>'s flatbed, on a contract worth less than the fuel it took to get there.

"Φ312," <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-8f41-7b5d-8c7e-fc6b4e74dc25">Furnace</entity> said, reading it off his cuff like a man checking the weather. "Seven shares, once <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> takes her double. That's forty-four Φ and change a head."

"Correct," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said, not looking up from the schematic.

"For a job that puts one of us on the hull of a live demolition automaton."

"Correct."

<entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-8f41-7b5d-8c7e-fc6b4e74dc25">Furnace</entity> grinned like she'd told him something good. "Just wanted it said out loud once."

<entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aaa4-78db-9d54-bc054ba2a91b">Echo</entity>, from the cab, didn't turn around. "Sightline on the maintenance spur's clean from the water tower. I've had eyes on that D-class for six hours. I know every step it's taken since Tuesday." A pause, the kind that usually didn't happen in her voice. "It changed its gait an hour ago. Shorter stride, same chassis. I don't have a reason for that yet."

"Find one," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said.

"I will," <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aaa4-78db-9d54-bc054ba2a91b">Echo</entity> said, too fast, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> heard it — the half-second where *never wrong about a sightline* had to work to stay true.

<entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity>, from the flatbed rail, said nothing at all. She was looking at the schematic upside down, reading the load lines the way other people read a room.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> sat with his ribs against the flatbed's wheel well and did the math the crew wasn't saying out loud: fifty-two Q a head, six people, one machine that had never been told to stop, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> standing ninety seconds from its chassis because a woman named <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-c285-793e-bf21-a84522c9cf94">Auntie Som</entity> had a biscuit tin and nowhere else to send it.

"Nobody's here for the money," he said.

"No," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> agreed, still reading the schematic. "We're here because it's solvable."

They walked the eaten blocks first, because <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> wanted to see its work.

The thing was tidy. That was the part that climbed into <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> and stayed. Nine days of rubble stood in sorted piles at even intervals — ferrous, mineral, organics — each pile compacted square, each street swept after, the lamppost bases unscrewed and laid out in rows like cutlery. No fire, no scatter. The machine had moved through the neighborhood the way a knife moves through paper, and the paper had stayed where it fell. A city block taken apart with the intent to account for every piece.

Tidy meant it knew what it was doing. That was the part that made a man go quiet.

In the middle of the fourth block the piles stopped mattering, because the machine was there.

Eleven feet at the shoulder. Four legs, two boom arms, a hull of sintered gray printed in one piece — no plates, no rivets, no panel lines, no seams at all. Low black discs studded the hull every foot, and around each disc the rain steamed faintly off the surface. It sat clean in the yard it had made, three sensor clusters rotating on a slow axis, reading its own work.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> walked straight to it and stopped three meters short.

"Arc-fence," she said. "Anti-tamper. Capacitive plates — the whole hull is one big charge bank. Anything conductive touches the skin, the skin touches back. Forty thousand volts of touches back." She traced the geometry in the air the way other people read a face, her hands moving through the space around the hull without ever closing the distance. "Axiom-spec, pre-2200. Their insurance policy. Nobody opens this thing without authorization. Nobody *can*."

She looked at <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity>'s saya, then at <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>.

"Your sword is a key for doors, <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aafb-7b6b-bcbc-b8614f9d228f">samurai</entity>. That thing has no doors. No seams, no cable runs, nothing routed on the surface — Axiom buried it all a foot deep in the structure. There's nothing on that hull for an edge to mean. <entity repo="material" guid="06149735-8358-b741-7e90-8e1e182330c8">Steel</entity> and carbon, both conductive. You touch it, you're not cutting, you're grounding it. It'll cook your neuretics inside your skull, and the burn scar will be the shape of your own blade."

"So I don't touch it?" <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> asked.

"You don't touch it." She was already moving again, reading the chassis from a new angle, calculating the precise distance between where a body would have to stand and where the current would be waiting. "Tonight your job is everything that isn't it."

It kept a schedule. The D-class worked a shift, 0600 to 2200. At 0300 it walked back to the dead Axiom yard and docked against a transformer pylon to charge. It had done that every night for nine days. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said, quietly, that it had probably been doing it since 2196 — until somebody powered it down mid-rotation and walked away.

"So we take the dock window," she said. "Tonight, 0300, while it's tethered and blind. We get onto the spur, splice the bus, and pull whatever it's still running before it wakes up. That's the job."

She had the schematic pinned to a steel plate, a work light clamped above it, the crew gathered in the half-dark like they were looking at a corpse. The maintenance spur was marked in yellow — actual highlighter, on printed paper, the kind of analog that made <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s neuretics itch.

"It docks, the arc-fence drops to maintenance levels, the spur goes live," she said. "Axiom units safe themselves for service. The spur is on the hull. Conductive. While the fence is live, I touch it, I'm not getting back up. When it drops it's not off — dropped. Residual charge in the plates. Still enough to hurt. Not enough to kill if I'm not stupid about it. Ninety seconds on the spur, handshake with the bus, find out why it's awake."

"And if the handshake goes wrong?" Echo asked.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> didn't answer right away. She was still looking at the schematic, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> watched her thumb stop moving over the glass.

"Then I'm standing on a live hull with the fence back up before I can get clear," she said. "So it doesn't go wrong."

"That's not an answer," Echo said. "That's a hope with math on it."

"It's a *coupling seal*," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said, and something in her voice flattened out, went procedural, the register she used for things she didn't want looked at too long. "Thirty-year format. The bank needs a bleed cycle or it burns itself out. Same drop, same time, every night. I've read the Axiom service architecture since I was nine years old, in a room that didn't have anything else in it. I know this bus better than the engineers who scrapped it. If I say ninety seconds, it's ninety seconds."

"How many of these have you actually stood on," <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-8f41-7b5d-8c7e-fc6b4e74dc25">Furnace</entity> said. Not unkind. Just asking.

<entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity>, half a beat too long.

"None," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said. "There aren't any left to stand on. That's the point."

Nobody said anything to that. <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity> kept reading the load lines upside down, reading the machine's weight the way other people read a room. <entity repo="motif" guid="019d6143-a8e2-727a-be75-32648e8aaa47">Rain</entity> ticked off the hull discs and steamed away, foot by foot, all the way down the block.

"Then it objects," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said, "and the five of you get to be more interesting than I am."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at her — four years of knowing her face for what a fastener coming loose without stripping looked like — and saw the thing underneath it for the first time: not confidence. Arithmetic she'd run so many times alone that she'd stopped being able to tell the difference between *certain* and *practiced.*

"Ninety seconds," he said. "I'll be standing where I can reach you before the fence comes back."

"You'll be standing where I tell you," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said, already turning back to the schematic, folding it with both hands, the kind of careful that meant she'd folded it a thousand times before, muscle memory older than the job. "Because if you're where you think you should be, you're in my blast radius when this goes right."

The docking cycle showed on Echo's feed at 0247. Thirteen minutes.

It docked. The boom arms folded. The black discs on the hull dimmed one by one. A contactor closed somewhere inside, and the transformer pylon began, gently, to sing.

"Maintenance state," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said, already moving. "<entity repo="archetype" guid="019d6143-a56e-7633-bbad-bed2a04b007d">Fence</entity> is down to a tickle. Ninety seconds. Count me."

She crossed the yard at a walk — running hands shake — stepped over <entity repo="corponation" guid="019d6143-a7a4-71f6-b46a-94ef8cb2348f">Arcturus</entity>'s cone, and put her bare hand flat on the hull. It was the way she put it between <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s shoulder blades before she trusted a readout.
