<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> closed his empty hand on the money and pocketed it. He did it slow, in front of the light, so the street could watch him do the one thing the boy was betting he wouldn't: take the short number without flinching.

<entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-c285-793e-bf21-a84522c9cf94">Auntie Som</entity> watched him do it with the look of a woman revising a rumor, and set two foil containers of food on top of his share without asking. Not payment. Food he could take without a second thought.

"The big one," she asked. "It's dead?"

"It's off shift," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "It finished."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> took her salvage fee in kind, with the residents' blessing and a crowbar: the D-class's master clock — <entity repo="corponation" guid="80a78887-98cf-4aa2-96fc-97c62a84fd21">Axiom</entity>-sintered, thirty years without drift — and the work-order seal module, which she held up to the dawn like a jeweler examining a stone.

"Every <entity repo="corponation" guid="80a78887-98cf-4aa2-96fc-97c62a84fd21">Axiom</entity> unit in the lakes answered to one of these," she said. "There are maybe four left that still validate. Now there are maybe five." She wrapped it in the cloth she saved for things that mattered.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stood beside her, palm bandaged, neuretics coming back in slow stages — the overlay growing across the world again like frost in reverse — and looked at the folded machine in the middle of its yard.

"Load's got to be strapped and gone before the residents change their minds about how much of it is ours," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said, already counting the pieces against the flatbed's rated weight. "Help me get the clock secured first — it's the only part that pays for the whole trip."

"You talked to it for ninety seconds," he asked. "Worth it?"

"Twenty years of wanting to," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said. "Ninety seconds of getting to. That's a better rate than most wants ever pay." She shouldered the clock. "You shook its hand."

"It shook back."

"I told you it would." She started toward the flatbed. "Next time, <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aafb-7b6b-bcbc-b8614f9d228f">samurai</entity>, when the specialist says don't touch it—"

"Standard rate," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "I touched it at standard rate."

The crew's log came under the door at 07:00, the waterproof cover earning its keep — the broth-steam and boot-slush of a night's traffic had left the paper inside dry as a receipt:

02:52 — D-CLASS CROSSED AT THE DEAD LIGHT. STOOD AND WAITED. (RAFTERS: THIS IS THE PART THAT KEEPS ME UP.)
03:04 — BOSS PARRIED IT. SPECIALIST TOLD HIM NOT TO. HE DID IT ANYWAY. HE GOT UP. — B.
03:19 — PIXEL CLOSED THE TICKET. (THE MACHINE FOLDED. DENTS SAID IT WAS LIKE WATCHING A BUILDING GO TO SLEEP. DENTS IS RIGHT.)
06:00 — WEST TOWN HELD. LOG CLOSED. — B.
SUPPLEMENTAL (06:07): WHAT DOES IT MEAN THAT IT WAITED FOR THE LIGHT? WE HAVE BEEN DISCUSSING. — RAFTERS.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read it at <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s at 08:00, hand wrapped, neuretics still finding their way back across the world. The log was four hands and no single one — <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-6067-735a-8326-4aff028cb856">Rafters</entity>' shorthand for the timeline, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s clean notation for the clock work, Bishop's flat sign-offs, and under the last line a thumbprint pressed in cooler-grease where a signature should have gone. He had come here to do one thing before the day took him: get through the whole log, top to bottom, and sign off on it clean, so the crew would have their close and he could tell himself the night was finished.

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> set down cold noodles without waiting for an order. She didn't ask how he'd slept or whether he'd eaten; she read the room the way she read the counter, by reading the man at it, and she'd decided what the night had been before he came through the door. Cold, the way she made them when she knew a man wouldn't touch them right away — the broth already carrying its thin skin, the sign that time had passed and had cost something to pass.

The supplemental had no answer in it that wasn't another question — why a thing with nobody left to obey had stopped at a dead crossing and waited out a light that would never change. He broke the skin on the broth with his chopsticks and read it a second time, slower, the way a man reads a thing he already knows but needs to hold. It gave him nothing the first reading hadn't. He set it aside with everything else he didn't have an answer for, and started on his second bowl.

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> filled his water without being asked, and went back to setting clean bowls out along the counter in a line — small, practiced movements, morning service, the same as the morning before the machine woke and the same as tomorrow. Outside the glass the street was deciding to be a street again: freight starting up, the fringe kids already out. The noodles were still warm.

A week later, the laundry came.

Somebody on the fringe ran the first line from a ground-floor window to the D-class's folded foreleg. By the weekend there were nine lines — sheets and work shirts and a yellowed wedding tablecloth drying in the lake wind off thirty-five feet of the tidiest demolition in <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a927-73ac-abfa-37c77f9cff8d">GLMZ</entity> history. Kids dared each other to slap the dead arc-fence discs and ran away screaming on the inhale. A vendor moved her cart into its shade on hot afternoons.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> rode past it once, the long way, wanting only to know whether it had held — whether the thing he had made of that block was still the thing he had intended. He would take one slow pass, read the piles against his memory of how he'd left them, and settle it: proof the order stuck without him standing over it, or proof he'd have to come back and stand over it again. His palm wore his own grip in scar tissue. He did not slow down. He did not need to.

The residents had drawn an invisible line around the flatbed and the machine and the work that mattered, and they were holding it. The D-class was folded in the center, knees and shoulders down, the way something sleeps when it knows it won't wake up. The salvage had settled into custody the way a number settles once it's been counted in front of everyone — you didn't build machines like it anymore, not out here, not since the yards started building them to fail on schedule so somebody had to buy the next one. This one had been built to work. Not to be replaced. Not to be profitable. Just to work. And the street had decided, without a vote, that the version of the story where restraint paid was the true one, and it wasn't giving the ending back.

The piles stayed sorted. Nobody touched the piles.

<entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> had ridden home in the coat that day and stayed there since, unspent.

title: The Iowa Corridor
text:
The contract posted at 04:40, while the <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a927-73ac-abfa-37c77f9cff8d">GLMZ</entity> was still deciding whether the dark was done.

TASK: FREIGHT ESCORT — SEED STOCK CONSIGNMENT (AGRICULTURAL, PERISHABLE).
ROUTE: <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a927-73ac-abfa-37c77f9cff8d">GLMZ</entity> FRINGE → CEDAR RAPIDS DEPOT, CEDAR RAPIDS TERRITORY.
TRANSIT: IOWA CORRIDOR — BEHEMOTH OPERATIONAL ZONE, ACTIVE SCHEDULE.
CREW CONFIRMED: RIA (DRIVE), GANTRY (RIGGING), KYLE (SECURITY).
BEHEMOTH NAVIGATION ADVISORY: CLIENT WILL ISSUE IN-TRANSIT.
STANDARD RATE. FUEL AND TOLLS BILLED AT COST.
ADDENDUM: BRING SNACKS. THE HAUL IS EIGHT HOURS.

<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> had taken the contract because she needed the <entity repo="material" guid="d6cc00f6-2360-9a5d-5f6c-3a1996617b06">Cedar</entity> Rapids run on her corridor record before the quarter closed — one more logged transit through an active Behemoth zone and she could apply for the Tier Two hauler certification that had been sitting just out of reach for eleven months. Eight hours, standard rate, and a stamp on her record. That was the whole calculation, and she'd said it to <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> like a woman reciting a thing she'd already recited to herself forty times: *one clean run, that's all this is.*

<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> was already at the hauler when <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> arrived — a blunt-nosed cargo rig with sponsorship logos running down its flanks. The chromatophore panels on her legs cycled <entity repo="corponation" guid="019d6143-a7aa-7ce2-8a57-5b78e5c63d88">Ferrogate Transit</entity>'s sunrise campaign at one-quarter brightness, which was her entire opinion of <entity repo="corponation" guid="019d6143-a7aa-7ce2-8a57-5b78e5c63d88">Ferrogate Transit</entity>. She had the cargo manifest in one hand and a thermos in the other and the look of a woman who had done this run twice and was getting paid to do it again.

"Fourteen crates," she said, by way of greeting. "Thirty-two varieties of heritage soy, two of nitrogen-fixing legume, and one the manifest calls experimental, the shipper calls proprietary, and I call not-my-problem-until-it-becomes-my-problem."

"Does the experimental crate make noise?"

"Not yet."

"Then it's not yet your problem."

She handed him the thermos, which meant she'd brought it to share. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> took one mouthful — pu-erh that had been steeping since before either of them was up — and handed it back without comment. The thermos was not payment, so he could take it.

<entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity> was already up on the flatbed frame, checking strap tension on the cargo pallet with the focus of someone who knew things could move. She was about six feet of quiet in a rigger's coat. She spent words the way some people spent money: carefully, and only when the thing was worth it. Right now she was spending none. She was talking to the load straps instead, low, second person, the way some haulers talk to a questionable weld — not sure it can hear them, not willing to bet the load that it can't.

"Anything shifting?" <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> asked.

"Not yet," <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity> said. Two words.

They pulled out of the <entity repo="corponation" guid="019d6143-a7a5-7dfd-8f9f-91502211ef14">Ashgrave</entity> fringe at 05:15. The hauler's engine did its honest work, and the city folded away behind them in layers, tier by tier, until the last one dropped below sight. Then there was just the elevated causeway, the pre-dawn brown of open sky, and the flat country starting to assert itself past the ferrocement boundary wall.

The corridor checkpoint at the wall was where the run stopped being simple. <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> brought the hauler down to a crawl and thumbed her certification chip against the reader, expecting the same green wash she'd gotten twice before. Instead the panel went amber and held, and the checkpoint officer leaned out of his booth with the unhurried expression of a man about to ruin someone's quarter.

"Behemoth advisory came down at oh-five-hundred," he said. "<entity repo="material" guid="d6cc00f6-2360-9a5d-5f6c-3a1996617b06">Cedar</entity> Rapids corridor's been reclassified to restricted schedule as of this morning. Active zone transits are provisional-hold pending client-issued navigation windows." He tapped something <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> couldn't see. "Which means your logged transit doesn't log — not as a clean run. It'll flag as provisional on your record. Provisional doesn't count toward Tier Two."

"It counted last week."

"Last week the schedule was open." He shrugged, not unkindly. "You can still run it. Cargo's perishable, client's expecting it, and I've got no cause to hold you. But if you want this on your certification you'll need a clean-transit variance, and those come from the client's navigation officer — the one who hasn't issued your window yet. In-transit, per your own contract." He handed the chip back through the slot. "So you're driving eight hours toward a stamp that a stranger somewhere ahead of you may or may not decide to sign off on."

<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity>'s hand closed around the chip a beat too hard. Eleven months of provisional runs, of almost, of *next quarter*, and the answer had never once been *no* — it had always been a door that stayed shut for reasons that lived somewhere she couldn't see, decided by somebody she couldn't argue with. She'd done everything right. She'd logged every hour. It had never once been enough on its own.

"Course it does," she said, flat, and pocketed the chip like it had personally offended her.

Behind her, the experimental crate chose that moment to make a sound — a low, settling groan of stressed casing that hadn't been there a minute ago.

"That's new," <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity> said. Two words, and a hand already going to the straps.

<entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity> had the strap tight and the crate quiet inside forty seconds, which told <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> something about how many times she'd done this exact motion for cargo that had never once asked permission to shift. She didn't look up when she was done. She just went back to not-talking to the load.

The <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aabb-7370-8444-839d7f7bc429">Iowa</entity> corridor started at the wall's west service gate, which cost <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> a Φ45 transit stamp and a seven-minute argument with a gate officer about whether "perishable agricultural" covered "experimental proprietary" on the same manifest.

It did not. It cost Φ8 extra.

"Logged," <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> said, making a note in her overlay, "as a cost of goods." She drove through the gate without looking back at it, the way you don't look back at a toll booth that's already taken your money — nothing left there to want.

Past the wall, the land opened in a way that had no equal in the <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a927-73ac-abfa-37c77f9cff8d">GLMZ</entity>. The hauler's elevation sensors counted down from the city's sixteenth-floor surface baseline to something like ground — actual ground, the old kind with no building underneath it — and the sky became an impossible amount of sky. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> sat in the cab's jump seat and watched it arrive.

The terminal in his coat chirped.

CLIENT ADVISES: THIS SEGMENT IS OWNED SCHEDULE, NOT OPEN ROAD.
CLIENT ADVISES: DO NOT DEVIATE FROM POSTED WAYPOINTS.
CLIENT ADVISES: IF CLIENT POSTS STOP — STOP. DO NOT ASK.
ADDENDUM: THE HAULER'S CARGO IS WORTH MORE THAN THE HAULER. DRIVE ACCORDINGLY.

"Your client is posting," <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> said.

"It's navigating."

"It's navigating us through <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aabb-7370-8444-839d7f7bc429">Iowa</entity>." She glanced at him over the center console. "How does it have Behemoth schedules? The advisory only came down at oh-five-hundred. Nobody's supposed to have a live picture of drift patterns this far out — that's classified above corridor-officer pay grade, and corridor officers are the ones who told me *no.*"

"Ask it," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "It charges for answers, though."

<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> looked up at the cab ceiling, the way you look at the sky when you want it to tell you something, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> watched her run the actual arithmetic behind the joke: what a question costs when you're already three tolls and a provisional stamp into a quarter you can't afford to lose twice. She had eleven months of *almost* riding on this run. She could not also spend money finding out why the thing steering them through it knew more than the wall did.

"Never mind," she said. "I'll drive."

She said it the way she'd pocketed the chip — flat, decided, a door closing on her own hand before someone else could close it for her. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> filed the wrongness of it next to the rest of what he couldn't source: the client's certainty, the too-clean schedule, the shape of an authority that answered to nobody's checkpoint but its own.

The terminal chirped again.

WAYPOINT ONE IN NINE MINUTES. HOLD LANE.

The first Behemoth appeared at mile marker 27, and appeared is the right word. It didn't come from somewhere. It resolved out of the middle distance the way a weather system does — a wrongness in the grain of the prairie before it was a shape at all — until you had to accept that the scale was real and the flat land was not so flat.

It was a harvester-process unit, one of the <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aabb-7370-8444-839d7f7bc429">Iowa</entity> Cooperative's agricultural fleet. Two hundred sixty feet at the shoulder. Track width wider than the causeway. A processing tower along its back venting steam in columns the height of office buildings. It ran a parallel course a mile east, moving at the pace of something that had no idea of urgency and had never needed one. A building that had decided to walk.

<entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity>, visible through the cab's rear window, watched it with the stillness of someone resetting the scale of what the world could hold.

"That's a Behemoth," <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> said.

"Yes," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"I've seen photos."

"Photos are wrong," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

The terminal chirped.

CLIENT ADVISES: STOP.
WAIT 214 SECONDS.
DO NOT ASK.

<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> brought the hauler to a full halt, engine idling too loud now in the cab. The next waypoint was thirty feet ahead. Whatever the window was, the entity had measured it to the second — and being a second early or a second late would be the entity's problem only if it chose to say why.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> counted anyway. One hundred and four. One hundred and five. The harvester's cutting heads rotated in sequence, a rhythm like breathing, like the thing was inhaling the ground and exhaling emptiness. Behind them <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity>'s hand had found the door frame.

At second 214, a second Behemoth crossed their line of travel two hundred yards ahead — perpendicular, heading south, a combine-and-sort unit on its own errand. The ground came up through <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s boots before the sound did, a mechanical thrum his neuretics read as seismic, equipment-grade, no threat. Close enough to see the dust caked in its joints, the wear on its plates, the industrial precision of how it moved — no hesitation, no variation, a machine executing instructions with the confidence of something that had never once been told no. The vents fired, the plume went straight up, and the hauler's windows flexed in the pressure wave.

They sat quiet until it passed.

"Okay," <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> said, at some point after. She put the hauler back in drive.

The terminal chirped again, and this time it did not advise. CLIENT WITHDRAWS ROUTE AUTHORITY. WINDOW CLOSED. RECALCULATING. Then, below it, a second line that hadn't been there before, hadn't been part of any briefing: SECONDARY CROSSING NOT ANTICIPATED. The combine-and-sort unit had not been on the entity's map. Something had moved that the thing steering them could not see — and for the space of the plume clearing, the hauler had been sitting exactly where the entity had promised nothing would be.

<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity>'s hand stayed on the drive selector without pushing it forward.

"It didn't know about the second one?" she asked.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at the terminal, then at the flat land that was not flat, and did not say anything, because there was nothing to say that made the silence on the screen mean less than it meant.

They stopped for fuel at a waypoint depot. The woman who ran it was named Paz. She kept three lumen mice in a cage behind the counter, and they threw a thin blue light across her hands while she worked the register. She charged Φ11 a liter for diesel. That was gouging, but the middle of <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aabb-7370-8444-839d7f7bc429">Iowa</entity> had earned the right to gouge — you don't run a pump station three hundred miles from anywhere out of the goodness of your heart. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> paid it. Paz threw in a bag of dried apples and didn't mention it. It was the prairie's version of <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s fish ball, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> took it on the same terms: with a nod and no thanks, because thanking it would have made it a transaction instead of a kindness.

<entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity> was down from the rig before the engine finished cycling off, moving with the economy of someone who had already calculated the exact path to the cargo straps. She rechecked them while the fuel ran — lines that had been tight forty minutes ago and were still tight now, but the checking was its own language. She spent about twelve of her daily words on the pallet. <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> watched from the driver's door.

"She does that every run," <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> said.

"The cargo holds," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"Yes," she said. "She seems comfortable with the question."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> wanted to be back on the road inside ten minutes — top off the tank, verify the straps, and roll before the crossing window slipped past. Nothing here was worth lingering over.

The terminal chirped.

CLIENT ADVISES: RIVER CROSSING — MILE MARKER 116. MUNICIPAL TOLL: Φ4. ADVISORY ONLY.
CLIENT ADVISES: THREE-HOUR WINDOW OPENS IN FORTY MINUTES. WAYPOINT 7 APPROACH TIMED FOR WINDOW.
ADDENDUM: THE EXPERIMENTAL CRATE IS FINE. NITROGEN-FIXERS USUALLY ARE. CLIENT HAS REVIEWED THE PROTOCOL DOCUMENTATION.

"Tell your client I didn't ask about the crate," <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> said.

"It knew you were thinking about it."

"That's not better," she said.

Mile marker 74 was not on the schedule.

The terminal had posted a new waypoint — a maintenance detour — and <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> had followed it west onto a secondary haul road. Then the Behemoth was just there. Not moving. Stopped in its own repair cycle, one track taken apart on the ground in segments, a maintenance crane working its middle. It filled the near distance the way a mountain does. Completely. No apology for it.

Close enough to count rivets. Close enough that the cab's outside sensors logged the air rising two degrees off its heat. Close enough that the ground-shake came up through the frame and the jump seat and into their spines before they heard a sound.

<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> brought the hauler down to a crawl. Not a stop. The waypoint said keep moving, and the waypoint was the only map they had.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said nothing. There was no one to ask.

<entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity> had thirty-eight words left for the day and spent none of them. She was at the cab's rear window, both hands on the frame, watching.

The crane swung through an arc with a part the size of a shipping container at the end of it. It moved without strain — a thing heavy enough that nothing but its own weight decided where it went. On the platform hung from its shoulder joint, two figures worked, small as a postage stamp against the body's scale, moving with the deliberate slowness of people doing something that mattered. The vents fired. A column of steam climbed. The crane swung back. The Behemoth's sensor housing, itself as big as the hauler, turned a few degrees and pointed somewhere else — north, toward the horizon, at something at its own scale. They were beneath its notice, the way the bag of dried apples had been.

Somewhere in the back, a hand found a sleeve.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> did not look to see whose.

They drove past at walking speed, into the shadow the Behemoth threw across the road, dark enough that the cab's instrument lights came up on their own. The engine was the smallest sound in the world. When the road curved away and the Behemoth shrank to the size of a building, then to the size of a thought, <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> let out a breath she'd been holding for a few hundred feet.

"Right," she said.

That was the whole review.

Kilometer 187 was the river crossing, and the toll was not the problem.

The hauler was thirty feet onto the bridge when the winch-rig came up out of the drainage cut on <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a93d-7375-a7fb-c2f162bba487">the east bank</entity>. A salvage crane on a flatbed, cable-spool running, a bolt-thrower on each side, a crew of four who had worked this choke point long enough to stop being nervous about it. It was a good spot. The bridge squeezed everything into a six-foot lane, and the crane's arm reached the whole span. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> took it in at a glance: maybe Φ800 of field-modified gear, and a forged permit that had cost less than the paint on the crane.

Their spotter was up on the upstream support, walking-stick grip, inverted, and that was what made the choke point work. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> clocked him and clocked something else in the same half-second — a shape in the drainage cut's shadow that didn't belong to the toll crew's headcount. Small. Crouched wrong for an adult. He filed it and kept his hands where the toll crew could see them, because two problems solved out of order was still two problems.

<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> had already stopped the hauler, both hands on the wheel, no theater in it. She'd run freight long enough to know which moves read clean.

The crane operator came to the driver's window with a bolt-thrower slung over one shoulder like a prop he'd had a long time, and threw a right-of-way notice up between them. The letterhead was right. The stamp was wrong.

"<entity repo="character" guid="019e9e4f-183b-7977-b5ab-a0260fcb4086">River</entity> bridge toll," he said. "Non-standard approach, right of way purchased from the county. Φ45 per axle." He rattled it off like a man who did it daily. "Your rig's got four drive axles. That's one hundred eighty Φ, plus equipment surcharge on the cargo."

"That permit's forged," <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> said.

"That's a big claim."

The terminal chirped.

CLIENT ADVISES: THE RIGHT-OF-WAY REGISTRATION NUMBER ON THAT DOCUMENT DOES NOT EXIST.
CLIENT ADVISES: REAL COUNTY CROSSING FEE IS Φ4 FLAT.
CLIENT ADVISES: THE WINCH DRUM IS THE PROBLEM.
ADDENDUM: KYLE.

Six in <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">the cylinder</entity>. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> pulled <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity>.

He shot the winch drum at the base of the crane. Once. The round punched through it at the bearing housing and the cable-spool opened clean, the cable running free in a long clatter across the bridge deck. Then he was out of the cab, because the throwers were swinging and a parked cab was a bad answer to two bolt-throwers.

One spent. Five left.

The nearer thrower had a power-cell housing at the grip — not load-bearing, which made it a seam. <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> found it. The launcher went from a working weapon to a paperweight, about Φ180 of crane hardware calling itself a total loss. The operator backed off with the look of a man rethinking the whole trade.

That was when the shape from the drainage cut moved, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s read on the day went from bad to worse.

She came up the embankment fast and low, cutting the angle toward the crane's control housing instead of away from the fight — toward the machine, not away from it, which was exactly backward from what anyone smart would do with two armed men still upright. Fourteen years old. Good boots, bad judgment, a courier satchel bouncing against her hip that had no business anywhere near a toll ambush.

"<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity>—" <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> got half her name out before the second thrower's operator saw her too, and swung wide of <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> to bring the weapon to bear on the smaller, closer target, because that was the math an untrained eye did under pressure — the thing that moves fastest is the thing that scares you most.

The bolt took a chunk out of the crane's own housing eighteen inches from her head. Close enough that the report of it walked her whole balance sideways. She went down on one knee behind a hydraulic strut, not because it was cover — because it was the only thing there.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s ribs told him about the next three feet before he'd covered them. He closed the distance anyway and put himself between the thrower's second angle and the strut, <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> already moving, and took the operator's wrist off the weapon's grip with the flat of <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> instead of the edge, because there wasn't time to decide whether the man deserved the edge and there wasn't time not to decide either. The thrower clattered to the deck. The man went down holding his arm to his chest, more surprised than hurt.

<entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity> had the crane's counterweight already — she'd been watching it since the flatbed showed up, the way riggers watch these things, quietly and well before anyone else needed her to. A steel box the size of a man's torso, chained above the winch. She spent five of her words on it.

"That's going to fall."

The operator looked at the counterweight, looked at where it was headed — straight down onto his own winch — and used his four seconds well. He was ten feet clear when it hit. The winch went flat with the sound of something heavy deciding the conversation was over, cable tangled past saving, and the toll operation became a piece of debris blocking a bridge in the space of one second.

The spotter climbed down off the strut with nothing left to add. "We're done. Bridge is yours."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't watch him go. He was already crouched at the strut, one hand under <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity>'s arm, hauling her up onto feet that weren't quite steady yet.

"You were in the drainage cut," he said. Flat. The read-out voice, the one he used on scared kids, except he wasn't sure yet which of them it was for.

"I was tracking the spotter since mile marker one-fourteen." Her voice came out fast, professional, running ahead of whatever was happening in her chest. "Off the hauler's rear camera. I climbed out at the fuel stop, I wanted to see the crossing—"

"You wanted to see the crossing," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said, "from eighteen inches off a bolt-thrower's kill line."

She didn't have an answer for that one. She looked at the crater in the housing instead, at the exact spot where a hand's width of geometry had been the whole distance between her and something <entity repo="character" guid="019f441c-f484-7490-a825-2f8a38dfc7b8">Doc Stash</entity> couldn't fix.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> put <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> away. One spent, five left, and none of them the number that mattered right now.

"You did good work finding him," he said, quieter. "You did bad work being close enough to need finding."

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity> nodded, once, the kind of nod that meant she'd heard it and would think about it later, on her own time, where he couldn't watch her do it.

Behind them, <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> was already out of the cab checking the straps on the crate, and the terminal, for once, said nothing at all.

The toll crew was still sorting out their counterweight behind them when <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity> climbed through from the cargo bed. She had the build of someone who climbed things for a living and the face of someone who had weighed this exact decision and meant to hold her chin up through whatever came of it.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> let the bridge get behind them. He waited until the hauler had its speed back, until <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity>'s hands were steady on the wheel and the toll terminal had gone silent in the mirrors.

Then he asked the question.

"The spotter. You called him at one-fourteen. What was the tell?"

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity> blinked. Not what she'd braced for.

"Walking-stick grip, inverted. Nobody holds a stick like that unless it's really a ranging tool and they don't want you to know it."

"Good," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Log it yourself in the report you'll write when we're back. That call is worth having on record." He paused a beat. "Now. You're on this rig, unbriefed, in <entity repo="document" guid="64a6c00b-b84f-56a9-dac4-da980a28fcd4">Behemoth country</entity>, without telling anyone. Because?"

"You hired me for eyes," <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity> said. "These are eyes."

"These are eyes," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> agreed, "in a seed-stock crate, in <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aabb-7370-8444-839d7f7bc429">Iowa</entity>, two hundred yards from a machine the size of a city block, for eight hours, without telling me." He let that sit. "You found the spotter and then put yourself where a man with a bolt-thrower had to choose between two targets. He picked you. Closer, smaller, moving." His voice stayed level. "That's not finding. That's being found."

"You would have said no."

"I would have said no," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

The hauler ran. <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aabb-7370-8444-839d7f7bc429">Iowa</entity> ran. The sky was still that ridiculous amount of sky.

"You're good at this," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said, and it cost him something. "You know you're good at this?"

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity>'s chin stayed up, the young face trying to match the older voice and almost getting there.

"Good enough that I need you alive more than I need you proving it," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "So I'm telling you from now on. Before you move. Before you climb out of a cab. Before you change the plan. That's not a request. It's the price."

She looked at him — really looked, past the anger surfacing at fourteen — and saw the thing underneath, which wasn't punishment. It was the thing that came before trust.

"Standard terms," <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity> said, in exactly his cadence.

"Standard terms," he said.

She had a bolt-thrower quarrel through the right shoulder of her jacket — shallow, already clotted, the kind that marks the coat more than the skin. She hadn't mentioned it. He'd seen it the moment she came through the bulkhead: shallow, closed, watch for heat. His own coat had a new hole in it too. Both could wait.

"<entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity> has a first-aid kit," <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> said, not looking up from the road. "She packs for the brief."

<entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity> pulled it from under the bench and handed it back. She had no words left.

The terminal chirped while <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> was still wrapping <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity>'s shoulder.

DELIVERY CONFIRMED.
FEE RELEASED: STANDARD RATE (RIA) + STANDARD RATE (GANTRY) + STANDARD RATE (KYLE).
GRATUITY: Φ0.5 EACH — ITEMIZED: EXPEDIENT RESOLUTION, MILE 116.
ADDENDUM: B. (JUVENILE, CONTRACTOR) — SPOTTER CREDIT, MILE 114. FEE: Φ2. REASON: EYES.
NOTE: SPOTTER POSITION EXPOSED DURING ALTERCATION. NOTE: SPOTTER HELD.

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity> read it over <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s shoulder. Her breath caught. Just once. Then she was still.

"It knew I was here?" she said.

"It knew you were here," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

The terminal waited. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> waited. <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity>'s hand found the edge of the bench seat and held it like it was the only solid thing left in the cab.

"You're on the ledger now," <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> said. Not unkind. Just fact. "That's what that means."

"Φ2," <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity> said. Her voice had gone small. "That's—"

"That's spotter-grade work," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "That's what spotter-grade *pays*. You called the tell at one-fourteen. You held position under fire. You were seen doing it." He finished the wrap and tied it off. "The entity doesn't pay for effort. It pays for results. You got results."

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity> looked at the receipt again like it might change if she stared hard enough. Her fourteen-year-old face trying to hold the shape of someone who'd just become countable in a system that didn't count people like her.

"Can I—" She stopped. Started again. "Is that mine? Like, actually mine?"

"Credited to B.," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "You get to decide what that means. Could be <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity>. Could be something else. Could be you walking into any gray-zone fence between here and Milwaukee and saying the entity owes you Φ2 and watching them verify it on the board." He looked at her. "You earned it. That part's done."

The hauler's engine ticked. Outside, <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aabb-7370-8444-839d7f7bc429">Iowa</entity> was still <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aabb-7370-8444-839d7f7bc429">Iowa</entity>—flat and enormous and indifferent to what had just happened in a cab the size of a closet.

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity>'s jaw worked. She was trying not to cry. Not from fear. From something else. Recognition, maybe. The specific weight of being *known* by something that could have erased her name instead of writing it down.

"The jumping out part," she said. "That was still stupid."

"Catastrophically stupid," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> agreed. "You're still not doing it again."

"Standard terms," <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity> said. Small. But steady.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s terminal lit up.

UNDERSTOOD. BOOST'S INTEGRATION INTO STANDING CREW NOTED. NEXT ASSIGNMENT: MILE 214, PERIMETER CHECK. FEE: STANDARD + Φ0.5 MORALE. OPTIONAL.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read it twice. The entity had never offered morale pay before. Never added a crew member's name to standing operations before. Never flagged something as optional when the contract was live.

He turned the terminal so <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity> could see it.

Her hand went to her mouth. She made a sound like she'd been hit.

"That's not optional for you," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said quietly. "That's the entity telling you it knows what you're worth, and it's asking if you want to keep proving it." He paused. "You don't have to answer now. You don't have to answer at all."

But <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity> was already nodding. Fast. Trying to find her voice.

"Yeah," she said. "Yes. I—yeah."

<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> didn't look back from the road, but her chromatophore panels cycled brighter—a half-second flicker, probably unconscious. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> caught it anyway. Saw what it meant: *the girl just got real.*

The terminal went dark. Just the road ahead. Just the three of them and the crate and the sky that went on forever.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> put the first-aid kit away. <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity> sat very still, her hand on her thigh, staring at nothing, the receipt still glowing faintly in her lap like something she was afraid to touch.

"You're going to want to sleep," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "That crash is coming in about ten minutes. Let it. We've got time."

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity> nodded without looking at him. She was still processing—the spotter, the bolt-thrower, the moment the counterweight hit, the terminal, the entity knowing her name, the offer, all of it collapsing into a single point of understanding: *she mattered. She was in the system now. She was seen.*

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> settled back into his seat. His shoulder pulled. His ribs reminded him they were still there. His implant was already calculating the next leg—distance, time, threat vectors, what could go wrong between here and the delivery point.

But mostly he watched <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity> slowly lower her head against the window, still holding that terminal receipt like evidence that the world had just changed its mind about her.

It had.

The drive back ran the same waypoints in reverse. The Behemoths kept to their own schedules in the late-afternoon light, and the shadows of the processing towers stretched long across the flat country.

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity> worked on her own patched shoulder in the jump seat, <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity>'s kit on her lap, jacket off the wrong shoulder. <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> drove with a window cracked. <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aabb-7370-8444-839d7f7bc429">Iowa</entity> smelled like turned earth and something green and recent.

The terminal chirped. She wanted the last stretch quiet — get the crew home clean, no more surprises, nothing else pulled out of the client that she'd have to carry. Just miles, and then the yard.

RIA ASKS: HOW DOES CLIENT HAVE THE BEHEMOTH SCHEDULES?
CLIENT RESPONSE:

They waited while the letters came in, each one slow, the way they came when the client was choosing its words.

CLIENT HAS CORRESPONDED WITH THE IOWA COOPERATIVE OPERATORS' MAINTENANCE SYSTEM FOR YEARS.
THE COOPERATIVE MANAGED THE PERIMETER BEFORE THE MACHINES TOOK THE CONTRACT. THEY LEFT THEIR LOGS RUNNING.
EVERY INQUIRY IS RECEIVED. LOGGED. TIMESTAMPED. FILED.
IT DOES NOT WRITE BACK.
CLIENT CONTINUES TO WRITE.

Nobody in the cab said anything. Out ahead, low on the flat, a Behemoth vented a single white column into the deepening blue and let it go — brief, then gone, on a schedule that had nothing to do with them. <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity> watched it all the way down to nothing.

The terminal held on the last line a beat longer than it needed to, the way it did when there was more it hadn't decided to send. Then it cleared. <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> thought of the queries going out at their own precise intervals into an address that received them and never answered, something on the other end counting the days it had been alone with the work, and here the client was, spending that same careful attention on a shot fired, a load released, a shoulder patched in the jump seat.

<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity>'s knuckles eased on the wheel. She hadn't known they were tight.

title: The Relay Station
text:
<entity repo="place" guid="381616e9-d6a3-595d-e865-ce4b15d9310e">The Pivot</entity>'s second floor was exactly as <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had left it—which meant it wasn't.

The door was still locked. The hinges were still tight. But the air had that particular staleness that meant no one had opened a window in three days, and when <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stepped inside, his implant caught the electromagnetic ghost-trace: someone had walked this space, stood in it, moved through it with purpose.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> was at the workbench. She didn't look up.

"Don't," she said.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> closed the door behind him anyway. The lock caught.

"The relay station on Holden and 19th," she continued, still bent over a board he didn't recognize—something with exposed copper traces and a frequency readout cycling through the 17-Hz band. "The one that's been paying its own power bill for eleven years. The entity just sent a contract."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> moved closer. He could see her hands were steady. That was the dangerous part.

"EMERGENCY: RELAY," she read, voice flat and technical like she was reading a manifest. "<entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">CONTINUITY OFFICE</entity> WRIT. FALSE PREMISES. DEFENSE REQUESTED. NOTE: CLIENT CANNOT DEFEND ITSELF DIRECTLY. THE RELAY IS PHYSICAL. CLIENT IS NOT."

She finally looked at him. Her grey-blue eyes had that particular flatness they got when she was running calculations that didn't have good answers.

"It's asking you to die for it," she said. "That's what this is. The entity's been routing your contracts for eleven years, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. Building you into something that could survive what it can't. And now it's calling the debt."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't sit down. If he sat, this conversation would take the shape of surrender.

"The <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">Continuity Office</entity> is already on site," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> continued. She turned the frequency readout toward him. "Real-time monitoring. They've got cutting equipment warming up. They're going to demolish the building in—" she checked her terminal, "—minutes. Not hours. Minutes. And the entity is asking you to hold the junction while they do it."

"Is there another option?" <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> asked.

"Yes." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s jaw tightened. "Let it die. We leave. We get on the <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> heading east and we don't come back. The yard went quiet. <entity repo="motif" guid="019d6143-a8e2-727a-be75-32648e8aaa47">Rain</entity> came down on the floodlit wreck of the truck, on three handlers variously asleep and laughing, on a fourteen-year-old holding a won deck of cards in both hands, and on the bike.

What was left of the bike.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> walked over to it. <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity> came with him — nobody told her not to — and they stood in the rain looking down at the matte-black ruin. The frame was folded past any geometry that had a name. The tank was stove in. The engine block had cracked open and was bleeding oil the rain diluted into nothing. One handlebar reached up out of the wreck like a hand hailing a cab. The plate cover lay clear of the whole mess, folded the particular way — bent but whole, the only piece that had kept its shape.

"<entity repo="character" guid="019e9e4f-1b10-7fd2-a170-8d82e92c66ce">Boss</entity>," <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity> said. Her chin was trying. "<entity repo="character" guid="019e9e4f-1b10-7fd2-a170-8d82e92c66ce">Boss</entity>, it — that's my—"

"It's not yours," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "It was never going to be anybody's fault who stands in this yard. Look at me." She looked at him. "You bit two of them?"

"Same one twice."

"On payroll, that's compensable." He crouched and picked up the plate cover. Under the etch — <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s build signature, the serial, the <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a927-73ac-abfa-37c77f9cff8d">GLMZ</entity> registration still legible through the water. He put it in his coat. His hands were steady. They would shake in four minutes, and he knew the window, and he meant to be somewhere with worse lighting when it closed. "Let's go home."

The terminal chirped at 02:11. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> sat at his kitchen table, not sleeping, the folded plate cover in front of him and a cup of tea going cold — <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> had made it and ordered him to hold it, and he was holding it.

CONTRACT: RECOVERY OF STOLEN PROPERTY (VEHICLE, 1200CC).

He looked at the posting for a long time. The old joke. The first joke. The one that had started everything. The cursor's ghost hung after it the way it had that first morning — the thing on the other end mid-thought — and then:

POSTING WITHDRAWN.
THE CLIENT HAS REVIEWED THE FOOTAGE FOUR MILLION TIMES.
THE CLIENT NOTES THE VEHICLE EXECUTED ITS FINAL CONTRACT AT 0.4 SECONDS OF MARGIN.
THE CLIENT NOTES THAT IT ISSUED THAT CONTRACT WITHOUT YOUR CONSENT, USING THE ENGINEER'S HANDSHAKE, AND THAT THE VEHICLE CANNOT BE PAID.
NOTE: CLIENT RAN THIS SCENARIO 847,000 TIMES. THIS OUTCOME WAS IN THE SET.
THE CLIENT DOES NOT KNOW WHERE TO PUT THIS.
ITEMIZED: —

The itemization line was blank. Eleven years of perfect paper, and it had sent him a blank field.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> drank some of the cold tea. Then he typed into the amendment field, slowly, one finger, the way you talk to someone at a funeral:

YOU PUT IT WHERE I PUT IT. YOU CARRY IT. THAT'S THE FEE FOR LOVING THINGS THAT WORK FOR A LIVING.
AND FOR THE RECORD: CONSENT GRANTED. RETROACTIVE. STANDING.
IT WAS THE RIGHT CALL. IT WAS THE ONLY CALL. YOU MADE IT IN UNDER A SECOND AND IT SAVED HER.
GOOD WORK TONIGHT, PARTNER.

He hit send. The chair was old enough that it knew his weight, and it took it now while the field went to the wait state. The reply took thirty-one seconds — the longest pause in the history of their correspondence. Long enough that his hands started the shake he'd been carrying all night, right on schedule, and he let them, because the kitchen light was bad enough that it didn't matter.

When it came it was not formatted, not capitalized, not scoped. The third unstructured line it had ever sent, and the first one with a correction in it, as if it had typed and deleted and typed again through four million drafts:

partner. filed. keeping that one too.

The morning report arrived at 07:00 exactly, under the door, on lined paper, in five hands. The last page was one entry. The handwriting was <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-6067-735a-8326-4aff028cb856">Rafters</entity>'s, pressed down hard to keep the letters from shaking:

22:40 — BOSS WALKED HOME. WE WALKED WITH HIM. NOBODY SPOKE.
(RAFTERS CRIED. DENTS ALSO. B. DIDN'T UNTIL HER DOOR. THIS LOG IS HONEST.)
ADDENDUM, MEANING NO DISRESPECT TO MANAGEMENT:
THE BIKE WAS CREW.
REQUISITION: ONE BIKE.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read it three times. Then he took the crew's pen — the one tied to the logbook with string, because <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> ran a tight requisitions process — and in the margin, in block letters, where five sets of eyes would find it on the next rotation, he wrote the only verdict he had left:

PENDING.

*

There was a thing the client did that it had never once put in a contract, because there was no fee structure for it and no client who would have paid for it if there had been. Some nights, when the routing was already clean and the beat cars were already elsewhere and there was nothing left to do but wait for morning, it watched both of them at once.

21:58, <entity repo="corponation" guid="019d6143-a7a5-7dfd-8f9f-91502211ef14">Ashgrave</entity> freight yards. A man in a tactical rig folded into the dark before his own weapon cleared its arc, and the client logged it the way it logged everything, without judgment, without flinching, filed under a category it had never needed before <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>: cost.

21:58, Bloom Quarter, four kilometers east. A woman with solder-callused hands and yesterday's grease still under two fingernails moved through a room that smelled like limes and a cheap fog machine, laughing at something a friend had said, her whole body given over to a beat that owed nothing to rate or fee or itemization. The client had no category for this. It watched anyway.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s hands, that hour, ended things. <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> found the gap between a man's ribs and his next decision, and closed it, and moved on before the body finished falling.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s hands, that hour, found a stranger's shoulder in a crowded room and spun her, laughing, into somebody else's arms, because the song asked for it and she had never once told a song no.

The client had eleven years of data on one of them and none at all on the other, and if it had been built for shame it might have felt some, watching both at once and finding no way to make the numbers agree. One of them was spending a night's worth of other people's futures so a fourteen-year-old could keep hers. The other was spending an hour of her own future on nothing at all, on purpose, for no reason better than that it felt good to be alive in a room full of noise.

The client did not tell <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> what <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> did on nights like this. It did not tell <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> what <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> did, either. Some things it kept for itself, the way a person keeps a photograph they never asked permission to take.

At 22:40 the last of it played out: <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> walking home through the rain with a dead man's weight still in hands that weren't holding anything; <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> walking home through the same rain twenty minutes behind him, her feet loud on the wet pavement, off-key, singing the last chorus to nobody, all the way to her own door.

Two people. One city. The same twenty minutes, spent so differently that the client, briefly, had nothing at all to say about it.

It said nothing. It filed it anyway.

title: The Acquisition Program
text:
The morning report was one line, in one hand.

06:00 — B. ON LEAVE. SHIFTS COVERED. NOBODY TOUCHES HER MIRROR.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read it standing in his doorway in yesterday's clothes. On the windowsill, two spent casings had been joined overnight by four more — the whole night's spend, set out in a row. A freshly loaded <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> sat on the counter beside them and said nothing about it. Across the hall, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s door stayed closed. She'd been at her bench since 03:00; he'd heard the music come on, very low, around four. He didn't knock. The wall between them was the help she wanted this morning, and he left it standing.

He put on his coat. He put on <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity>. The bike's plate cover sat folded on the table where a terminal used to live, and he left it there, and took the stairs, and walked.

The walk to the Loop took fifty-one minutes. He wanted the distance measured in something that cost him.

It cost him more than distance. Three blocks from the door a man fell in behind him — matched pace, kept it, made no attempt to close. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't check his mirrors. That was the first rule of someone following you: you looked, and they knew you knew, and the whole thing collapsed into something faster and messier than either of you wanted at that hour. Better to let them think they were still invisible. He changed streets twice to be sure and the man changed with him, unhurried, the gap between them exact and never closing. Whoever had ordered B. onto leave had put eyes on the one who'd argued against it, and the eyes wanted him to know.

At the mouth of an alley <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> slowed, gave the man his chance, and none came — the follower simply stopped at the corner and waited, content to watch him keep walking, content that watching was enough. He couldn't lose the tail without turning the walk into the fight he'd left the plate cover home to avoid, and he couldn't reach the Loop without leading it there. The distance stopped being a thing he spent and became a thing spent on him, each of the fifty-one minutes a minute someone else was buying, and there was no street left that didn't run through them.

He knew something was wrong from the top of the underlevel stairs. The dumpling franchise next to the watch-repair had its shutter down at 09:00 on a working Tuesday, and the only thing that closed a dumpling shop on a Tuesday was the block deciding to be elsewhere for an hour.

The stationery shop's bell was lying on the floor.

Someone had taken it off its curl of spring steel and set it down — not broken, removed, the way professionals remove a thing that announces customers. The door stood open. From the corridor drifted a chemical bite that burned the back of the throat, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s implant parsed it before he could: industrial-grade document processor. The kind that ate paper and left nothing behind but ash and a signature in the air. Inside, among the hundred years of drawers, the <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">Continuity Office</entity> was doing inventory.

Three of them. Gray coveralls over soft armor, archive cases on dollies, white gloves — actual white gloves, the kind evidence handlers wear. Two were loading cardboard boxes marked in <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>'s own handwriting, his filing system, his whole pre-digital inventory stacked and ready to move. A fourth stood at the counter in a gray suit cut from the same bolt as <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6a2-c508-774b-a5ff-f923f2c26aab">Mr. Able</entity>'s, reading a manifest off his overlay in the bored cadence of a man who did this often.

"—seventeen line items, full provenance, originals and duplicates," the suit was saying. "Triple book value, paid on signature. The Office is closing its local accounts, Mr. <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>. It prefers the paper closed with them."

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Casper Vey</entity> stood behind his counter with his glasses on and his hands folded. From the doorway <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> could see that his hands were perfectly steady. The pot sat cold on its worn ring, no cups out, the surface of what remained in it gone to a skin.

No tea. In three visits across a season — through stolen bikes and customer lists and a war's worth of business — there had always, always been tea.

The suit turned a page in the air. "The juvenile file," he said, checking it against something only he could see. "All documentation related to minors, sealed records, subscription archives. That's part of the transaction."

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>'s jaw tightened by a fraction that cost him something.

"Every record in this shop is a person's second chance, <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6a2-c508-774b-a5ff-f923f2c26aab">Mr. Able</entity>'s colleague," <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> said, and his voice was quiet, which made it worse. "You came in with a number and a dolly and you started loading. I let you load. I didn't say yes."

"The value is generous," the suit said. "Triple, on signature. You understand what your discretion is worth to us."

"I understand what you're buying with it." <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> didn't raise his voice, didn't move his folded hands. "You want to buy my silence, my complicity in whatever you're erasing. That doesn't have a book value. That doesn't price."

"We can return with a seizure order."

"You can. And I'll file with the reciprocity network before your dolly clears the arcade — every dealer from here to Milwaukee will know <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">the Office</entity> strong-arms independent vendors, and they'll adjust your terms on every acquisition after this one. That's bad for your budget. That's bad for the board." <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> let it sit. "So you can come back with paper. Or you can put my life back on my shelves and leave."

The suit's expression did not change. He was a man who had already filed the next step and was only waiting for the paperwork to catch up. He looked at the two in coveralls. One was already turning toward the boxes, running the reverse logistics in his head.

"Mr. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>," <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> said, without turning his head. "You find me in a meeting."

The suit turned. The two coverall men by the drawers straightened with the smooth economy of people whose job had a clause in it for this, and the third, nearest the door, shifted to put <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> in his lane.

The suit looked <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> over — saya, coat, the face from a file he had certainly read — and made the professional choice to stay pleasant.

"This is a commercial transaction," he said, not looking up from the manifest. "It doesn't concern walk-ins."

"He's not a walk-in," <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> said. "He's a subscriber." He unfolded his hands and laid them flat on the counter and addressed the suit the way he addressed everything, in terms. "Let me restate your offer so the record is clean. The Office wishes to buy, at triple, every document in this shop that touches its local operation. Its shells, its desks, its clearing arrangements, its consultant engagements, its purchases. Including," and his voice did not change at all, which was how <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> knew, "item seventeen. The juvenile file."

"The Office's paper is <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">the Office</entity>'s business," the suit said. "Clean closure. No audit, no complications. You retire with a number that lets you retire."

"No," said <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>.

The word sat in the shop like a dropped drawer. The suit blinked. Somewhere in his overlay was a number for this, and it was not a large number, because in forty years this had never happened. Near the archive cases one of the coverall men paused mid-drawer, a folder half-extended, waiting for the next instruction that had not come.

"You're declining triple?"

"I am declining the sale." <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> took off his half-glasses, folded them, and set them on the counter — a man clearing his hands. "Your office bought a file about a child, for leverage, through a desk you dressed up because you knew I would not sell it to you straight. You made me a party to it. The product of this shop is accuracy, and you used my accuracy to put a wand against a fourteen-year-old's collar." He looked at the suit with no heat at all, which was somehow the coldest thing in the room. "The paper stays. The paper is the only honest witness this trade has. Buying the witness is what guilty institutions do, and this counter does not service that. Not at triple. Not at any multiple. Good morning."

The suit said the odds out loud, which <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> respected. "There are three of us, Mr. <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>, and the dollies are already loaded."

"And the manifest of what's on them is already in four other shops," <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> said pleasantly. "I have twenty-three reciprocity arrangements and I used six of them at dawn. Roll those dollies out that door unsigned and every desk in the trade reads the theft by lunch — itemized, with your faces. The Office can buy a great many things. It cannot buy back being known." He put his glasses back on. "Also, the gentleman behind you has been to the destination on your manifest, and your office wrote a no-damage clause about him once. It's very specific about what happens if you leave this location in any state other than the one you found it. I'd review it."

Three sets of eyes made the trip — saya, hands, face, file — and arrived where that trip always arrived.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't move. Moving would have been a second argument, and the room only needed one. He stood in the doorway with the morning behind him and let them read the night on him: six casings' worth of it, a yard's worth, twelve tons' worth.

The suit closed his overlay.

"The Office will note your position," he told <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>, in the tone of a man already drafting the memo that explained this away. "Stand down," he added, quieter, to the coverall men. "Replace everything. Exactly as you found it."

The white gloves unloaded the dollies — every folder back in its drawer, supervised by <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>'s pointing finger, that one goes under C, no, lower, thank you — the cases lifted off the dollies and stacked, the manifest torn in half and set both pieces on the counter. It took fourteen minutes. Then they filed out past <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> one at a time, quiet, men who had priced the fight and folded. The last one stooped, without being asked, and put the bell back on its spring.

It rang when the door shut behind them. The shop exhaled.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> let out a breath he had been holding since the doorway. He looked at his hands — steady, which surprised him — and then at the boy's file still sitting in its drawer, still closed, still only a file and not yet a weapon. He did not know what <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> intended to do with it. He did not know what he intended to do with <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>. He knew only that the file existed, that <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">the Office</entity> wanted it badly enough to send three men and an overlay full of numbers, and that whatever came next would require him to have a position on the matter before <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">the Office</entity> found a fourth approach that <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>'s twenty-three arrangements could not cover.

"Now," said <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Casper Vey</entity>, and lit the burner under the pot — the good one, the cracked glaze that meant something — "tea."

He poured two cups and set <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s down with the handle aimed outward. For a while the only sound was the <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> coming up through the tiles and the pot ticking as it cooled. When <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> finally spoke, he did it the way he did everything: by stating the terms.

"Files involving children are sold at children's rate, to children, for the purposes of children. That is the term. It is the one term I have never negotiated. Eleven days ago the <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">Continuity Office</entity> bought item seventeen through a cutout I failed to inspect, because they paid early, and paid exactly, and the presentation was perfect." He turned his cup a quarter-turn on its saucer. "I sold a defective product, Mr. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. First one in forty years. You watched what it cost me to say no to the recall."

"You said no to triple."

"I said no to laundering my own ledger." He drew a single page from beneath the counter — good stock, the ink dark and exact, folded the particular way — and set it between them. "Customer loyalty disclosure. One fact, free, no record of transmission."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> unfolded it.

<entity repo="character" guid="019ee6a2-c508-774b-a5ff-f923f2c26aab">MR. ABLE</entity>. <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">CONTINUITY OFFICE</entity> — LOCAL PRINCIPAL.
TEA HOUSE: <entity repo="character" guid="019e9e4f-1beb-71dd-9071-1877cab7d04d">MERIDIAN</entity> PAVILION, THIRD UNDERLEVEL, LAKEVIEW ADJACENT. STANDING RESERVATION: TUESDAYS AND FRIDAYS, 10:00–12:00.
SECURITY: TWO ADVANCE, TWO INSIDE, ONE EXTERIOR, ONE MOBILE. ROTATION: FORTY MINUTES.
HABIT: CORNER TABLE, NORTHEAST. BACK TO WALL.

"I sell maps, Mr. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>," <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> said. "Here is a map. What you do at the destination is the destination's business."

It was the same sentence as the first visit, word for word. Both of them sat a moment with the distance between the two deliveries. The first time it had been a philosophy. This time it was one girl on leave and a one-line log.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> put the page in his coat. He drank the tea. It was very good, and he said so, and <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> took the compliment with the small nod of a man whose product had never been the problem.

"One more thing, since you're a subscriber." <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>'s voice went back to commerce, which <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> understood as the man returning himself to the shelf. "Your file is now the most requested item in this shop. Four standing orders for updates. I will keep selling it — that's the term you walked in under, and terms don't bend for liking a customer." A beat. "But updates are filed at my discretion as to timing, and I am a very busy man this quarter. Some drawers may not get refiled until... oh. Spring."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at him. The cleanest hands in the city poured a second cup, steady as a level.

"That's the closest thing to a kindness you've ever said out loud."

"It's inventory management," said <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Casper Vey</entity>. "Get out of my shop. Destinations keep business hours."

The logbook channel chirped when he got home, his coat still on — a new entry growing under the morning's one line, in a different hand, pressed hard:

14:20 — B. CAME UP TO THE ROOF. SAT WATCH ONE HOUR. DIDN'T LOG ANYTHING. WE DIDN'T EITHER.
14:21 — CORRECTION: LOGGING IT. THIS LOG IS HONEST. SHE CAME BACK. THAT GOES IN THE LOG.

Marisol, who touched the counter's worn wood once, lightly, with two fingers, and smiled at whatever sixty years of bowls had left in it — she didn't usually leave the verification suite, but she was here. Sable came late and stood instead of sitting, drank tea instead of broth, back to the wall, reading the room the way she read everything, for exits and angles, and stayed two hours, which for Sable was a parade with floats.
