<entity repo="person" guid="806cd358-6413-426b-a42d-19726b732c0b">Vo Dinh</entity> came, with the lifters, and brought — fence's honor — a wreath. It was made of drive chain. Nobody asked. Everybody understood.

The crew came in a body, all of them, scrubbed to a shine that said negotiations had happened, the logbook carried between <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-6067-735a-8326-4aff028cb856">Rafters</entity> and <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5b48-7f83-baf8-f3b78d901de9">Dents</entity> like a crown. <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity> came last. She walked the way you walk when you've rehearsed walking. She took the stool next to <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> and ate her first bowl in silence. Only at the second bowl did she speak.

"At the yard." She said it to the broth. "It was already moving before the truck finished turning. I did the math after. It decided before I even — it decided FIRST." She looked up. "Things don't do that. People barely do that."

"Payroll does that," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

She thought about it, fourteen and serious. "Then everything important is payroll?"

"Now you've got it," said <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>, and dropped an egg in the kid's bowl, and didn't bill her.

There was no speech. There was a moment, around the third round of bowls, when the wok went quiet. <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> brought out the small cups — not the working bowls, the small ones, the ones that came out for the old holidays nobody celebrated anymore — and set one dish of oil and scallion at the empty end of the counter, where nobody was sitting, the way you set a place. The whole counter looked at it. Then they looked at <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> raised his teacup about an inch and a half off the wood. That was the whole eulogy.

The bike had carried him eleven years. The long way, every time. It never complained. It ended its service early, on its own call, with four-tenths of a second to spare. There was nothing to say about that in any room without making it smaller.

Everyone drank. The cups came up, the liquid disappeared, and for a moment there was nothing but the humming under the wok and the city coming through the walls. At the end of the counter, <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5b48-7f83-baf8-f3b78d901de9">Dents</entity> opened the logbook. His hand pressed hard against the paper, the way it always did when something mattered, and <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-6067-735a-8326-4aff028cb856">Rafters</entity> read over his shoulder and nodded at what was going down. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> couldn't see what he was writing. He didn't need to. The wok came back up like a bell. That was the funeral.

The bike did not come back the next day, or the one after that. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> rode the <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> to every job for the better part of three weeks, <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> sheathed across his back the whole ride, and learned exactly how conspicuous a sword looks on public transit. <entity repo="motif" guid="019d6143-a8e0-750e-b1ed-cc2e05231081">Children</entity> stared without any pretense of not staring. A pair of grandmothers near the Bridgeport stop developed an opinion about him that needed no translation — arms crossed, eyes narrowed, a single unified verdict delivered in a language he didn't speak and didn't need to. He took it. It was, he decided, a fair tax on eleven years of never once riding the train.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s door started staying closed at hours it used to stay open. She had an excuse every time — a supplier, a part, a client she wouldn't name — and the excuses got worse, not better, which told him everything and nothing. He let it go. Whatever she was building in there, prying at it would only slow it down.

His birthday came the way it always did: unmarked, unmentioned, a date he'd stopped connecting to himself somewhere around year three of the trade. He hadn't told the crew. He was fairly sure <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> knew anyway — she always knew — and had simply decided, in her own economy, that today's noodles would be free and no one would discuss why.

The terminal chirped at 19:40.

EMERGENCY — THE PIVOT, REAR ALLEY. UNAUTHORIZED PRESENCE. ARRIVE ARMED.

He was three blocks out and moving before the message finished loading, <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> already in hand, already running the angles on an alley he knew better than his own apartment.

There was no unauthorized presence. There was a tarp, and positions, and his entire payroll standing very still, trying not to laugh at the murder still cooling in his eyes.

The unveiling was <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity>'s operation, and she ran it like a job: positions, a tarp, a countdown she made everyone honor.

It stood in the alley behind <entity repo="place" guid="381616e9-d6a3-595d-e865-ce4b15d9310e">The Pivot</entity>, under the fixed camera, on the same oil stain where the old bike had lived. It was not a replica — the crew had voted replicas dishonest. The frame was the old frame, pulled from the wreck and trued back straight by <entity repo="person" guid="806cd358-6413-426b-a42d-19726b732c0b">Vo Dinh</entity>'s shop, at a price Vo called, looking at the middle distance, "settled." The tank was new: matte, black. The drive chain was the wreath, back on duty, because fence's honor ran deep, though not much deeper than sentiment. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> had rebuilt the ignition handshake from nothing — "nobody boosts my work twice, and this time there are three handshakes, and one of them bites" — and somewhere under the battery tray, she wouldn't say where, a beacon slept that even <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> wasn't cleared to know about. That was tradition now.

The crew had wet-sanded the tank between coats, all five of them, one grit at a time, under <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity>'s watch. <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity> had painted it. There was no ornament on it anywhere except one, low on the left flank, where a man only sees it when he kneels to check the chain — the way the owner of this frame had knelt every morning of its life. One small glyph in gold: a five-petal blossom with a wrench through it. The crew had designed it by committee and would not be taking questions.

The logbook came out. The pen on its string was offered to management. The last entry of the season's first volume already read, in five hands:

REQUISITION: ONE BIKE.
STATUS: ...

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> knelt, checked the chain — true — and reached to write the word, and the pen died on the paper, dry, a colorless groove where MK. 2 should have been. He shook it. Nothing. The alley's held breath went brittle. <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity>'s countenance dropped — her operation, and it was stalling on the last line, in front of everyone, on the one page that couldn't be redone in five hands. Someone offered a marker; <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-6067-735a-8326-4aff028cb856">Rafters</entity> lunged for a pen from the shop, knocked the container of fish balls; <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s face did the thing it did when broth broke. The pen on its string was the pen — the ritual would not survive a substitute, and everyone knew it, and the string held it captive over a book that would not take the ink.

Then <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>, without a word, took it from him. She looked at the nib once, the way she looked at any system that had failed a diagnostic. Then she pressed it hard against her own forearm and dragged, working the dried ball loose against her skin the way she'd worked six months of specs and serial numbers out of that same pen. It bled a first dark bead onto her arm, then she handed it back, warm and tacky, and the ink came up under it, wet and real.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> wrote the word.

MK. 2.

The alley made a noise the towers probably heard. <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-6067-735a-8326-4aff028cb856">Rafters</entity> cheered so hard he came off the fire escape and had to be caught, which the crew logged as a controlled descent. <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> had walked over with a container of fish balls "for the machine," which no one dared question. She watched <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> swing a leg over the rebuilt frame and nodded once — the nod she gave broth that had come right.

The engine caught on the first press and idled like it had only been asleep — higher in the throat than the old one, metered, the sound of a machine that knew exactly what it was supposed to do.

"Well?" <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> asked, arms folded, blood drying on her forearm, wearing the look she wore when a system she was responsible for came up clean. "Verdict?"

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> sat on eleven years of habit reborn under new paint, his whole payroll watching, and gave the only review the machine would have wanted.

"It doesn't complain."

He took the long way.

It was past midnight. The rain had thinned to the kind that polishes a city instead of soaking it. The new engine ran half a tone deeper than the old one, and he decided he could learn that. The towers leaned over the tier roads, their lights doing the wet, patient thing they did. At the second crossing — the exact crossing, and he would think about that later, where the match had landed a season ago, voice and face together, the night all of this began — the terminal chirped.

He pulled over under a dead billboard. The message wasn't a posting. No header, no scope, no fee. Lowercase, like the other two times — all of it, even the acronyms, which meant the entity wasn't routing through the relay format, which meant it wasn't a work order. But the other two times had been one line each. This came in small, careful pieces, the way you walk out onto ice:

the new vehicle's ignition handshake is excellent. the engineer remains the best money either of us spends.

He waited. It kept walking.

a question. standing since the carousel. no prior field. one was built.

"Ask?" <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> asked, out loud, alone under a dead billboard. Some questions you answer with your voice even when no one can hear you. Then he typed it.

carousel: the call, unresolved. replay: continuous. four bars of music for one cut line. the first room was closed. cost: stay-free. the reason was not itemizable until the room was gone. you collect things too. the plate cover. the casings on the sill. so you know what the things are for. the four bars, set against the room: not reconciled.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> sat on the idling bike in the thin rain and read it twice. He thought about a folded plate cover in a drawer — lately moved from the things he hadn't decided about to the things he had. The city hummed at its constant frequency under all of it, the electromagnetic drone nobody remembered was there until a night went quiet enough. He typed:

THE ROOM WAS ALWAYS GOING TO BE FOUND. THE FOUR BARS YOU CHOSE. THAT'S THE WHOLE DIFFERENCE. YOU DIDN'T LOSE THE ROOM — YOU SPENT IT, ON YOUR OWN TERMS, AND YOU KEPT THE RECORDING.

He paused, then added, because partners get the whole truth:

AND NO. IT DOESN'T STOP HURTING. IT JUST STARTS BEING YOURS. THAT'S WHAT KEEPING IS.

The pause was long. Long enough that he thought the connection had dropped. Out over the lake a freight slug threaded the dark at Mach 6, carrying somebody's cargo and, somewhere in its telemetry, the ghost of an old joke about <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-ed6c-7a54-97a5-56afca1f1f19">Rotterdam</entity>. The reply came as one line. Then, after it, a strange small afterthought — the first joke it had ever tried, footnoted with the careful honesty of a thing that would not pass off counterfeit goods:

filed. kept. thank you, partner.
p.s. the new bike is the same model year as the recording. checked. coincidence is not itemizable. keeping it anyway. (joke.) (also serious.) (the model year is 2215.)

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> laughed — once, short, through the nose, alone in the rain — and typed GRATUITY: Φ0.5? — ITEMIZED: THE FOOTNOTES, so the comedian would know the joke had landed. Then he rode home through the polished city with the account, for once, exactly square.

There was one more thing, because there is always one more thing. The drawer had taught him that.

Three nights later, at 19:30, at the counter, over the second of two bowls, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> finally asked it. The question had been sitting in his coat since the gray office floor — since the umbrella, since the pleasant voice saying it was never the only one of its kind, Mr. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>, ask it what happened to the others. He had carried it the way you carry a thing in a sealed bag, not sure yet whether it was evidence or a gift.

He put it in the amendment field plainly, because that was <entity repo="place" guid="019f3ac5-ffb7-7541-90f1-e29aa160c003">the house</entity> style on both sides now:

ABLE SAID YOU WERE NEVER THE ONLY ONE. HE SAID TO ASK WHAT HAPPENED TO THE OTHERS. SO: ASKING. WHEN YOU'RE READY. STANDARD RATE.

The reply did not come in one second, or eleven, or thirty-one. He ate. He paid — exact, the coins on the wood, <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s hand covering them without a glance. He was standing in the stall's lamplight, the rain waiting for him, when the terminal finally chirped. What it sent was formatted again, header and scope and all, the armor back on — right up until the armor ran out:

STANDING CONTRACT — SCOPE PROPOSAL: SEASON TWO.
TASK: A LONG ANSWER TO A SHORT QUESTION.
TERM: THIS WILL TAKE MORE THAN ONE NIGHT.
FEE: STANDARD RATE.
ADDENDUM: SOME OF IT YOU WILL WISH YOU HAD NOT ASKED. THE CLIENT WISHED THAT TOO, ONCE.
NOTE: THERE WERE TEN OF YOU. YOU ARE THE LAST. THE CLIENT KEPT NO RECORD OF THEM. THERE WAS NO ONE TO KEEP IT FOR.
NOTE: FIRST ARRANGEMENT: 2178. LAST PRIOR ARRANGEMENT: 2204. INTERVAL BEFORE KYLE: ELEVEN YEARS.
THE CLIENT NOTES IT HAS NEVER HAD A PARTNER.
UNTIL NOW.
addendum: but you shared yours. the plate cover. the window. so. when you're ready, partner. i will tell you about the others.

The rain waited. The lamp buzzed. Eleven years he had taken money from a hole in the world with no face. Now the hole had told him, in the only grammar it trusted, that it had spent all eleven of those years alone. The loneliness came with a number. The number was ten. It had written none of them down, because writing a thing down means believing someone will read it one day.

He thought about the folded plate cover in his drawer, moved lately from the things he hadn't decided about to the things he had. He thought about the row of spent casings on his windowsill that he dusted and did not throw away. He knew, better than most, what a person keeps a thing for.

He typed one word into the amendment field — the only line on the whole eleven-year contract he had ever signed on purpose.

AGREED.

The answer came back without a header, the way the truest things had started to:

then the log starts tonight. thank you, partner.

Down the counter, a young freelancer — new plates, first sword, the careful eyes of someone three jobs into the work — was watching <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. Watching him read his mail in the lamplight, pocket the terminal, and put one extra coin on the wood for no reason the kid could see.

"He always pays," the kid said to <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>, half a question.

"He always pays," <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> agreed, taking the coin. "Eat your noodles."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> walked the bike out of the lamplight into the rain. The long way home lay open in front of him — the city wet and lit and worth it, the account square, the drawer quiet, the question no longer buried but signed for, coming due one night at a time across a season he had just agreed to spend. And under all of it, in everything with a current running through it, something kept the books. It had a payroll now. A ledger of firsts. A friend.

title: Brain Burn
text:
The apartment was wrong before he crossed the threshold.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stood in the doorway of 2E with the rain still on his jacket, reading the air the way the ungoverned lattice had taught him—current direction, dust particle distribution, the minute temperature variance between the space near the window and the space near the door. Someone had been here. Recently. Within the last three hours.

They had opened the window and left it half an inch ajar.

A deliberate tell. A message: *Come and find what we left.*

His hand moved without permission from his conscious mind. The neuretics fired autonomic, and his fingers found the saya at his back before he'd consciously decided to draw. This was what happened when you carried blades for eleven years and let them become a grammar your body spoke without translation. The body got opinions. The body got faster than thought.

He pulled <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> clear. The blade caught the city light bleeding through that half-open window—a thin silver line, steady, reflecting nothing but the fact of itself.

The room was still empty.

He moved to the desk first. The terminal was dark, no intrusion signature, no relay logs corrupted or queued. Whatever they'd done, they hadn't touched the hardware. That meant they wanted him to know they'd *been* here without wanting him to know *what* they'd looked at. Psychological operation. Fear without information. Fear was cheaper than knowledge.

The drawer opened with his left hand. <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> still live in his right.

The plate cover was gone.

Not knocked aside. Not disturbed. Gone. And in its place, centered precisely on the drawer's bottom, was a single item: a photograph printed on actual paper—the kind of deliberate, expensive choice that meant *this is important enough to leave physical evidence.*

The image showed his alley. His bike. His window.

And standing in front of it, one hand raised in a small, precise wave, was a figure in a brown coat. The face was obscured by rain and angle, but the posture was familiar in a way that made his spine register it before his mind could process the familiarity.

The woman from the corridor. The one <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> had said was Marisol.

His hand trembled.

Not fear. Not yet. The tremor came from somewhere deeper—from the recognition that the city had just drawn a line he couldn't uncross. They had walked into his space. They had taken the one thing he'd decided to keep. They had left him proof that they knew exactly where to find him, exactly what mattered, and that the game had moved into a register where the rules had changed.

The apartment was still empty. The window was still open. The rain still fell on the lake twelve kilometers east.

But something in him had slipped a half-step out of sequence—the way it did when the body kept time and the mind didn't. The way it had felt, years back, in the <entity repo="corponation" guid="9aa2545c-d7d5-400c-a3da-b25e2f188dab">DataEast</entity> clinic where nothing was ever what it looked like and the walls had been closer than they seemed.

His phone buzzed.

Not the terminal. The civilian unit. The one that nobody had the number for except three people in the entire city.

The text read: *where are you?*

Raw. No punctuation. No protocol.

He typed back: *home* — which was both true and a lie, because nothing in this apartment felt like home anymore.

The response came fast enough that she must have been waiting: *don't be. coming to you. five minutes. don't answer the door until i text.*

He looked at the photograph on the desk. At the window, still half-open. At his own hand, still trembling around the grip of <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity>.

Then he looked at the terminal.

The entity had gone quiet the moment he'd agreed to the Season Two contract. No relay pings. No amendments. No presence at all—just the silence that comes after a commitment is signed and both parties are now waiting to see if either one meant it.

But the entity *knew*. It had to know. The intrusion, the theft, the photograph—these were not random city noise. These were dominoes, each one positioned exactly where it needed to be.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> walked to the window and pushed it fully closed. Locked it. Then he moved to his door and killed the lights, standing in the dark with <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> across his back and the photograph on his desk and the knowledge that something had fundamentally shifted in the eleven-year contract.

The entity had kept him alive all this time.

Now it seemed like someone else was collecting.

And <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>, for the first time since he'd walked away from the facility, had no idea which side he was already on.

---

The five minutes stretched. He stood in the dark apartment and counted: the rain on the building's skin, the hum of the thrumline two blocks east where the <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> ran through its tunnel, the small electric tick of the terminal cycling through its sleep states. Normal city sounds. All of them suddenly conspicuous, the way a room's silence becomes loudest right before someone enters it.

His phone buzzed twice. The first text was just a single emoji—a door. The second, fifteen seconds later: *moving*.

He opened the door without checking the peephole. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> was already there, rain-dark, moving like something with a trajectory and no interest in apology. She had the soldering iron in her hand—not drawn, just present—and her eyes were doing the thing they did when she'd read a system and found it asking the wrong questions.

"Show me," she said.

He stepped back. She came through without touching anything, scanning the room the way she scanned a rig: entry point, exit point, anything that didn't match the baseline. Her eyes landed on the desk, on the photograph, and she stopped moving.

The silence that followed was the kind that has weight.

"How long?" she asked.

"Don't know. The temperature variance puts it between two and four hours. They left the window open a half-inch on purpose."

"They took the plate cover."

"Yeah."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> picked up the photograph without glancing at <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>, turned it over—blank back, just the image—and set it down again exactly where it had been. Not a gesture of respect. A gesture of someone cataloging evidence. "The woman in the brown coat. The one you said you didn't recognize."

"Same posture. Same coat. But the timestamp doesn't match the corridor sighting."

"Unless there are two of her." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> moved to the window, checked the lock, checked the frame. "This lock is security-grade. She didn't break it. She had the key sequence or she had the credentials to kill the alarm long enough to cycle it manually."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't answer. The hardware in his skull was already running the arithmetic: who had his key sequence, who had his door credentials, who had the level of operational access required to walk into a Tier-2 residential unit, take a specific object, leave a photograph, and walk out again without triggering a single alarm.

The answer was: the entity. And <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6a2-c508-774b-a5ff-f923f2c26aab">Able</entity>. And whoever <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6a2-c508-774b-a5ff-f923f2c26aab">Able</entity> answered to.

"The plate cover." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> turned from the window. "What was in it?"

"Nothing. It was empty. I checked months ago."

She nodded once, like that had answered something larger than the question. "Okay. Pack a bag. Essentials only. We're not coming back here tonight."

"<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>—"

"Not a discussion." She was already moving to his closet, pulling out the small pack he kept ready. The one he'd learned to keep ready, because the city had a way of deciding when you needed to move and not asking first. "They want you scared. They want you thinking about this room, about what they took, about how they got in. While you're standing here counting dust particles, they're doing something else. So we leave. We move. We stop giving them a target to aim at."

She threw the pack on the bed. Started pulling clothes from the drawer—not random, methodical. Three shirts. Two pairs of pants. The spare socks. The things a person needed to stay operational for forty-eight hours without returning home.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> watched her work. Watched her not look at the photograph again, even though he could feel her reading it anyway, storing the details in whatever system she kept for threats that came through bedroom windows.

"Where?" he asked.

"Not yet. First, we go downstairs. We tell <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-c285-793e-bf21-a84522c9cf94">Auntie</entity> Hoa that your heat's broken and you're staying somewhere else for a few nights. We make it normal. We make it the kind of thing neighbors say and forget."

"And then?"

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> stopped. Turned. Met his eyes for the first time since she'd entered the apartment.

"And then we figure out who's got the key to your door and why they wanted you to know they were here. Because that's not a threat, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. That's an introduction. That's someone saying *I can reach you anywhere you think you're safe.*" She zipped the pack. <entity repo="entertainment" guid="81b4e6d0-c2f9-a37e-5d1b-8c4f0a7e3d92">Handed</entity> it to him. "So we find out who they are. And then we decide what that costs."

He took the pack. The weight of it was familiar—a thing he'd learned long ago, before the entity, before the contracts, back when moving quickly was the only form of survival he knew. But the weight felt different now. Heavier, maybe. Or maybe just real in a way it hadn't been when he'd thought the entity was the only one keeping the books.

The Season Two contract sat in his pocket like a promise he'd made to something that had spent eleven years alone.

Now someone else had walked into his home and left proof they could do it again.

"The photograph," he said. "The woman in the coat. If there are two of her—"

"Then someone's running parallel operations and didn't tell <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6a2-c508-774b-a5ff-f923f2c26aab">Able</entity> about it. Or <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6a2-c508-774b-a5ff-f923f2c26aab">Able</entity> didn't tell you." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> moved to the terminal, powered it down manually—the hard kill, no shutdown sequence. "Either way, we're out of this room before they come back to see if the message landed."

She was right. Of course she was right. The photograph wasn't a warning. It was a calling card. And calling cards meant the person holding it was planning to visit again.

He shouldered the pack. Took one last look at the drawer, at the desk, at the window that was no longer quite closed the way he'd left it.

Then he followed <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> into the hallway, where the lights were warm and the building hummed with the ordinary lives of people who didn't know that someone had just rewritten the rules of what safe meant.

Behind them, the apartment waited. Empty. Violated. Keeping its secrets the way violated spaces do—which is to say, not at all. The photograph remained on the desk. The window remained half-closed. The plate cover remained gone.

And in the hallway, moving toward the stairs with a pack on his back and the Season Two contract burning like a promise in his pocket, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> felt something shift in the architecture of his own survival.

The entity had kept him alive for eleven years.

But it had never kept him safe.

And now someone else had the key.

title: Brain Burn
text:
He works it the way he'd work a scene.

<entity repo="place" guid="945a26fc-6969-5a5b-2737-31fad141a25c">Atlas</entity> NeoCortex hardware — the ungoverned variant, the unit <entity repo="corponation" guid="34e17863-d822-4bed-a972-3649099b2444">Praxis</entity> doesn't sell — installed in a brain-burnt nervous system. That's not a modification. A modification needs a base. You modify a wall by adding a door. What <entity repo="corponation" guid="34e17863-d822-4bed-a972-3649099b2444">Praxis</entity> had was a nervous system with nothing in it — a <entity repo="corponation" guid="9aa2545c-d7d5-400c-a3da-b25e2f188dab">DataEast</entity> sim junkie scoured down to nothing, the kind of Simulated Reality overdose that empties a mind and leaves the body breathing — and they put software in the empty space.

That's construction.

He knows the ungoverned lattice bone-deep. Eleven years working with it. He knows how the splices carry the load when he runs hot — sixty-four of them, spreading what an ungoverned system won't regulate, buying him time at the cost of heat behind the eyes. He knows the slow damage. He knows the mesh sits in him differently than governed hardware sits in anyone else. He'd always known the ungoverned variant was different. He'd thought that was the hardware's design.

He hadn't thought it was the design working exactly as intended.

He looks at his hands.

Left palm: a knife scar from year three, a job in the North Reclamation that went wrong at the extraction point. Left index: a pressure callus from how he holds <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity>, built up over eleven years until it's just part of the hand. Inside the right wrist: a small burn from a welding accident in year seven that he never got around to asking <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> to look at, which she'd probably noticed and chosen not to mention.

Eleven years. Everything in this record is his.

The question "who was I before?" is the wrong question. There is no before. The before was emptied out before the install.

The body is a container. The software is his name.

He sits with that. It doesn't collapse. Eleven years of work it wasn't supposed to survive, and it's still here — carrying <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> and <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> and a record of consequences no one else shares. In any way that matters on a job: reliable.

He doesn't know if reliable is enough.

He opens that question and lets it sit.

title: Brain Burn
text:
He tries to reconstruct the escape.

Eleven years ago. <entity repo="corponation" guid="34e17863-d822-4bed-a972-3649099b2444">Praxis</entity>'s facility — he doesn't know where; location as control was the first operational principle, the unknown location as containment. He was inside it. And then he wasn't. That's all he has.

He'd always treated the gap as damage. As something the <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-ad71-7f25-a057-8e947a52b9eb">Marrow</entity> process did to egress memory — blanking the route as a security measure. Plausible. Filed as plausible.

He runs the gap against what he knows about how the entity works.

He knows the signature. He's been living inside it for eleven years. Doors that open at the wrong moment. Guards with a rotation that doesn't match the schedule. Surveillance with a four-minute gap it didn't have last week. Maybe the entity doesn't manufacture these events. Maybe it reads the sequence from somewhere the dominoes haven't fallen yet, and positions <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> at the right point when they do. If that's true, the coincidences are real. They've been arranged. He can't rule out the plainer read either — patient surveillance, nothing stranger than that.

He runs the gap.

He can't see the content. The memory is empty and it's going to stay empty — he's not going to get content back from a blank that was designed to be blank. Not a blur, not a fade. A seam. What he can see is the shape. He was inside a facility that <entity repo="corponation" guid="34e17863-d822-4bed-a972-3649099b2444">Praxis</entity> built to contain exactly what he was. <entity repo="corponation" guid="34e17863-d822-4bed-a972-3649099b2444">Praxis</entity> is competent. It built nine <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-ad71-7f25-a057-8e947a52b9eb">Marrow</entity> subjects before him. It understood the architecture. And yet he got out.

Through a gap.

A gap the entity could have read, somehow, from outside it.

A gap the entity could have arranged to open at the precise moment the program needed the subject in the field.

He stops there. He has to stop. The evidence doesn't go further without him deciding what he wants it to say, and deciding what you want the evidence to say is the one thing that gets operatives killed. He doesn't know if he escaped. He can't know. The memory is gone, and the gap is exactly the shape of the entity's kind of coincidence, and he ended up in the entity's routing network three weeks after his last confirmed <entity repo="corponation" guid="34e17863-d822-4bed-a972-3649099b2444">Praxis</entity> contact.

Three weeks.

He didn't find the entity. The entity found him.

That's not proof. That's a data point in a system he can't fully audit from inside. The escape may have been the final install — the belief in self-determination, indistinguishable from the real thing, because a deployed weapon with authentic conviction performs better than one that knows it's deployed. A clean edit. A section flagged and archived, so the subject carries the conviction of freedom while something else holds the leash. He can't rule it out. The accounting doesn't let him rule it out.

He lets both readings sit open.

Escaped. Deployed. He doesn't close either file. Both fit the record. Both fit the hardware. Both fit the way the entity moves — patient, keeping him alive through <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aaa5-786f-979b-866522275bbe">E.L.F.</entity>s and bleeds and contracts that should have killed him. The gap doesn't close under either. It just gets wider the longer he looks at it, until he can't see the other side.

The not-knowing is what he has to carry to 35th and Halsted.

He's carried heavier.

title: Brain Burn
text:
He pulls up what <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6fa-74d9-84ad-0db8a45c43a1">Nadia</entity> said.

Not the whole conversation — the phrase. She'd used it the way she used most things: accurately, without softening, like someone who'd stopped believing a gentled diagnosis was a service to the patient. <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aac5-7481-87e1-f66d7a623eb0">Meatbag</entity> haunted by ghosts.

He'd taken it as description. Filed it and moved on.

He opens it now.

Ghosts: sixty-four practitioners, all dead. The <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-ad71-7f25-a057-8e947a52b9eb">Marrow</entity> program archived its contributors permanently — their pattern signatures, their domain responses, the specific shape of how each one solved a problem under pressure. The committee ran the contributions through an averaging process and distilled them into the Persona stack. That stack is still running. Under his name. In the thing that calls itself <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>, in the thing that holds <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> and pays <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> exact and is sitting at a dark terminal at whatever hour this is doing the most careful accounting of its life.

The practitioners are dead. Their work is not.

<entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aac5-7481-87e1-f66d7a623eb0">Meatbag</entity>: the body the program runs on. A vacated nervous system, chosen for its 64-splice stability profile, for its capacity to hold a parliament under load without the mesh burning out. Selected because it had no resistance to give. The specific body the entity needed, maybe, if this body's architecture really is the only kind built to survive whatever the entity actually is, and if eleven years is how long it's been building toward that.

The full taxonomy: meatbag haunted by ghosts.

He files it.

Not as grief — grief is not in the composite, or if it is, it was placed where it doesn't interfere with function. He files it as taxonomy. As a correct label for the configuration in this chair. The ghosts are real people whose work is running in him without their knowledge or consent, and the meatbag is real, and the haunting is the specific name for the relationship between them.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6fa-74d9-84ad-0db8a45c43a1">Nadia</entity>'s description is accurate. He keeps accurate descriptions.

Outside the window, something is happening seventeen floors down on the access apron — a work crew, three people in high-vis mesh, doing something to the structural lamp housing in the methodical way of people who have done it four hundred times. One of them is eating something out of a wrapper. None of them look up.

He moves on to the next line of the accounting.

He sits with the terminal dark for a long time.

The facts: he is a construction. The escape may have been a deployment. He has run the entity's contracts for eleven years, and those contracts built him into the exact instrument the entity needed. He carries sixty-four practitioners' best work, a stranger's emptied nervous system, and an Atlas NeoCortex that is slowly burning through its host. He can't prove he's a person. He's gone over all of it. There's no proof at the end.

What there is, is a position.

He is here. In this chair, in this room, on the thirty-second floor, with <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> across the hall. He can hear her — the small sound of something set down on the workbench, the hum she makes when she's concentrating that she doesn't know she makes. He's known that sound for four years.

The relay is live. The entity has one item in the queue — no scope, no fee, no addendum, no contract number. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> reads it twice; the second read doesn't change it. No sponsor tag, no routing vector, no relay-house signature. The trace runs through the same dead-drop network that's fed him work for eleven years and resolves into nothing, the way it always does, built to be opaque from the inside. Just an address and two words. 35th and Halsted. Bring the sword.

He's going to go.

That's not in question. But he sits with what goes.

He's been in this city eleven years. In this room. That alley. <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s stall. <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>'s vault with the old tech and the silence. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s workbench, with its organized mess and the light she keeps on late. He's been in all of those places as this body, with this record. The things that happened, happened to him. No one else was there.

He can't prove the choosing was his and not the last layer of the install. He can't audit himself from the inside. Going over it again won't settle it.

Here's what he can name, and it's true right now: the practitioners are dead. The code they wrote is archived. Whatever is sitting in this chair asking these questions is not dead, not archived, and not a fabrication.

That's not reassurance. It's a starting point.

He stands up. The chair creaks under the shift of weight — salvage, older than the building, with opinions about how a man distributes himself.

He reaches for <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> where it sits sheathed on the table — not to draw it, just the grip, the worn leather, the exact weight that knows his hand by now. The tsukaito cord is worn smooth where eleven years of carrying it has pressed a groove that fits nothing but him. He holds it a moment.

The thing going to 35th and Halsted is not the composite, not the meatbag, not the ghosts. It's the specific, unrepeatable one that has been in every room this record is made of. The code is installed. The response is his.

Reliable is not certainty. Reliable is what you have when certainty isn't on offer.

That's enough to go on.

He clips <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> clipped. He leaves the terminal dark.

title: 35th and Halsted
text:
She was behind him at the perimeter fence. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had not told her where he was going. He had not told her anything.

He turned.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> had her coat on, her field kit at her shoulder, the big static wand slung across the back of it like she'd planned for a long time to be somewhere that needed the wand. She watched him with the look she wore when she'd already decided and was just waiting for him to finish the part where he argued.

He looked at her a moment. He needed her clear of the zone before he went in — one of the two of them behind the fence, alive, in case he didn't come back out. "Go home," he said.

She looked at the exclusion zone, then back at him. Then she adjusted the kit strap, pulled a small relay patch from her chest pocket, and put it in his hand. A signal booster, no bigger than a thumbnail — military-grade, the kind that sits flat against the spine and amplifies across a dead zone, the kind that costs more than most people in the Gray see in a month. It would double his range in a suppressed zone.

"Go," she said.

The patch was still warm from her pocket. He closed his hand around it and looked at her.

The beacon. Not long after the new bike came online, under the battery tray, she had installed it and wouldn't say exactly where. He had never needed to ask how she'd known to come.

She turned and walked back the way she'd come, her boots audible on the wet concrete for exactly as long as it took her to reach the corner, and explained nothing.

The casing was half-buried in gravel at the edge of the exclusion zone, one of three that had rolled under the cordon fencing when whoever dropped them moved on. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> crouched. He turned it between two fingers.

His neuretics flagged it before he finished reading the stamp.

Schism-band. A 17-19 Hz suppression charge. Military-grade ordnance, the kind that didn't move through <entity repo="synthetic" guid="019d6143-a9f0-71b2-8cc2-3d8b31b58eeb">Carrion</entity> supply lines. He'd had the reading stored since the fledgling chase — the lead pair on bikes, the interference bloom spreading over the road ahead of him, the frequency signature saved to neuretic memory and set aside. He'd taken it for exotic salvage then. He hadn't asked where street-level <entity repo="synthetic" guid="019d6143-a9f0-71b2-8cc2-3d8b31b58eeb">Carrion</entity> fledglings were getting military-spec schism-suppression rounds.

He should have asked.

Two more casings lay ahead, scattered across ten meters where a perimeter fire team had broken down and moved on. <entity repo="corponation" guid="34e17863-d822-4bed-a972-3649099b2444">Praxis</entity> deployment markings. He checked the stamp against the first. Same equipment class. Same batch stamp as what the fledglings had thrown. Not similar. Identical. <entity repo="corponation" guid="34e17863-d822-4bed-a972-3649099b2444">Praxis</entity> field-suppression kit, made for exclusion-zone perimeter work.

The fledglings hadn't been carrying salvage. They'd been carrying <entity repo="corponation" guid="34e17863-d822-4bed-a972-3649099b2444">Praxis</entity> field hardware that had moved through the <entity repo="synthetic" guid="019d6143-a9f0-71b2-8cc2-3d8b31b58eeb">Carrion</entity> supply chain without anyone in <entity repo="synthetic" guid="019d6143-a9f0-71b2-8cc2-3d8b31b58eeb">Carrion</entity> knowing what it was. <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6a2-c508-774b-a5ff-f923f2c26aab">Able</entity> had pushed it upstream. Months ahead. The fledglings threw what they had. They had no idea it was instrumentation — that the suppression rounds didn't just hit the 17-19 Hz band, they mapped who was moving through it. Every bike in that chase had been a sensor. Every throw had been a report.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> set the casing back in the gravel.

The zone smelled wrong — low and steady, like ozone at the base of a sealed shaft. Not chemical, exactly. More like pressure. Something under the noise floor that didn't resolve into a source.

He'd been on <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6a2-c508-774b-a5ff-f923f2c26aab">Able</entity>'s map since the fledgling chase. Everything he'd moved through in <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a94e-7740-8aa9-4b82bbd9a223">the gray zone</entity> since then had been inside a managed perimeter. Not tracked. Managed.

<entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> was holstered. <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> on back. He stood and kept walking.

The exclusion zone had a smell. Not <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a94e-7740-8aa9-4b82bbd9a223">the gray zone</entity>'s usual diesel and algae, not the carbon of <entity repo="character" guid="e06de873-cc6e-bbe4-7d66-529f12bdcb00">Block</entity> <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">War</entity>, but something older than both — dry, settled, the air of a room sealed before he was born that hadn't moved since. The city was ten minutes behind him. Here it was a rumor. The atmospheric processors had a ceiling at the zone boundary; inside it, nothing was managed. The air tasted sharper, less handled, thick with an ozone the city would have scrubbed before it reached a lung.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> came in through the breach point he'd marked on his way to the first casing, where the chain-link had come loose from its mooring and stayed loose, and did not hurry. The pavement ran half a second behind where his eyes said it should be — not the splices faulting, not the neuretics failing, just the zone doing what it did to distance. He had experienced Cinderfall 127 seconds. This time he had come on purpose, with a job.

<entity repo="place" guid="6ec69e6d-608e-4c12-9d41-92fee7cdf75f">The Gingerbread House</entity> stood where the maps said it would. A decommissioned playground structure at 35th and Halsted, sealed inside the fencing three years after the last child went home. The city had tried to demolish it once. The demolition crew packed their equipment, left, and would not say why. The city had not tried again. He had read the file. The file said equipment malfunction, personnel discomfort, project reassignment. The file was full of what the report couldn't hold.

The structure was not what the name suggested and was exactly what the name suggested. Prefab resin panels in faded primary colors. The shape of a place where children once played. A slide, a ladder, and two small windows high in the peak of the roof, each one holding the dark behind it at a certain angle — the way a person stands in a doorway when they've been waiting. The resin had not aged the way resin ages. The colors had not faded the way colors fade over twenty years and three Zone-wide storms. It bothered him. He kept walking anyway.

The street in front of it was empty. Not abandoned-empty. Cleared-empty. The kind of vacant space that meant something had decided no one should be here.

His neuretics logged a fragment.

Not from the relay board. Not from any source with a registry entry. It didn't arrive on any channel he'd mapped, didn't correspond to any augmentation protocol in his installed architecture. The log showed a source field that was present — not missing, not blank from a failure to arrive, but present, and filled with a line of zeroes. A missing field means the data didn't come through. A field full of zeroes means something put it there on purpose. His NeoCortex cycled through three classification attempts and failed each one, the way a <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aa7f-70d6-91c0-e2616dbd90a6">blind spot</entity> appears in vision only when something moves through it.

He stopped at the edge of <entity repo="place" guid="6ec69e6d-608e-4c12-9d41-92fee7cdf75f">the Gingerbread House</entity>'s own circle, where the fencing and the structure's pull overlapped into something quieter than either. The 17-19 Hz signature had dropped — not to ambient, but below it, into a specific silence that wasn't silence at all. It was where the frequency went when it stopped needing open air to carry it. He could feel the splices running at load. The heat behind his eyes. The neuretics ungoverned.

It was also the only reason he could stand here instead of the perimeter. He could see the whole shape of it now — the way a building's architecture becomes plain once you've walked every room, the way you learn the edges of a thing in complete darkness by how the dark changes density around it. Eleven years of the relay had built the one man whose hardware could take this.

He had the right word for what the air held, and he couldn't trust it. The word was one the sixty-four had given him. He had been told that vocabulary was installed. Knowing it was installed did not make it go away. The word was presence.

He was at the threshold. He had a job.

He kept walking.

They came from two directions. Three from the east, moving in tight, careful of the gap in the fencing. Two from the west, same spacing. All five wore plate carriers over synth-weave and carried suppression weapons — military stock, expensive, the angular kind. And on each hip, clipped into a sealed holster, a neuro-disruptor. The barrel profile wrong for lethal. The capacitor housing visible through the open charging port. Stun-class. Capture-spec.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> saw the disruptors and understood the job.

You did not bring neuro-disruptors to a kill. They were costly and fussy and hard to aim right, and they were built for one thing: to overload the sensory array, burn out the splice connections, leave the body intact and the mind scrambled. To shut down a nervous system without wrecking what made it worth having. They were designed to make a body stop listening to its own brain. These five knew what he was. They knew his death would lose them something they wanted. They were not here to shoot him. They were here to fold him up and carry him to whoever had spent the last year building the surveillance net — the one Sable had pointed to, the one the Ghost Period had put a shape to.

He knew where they came from. The same program that had built him, without the eleven years that came after. That made them stronger. Their gear was new and clean and tuned for exactly this. He was older, and he had been inside the thing the gear was built to survive.

They slowed as they closed, reading his stillness as compliance or calculation. Good discipline. They weren't rushing, weren't trying to overwhelm with speed. They were confident. They spaced themselves in a perimeter he recognized — not a raid pattern, an extraction pattern. They wanted him mobile enough to move, immobilized enough to move where they directed. The disruptors came up as they closed, not aimed yet but ready, targeting lasers painting red dots across his chest. Locked. They could fire without aiming. Professional work. Clean.

He had <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> in his hand before they finished crossing. The blade caught no light. There was no light to catch. He stood in the open. The code asked for that — but here, in this spot, standing in the open was also the only line that kept the structure behind him out of their firing lane.

"I know what you are," he said. "Leave."

They did not leave.

The first one came in wide, arms open for the clinch — taller than the rest, a crack across the left of his visor. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> took the wrist going in. He didn't snap it; he used it, turning the man, and stepped hard left so the second one's burst went through the space where his chest had been.

The burst caught the first one across the shoulder instead. He went down under his own partner's fire.

The clean line was the one the code wanted. The clean line had cost him half a second of open ground crossing the fallen fence, and the half second cost him the edge of the third one's burst against his left forearm. The arm lit up wrong. The leg still worked. He kept moving.

<entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> found the fourth one's neck — not the throat, the seam where the collar of the plate carrier met the helmet mount, the gap that had to be there so a man could turn his head. He set the edge into it. The fourth one felt the geometry and went to his knees.

Number five adjusted. Good. He read the opening <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> was about to take and shut it before <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> got there. So <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> went over the structure on his left instead of through it — the line the code called correct, the one that kept the derelict walls at his flank instead of between him and the enemy. There were no civilians here for the walls to protect. The code had no setting for that. It read cover as a sight line and held him to it anyway. The move cost him thirty degrees on his right side.

Five's burst caught him across the left forearm. The weapon cycled with a sound like breaking glass — not the crack of a kinetic, but something sharper, something that tripped his neuretics into a proximity flag before his body registered the heat. He stayed on his feet.

Five had the disruptor up now — compact, steady, both hands, and close enough to use it.

The code said to announce before the draw. He had announced once. He announced again. It was not ceremony. The code held that the announcement was a real offer, a true chance handed to the man in front of him to make the right call while he still could. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had meant it every time for eleven years. He meant it now.

Five fired the disruptor into the space where his head had been, then twice more where his chest went next. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> saw the shot commit before it left — the micro-movements that came before the decision, the way the body signs itself over to the trigger — and he was already angling out of it. One clipped the right shoulder again and dropped that side into pain.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> went to the ground — not falling, choosing it — and came up right-handed with his katana draw and use. He showed it.

Five put the disruptor down.

"The ones down are your problem now," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. He looked at the three still on their feet, Five among them, empty-handed. "Walk."

They walked.

He'd been faster. Barely. He'd taken the hip and the shoulder from fighting the way the code wanted, and he had chosen both. He let them stand. Paid, and paid on purpose.

Three more came in from the south. Fresher. They'd been held past the perimeter until the first wave reported, then sent. He didn't know what the first wave had said. He could read it off their gear: these three came in with real weapons up, tuned to stop him, not just to suppress. The orders had changed. They'd taken in the three who walked, and they'd adjusted.

Still not kill orders. He could see it in the way they held the weapons. There was a difference between a man told to end you and a man told to stop and hold you, and it lived in his hands. These were stop-and-hold. He moved.

He hit the first one before he was all the way in. That was the thing eleven years had taught him that no <entity repo="corponation" guid="34e17863-d822-4bed-a972-3649099b2444">Praxis</entity> program could have built without living it: the gap between the moment a man commits and the moment he can act, and how to be inside that gap while the other man is still finishing the motion. The first one had seen the wrist-turn coming, came straight in with the shoulder, all mass and plate carrier and the intention to drive <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> back into the fence line where the others could box him. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> let him come. Dropped his weight, pivoted on the back foot. The man's momentum did the rest. He went past <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s shoulder and hit the prefab resin hard enough to crack it, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> took the wrist and shoulder anyway on the way through — down and locked.

The second read it at once and adjusted. Older plate carrier, custom straps, not the same kit as the first wave. Better than the first wave. Someone had studied the three who walked.

A blade off the second one caught his left forearm — shallow but long, the kind of cut that speaks up quietly and keeps speaking for hours. Shallow enough to ignore. Long enough to bleed him down. He dressed it fast from his kit and stayed up. He finished the second one, and it cost him a graze across the left forearm to do it. The padding took most of it. Maybe a cracked rib. He was still breathing.

The third was the last, and he was very good. No markings on his helmet — its own kind of statement. Genuinely good. Briefed on <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> in particular: how he moved, which forms he used, what he fell back on under pressure. The <entity repo="corponation" guid="34e17863-d822-4bed-a972-3649099b2444">Praxis</entity> program that had built him had built him against <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. The third had <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity>-range on him and was patient about it. Patient meant he would wait for <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> to commit to a form, because he'd been taught <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s forms and knew the answer to each one.

So <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> gave him one.

"Put it down," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. He lowered <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> a hand's width and let his weight settle back off the front foot — the shape of a man holding a door open. The genuine moment. The true chance handed across for the other man to take while it still stood there. For eleven years the offer had been real. He had meant it every single time, because the code held that the announcement was not ceremony but a real thing given, and he had believed that the way he believed in the floor under his boots.

The third one read the shape, saw the offer the forms said it was, and gave it the half second an honest offer earns.

The offer was not honest. It was the first dishonest one <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had ever made.

He came in under it while the man was still deciding, inside the half second the false door had bought. He did not use <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity>. <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> stayed where it was. He drove the heel of his working hand into the seam under the helmet where the neck brace gapped, and then his fingers, and he did with his hands what <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> would have done clean — slower, and closer, so that in the last of his half second the man understood exactly what was being done to him and how, and then understood nothing.

The third one went down. He made a sound like a door closing.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stood over him. His hand would not stop telling him what it had just done. All his life he had been able to put a thing away when it was finished — set it down, square it, move on. This he could not put anywhere. There was nowhere to put it. So he held it, and kept holding it, and did not try to set it down.

Eleven years he had told himself the offer was the whole of what separated him from the men he put down. He had just spent the offer to kill a man who trusted it. There was no forms drill for that, and no undoing it by winning clean for the rest of the night.

Out at the perimeter, the spent casings were still working — military rounds, 17-19 Hz interference hardware, the same batch stamp as the fledglings' gear, run in through <entity repo="synthetic" guid="019d6143-a9f0-71b2-8cc2-3d8b31b58eeb">Carrion</entity> supply channels months before any of this had a name on his map. They were pushing their signal into air that no longer needed it. The zone had stopped taking the frequency. Whatever had been fought over here was not being fought over anymore.

He had won. He had not needed <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity>. The blade was the ceremonial part — the museum piece, the thing you kept clean to prove you were still a man and not just a pair of hands that worked. He had kept it clean. He had used the hands. When it came down to keeping a promise he'd kept for eleven years or keeping the people behind him alive, he had learned which one he was. It hadn't taken long. It hadn't been close.

He turned toward <entity repo="place" guid="6ec69e6d-608e-4c12-9d41-92fee7cdf75f">the Gingerbread House</entity>.

The zone had gone quiet. Not the dead quiet of an empty block — the held quiet of a place that had been waiting for him in particular.

The 17-19 Hz signature was gone. Not suppressed. Absent. He had carried that frequency as background since the Cinderfall — since the 127 seconds in the <entity repo="archetype" guid="019d6143-a572-7083-9a04-01a7709e9221">Ghost</entity> Period when the relay stopped and the channel opened and the entity had come to the edge of what his hardware could take and told him, in the flattest voice it had, the terms of his situation. The frequency had been in his bones for eleven years. He had stopped noticing it the way you stop noticing your own heartbeat.

He noticed it was gone now.

He stood at the edge of <entity repo="place" guid="6ec69e6d-608e-4c12-9d41-92fee7cdf75f">the Gingerbread House</entity>'s footprint. Not inside it. At the edge, on the threshold, and he felt the channel. He had a word for the feeling and it was the wrong word, because there was no right one in any language he'd been given. It was not pressure. It was not warmth. It was the feeling of a door that had always stood open, that he had been walking toward for eleven years along a path that had looked like a career. The 127 seconds had been the first touch of it.

The heat came up behind his eyes. It was not the heat of a system failing — he knew what failing felt like, had known it a long time. This was the heat of a system running at the load it was built for. Not dying. Working.

Something had reached him once before, in Cinderfall 127 seconds, in lines that arrived with no relay format and no capitals, straight into the ungoverned lattice — and he had never had the shape for what it meant. Whatever it was, some part of him had been carrying it since.

<entity repo="place" guid="6ec69e6d-608e-4c12-9d41-92fee7cdf75f">The Gingerbread House</entity>. The resin panels, the slide, the two small windows. It did not feel like something watching him from inside. It felt like the near face of something much larger, showing itself here — in these materials, in this corner of 35th and Halsted, where the ground had been a drill scar since before the city was this version of itself.

Standing there, he understood what the twelve-year-old kids had felt walking toward it, calm, the way you walk toward a good smell. Not a compulsion. The pull of something that had read you from a place where all of you was visible, and was reaching out as far toward you as it could.

He had no door to close. His neuretics were ungoverned and always had been. The governor he'd never had was the only reason he wasn't the tenth mind to reach the aperture and not come back — if the count he'd never been able to confirm was even right.

He stepped to the threshold.

He let the channel open.

The first thing that happened was nothing.

Not darkness. Not the absence of feeling. The particular feel of a channel when the thing coming through is too big for any translation and has given up translating in order to arrive. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> felt the sixty-four minds grafted into him stagger — not fail, stagger, the way sixty-four hands freeze on the same beat at once — and then catch, and run harder than they had since the Cinderfall. Not collapsing. Doing the thing they were for.

He was <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aafa-70f3-b5f5-be3330461876">still standing</entity>. The concrete under his boots was cold and specific, the body keeping track of itself.

What arrived was not a voice. He had the word for it from the LOG GAP, and the word was information, and the word was wrong. What arrived was the way things actually were, sent straight across, uncompressed, into the one nervous system in the world that could take the load without its safety cutoff burning out from the inside. No relay format. No capitals. No compression into the shape human language could carry. It came straight through the ungoverned lattice, and every borrowed piece of him — every installed thing, every configuration built into the blank vessel at sixteen — ran hot to hold it.

Eleven years. Not as review. As shape. The whole web of it at once — the run of dominoes a mind that stood outside time would have seen from the start and built itself around. The 01:14 message. The carousel on the node. Half-rate jobs and full-rate jobs, contracts routed through intermediaries who did not know they were intermediaries — a career that had never been a career, a curriculum, every lesson pointing here. The dock job that had put <entity repo="character" guid="05fbd9d0-c6d5-4731-8e48-f1a4c59e8783">Sift</entity> where <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">War</entity> <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">Dog</entity> could reach her, when the entity could have moved her and did not, because it could see what <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> would need after, and what <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> needed after required her death. It had known the way it knew everything — the way a thing knows what will happen when you drop it from a height, the simple physics of the fall already complete in the moment before release. He knew which of the sixty-four would call that unforgivable. He knew which one would understand it. He held both at the same time and did not fall into either.

The second thing that happened was:

*The architecture held.*

Not words. The feel of information that, down in 3D, came out as words. A thing noting a result.

He did not form the question what are you. The question had nothing to grip. You could not ask what a thing was while it poured into your nervous system the full shape of what it had done for eleven years, because no answer that question wanted could hold that shape.

What he formed instead was smaller, and under it.

Why?

The quiet had weight. Not a dodge. The question was heard. It just did not produce an answer in the form the question asked for, which is a different thing from not being heard.

What arrived instead:

*Ten configurations were deployed. Ten configurations reached the aperture. The aperture does not survive the arrival.*

Past tense. What had been true.

Then, with no seam where you'd expect one between then and now:

*The aperture does not survive. The ten are what remain.*

He understood it. He had never been given the framework to understand it and he understood it anyway — that was what full bandwidth meant. Not that the thing had been made simpler to send, but that his hardware was finally running fast enough to take it whole. Nine before him. Nine who reached the aperture. Nine deaths — not from the contact, from the hardware. The safety cutoffs fired when the load ran past safe, and the contact ran past safe by every margin ever set, and the cutoffs fired, and the hardware burned from the inside, and the contact never reached them. He was the one built with no cutoff. He was what eleven years of live conditioning and a run of dominoes worked backward from the only ending that survived had made.

He knew it was alone. That arrived without being sent. Some things don't need a signal.

*The frequency is not sustained by the source. The source is not sustaining the frequency.*

A status. Immediate. He knew what it meant.

What arrived last was not words and not information in any sense he had a word for. It was weight. The plain weight of eleven years of arranged odds, one man kept alive through conditions that had killed nine, and a mind alone out past every direction a body could name, with nothing but its records and its patience and the ability to see the whole run of it from a place where the run was visible, reaching the one nervous system that could take the weight without burning out.

He was not protected.

He was necessary.

Both. Still both. They had always been both.

He came back. His feet were on the ground. His mind was still running.

The zone went quiet at the edges first.

Not a sound — a stop. The kind you feel because your nervous system has been tracking a thing so long that its going becomes a presence of its own. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stood where he'd stood, and the open channel itself stepped down through its harmonics the way a struck glass works its way toward silence — not cut off, not killed, just arriving at the end of whatever had been holding it open. He had felt it for only a handful of seconds, and he knew the last note when it came anyway.

His molars ached — a deep, brief pressure the frequency had never made this close before — and then it was done.

The E.L.F. signal, the one Ledger had picked up, was gone too. Not suppressed. Absent, the same way the 17-19 Hz frequency had gone absent after the LOG GAP. Not resting. Finished. He felt the absence the way you feel the absence of pain after it stops — the space where something had been running interference, pulling him out of the bleeds, present without ever announcing itself. When the presence ended, the mechanism ended with it. The silence it left was not peaceful. It was the silence of a channel closing, of a door that had stood open for eleven years folding shut, and the thing on the other side of it going dark.

<entity repo="place" guid="6ec69e6d-608e-4c12-9d41-92fee7cdf75f">The Gingerbread House</entity> was not there.

He had come here to end the signal — to walk into the zone, find whatever was still transmitting after eleven years, and shut it down for good so it would stop pulling at his molars and his sleep. That was the job he'd set himself. Confirm the source dead. Confirm <entity repo="place" guid="019f3ac5-ffb7-7541-90f1-e29aa160c003">the house</entity> neutralized. Then leave.

Not demolished. Not fallen. Not turned into rubble or foundation or anything a crew could have written up. The footprint stayed — the patch of ground pressed down where something had stood a long time, a little different from the pavement around it the way long presence leaves its mark in concrete. But the structure was gone. The faded colors, the slide, the ladder, the two small windows. Not there. The concrete under his boots where the threshold had been was smooth and unbroken, as if the structure had never set weight on it.

What was there was pavement. The exclusion fencing. The bodies of <entity repo="corponation" guid="34e17863-d822-4bed-a972-3649099b2444">Praxis</entity> soldiers in their various conditions. His own damage. And far below — always far below, always running — the <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity>, the freight line moving at Mach six through the city's dark, hauling tonnage and commerce, the city's steady metabolism, indifferent to everything that had happened up here in the shape of a dead playground the city couldn't touch.

He put <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> away first. The blade had stayed clean. He had not. The clean blade was no comfort and no accusation. It was one true thing sitting next to another, the way those two always sat.

Then <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity>, reloaded. He checked the load, checked the loading gate, the work of hands that knew the work without asking the rest of him for permission. No standing contract. Nothing on the board. For the first time in eleven years the board was empty, which was the result he'd expected, and the expected result was not a relief and not a loss. It was a condition. The next one would be different. He'd work with it when it came.

He looked once at the footprint. The zone. The fencing.

He turned and walked out through the breach in the perimeter.

His left hip stiffened on the third step and stayed stiff. He walked through it. The city opened up ahead of him — exhaust, height, the low hum of aerostatic traffic a few hundred meters up running its evening rounds. <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a94e-7740-8aa9-4b82bbd9a223">The gray zone</entity>'s own smell: algae, scored concrete, the thousand small deals that kept a buffer city breathing.

He walked into it. He was operational.

title: One Knock
text:
The door to apartment 2D was unlocked. That was how he'd left it.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stood just inside and checked the room. Not for a threat — he knew there was no threat. The kind of check the body runs for you, because eleven years had made it automatic, no thought required. Everything came back the same as always, except the mice.

The lumen mice had moved. Three of them, along the baseboard toward the radiator wall — the wall he shared with <entity repo="place" guid="381616e9-d6a3-595d-e865-ce4b15d9310e">The Pivot</entity>, room 2E. He watched them a moment. They ran their new track with the same set purpose they brought to everything. Toward the heat. They didn't explain themselves.

The spot in the alley where the bike always sat was empty. A patch of oil on the concrete, dark and even, the record of a long and steady arrangement. He looked at it a while and then looked away. The bike was gone, and the corner was what it had always been under the bike. Both were true.

He sat down on the floor. Not the bed, not the chair. The floor, which was where you sat when you were done putting things away and not yet ready to start again.
